News.title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
News.content:
The meeting hasn't even happened yet.

But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.

Whatever the outcome.

Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down â just the three of them â for talks.

That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.

It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.

That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.

But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.

One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.

In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."

But what of those who are not at the table?

Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States â Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.

Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.

Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula â carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.

It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.

The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.

It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

News.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
News.content:
Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by Â£443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.

Some households will get a Â£100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.

Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand Â£100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach Â£2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."

News.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
News.content:
That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay Â£2,166 a year - that's an increase of Â£443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a Â£100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, external, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

News.title: Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident
News.content:
An investigation has been launched into the death of a three-year-old boy following an incident at a nursery in Greater Manchester, police said.

The boy became critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton shortly before 16:00 GMT on Monday 2 November.

He was rushed to hospital, where he died three days later.

Greater Manchester Police said his family were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family."

Police said an investigation had been launched in line with standard procedure following a child's death in a care setting.

No arrests have been made at this time.

News.title: Council wins legal fight over flags on lamp-posts
News.content:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court bid to prevent unauthorised flags being put up after a legal battle with campaigners from an anti-migrant group.

The local authority had sought an injunction against members of the group Raise the Colours, who have placed thousands of St George and Union flags on lamp-posts since the summer of 2025. Supporters of the group protested outside the court, wearing Raise the Colours shirts and hoodies.

The council's lawyers said the flags were a road safety risk and created tensions, but supporters argued an order would breach the European Convention on Human Rights.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the injunction could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

In her ruling, the judge said the order would last until trial or further order of the court.

The judgment grants the local authority an interim injunction against Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning the police could arrest someone immediately without a warrant if they reasonably suspect the order has been breached.

In her adjudication, Kelly said: "The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is. It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the Union Jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

News.title: Gamers react as New Zealand first to see Grand Theft Auto 6
News.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 has now officially been released in New Zealand and players have had the chance to take their first look at the game.

POPE NZL and Hayden 'Prawln' Tresch, both New Zealand streamers and among the first to download the newest version in the series, praised its soundtrack and graphics.

It will now launch in successive countries at midnight local time with those who had preinstalled it able from then to download it to their consoles.

Its launch had been delayed twice and comes 13 years after GTA V.

More on this story.

News.title: Test cricket's sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
News.content:
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted â the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.

Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.

Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.

"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.

He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.

"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.

"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.

"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."

News.title: Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message
News.content:
Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence.

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment.

ITN News chief executive Ian Rumsey told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show that the company's newsrooms, including ITV News and Channel 4 News, took the decision not to play the video.

He said: "You didn't need to show it. You could discuss, you could describe what it was, and I'm very pleased and proud that every area of ITN chose not to show it at all, and I think that's exactly the right decision."

YouTube said it is aware of the video and investigating, and that Brand's channel on the platform hasn't been able to make money since being suspended from its advert revenue scheme for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy" after allegations against him emerged in 2023. But the channel is still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

News.title: 'Good for the people' if politicians stopped doing media, says NI secretary of state
News.content:
The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has said that if politicians stayed off the media for a month it would "probably be very good for the people".

Sir Chris Bryant said it breaks his heart that because of the crisis over agreeing a budget he can't get round to issues like violence against women and girls, or resolving community tensions.

He told a committee of MPs that was "one of the symbols of the kind of complete abnormality that now seems to pervade Northern Ireland politics".

Ministers on the Stormont executive say they can't strike a budget without additional money from the Treasury.

The government has offered around Â£1.5 billion in extra funding over the next three years but ministers say they need more.

It means Northern Ireland faces the prospect of strikes by public sector workers because there is no way of meeting pay claims.

Asked by the committee chair Tonia Antoniazzi how much money ministers required he said: "Oh I mean it changes every week. One version is another billion pounds."

He added that some politicians "won't sit in the same room as each other".

He told members of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee: "The point is that Northern Ireland is getting fair funding, and whatever the envelope is, if you were a councillor, you would have to set a legal budget.

"You just have to make the sums add up. And what really frustrates, I think, all of us is, I've tried processes of adjudicating between the different parties, because let's face it, the parties aren't talking to each other at the moment."

News.title: Ivan Toney loses bid to avoid Euro 2028 court clash
News.content:
A bid to move the date of England striker Ivan Toney's assault trial to avoid a clash with Euro 2028 has been refused.

The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva during a confrontation at a nightclub in Wardour Street, central London, on 6 December.

Toney denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm at a court hearing last month and a date for a trial of up to four days was fixed for 12 June 2028, which is three days into the Uefa Euro 2028 tournament.

He represented England at this summer's World Cup and has made 10 international appearances. It is not yet known if he will be selected for Euro 2028, but the application was made in case.

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, where Toney did not appear, his barrister Mozammel Hossain KC said: "It came to our attention thatâ¦ there may be potentially a football match called the European Championship in 2028 between 9 June and 9 July."

Hossain proposed a trial date in August that year, adding: "We ask you please that the matter be put back to then for a trial so that if the defendant is included in this football tournament he can play.

"My knowledge of football is very limited but I am told he was included in the last one in 2024 and the England squad for the World Cup."

Judge Tony Baumgartner called it a "speculative" application.

He refused the request, saying: "It does not seem to me to be in the interest of justice to disturb the date that was already fixed."

The judge said the application could be made again if Toney is selected for the England squad.

Toney missed out on the latest squad for the country's Nations League ties.

Toney started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.

He scored 72 goals during four years with the Bees before making a surprise switch in 2024 to Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.

News.title: Water queues build as 8,500 without supply
News.content:
Thousands of properties across Stourbridge, in the West Midlands, remain without water on Wednesday as teams work to locate a burst pipe, with repairs potentially taking until the weekend.

Ridgewood High School and Ashwood Park Primary School remained closed, and residents said they had been unable to cook, wash or flush their toilets.

Emergency bottled water stations have been operating since 08:00 GMT, although supplies temporarily ran out at one site before a fresh delivery was arranged.

Severn Trent said bottled water would be available until 22:00 on Wednesday and every day until supplies were restored, but warned the complex repair could take several more days.

On Wednesday morning, it was reported that 6,000 homes and businesses were without water, but by lunchtime that had risen to 8,500 as engineers attempted to find the source of the leak.

Howard Perry, head of water quality at Severn Trent said some residents could be without water for four days.

"We are very hopeful we can get customers back on supply before that," he said.

News.title: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish, Sam Fender and Cher to headline Glastonbury 2027
News.content:
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.

It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.

In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.

Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.

At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.

Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.

Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.

She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.

In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.

Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.

Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.

She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.

Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.

More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

News.title: Raise The Colours member guilty of dancefloor murder
News.content:
A member of activist group Raise The Colours has been found guilty of murdering a pub landlord who was killed by a punch to the neck on the dancefloor at a bar.

Matthew O'Gara, 44, was attacked by Billy Allison in the incident at Rico and Loren in Lichfield, Staffordshire, on 24 May.

Allison was also found guilty of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to O'Gara's friend Adam Cooper, 62, who was punched twice and was left with a fractured eye socket and nose.

O'Gara, who ran The Plough on the outskirts of Lichfield, suffered two broken bones and a split artery in his neck, which caused a massive bleed and rendered him unconscious until he died in hospital two days later.

The trial at Stafford Crown Court heard the punch could be heard over the bar's DJ sound system.

Allison, who wore a black suit and tie and white shirt in the dock, appeared shocked by the verdict, sighed and held his head in his hands as he left the dock without being granted permission by the judge.

He is due to be sentenced on 5 January.

News.title: Police treating 'targeted' shooting of woman as attempted murder
News.content:
Police are treating the shooting of a woman in Glasgow on Monday night as attempted murder.

The 27-year-old was taken to hospital after emergency services were called to Eynort Street in the city's Lambhill area at about 23:45.

The victim suffered serious injuries and is in hospital, where she is in a critical but stable condition.

Police Scotland described the attack as being "an extremely reckless act with no regard for the safety of the local community".

News.title: Joanna Page says male actor made 'awful' and 'inappropriate' comments to her on set
News.content:
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.

The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrityâ¦ Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.

"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.

Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.

Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".

"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

News.title: Brain cancer patients demand public inquiry into chemotherapy scandal
News.content:
"I have two young children and to think once upon a time I might not have been there for their future kills me every day and it's all down to one person," the 35-year-old added.

She is one of more than 40 patients taking legal action against the NHS Trust. The mum-of-two was 21 when she was told she had a grade 4 glioblastoma and six to 12 months to live.

After more than 100 cycles of chemotherapy it was found she had never had a brain tumour and that her imaging was consistent with tumefactive demyelination, a less serious lesion.

She said of the report: "The findings are worse than I ever expected them to be.

"A national inquiry needs to happen and things need to be tightened up so it can't happen to anyone else.

"I don't think I'll ever find closure until the trust accept what they have done wrong and are held accountable. I would like answers."

The review, released on Wednesday, was commissioned by the trust following the retirement of one of its doctors.

Brown, referred to as Dr Y in the RCP's report, did not take part in the review and refused to comment when approached by the BBC at his home.

University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust has apologised for "failures" within its neuro-oncology service under the care of the retired clinical oncologist.

Chief executive Professor Andy Hardy and trust chair Sue Noyes said in a statement: "This is far below the standards our patients deserve and that we expect. We let you down, and for that we offer our sincere apologies."

News.title: Prince Harry says he would join the army again to fight against Russia
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prince Harry says he would rejoin the British Army to fight against Russia if needed, saying he believes Europe has finally “woken up to the threat” of Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.

On a visit to Lviv in western Ukraine, the Duke of Sussex told The Telegraph he believed the UK and Russia had effectively been in conflict for the past decade.

“Just because there’s not drones, bullets and rockets flying at us, it doesn’t mean that we’re not at war,” he said.

The interview is his first since returning to the UK earlier this year.

The Duke said the UK could learn a lot from Ukraine’s resistance against Russian aggression, adding: “If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100 per cent be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel.”

“There is a lot that we can learn from Ukraine. I think there’s a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine,” he said.

Asked whether he was concerned about today’s geopolitical situation, Harry said: “I think we should all be nervous, absolutely. And I think we should be prepared, and I think that those of us that have served should be ready to serve again.”

More to follow...

News.title: Damian Lewis hits back at critics who mock his music career
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Damian Lewis has addressed criticism of his music career, saying there will “always” be “people who sneer”.

The Emmy-winning Homeland star released his second studio album Sweet Chaos earlier this year, three years after his debut record, Mission Creep.

However, the 55-year-old has faced some mockery over his pivot to music over the years, including viral reactions to his “King” music video and an on-air slip by a BBC Radio 2 presenter.

“There are always going to be people who sneer, right? Especially in England, but they should be ignored,” he told the Press Association in a new interview.

“They’re anti-adventure, they’re anti-fun, and they’re anti-creativity, and it’s not unexpected that there’ll be people that respond that way.

open image in gallery Damian Lewis released his debut album in 2023 ( Getty )

open image in gallery Lewis’s new album, ‘Sweet Chaos’, is out now ( PA )

“It’s not very strange, it’s the truth of it, it’s not that odd, it’s just because I became so well known for one thing that I think it’s difficult,” he continued.

“It can be difficult for some people to get their head around the other thing, but if someone’s fallen in love with me as Henry VIII or is obsessed with Captain Winters from Band of Brothers, and they go, ‘oh, bloody hell, Henry VIII’s written an album’.

“Well, yeah, that’s that. I think that’s quite a different time and energy; you’re trying to put a square peg in a round hole because the first thing to say is Henry VIII didn’t write an album.

“I played Henry VIII, and I also write songs, and it’s really not that weird; the important thing is the music, and that’s the bottom line, just listen to the music, and if you like the music, get into it.

“And if you don’t like it, there’s not much I can do about that, but even the Beatles couldn’t make music for everybody.

“The first album got really got well reviewed, I’m very happy to say, and I feel very blessed with that.

“And I find music fans are overwhelmingly generous and curious, and open-hearted because music fans are always looking for new music, they always want to find new music, so they always come with curiosity, and I think with real imagination, it’s people sitting on the sidelines.”

Lewis’s comments come months after BBC Radio 2 traffic presenter Sally Boazman accidentally called Lewis's new track a “dirge” live on air while he was in the studio promoting Sweet Chaos.

The star appeared on Romesh Ranganathan’s show to share his latest single, after which Boazman, also known as “Sally Traffic” admitted she had asked, “What is this dirge?” Lewis responded, “It’s my record”, before the studio burst into fits of laughter.

In May, fans and social media users poked fun at the video for his song “King”, calling it “unintentionally hilarious” and likening it to a parody due to his pout, bare chest, and white slip-on loafers.

Sweet Chaos is out now on streaming, CD and vinyl record.

When is Black Friday 2026?

Black Friday officially falls on Friday 27 November 2026, but you can already shop hundreds of early deals. The likes of Sephora, Lookfantastic, and PlayStation have all launched their sales, with more retailers joining them as November progresses. So, while we're still more than a week away from the date itself, Black Friday shopping (and the savings that come with it) is well under way.

For those wondering why the date changes each year, Black Friday takes place the day after Thanksgiving in the US, which is always celebrated on the fourth Thursday of November. Whether it's worth waiting until then is another matter. Some of the strongest offers can appear well before the main event, so I'd recommend checking historical prices before deciding whether to buy now or hold out. Lucky for you, this is something myself and IndyBest’s shopping experts usually flag in our guides – so make sure to browse our descriptions in full before heading to the checkout.

When does Black Friday end?

Cyber Monday (30 November) marks the unofficial end of Black Friday each year, although there's technically no forced cut-off for retailers. Some will pull their discounts at 11:59pm that evening, while others will keep the offers running into early December.

Last year, for example, Lookfantastic continued its promotions until 3 December, and several retailers ran extended Cyber Week sales. However, I wouldn't count on every deal sticking around. Popular products can sell out long before the advertised end date and plenty of discounts are only available for a limited time. If you've spotted something at a jaw-droppingly good price, it's worth checking when that particular offer expires rather than relying on the retailer's wider sale dates.

When is Cyber Monday?

Cyber Monday is on 30 November 2026.

Cyber Monday is the online shopping event that follows Black Friday. It takes place on the Monday after Thanksgiving weekend in the US. It was originally created to encourage shoppers to buy online. But given that everyone shops on the internet, the concept of Cyber Monday is slightly redundant. It’s now just an extension of Black Friday, giving you a final chance to save before Christmas.

Some brands and retailers have tried to popularise other shopping events, but most have had about as much success as Gretchen Wieners trying to make “fetch” happen. There’s Travel Tuesday, for example, which takes place on the day after Cyber Monday and focuses on deals for flights, hotels and package holidays, and Small Business Saturday, which encourages shoppers to support independent retailers instead of the big chains.

How can I tell if a Black Friday deal is genuine?

The easiest way is to check a product’s price history. If it’s been the same price for weeks before Black Friday, or the discount is only a few pounds, it probably isn’t as impressive as it looks. Make sure to write a list of everything you want and need, noting down the current price so you can check the discount in November. I also recommend comparing prices across multiple retailers. Just because something has a big percentage off doesn’t automatically make it a good deal. Having covered sales for more than a decade, I’ve written a detailed guide to my top shopping tips for Black Friday.

News.title: Man United’s players can’t play Mauricio Pochettino’s style – but there is a solution
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Mauricio Pochettino does not have much time between landing in England on Thursday afternoon and travelling to Manchester United’s greatest rivals Liverpool on Sunday but, within those three whirlwind days, he will still seek to do something that he feels just keeps everyone grounded. He will pay for a dinner out with all the players and staff.

Pochettino usually does this on the eve of every season, a custom he started in his first English job, at Southampton. Then, as now, it had to happen mid-season but at least gave him an initial sense of the squad as a group while encouraging togetherness.

It will also allow Pochettino and his staff to quicker detect the group dynamics, in lieu of an actual pre-season.

open image in gallery Mauricio Pochettino will want to impose a very specific style at Manchester United ( PA )

That touches on something else that Pochettino sees as a fundamental. Or, rather, the fundamental.

“The most important thing is the players’ fitness,” he said in Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs – his 2017 book in conjunction with journalist Guillem Balague – and everything he and assistant Jesus Perez do radiates that.

It perhaps forms the single greatest issue in this season at Manchester United, and is something Pochettino himself is going to have to work out how to adapt to.

open image in gallery Man United’s squad is not suited to heavy pressing ( Getty )

That opening meal might even be seen as the buttered carrots before the sticks used to drive these players – and regular body-fat tests.

Except, even that poses another dual-sided problem.

On one side, there is the manner the fitness of this specific squad has been questioned all season. You can go through the data or just use the eye test, to see a team regularly ripped apart. Pochettino will have to work to get them up to scratch.

But there’s then getting them up to his own levels, the standards required to really play Pochettino’s style.

As the Argentine has said, he demands his teams play “with intensity and at a high tempo”, to be “prepared for battle” in a way that provokes “a controlled disorder, to create so much movement that it distresses the opposition”.

open image in gallery Pochettino teams play with high intensity and tempo ( Getty )

That comes from initially distressing his own squad. Some of Pochettino’s former players have commonly remarked about how they thought they were fit, and then realised they were nowhere near what their boss actually means by that word.

Duly, the manager and Perez have their own adapted fitness exercises based on the Gacon test, named after French fitness coach Georges Gacon.

“We did a lot of them in pre-season,” Harry Kane has said.

Ben Davies talked of “crazy sessions”, that his international teammates couldn’t believe, and that then-Watford boss Quique Sanchez Flores said produced “animals”.

open image in gallery Pochettino had Harry Kane and the Tottenham squad incredibly fit ( Getty )

A further problem with United, however, is that it’s not just that Pochettino doesn’t have a pre-season. He barely has time between games. This truncated first week sets a tone. United now enter the busiest period of the season, where the Champions League group stages are at their most intense and then it’s Christmas.

Elimination from the Carabao Cup may actually be seen as a gift.

Worse, if Pochettino does attempt anything like his usual fitness approach, United’s under-cooked players are likely to break down with injuries. He is consequently going to have to adapt as much as his squad.

Pressing has long been described as the core principle of Pochettino’s game but the reality is that it is now the core principle of everyone’s game in the Premier League. Teams operate with multiple varied systems. And, as one Premier League coach says, if you get your pressing wrong, or it’s not calibrated correctly, modern teams can so easily play around you.

It is described as one of those unseen elements of the modern game that explains why teams can suddenly get badly beaten.

open image in gallery Pressing has become a staple of every Premier League team ( Getty )

Pochettino did arrive in mid-season at Southampton and immediately got them pressing – to the point that Sir Alex Ferguson even commented approvingly after the Argentine’s very first game: a valiant 2-1 defeat at Old Trafford. That was nevertheless in a very different Premier League, that hadn’t properly gone through the Pep Guardiola-inspired pressing revolution. What Pochettino was doing was itself revolutionary, and he enthused about how he had “hungry players who didn’t want to be relegated”.

This is at least where his time at Paris Saint-Germain may offer necessary experience beyond weathering an immense weight of expectation.

Pochettino instantly realised that Neymar, Kylian Mbappe and later Lionel Messi just weren’t going to run or press in a way anything close to what he expected, so he essentially had to abandon his usual approach.

Eight players would instead have to compromise for the three stars. And, without a full XI running, this wasn’t a true Pochettino team.

open image in gallery PSG couldn’t press the way Pochettino wanted with Kylian Mbappe (picture), Lionel Messi and Neymar in the team ( Getty Images )

He and Perez would still point out that they had PSG’s best Champions League performance in getting to the semi-finals in a full season – Thomas Tuchel’s final was in the Covid campaign – before the club belatedly decided to change approach. They have often remarked with a touch of envy how they would have loved to work with the youth-defined approach that Luis Enrique has enjoyed.

That may be one way Pochettino gets around these various problems. He’s spoken before about how gaps were “filled by youngsters”.

Such a commitment to youth has been another core principle of his career. And, aside from being willing to take instruction and run harder with more energy, young players also give you something else.

“There’s nothing quite like winning with the team you joined at 13 or 14 and have given your heart and soul to,” he explained in his book. “You then move on to play for the first team with a feeling of identity that offers the team an added extra. It’s something that will be stamped on every side I coach.”

open image in gallery Could Man United’s youngsters such as Shea Lacey hold the key for Pochettino? ( Getty )

It was similar at Tottenham, where Pochettino described a squad that sounds someway similar to United now – “figures who at some point in their careers had been considered stars but had lost their way. And the team didn’t come first”.

That’s what Pochettino will demand. Now, he will coach a side arguably more associated with youth than any in the game, but one thing they don’t have is time to grow.

Pochettino’s United have to hit the ground running, when running is one of the issues.

News.title: Markwayne Mullin says people would have feared flying if he didn’t go to LSU game after air traffic ground stop
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that if he did not fly to an LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide air travel ground stop, it could have sown “confusion” and “distrust” for others hoping to fly.

Mullin appeared Wednesday in front of the House Homeland Security Committee for the annual “Worldwide Threats” hearing, which happened to fall days after a meltdown of the U.S. air traffic control system, a major Microsoft outage and glitches with online banking systems that temporarily prevented some customers from accessing their accounts.

The Homeland Security chief, alongside Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia, answered questions from lawmakers about the timing of the tech outages, which have sparked concern among Americans.

Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the top-ranking Democrat on the committee, said Mullin was “tone deaf” for attending Saturday’s game between the LSU Tigers and the Texas Longhorns in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, amid the travel and security chaos that unfolded Friday afternoon.

“While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game and visited the private suite of a company that DHS had awarded a $2.2 billion contract for the secretary of Homeland Security,” Thompson said.

open image in gallery Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that if he did not fly to an LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop, it could have sown ‘confusion’ and ‘distrust’ for travelers ( Reuters )

His remarks prompted a defensive response from Mullin, who also said he was going to the game to be a “good uncle” to his niece, “who has never been to an LSU game.”

“We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace that was completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there,” said Mullin, who represented Oklahoma in the U.S. House, a rival of Texas. “That would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly.”

Thompson referenced that Mullin was seen in the private box of Bollinger Shipping CEO Ben Bordelon, who holds numerous contracts with the DHS.

Mullin accused the Democrat of “hypocrisy” and said he had never met the executive.

When it was the turn of New Jersey Democrat LaMonica McIver, she had a heated exchange with Mullin and asked whether he would support fixing the air traffic control system by “redirecting some of the funds from ICE.”

“Well, by statute, I'm limited on what I can spend those funds on,” Mullin responded.

“So I guess that's a no,” McIver said, and asked Mullin whether he had any regrets about the role he is playing in the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.

open image in gallery Mullin appeared Wednesday in front of the House Homeland Security Committee where he was quizzed on the recent tech outages and the shut down of the nation’s skies ( Reuters )

“I will never apologize about enforcing our nation's laws,” the secretary said.

“Not about even killing people?” McIver followed up.

“We’re not killing people,” Mullin claimed. Six people, including three American citizens, have died after being shot by federal immigration agents since last year, according to analysis.

Elsewhere in the hearing, Mullin distanced himself from the Nvidia controversy when asked what he knew about ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“The way that I understand it is because this is a spy outside of just our network, and they were handling it in different agencies,” he said. “If it was a direct threat to the homeland, I would have been read in on it.”

Democratic Rep. Seth Magaziner asked if Mullin was concerned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had resisted implementing export controls on certain chips sold by Nvidia to China that others in the administration supported.

“This wasn’t something I’m dealing with. It’s outside of my lane,” he said.

FBI Director Kash Patel refused to appear at the hearing, according to GOP committee chairman Andrew R. Garbarino, who said he was “disappointed” by his absence.

News.title: Trump, Putin and Xi meet ahead of unprecedented three-way summit as China rolls out red carpet
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

US president Donald Trump has met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China ahead of their unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday.

China’s presidentpersonally welcomed Trump upon his arrival at an airport in Shenzhen on Wednesday, an unusual honour for a visiting foreign leader. He said China has a “tradition of reciprocating courtesy” after Trump

Xi said China has a “tradition of reciprocating courtesy” after greeting the US commander-in-chief with a rare hug following a similar reception at Joint Base Andrews in September. The pair later welcomed the Russian president with handshakes, beaming smiles and a group photo ahead of an evening banquet.

open image in gallery US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands as China's President Xi Jinping looks on ( AP )

According to China’s Xinhua news agency, Trump said every meeting with his Chinese counterpart has been “very pleasant”.

The three men will meet on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.

Ahead of the high-stakes trilateral, Xi took the opportunity speak out against trade protectionism, while Putin lashed out at the growing pile of Western sanctions against Moscow.

The Russian president, who took the stage after Xi, described Western powers as “former hegemons”, claiming Europe was in “humiliating decline”. It is the latest attack by the Kremlin, which has repeatedly sought to test the Nato alliance in recent months.

The three-way gathering has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.

open image in gallery Donald Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese president Xi Jinping ( Getty )

But it has also unnerved leaders of smaller and medium economies, especially in Asia and Europe, who fear the three world powers will disregard or undermine their interests.

The warm reception for the Russian leader will be of particular concern for Ukraine, as Kyiv urged Trump and Xi to pressure Putin to end the near five year war rather than trying to appease him.

”It is very important that through this meeting the two leaders do not give Putin the false impression that we are returning to a period of divided spheres of influence. The tone needs to be different - pressure,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha told reporters on Wednesday.

Since taking office in January 2025, the US president has deepened ties between Washington and Moscow, while repeatedly castigating Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - sensationally even blaming him for starting the war, which began with Russia’s invasion nearly five years ago.

On the eve of the summit and sidelined by the trilateral, Ukraine struck a symbolic blow to the Kremlin with two strikes on Putin’s prized Crimea Bridge this week.

open image in gallery AI, nuclear weapons and global conflicts are expected to be on the agenda ( AFP/Getty )

With peace talks stalled, the back and forth strikes between Moscow and Kyiv have continued unabated, with four people killed in an overnight Russian attack on the port city of Odesa.

The summit also comes against the backdrop of war Iran, a conflict launched by the US and Israel on 28 February that has sent shockwaves through the global economy.

Both Moscow and Beijing have criticised the Iran war, with Xi repeatedly calling for countries to avoid a return to “the law of the jungle”, in a thinly-veiled dig towards Trump’s approach. The war is set to be discussed, with the Strait of Hormuz still all-but closed nearly nine months after the war was launched.

Winding down nearly two years of trade warfare, another defining characteristic of the US-China relationship during Trump’s second term, will also be on the table.

open image in gallery Donald Trump is expected to meet Xi Jinping along with Vladimir Putin on Thursday ( AFP/Getty )

In his opening address, the Chinese president called for “free and open trade”, a direct rebuke of Trump’s protectionist and aggressive policy of trade warfare during his second administration.

The US president imposed sweeping tariffs soon after taking office, prompting a tariff war between Washington and Beijing which saw the US impose duties as high as 145 per cent on Chinese goods.

Xi’s remarks came after Washington announced restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies including Nvidia. The Chinese premier has sought to position Beijing’s trade policies in contrast to Trump’s tariffs and the US administration’s adoption of a muscular foreign policy.

The trade war has since settled, with the sides agreeing to produce a trade deal next year and agreeing a truce on tariffs.

open image in gallery The Russian leader was all smiles as dignitaries greeted one another in China ( Sputnik )

“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” the Chinese president told an audience of business executives.

Chastising the West for the sanctions imposed on Russia following the invasion of Ukraine, Putin added: “Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having lost much of their intimidating ​power."

“While sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth—let alone crushing the economies of competitors.”

He also praised close partnership with China, pledging more measures for a “multipolar world”.

open image in gallery The world leaders are expected to discuss war on Ukraine, along with AI and trade ( Getty )

The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons with the Yalta Conference as “games of political scientists”, but said the meeting will have a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral will promote world peace.

Putin described the world as "turbulent" but said disagreements can be addressed by “sitting at the table”.

“I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” he said.

Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy have added to the tension.

News.title: Sanctioned Russian billionaire told to pay more than £2.1bn to ex-wife in largest divorce battle in English history
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A sanctioned Russian billionaire has been told should he pay more than £2.1 billion to his ex-wife in what is believed to be the highest-value divorce battle in English legal history.

Natalia Potanina is seeking the money from businessman Vladimir Potanin, who is estimated to be worth billions.

Mr Potanin, who has said he earns £42.2 million per year, argues she should not receive the money and has offered £25 million.

The 65-year-olds married in Russia in 1983 and have three adult children, but divorced in Russia in 2014 and have been engaged in divorce proceedings in English courts since 2018.

Charles Howard KC, for Ms Potanina, said in written submissions for a hearing on Wednesday that she and Mr Potanin enjoyed a “lavish lifestyle” when they were together, and had “fabulous homes” and luxury yachts.

He said in court that the then-couple paid George Michael £1.7 million to perform at their 2006 New Year’s Eve celebration.

Mr Potanin claims the pair separated in January 2007, but Ms Potanina contends they did not separate until 2013.

Mr Howard said that after the couple divorced in 2014, Russian courts only considered Mr Potanin’s legally owned assets when determining his wealth, rather than also evaluating assets he beneficially owned.

This meant the latter “fell off the radar” and Ms Potanina was “deprived of anything like a fair share of the parties’ wealth”.

open image in gallery A picture taken late on December 04, 2017 shows Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) meeting with metals magnate Vladimir Potanin at the Novo-Ogaryovo state residence outside Moscow. ( AFP/Getty )

The barrister said: “Ms Potanina has ended up with less than 1% of the wealth generated during this long marriage.

“On any objective analysis, that is hugely unfair and a huge injustice, particularly when it entails her being deprived of billions of dollars.”

He continued that the English courts should “remedy the injustice” and award her a “meaningful share of the assets”.

This included more than £172 million for UK property, and annual income of £12.3 million.

Mr Howard said that while his client was “undoubtedly seeking a considerable amount of money”, this was “the inevitable and natural consequence of the level of wealth generated during the marriage”.

He said: “There has never been a contested case in the family court… with this level of wealth, after a very long marriage, and where the parties started with nothing and all the billions were created during the marriage.

“But the scale of wealth cannot justify discriminating against Ms Potanina.”

Lord Faulks KC, for Mr Potanin, said Ms Potanina received a “big money” award in the Russian divorce proceedings and left the marriage as a “very wealthy woman”, but is now seeking £2.174 billion.

open image in gallery Russia's mining giant Norilsk Nickel President Vladimir Potanin attends a meeting with Russian President in Moscow on July 15, 2026. ( AFP/Getty )

He continued that she “wishes to turn back the clock 20 years” to “return to living an ultra-high net worth lifestyle”.

But he added she “has already transitioned to independence without undue hardship” since the separation and lives a “very nice and fulfilled life”.

The barrister said that while Ms Potanina “plainly has significant financial aspirations”, they “do not bear scrutiny as relationship-generated needs”.

He said: “Properly viewed, she has sufficient resources to meet her needs at a reasonable level, or, putting it differently, she has no needs which it would be reasonable for this court to order Mr Potanin to meet.”

He added: “Mere disparity between what would have been ordered in England and what was ordered in the overseas jurisdiction, and/or between what the spouses respectively received, cannot alone amount to injustice.”

He said: “The rationale behind why the Russian courts made the award they did is irrelevant and a very dangerous path for this court to go down.”

Lord Faulks said it would be “impossible to enforce” any order made by the English courts in Russia, and that even if Ms Potanina was awarded the money she sought, “there can be no certainty” that she would be able to access the money due to “brutal” sanctions against Mr Potanin.

Mr Potanin has been sanctioned since 2022 after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, due to his ownership of the Interros conglomerate.

The hearing before Mr Justice MacDonald is due to conclude in December, with a judgment expected in writing at a later date.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

News.title: ‘I lost my family when I contracted HIV’: why virus is still taboo in Iraq
News.content:
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.

The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.

His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.

“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph, his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”

The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.

When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.

He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.

“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.

To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.

News.title: Bosses ‘increasingly reluctant’ to hire as employment costs soar
News.content:
Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in 12 years outside the pandemic as employers braced for the impact of the Government’s workers’ rights reforms.

Vacancies dropped by 22,000 to 690,000 in the three months to October, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This was the lowest since February to April 2021 – and the worst performance since the three months to September 2014 when taking out the impact of Covid lockdowns.

Bosses are grappling with higher employment costs in addition to the Government’s looming deadline to implement the Employment Rights Act on Jan 1. Under the changes, a cap on claims for unfair dismissal will be scrapped and the time a worker needs to have been employed before they can make a claim will be cut from two years to six months.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “The problem isn’t that businesses are firing workers. It’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them.”

KIM HELLBERG needs zero assurances over Will Lankshear’s future — declaring the red-hot striker has no interest in ditching Middlesbrough.

A host of scouts from the Premier League, including former club Tottenham, have watched the 21-year-old fire 15 goals in his first 16 games for the Championship side.



Promotion-chasing Boro forked out an initial £10m to Spurs for the England U21 striker last summer and now value him at around £70m.

Boss Hellberg, October’s Sky Bet Championship manager of the month, claims he has not felt the need to seek any promises from club chiefs that his prized asset will be sold in January.



The Swede, 38, said: “I don’t think in this business you can be assured of anything. Who knows what’s going to happen in terms of that?

“What is important is that the club has no interest in selling Will, and Will, I don’t think he has any interest in going anywhere.

“So that is reassurance enough, and I don’t go and ask people for reassurance. I believe that if people want to be here, people will be here.

“There’s very few places in this country, or in general, that is a better place to be in to develop and to work hard and to be part of a team that plays very good football.”

Boro dropped from top spot into second without Lankshear and failed to score in their past two games with the star ruled with a hamstring injury.

Hellberg desperately hopes to have him back when Bristol City head to the Riverside on Saturday and is confident the growing transfer speculation will not get into his red-hot ace’s head.

He added: “Everyone is a human being and Will is the best one to answer that himself, but if you look at him every day, he’s working very, very hard. He’s a brilliant boy.

“I’m just seeing a boy very focused on doing everything to get the best version of himself. That’s what everyone owes themselves as a footballer, because you know the career is short, you know that you don’t have all the time in the world.

“My job is to remind them that every day is important to get where you want to get. So I’m just seeing a balanced boy working very hard to improve every day, and one day he will get there.”

The ultimate ambition for Hellberg is to be in the Premier League himself next season. But does he feel he already possesses a top tier striker in Lankshear?

Sports.title: Brazil legend Romario calls for Carlo Ancelotti to be SACKED before Real Madrid legend hits back

CARLO ANCELOTTI has responded to a scathing attack by Brazil legend Romario, who demanded he leave his role as national team head coach.

The 1994 Fifa World Cup winner didn’t mince his words when posting a damning verdict about the Italian’s tenure so far on Instagram.



He wrote: “I want to tell Ancelotti this: I speak out a lot because, when it comes to the national team, I have the stature, the influence, and the power to speak.

“I don’t speak to gain followers, I don’t speak to please people. I speak my mind.



“The national team means a lot to me! I wore this shirt for many years, and I’m sure I was one of those who helped the Yellow Submarine earn respect worldwide.

“Ancelotti, you still have my respect for what you did at the clubs you managed.



“Tomorrow we face Singapore, who beat Paraguay 2-0.

“With all due respect to Paraguay, who by the way had the same number of points as us in the qualifiers, we can’t stay at this level.

“You haven’t added anything new to our football. I repeat: I demand you leave! We’ll find another coach who will do a better job than you.

“And I’m telling you this to your face, without sending a message, not even to the CBF president, who would have sacked you a long time ago.”

The Selecao would go on to claim a 7-0 victory over Singapore on Tuesday, but that win over the international minnows is unlikely to change the 60-year-old’s opinion.

This result came after a 3-2 defeat to Japan on Saturday, as Coventry City winger Tatsuhiro Sakamoto scored a stoppage-time winner with Ancelotti and Raphinha both sent off in the aftermath.

Ancelotti gave a measured response to Romario‘s comments in his press conference ahead of the Singapore game.
