Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement

Chris Eubank Jr is in talks to fight Kell Brook in his return to the ring.

Brook, 40, has not fought since beating Amir Khan in 2022, but has emerged as a potential option to fight Eubank in his first fight since losing to Conor Benn late last year.

According to Elliott Amoakoh, the executive director of Eubank Jr's management team, Nova Sport LLC, any agreement is still a way away.

He told Sky Sports: 'Talks are ongoing but the date, purse and location are yet to be confirmed.'

Ben Shalom, however, who has represented both fighters in the past, told talkSPORT: 'It's a fight that we have been trying to make for a couple of months.

'They have pretty much agreed terms on both sides, there is just some final bits to go. It is one of the biggest fights in British boxing. I think you are right on February and in Manchester.'

Chris Eubank Jr (pictured) is in talks with Kell Brook to face off in his return to the ring

Brook (pictured) hasn't fought since 2022 and retired after beating long-term rival Amir Khan

Brook retired after beating long-time rival Khan in Manchester, having been linked with a fight with Eubank in the aftermath.

Brook has seemed almost certain to return to the ring, having revealed his return fight would be 'announced soon'.

He retired with 40 wins from 43 fights, and is a former International Boxing Federation welterweight champion.

Having debuted as a professional in 2004, he didn't lose until September 2016, when he was stopped in the fifth round by Gennady Golovkin.

Eubank Jr, meanwhile, had faced questions over retirement following his defeat by Benn but has refused to call it quits on his 15-year career.

He had claimed to have major fights scheduled for 2026, but has taken a whole year out of action.

Sports.title: English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man
Sports.content:
English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man

A teenage English boxer has said they have been left 'broken' after being denied the chance to compete at the World Championships due to officials failing to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, had been due to represent England at the Under-19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro last month.

Francis was withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event after an administration error by England Boxing, with the governing body having failed to arrange the necessary sex verification test.

'They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,' Francis told the BBC.

'The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

'Somehow I wasn't on the system.

George Francis, 18, missed out on competing at the Under-19 World Championships after England Boxing failed to arrange a necessary sex verification test. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

'It was the worst news I've ever had in my life.

'I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated.

'I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there.'

Francis's situation, first reported by The Times, followed the mandatory introduction of sex verification tests by the sport's governing body World Boxing.

World Boxing announced the move last year, with genetic sex testing initially introduced for female competitors aged 18 and above. The governing body stated the move was due to a 'duty of care to deliver safety and competitiveness fairness'.

It followed controversy at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where boxers Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting won gold.

Khelif and Lin had been disqualified from the previous year's World Championships, with boxing's former governing body – the International Boxing Association – claiming the pair had failed sex eligibility tests.

Earlier this year, Lin was cleared to compete in women's events following a review of her sex eligibility.

World Boxing's mandatory tests were extended to include male boxers earlier this year.

Francis had been required to undergo a test due to turning 18 four days before travelling to the World Championships.

Francis, a multiple national champion, had been required to undergo a mandatory test after turning 18 days before the World Championships. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

World Boxing introduced sex testing last year amid the controversy surrounding Algerian boxer Imane Khelif's participation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games

The multiple national and GB champion has claimed he is considering turning professional following the mix-up.

England Boxing reportedly contacted Francis's father to apologise for the 'administrative oversight', with the governing body stressing it will 'strengthen processes' to avoid a repeat incident.

'We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible,' an England Boxing statement read.

'George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

'England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence.'

World Boxing's policy requires boxers to undergo a once-in-a-lifetime PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to determine their sex and their eligibility to compete in either the male or female category.

The PCR test is a laboratory technique used to detect specific genetic material, in this case the SRY gene, which reveals the presence of the Y chromosome that is an indicator of male biological sex.

A dozen boxers, representing five nations, were last year blocked from competing at the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

Under World Boxing rules, national federations are responsible for testing and will be required to confirm the sex of their athletes when entering them into World Boxing competitions

Sports.title: Viddal Riley opens up on why he stuck with his dad instead of moving to Las Vegas to train with a Mayweather as he eyes fighting Oleksandr Usyk
Sports.content:
Derrick Riley almost never speaks publicly. Ahead of his son's European title defence against Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday, father and son sat down together to talk about trust, tough love, Joe and Enzo Calzaghe, and why Oleksandr Usyk returning to cruiserweight is 'a little bit greedy'.

But to understand where Viddal is going, you first have to understand the man in his corner.

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since he was a little boy. He still can't put into words what it does to him.

'It's strange,' he exclusively tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I've been doing it for a long time. But you have to try and separate it. You have to shut off the emotion and the sentiment. If you let that sentiment in, I think that's a bad thing. That's your boy in there. He's getting hit and he's getting hurt. I would say it's not easy, and some people can't separate it.'

It's rare to hear Derrick say anything at all. He stays out of the spotlight, and he leaves the talking to his son. Sitting beside Viddal days before the biggest night of his career, when the unbeaten Londoner headlines OVO Arena Wembley against Frenchman Coupe, you quickly see how their relationship works.

'Only my dad would be able to speak to me the way he does,' Viddal says. 'But it comes from a place of genuine care. It's not a job. Someone can only care so much when it's a job. It's like being an employee at a company and having your own business. It's a completely different mentality. This is my business, so he cares and I care.'

WATCH THE EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW ON THE DAILY MAIL BOXING YOUTUBE CHANNEL

Derrick Riley (R), the father and trainer of son Viddal Riley (L), almost never speaks publicly

Viddal is set to take on Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday evening, headlining the event

Derrick added: 'Part of caring too is the fact it's the same brain you've got now that you're going to need after boxing. You can't go to the shop and buy a new one, so you need to protect it. That's why it's difficult to separate the two.'

Viddal grins and says: 'It's the same brain I need for the grandkids.'

The partnership was not always a given. At 21, Viddal went looking for something of his own.

'I was at a stage where I was trying to find some independence. That's the truth,' he says. 'I was presented with the opportunity to go to Vegas, train with a Mayweather and work with Jeff Mayweather. I was thinking, "Yeah, I'm doing this my way. I'm doing things differently."

'But the truth is, I knew my ceiling was getting lower. And I knew the only person who could push that ceiling higher, and continue to do so, was my dad.

'So when I came back to the UK, I said, "Dad, can you train me?" He was like, "Nah, I'm alright. I'm not doing it." And I was like, "Nah, I need you to do it, because that's the only way this dream we've been talking about is going to be fulfilled."

Derrick's refusal was not stubbornness. It was self-preservation.

When asked why he initially said no, Derrick admitted: 'I know what the game is about. I know what boxing involves, and I thought to myself, do I want that in my life? It's a good question when you're in your 50s. I've lived life. There are no rose-coloured glasses. I know what boxing is. But I had to think about it.'

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since Viddal was a little boy

The irony was that he was already qualified for the job. 'By this point I already had a British Boxing Board of Control licence, because I was in the corner with Viddal in Dubai,' he laughs. 'So, funnily enough, I already had the licence.

'He looked at me with those puppy-dog eyes, and I thought, you know what? We've got to do this. But I did say to him, "It's not going to be easy, son. We're going to have to do this properly. You're going to get no ranking belts, no intercontinental belt, nothing like that. You're going to have to do it the old-school way, with the British, Commonwealth, European, and it's going to be hard." And we've done it, man.'

The record backs him up. Viddal is 14-0 with seven knockouts. He won the European title in April with a wide points win over the vastly experienced Pole Mateusz Masternak at The O2, a fight that also served as an IBF world title eliminator. Saturday is his first defence, and it's a mandatory one against a challenger who is also unbeaten in 14.

For a template of what father and son can achieve together, Derrick points to Wales.

'I appreciate Enzo [Calzaghe] more now than I did before,' he says. 'I've always appreciated him, but I appreciate him even more now because I'm doing it myself. People have no idea what it takes, and for him to do what he did with Joe was absolutely amazing. I take my hat off to him.

'Don't get me wrong, I had a boxing background. I wasn't great, I wasn't pulling up trees, but I had a boxing background. Enzo had no boxing background whatsoever, yet he managed to do what he did with Joe. That is amazing.

'It's funny. During the fight with Bernard Hopkins, I think Enzo was saying something to Joe, and Joe gave Enzo a look. I know that look. I give Viddal that same look.'

Viddal and his father have become a force to be reckoned with but they've faced criticism

Joe Calzaghe has described his own brief split from his father, and how he came back because he realised he wanted those highs to be shared with Enzo. Viddal sees the same story in his own.

'We relate to that story because we were severely doubted,' he says. 'It wasn't celebrated. The partnership is only now starting to get some recognition, with people acknowledging that it works. It wasn't like that at the beginning.

'It's been suggested to me that my dad shouldn't train me and that there are people better suited to the job. That's what we walked into. It wasn't accepted as, "Oh yeah, this is a nice family dynamic, let's get it going." It was challenged. The aim was to separate us.

'When we're up against it, we just keep proving ourselves, time and time again. That's what I take from Enzo and Joe. It wasn't celebrated either. They had to keep doing what they were doing, and he turned his son into a 46-0 fighter and one of the best to have ever done it.'

Fathers who train their sons are often accused of living through them. John Fury, so often more visible than Tyson, is the obvious example. Derrick, a former boxer himself, rejects the comparison.

'I don't live vicariously through Viddal. I don't want that,' he says. 'I'm not hogging the camera. It's not about me. It's about Viddal. He asked me to help him, and I'll help him.'

Viddal is just as clear about who he fights for. 'I do it primarily, first and foremost, for me,' he says. 'And very quickly after that, it's for everyone around me that's put work into me achieving it, because it couldn't be done by myself.

Derrick has said he resonates with Enzo (pictured right) and Joe Calzaghe (pictured left)

'When I became British champion, it made me give my dad the belt. We sat down at home for years watching people pick up the Lonsdale belt and hold the Lonsdale belt. So I heard the announcement, "British champion", and I'm like, "Dad, hold this." That's something he's always deserved.'

By rights, Viddal should already have fought for a world title. When Jai Opetaia was stripped of the IBF belt after signing with Zuffa Boxing, the Masternak win put Viddal in line for a shot at the vacant title against New Zealand's David Nyika. Then Opetaia sued the IBF, the governing body held off sanctioning the fight, and Viddal was left waiting.

At the same time, the division has been turned upside down. Opetaia is moving up to heavyweight to face Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua card in Cardiff on December 11. David Benavidez holds the WBA and WBO belts and faces WBC champion Michal Cieslak next month. And now Oleksandr Usyk wants to come back down.

'As I have been saying, it's messy, but I'm trying to get in the mess,' Viddal says. 'I don't want to be on the outskirts of that mess. I'm trying to be in it.

'Right now, I'm just on the outside of the door. I can hear the music in the club, I can hear the bassline. I know there's a vibe in there. I've been seeing the people getting in the door, walking past me. I want to get in there. And Coupe this weekend is another step towards that.'

The most famous person trying to get through that door is Usyk. The Ukrainian became undisputed at cruiserweight, moved up to become undisputed twice at heavyweight, and his team says he now plans to return to 200lbs to chase Benavidez and become undisputed at cruiserweight again. He hasn't fought at the weight since knocking out Tony Bellew in November 2018, and he turns 40 in January.

Viddal admires him. But he isn't convinced.

'It's a bit greedy. It's a little bit greedy,' he says. 'He's completed the level here. He's gone up, he's completed it there, and I think he's just needing that challenge. He's a guy you can tell lives for challenge. All he does is take challenges. "If I'm fighting for a world title, I'm going to go to your country and I'll beat you there." He's that character. That's what makes him a GOAT. That's what makes him a legend.

Viddal has said Oleksandr Usyk is 'greedy' for returning to the cruiserweight division

'But it's dangerous too. Forty years old, dropping all that weight. He hasn't been a cruiserweight since 2018. If I'm in his circle, I'm saying, "Bro, you ain't got to do this. Why? There's no need to." It's not going to be financial. It's just that craving for a challenge.'

Regardless, Viddal is happy with where he is at.

'What I like is that if I'd done this interview four or five years ago, everyone would have asked me, "Do you want to fight Tommy Fury or Jake Paul?" he says. 'Now people ask me, "Would I fight Usyk?"

'Clearly, I'm doing something right.'

Sports.title: What REALLY triggered HSTikkyTokky's boxing night riot between Tommy Robinson and Mo Deen, as Muslim influencer breaks cover to claim 'set up'
Sports.content:
What REALLY triggered HSTikkyTokky's boxing night riot between Tommy Robinson and Mo Deen, as Muslim influencer breaks cover to claim 'set up'

The Muslim influencer at the heart of HSTikkyTokky's shut-down influencer boxing night claims he was 'told to' attack Tommy Robinson in a 'scripted' moment that sparked a riot which saw a man stabbed and two arrests made.

The 'Unhinged' event, held in Kilkenny, Ireland, and streamed to millions online was held 'without any authorisation from anybody', sources say, and promised to be a 'proper scrap between the most chaotic names in the internet scene' – with Muslim influencer Mo Deen and a rival calling himself MrTikTokUK on the undercard.

But the night, with a capacity of up to 2,000 young fans, had to be cancelled three fights before its conclusion when venue owners refused to let it continue.

HSTikkyTokky, the controversial British 'manosphere' influencer whose real name is Harrison Sullivan, is behind the Unhinged event company. He now claims it has been banned 'worldwide' in the wake of the carnage, while simultaneously talking up a fight card for next month – with hopes that far-Right activist Robinson will fight on it.

At the point of cancellation, Mo Deen had jumped from the ring to attack Robinson, metal chairs were being hurled across the crowd by fighting fans, Sullivan had been hit in the head by a glass bottle and racist and sexist comments were being broadcast on commentary online. Later, one man was stabbed and two people were arrested. One teenager has been charged.

Sullivan suggested the event had run 'absolutely brilliantly' because it was trending online. His claims of his company being cancelled appear to have little substance, sources close to boxing authorities say.

Mo Deen now says he has received death threats from Robinson's supporters and, in one video, suggested he feared a 'hit' would be put out on him.

For all those people who claim Tommy Robinson was simply the victim in what became a mini-riot in Dublin, watch this video.



TR might have well been kicked by MoDeen earlier )or attempted flying kick but debatable if there was actual contact), but it was after that incident had… — Nick Lowles (@lowles_nick) November 8, 2026

A mass brawl erupts at HSTikkyTokky's Unhinged 003 boxing event in Kilkenny on Saturday

Far-right activist Tommy Robinson sparked the violent riot with an altercation inside the ring

Muslim influencer Mo Deen has claimed he was 'told to' attack Robinson in a 'scripted' moment

At the Hub in Kilkenny, a 1,900-capacity community venue which hosted The Boomtown Rats at the start of the year and is welcoming Irish singer Gavin James next month, an already violent event broke out into a brawl after an altercation between Robinson and Deen – whose real name is Mohammad Kubba.

Robinson, currently on bail after being found guilty in October of harassing two Daily Mail journalists in a campaign that caused them to fear for their safety, arrived in Kilkenny as a ringside guest, accompanied by a large contingent of his supporters. He is due back in court on December 16 for sentencing, with the hearing potentially to result in a custodial sentence.

The chaotic scenes in Kilkenny were preceded by an equally unruly press conference on Friday evening, where multiple fighters launched themselves at one another in a series of violent clashes involving streamers, rappers, OnlyFans models and convicted sex offender-turned-YouTuber Paul Flaherty.

Flaherty, who was jailed for five years in 2018 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a woman he met on Tinder, had already been embroiled in a chaotic brawl at a Unhinged promotional event in September, with footage of the confrontation quickly going viral online.

Tensions rose on Saturday night when Sullivan and his influencer friend Ed Matthews, who starred alongside HSTikkyTokky in Louis Theroux's documentary Inside The Manosphere, invited Robinson to join them at the commentators' desk before Deen's fight.

Holding a copy of his book, The Grooming Gang Cover-Up, the 43-year-old activist made a series of inflammatory remarks about Islam, claiming that 'Muslims have been raping our country for 100 years' and citing false statistics about Muslim men and sexual offences.

After defeating MrTikTokUK, Deen – whose real name is Mohammad Kubba – climbed out of the ring and launched himself at Robinson with a flying kick, in a moment he has since claimed was staged and designed to raise tensions ahead of a potential future bout between the two.

Deen took to social media to claim his attack was staged as he sought refuge in a utility room

The initial brawl spilled into the crowd but was largely contained by security, who managed to defuse the situation. Deen, 41, subsequently left the venue as the remaining bouts got underway, only to be escorted back inside by event security after it was claimed Sullivan called for him to return and face Robinson in the ring.

Sullivan has denied the claim as well as the claim by Deen that he was following a script.

With tensions through the roof, and many racially diverse spectators left furious at Robinson's previous remarks, the far-Right activist launched his book towards Deen, sparking a physical brawl that violently went out of control.

Robinson was grabbed as punches were thrown, while people from both entourages were caught up in the melee.

Violence quickly spread through the crowd, with chairs and metal barriers hurled across the venue, spectators exchanging blows and others scrambling to escape the commotion as security desperately attempted to intervene.

A string of videos showing people screaming, pushing and throwing punches were published to social media in real time as the chaos continued for approximately 20 minutes. Shouts of 'Oh Tommy Robinson' bellowed out from the riot before the livestream, which was broadcast on platform Kick to approximately 1.8million viewers, eventually cut to black.

Police, who had been alerted to disturbances at the venue before the mass brawl broke out, arrested and detained a man in his 20s after another man was stabbed and rushed to hospital earlier in the evening.

A teenager was also arrested by the Gardai and charged with violent disorder.

‘Gardai attended the scene of a number of incidents on the night of Saturday 7th November, 2026 at approximately 9pm at a premises on the Dublin Road, Kilkenny,’ a police statement read.

’One male, aged in his 30s was assaulted and removed from the scene to St. Luke’s Hospital. A man, aged in his 20s was arrested and is currently detained under Section 4 at a Garda station in the South East.

‘A second male was arrested, an adult in his teens, for violent disorder and has since been charged. He is due to appear in court later today, no court sitting has been set at this time. Investigations ongoing.’

Despite the arrests and widespread violence, Sullivan attempted to restart the remaining bouts without spectators, solely for the event's livestream, before a visibly upset venue representative intervened to stop him.

Robinson brawled with Deen and his entourage after being invited into the ring by Sullivan

Robinson greets the event's organiser HSTikkyTokky, whose real name is Harrison Sullivan

HSTikkyTokky CRASHED OUT after someone in the crowd THREW a GLASS BOTTLE at him while he was interviewing a fighter 😳 pic.twitter.com/Uq8uSghkXC — clipmate (@clipmxte) November 7, 2026

A spokesman for the Hub has since said in a statement to Kilkenny Live: 'Following an incident the decision was made by the management of the venue to step in and stop the promotions company from continuing with their event.

'The Hub has a zero-tolerance policy towards violence, aggression or disorderly behaviour.'

As the violence unfolded, Deen took to social media claiming his initial confrontation with Robinson had been staged for entertainment but spiralled out of control.

As he and his entourage sought refuge in a small utility room, Deen urged that his post-fight fly kick was scripted as he hurriedly told his crew to 'lock the doors'.

'The whole place is surrounded,' a concerned Deen said as wild shouting could be heard in the background.

'There's fights everywhere, we're locked in a room right now. Listen I'll make this clear to every single person in the UK. I'm not trying to cause problems. This is like WWE, they said this is what the situation is. I followed the script.

'I'm getting death threats, people trying to kill me. I don't know about this, I just know this is what we had to do. Why is everyone trying to kill me right now?

'This is a message to all supporters of Tommy, supporters, gangs, whatever you are. I just followed the script they told me to agree with. Tommy's agreed to it, they've agreed to it, I followed it.'

'Look at my hands bro,' he added looking visibly shaken. 'My guys are getting rushed, look at my friend's face bro. This whole thing is crazy.'

Deen went on to plead with Elon Musk, whom he described as one of Robinson's 'friends', and the activist's wider network of supporters not to 'put a hit out' on him.

'A fight is a fight, hopefully anyone who is with Tommy and is friends and that, Elon Musk or whatever, don't put hits out on me,' he added, holding his hand to his heart.

Sullivan, who initially stated that the event went 'absolutely brilliantly' because it was trending globally, has refuted Deen's claims that the fight and aftermath was staged.

In a video on his YouTube channel, Sullivan said: 'I was sat next to Tommy. Do you think that I wanted to get f***ing fly-kicked and f***ing some fat belly over me? My watch nearly got popped off. Do you think that that was a plan? No. The plan was for them to face off in the ring.'

The 25-year-old manosphere influencer also dismissed claims that he intentionally attempted to stage an impromptu bare-knuckle fight between Robinson and Deen when the Muslim fighter was escorted back into the venue.

According to The Guardian, Sullivan repeatedly shouted 'let Tommy fight him' while Robinson's entourage – referred to by the YouTuber as 'Tommy's boys' – were permitted to enter the ring to face off with Deen and Co.

He added: 'What is that nonsense? You think I would want them to have a bare-knuckle fight for free, not to just face off and hype up the next event?'

🚨MUST SEE: Hstikkytokky has OFFICIALLY SOLD AWAY his UNHINGED PROMOTIONS COMPANY…



He goes on to apologise to all fans and every supporter 😳



HS: “I’ve had message from police and the boxing commission, I am no longer able to host @UnhingedEvents pic.twitter.com/6EopqIhyMr — KickClipz (@Kickclipzfeed) November 8, 2026

Chairs were hurled and punches were thrown as the event descended into absolute chaos

HSTikkyTokky appeared on Louis Theroux's Inside the Manosphere documentary this year

Sources have told Daily Mail Sport influencer events such as Saturday's Unhinged 003 tend to take place without authorisation from any official boxing body.

HSTikkyTokky had promoted the event as a 'proper scrap between two of the most chaotic names in the internet scene', with British rappers Russ Millions and Kirky set to headline a card that was ultimately abandoned before their bout could take place.

After initially hinting that a potential bout between Robinson and Deen had been in the works for next month, Sullivan appeared crestfallen on a later video as he called an end to Unhinged Promotions, claiming they had been shut down from operating 'worldwide'.

'I've had a lot of messages from police around the world, message from the boxing commission... I am not allowed to put an Unhinged event on anymore after Tommy Robinson riots at Kilkenny last night,' he said on his channel.

'Obviously it's massively disappointing, I wanted to grow the company Unhinged Promotions, I wanted to make it massive and huge and take over the world but the risks that have come in play from the decisions some of my staff have made has now led to us having to cancel any future event. We won't be back, but I will sure be supporting some of the other promotions around the world.

'I just want to apologise to the internet. I didn't want to ever have to put on events that risked the safety of people that came to support. I'm super sorry and I won't be doing an event again. I wish I could, but I'm not allowed to now.'

In case the message wasn't already clear, he stated again: 'There is no venue around the world that will take me, there is literally nothing I can do. I feel cornered, I feel lost, I feel gutted. I feel jobless, this was my passion, my desire, my life.

'Now it's been taken away from me over something that was meant to be a light-hearted promotion for the next event. I'm gutted and I want to say again, sorry to everyone.'

Sullivan's self-pitying demeanour offered a stark contrast to the buoyant figure he immediately cut after the chaotic event, which he claimed went 'absolutely brilliantly'. Footage from earlier in the night had shown him being hit by a glass bottle thrown from the crowd while he stood in the ring.

Thrilled that Unhinged's third event had trended globally on social media platforms as a result of the riots, he said: 'I think it went absolutely brilliantly. Listen it was controversial as f*** but please tell me other promotion on their third event is trending globally on Twitter like this, has generated over 200 million views across TikTok, Twitter and Instagram.

'So everyone who's hating, you're clearly still watching. The fights were absolutely brilliant up until the venue got closed down.

'I'm gutted that we didn't get to see the final three fights but s*** happens. I totally hold accountability for misjudging the amount of security that was needed and the types of people that were coming. I misjudged that.

'But what I won't listen to is that wasn't a f***ing great night of entertainment. It was huge. Every single person is watching what I do. Every single person likes to talk about what I do because I'm the number one at what I do.'

Robinson was holding a copy of his book, The Grooming Gang Cover-Up, as he entered the ring

Robinson, who is on bail before his sentencing in December, said 'Muslims have been raping our country for 100 years' as he riled up the crowd with inflammatory remarks about Islam

Irish mobster Paul Flaherty just KNOCKED OUT a boxer at HSTikkyTokky’s Unhinged boxing press conference 😳 pic.twitter.com/NHVJFG10Ij — vxdeo (@vxdeo) September 17, 2026

Sullivan has seen other boxing events shut down in the past. In January, he complained that 'hundreds' of complainants had called the local council and police to cancel a show in Basildon, saying that one of his fighters was a 'convicted child predator'.

The mayor of Kilkenny called the scenes this weekend 'absolutely disgraceful'. Andrew McGuinness said on local radio station KCLR: 'I am absolutely disgusted Kilkenny was used as a backdrop for such a horrendously managed event.

'They are grooming young people to behave in a way that's absolutely disgraceful. They have no respect for themselves, no respect for other people and particularly no respect for women.

'They groom thousands of people into going to these events. The fact there were minors and teenagers at the event is just absolutely appalling.'

Sports.title: Troubled ex-boxing world champion Adrien Broner wheeled out of concert and slumps over couch after falling unresponsive
Sports.content:
Troubled former boxer Adrien Broner has sparked major concern after viral footage showed him falling unresponsive at a concert on Saturday night.

Former four division boxing champion Broner, 37, was seen in the worrying state during a livestream while attending a 'Skilla Baby' concert in downtown Los Angeles.

In the viral footage, Broner could be seen looking dazed before slumping over on a couch. An EMS worker attended to him and helped carry him to a flight of stairs.

While taking Broner down the stairs, the ex-boxer appeared to fall in and out of consciousness before eventually regaining enough composure to walk down.

In the end, Broner was loaded into a wheelchair by friends and the EMS worker before being taken backstage and into a car outside the music venue.

It marks the latest concerning incident involving Broner, who recently had a run-in with police in Beverly Hills.

Troubled former boxer Adrien Broner has sparked major concern after viral footage showed him falling unresponsive at a concert

Broner had to be helped down a flight of stairs by an EMS worker while at the concert

At the end of October, Broner was among a group of men recording content on the streets of Beverly Hills for the social media platform, Kick, when local police arrived.

Viral footage from the incident shows the group recording what appears to be a music video involving both Broner and his fellow content creator, Deen The Great.

A separate clip showed Broner with his arms raised and walking backwards towards a pair of officers, who ultimately placed him in handcuffs.

Broner was seen trying to poke fun at the situation by doing a funny walk for the officers' benefit, but they did not seem amused.

'Broner was detained during a traffic stop as part of an investigation into a large street gathering in a residential area,' Beverly Hills police told TMZ in a statement. 'He was released from the scene and a citation was not issued.'

Broner is also currently among several defendants being sued in Los Angeles County over allegations of sexual battery, battery and assault.

'Plaintiff alleges that Broner repeatedly pressured Plaintiff for sexual activity after repeated refusals, attempted to isolate Plaintiff, repeatedly pressured Plaintiff while intoxicated, attempted unwanted physical contact, publicly humiliated Plaintiff, and made false sexual statements about Plaintiff to a livestream audience,' read the complaint, obtained by The Daily Mail.

Broner has denied any wrongdoing in the case.

Previously, in September of 2025, Broner was kicked off rapper Cam'ron's popular podcast after ignoring the host's warnings to stop flirting with his on-air co-host.

Sports.title: Scottish boxer Willy Hutchinson fulfils boyhood pledge by becoming world champion after famous victory
Sports.content:
Scotland is celebrating a new boxing world champion after Willy Hutchinson produced the performance of his life to beat Joshua Buatsi in Manchester and claim the vacant World Boxing Council (WBC) light-heavyweight belt.

The 28-year-old from Carstairs was superior in every department and toyed with his London-based rival while avenging the 2024 defeat he endured at the hands of Buatsi.

Hutchinson had insisted in the build-up he had matured since that setback and was a more complete fighter, and he went about proving it in devastating style by showing off expert footwork, evasive movement and sharp counterpunching to flummox Buatsi.

The judges scored the fight 117-112, 115-113 and 115-113, all in Hutchinson’s favour, and the majority of the crowd in the AO Arena went wild to acclaim the new champion.

The contest was initially for the interim title but was upgraded when American David Benavidez gave up the WBC gold to move up to cruiserweight. And it proved a dream come true for Scotland’s Hutchinson, who had told before the fight about how he’d targeted becoming a WBC champion at the age of 13.

As he celebrated a famous victory in the ring, an emotional Hutchinson said: ‘I want to tell the story one more time. I was 13 years old. My dad was working in Sweden. I signed it in a book, I said I will become a world champion. Let’s go!

Scotland's Willy Hutchinson lands a punch on Joshua Buatsi at the AO Arena in Manchester

Hutchinson proudly holds the WBC light-heavyweight title belt after outclassing his opponent

‘Can I say thank you to my coach because I’ll tell you one thing, without him I don’t think I’d be here today, let alone boxing. This man dug me out of a hole that I never thought that I would get out of, so this is all a bonus, baby.’

Hutchinson immediately set his sights on an all-British showdown against three-time former world title challenger Anthony Yarde, who was ringside in Manchester.

Eyeing up the Londoner, Hutchinson said: ‘Anthony Yarde, do you want some of this?

‘He’s no walkover but let’s go. Him next.’

Yarde, 35, responded: ‘It’s 100 per cent a fight I’d love to take.’

Another option could be the winner of next month’s mouth-watering tussle between Dmitry Bivol and Callum Smith in Yekaterinburg, Russia, where the other three light-heavyweight titles are on the line.

Beat the winner of that one and Hutchinson – who now boasts a record of 21 victories with two defeats – could find himself the undisputed light-heavyweight champion of the world in 2027.

Suddenly, things just got a whole lot brighter for Scottish boxing.

Sports.title: The factors behind the abortive 2030 F1 rules announcement
Sports.content:
Famously, when the papal conclave gathers to elect a new pope, a successful vote is communicated to the huddled masses via smoke from the Sistine Chapel chimney as the chemically impregnated ballot papers are burned: white smoke signifies a decision, black means yet another round of voting. The practice derives from the 13th century, when the cardinals took three years to debate a successor to Clement IV, prompting the frustrated local faithful to lock them inside the palace with only bread and water to subsist upon.

All this came to mind when Monday's much-anticipated meeting between the engine manufacturers, the FIA and the commercial rights holder to discuss the next generation of Formula 1 engines was followed by the 21st century F1 equivalent of white smoke billowing from the chimney: an Instagram post by FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

“You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon,” he wrote underneath the ‘asset', an FIA-branded graphic illustrating sound waves and accompanied by the unmistakeable scream of a high-revving V8 engine.

And then, almost within the blinking of an eye, the white smoke turned black. Various related promulgations on the FIA's other social media channels were deleted, kept for posterity only by those with the foresight to screenshot them.

Ben Sulayem has been among the most vocal exponents not only of a return to ‘purer' racing engines than the current turbocharged hybrid V6s, but also of an earlier timing for that change. Although the balance of electrical deployment to internal combustion engine power is shifting over the next couple of seasons, the essential concept is due to remain in place until 2031.

Speaking earlier this season, the FIA president made it clear he wants to bring forward a new generation of engines in 2030, and would use all the powers at his disposal to make it so. But while it is within Ben Sulayem's bailiwick to set the F1 technical rules, whether the other stakeholders in grand prix racing would sign up to that is another matter, and bound into the commercial settlement known as the Concorde Agreement.

Realistically, Ben Sulayem requires a consensus between the FIA, the teams, the manufacturers and the commercial rights holder. Aligning these parties – some of whom are in competition with one another – is usually a process that is both tormented and tormenting.

It's in that context we must view this week's announcements and their subsequent striking from the record.

What is understood from various briefings is that there was broad agreement for a turbocharged 2.1-litre V8 with a smaller electrical element. Even to get to this point has required a great deal of compromise, since Ben Sulayem's spoken preference was for naturally aspirated V8s with token electrical input, similar to the Kinetic Energy Recovery System (KERS) first seen in 2009.

The president sees simplification as the way of creating a virtuous circle: manufacturing and development would cost less, potentially opening the way for non-manufacturer engines, while the engines themselves would be lighter. This would make a lower minimum weight for the cars realistically achievable.

This met with considerable resistance from the car manufacturers – although, to complicate the debate further, these are not all aligned with one another. Ford and Cadillac, for instance, with their broader focus on the US market, are understood to have been supportive of dropping turbos and having a smaller but still significant electrical element. At the other end of the scale, Audi and Honda saw natural aspiration as a deal-breaker and were insistent on a strong element of hybridisation.

Adding two cylinders was much less of an issue since V8 engines still figure largely in several key road car markets. In racing terms, V6s make a much less inspiring noise owing to their ugly firing order, even when not breathing via a forced induction system which mutes the soundtrack.

Nico Hulkenberg, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Brett Farmer / LAT Images via Getty Images

Although the principle of turbocharging will most likely remain, it will be based on smaller compressors running with lower boost pressures, which will reduce lag. The electrical motor's output will be reduced from the current maximum of 350 kilowatts (kW) to 100kW in general running, with another 100kW available to augment overtaking.

While this was the understanding, it's clear now that several of the parties in Monday's meeting emerged with a different perception to the governing body about what had actually been agreed.

This isn't necessarily a setback to the process, even though it has exposed a certain lack of consensus as we approach the point where the rules must be set. One thing all the manufacturers appear to agree on is that they need clarity by the end of this year to have enough development runway for a 2030 introduction.

To that end, the FIA wants to present a definitive 2030 regulatory framework to the World Motor Sport Council meeting in Shanghai on 10 December. This, though, would essentially be a rubber-stamping process. The real agreement must be secured before then.

This week's premature celebration suggests that this agreement is close enough to have the press releases written, but not yet at the point of clicking ‘send'. Perhaps we should lock the stakeholders in a nearby palace and feed them only bread and water until unanimity breaks out?

Sports.title: What McLaren has learned from a tough 2026 as it aims for a return to glory in 2027
Sports.content:
McLaren's 2026 Formula 1 season has been characterised by a recovery effort that never quite came to fruition.

Yet, team principal Andrea Stella insists the reasons for this are well understood, so he can be optimistic about 2027: "We are in a completely different place compared to the start of the season," he told Autosport.

Whenever it seemed to have caught its rivals, McLaren found itself falling behind once again. A difficult start, followed by progress that culminated in a period of the championship when the MCL40 appeared capable of setting the technical benchmark, then a gradual decline in competitiveness and a return to the front at the Brazilian Grand Prix. This trajectory is not easy to interpret.

Stella has an explanation that goes beyond the performance of individual upgrades. He traces the team's 2026 difficulties back to what happened during the previous season, identifying three decisive factors: a delay in developing the new car, the consequences of the demands placed on the team by the 2025 championship battle, and the disadvantages of being a Mercedes customer team at the beginning of the new regulatory era.

"I don't think there have been any upgrades this season, at least among the top teams, that haven't worked," Stella explained. "Even when we introduced some new parts in Baku, after which it appeared that we had taken a step backwards, that wasn't actually the case. Competitiveness has to be assessed in relation to your rivals, not simply by looking at your own progress in absolute terms. And from that perspective, I don't believe we ever took any steps backwards during the season."

The distinction is fundamental. McLaren improved gradually throughout the season, but not enough to compensate for the progress made by its rivals. Above all, it had to recover from an initial deficit that was considerably greater than anyone might have imagined.

A three-month development deficit

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

"We established that, at the start of the season, we were three months behind in terms of development," said Stella.

This is a significant admission, particularly because the Italian makes clear that this was not an assessment made retrospectively by translating the gap in lap times into months of work. McLaren had already identified the problem by analysing its development trends during 2025.

Stella acknowledges the impact of what happened during the previous championship battle. McLaren had planned to gradually redirect its resources towards the 2026 project, but Red Bull's resurgence in the second half of the championship meant it had to maintain a strong focus on the MCL39 which was still competing on track.

On top of this came an especially complex management challenge: supporting the championship ambitions of both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri while maintaining an internal balance that would not jeopardise the team's future.

"For me, it was probably the season in which I worked harder than in any of my 26 seasons in F1," said Stella. "Every day, you had to pay attention to managing the team's environment, as well as the technical and operational aspects."

This is one of the less visible aspects of McLaren's story. The team had to devote its energy not only to developing the car and defending its competitiveness, but also to managing a delicate sporting situation. This effort, combined with the technical difficulties, contributed to slowing preparations for 2026.

The customer-engine factor

Mercedes' double championship demonstrates that it's now more challenging for engine customers to be competitive with their suppliers Photo by: Hector Vivas / Formula 1 via Getty Images

There is, however, a second element Stella considers decisive. For years, McLaren had demonstrated that a customer team could win a world championship using the same power unit as a works outfit. In 2026, that situation changed.

"In 2025, I was often asked whether not being a works team was a problem," said Stella. "I always said no, and in fact it had never been a problem until the end of last season."

With the introduction of the new power units, the situation became considerably more complicated. Integrating the engine into the car and optimising energy-management parameters took on decisive importance. Mercedes HPP, tasked with developing a competitive and reliable power unit, had to establish its priorities.

"When you're a customer team, you're not the priority," Stella acknowledged. "When it came to understanding the engine's power curves, certain cooling aspects or optimising the integration, we arrived a little late."

One concrete example involved the gearbox ratios, which had been defined using power curves that did not perfectly match those subsequently observed on track. These might appear to be marginal differences, but under the new technical regulations they can translate into significant disadvantages.

"In such a competitive F1 environment, you cannot afford to give away one or two tenths as a structural disadvantage simply because you're not in a position to be at the cutting edge of development timing," he added.

The most sensitive issue, however, concerns the tools used to optimise the power unit's operation. Some software developed jointly by Mercedes HPP and the works team contained proprietary elements that could not be shared with McLaren.

"They told us that these tools contained a significant amount of Mercedes intellectual property and that they couldn't give them to us," Stella said. "I didn't have particularly strong arguments with which to say, 'You have to give them to us anyway'."

The solution was to develop equivalent tools with HPP, essentially repeating some of the work that had already been carried out between Brackley and Brixworth. This process took time, and it is only in 2027 that McLaren will have full access to the same optimisation capabilities.

Nevertheless, Stella avoids any criticism of his engine provider. He acknowledged the difficulties faced by HPP, including those relating to reliability, and ruled out any deliberate attempt to disadvantage McLaren. The working relationship has remained positive, but that has not eliminated the structural disadvantage.

A recovery effort that wasn't enough

Developments have added performance, but not enough to ensure consistent winning form Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

McLaren attempted to make up the lost ground via the upgrades introduced throughout the season. The developments brought to Miami and Hungary produced clear improvements, but they were not enough to close the gap consistently.

"Every time we brought an upgrade, we saw a step forward, but we also saw that our rivals weren't standing still. The other teams brought their own upgrades too, and we weren't able to close that gap," Stella admitted.

Baku is a particularly telling example. At a circuit where electrical energy management is crucial, McLaren paid the price for its difficulties in optimising the power unit: "We weren't able to deploy all the battery energy from the final corner in Baku all the way to the end of the main straight.

"At that point, you're carrying a crucial disadvantage at a circuit that is so sensitive to power."

The problems had already emerged in the opening races. In Melbourne, the team discovered how a single suboptimal parameter could compromise energy management for an entire race, while reliability issues in China prevented both cars from starting.

The complexity of the new regulations had been anticipated, but not to this extent. Stella admits that McLaren underestimated just how decisive the power unit would become and how high the price would be for every parameter that wasn't perfectly calibrated.

The return to winning ways in 2027

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The 2026 season hasn't diminished McLaren's ambitions, though. Stella believes the team now has a much deeper understanding of the car and, above all, of the Mercedes power unit.

"I'm optimistic about 2027," he said. "Compared with the start of the season, we're in a completely different place in terms of how we're using the power unit."

The technical relationship with HPP is also set to change. The tools that were unavailable at the start of 2026 will be fully accessible next season, albeit a year later than for the official Mercedes team.

There is another factor that Stella considers important: with 2026 being less demanding in terms of sporting management than the previous season, McLaren's leadership has been able to devote more energy to technical work and preparing the new car. The aim is to avoid starting next year's championship with the same deficit that has hampered the team this season.

"We are a team that, over three years, has had a rate of development that has taken us to two consecutive constructors' championships," he said. "We cannot now back down and say that finishing third or fourth is good enough. Our ambition is to remain world champions."

McLaren therefore ends 2026 with a different perspective from the one it had at the beginning of the season. Stella made no attempt to hide the mistakes and delays, but he stands by the quality of the work carried out throughout the year.

The challenge now is to turn what the team has learned into a competitive advantage, and to look back on 2026 as a transitional year that laid the foundations for a future back at the forefront of F1.

Sports.title: The Antonelli you don't know: Daily life with F1's newest champion
Sports.content:
There is one thing that physiotherapist Sergi Avila took a little while to understand. When Kimi Antonelli finally found himself with a free weekend, after weeks being spent between circuits, airports and training, the most logical choice would have been to stay at home: sleep a few extra hours, meet friends and switch off. Antonelli, instead, got in the car and went to a race track - perhaps to watch karting or MotoGP.

At first his performance coach inevitably tried to dissuade him, but then he understood that he was making a mistake as for Antonelli, simply going to a track does not mean working, but returning to the place where he feels happiest.

“The track is his natural habitat,” said Avila, “the place where he feels most at ease, where he can be completely himself. At first I thought it would be better to stay at home, rest, sleep a bit more. Then I understood that for him the balance is positive. Going to the circuit gives him something he would not have by staying at home.”

It is a small detail, but perhaps it is one of the best ways to begin getting to know the new Formula 1 world champion. Not the one witnessed on television, talking to the engineers and celebrating on the podium, but the one known by the people who live alongside him, sharing with him much more than the 24 Sundays of an F1 campaign.

The first time in F1: “How can he already brake like that?”

Riccardo Musconi, now chief engineer, virtual world at Mercedes, was one of the men tasked with accompanying Antonelli for the testing programme organised in 2024 to prepare him for his F1 debut. His first memory, however, dates back a few years earlier, during a single-seater presentation at Silverstone.

“I had heard about Kimi,” said Musconi. “I saw him in the garage and asked him if it was him. He answered me in English, so I explained that I was Italian too. Then I spoke with his father Marco. He told me how the conditions had come about for Kimi to enter the Mercedes programme. It seemed as if all the planets had aligned.”

Riccardo Musconi, Brazil 2022 podium Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

When the time came to start testing, Musconi found himself facing a boy who was not yet 18 years old. The first episode he remembers, however, does not concern a single-seater, but a van. “We were at the Spielberg circuit,” he recalled. “He took us for a lap of the track, in heavy rain - well, I didn't imagine a van could go that fast! He scared us to death. It didn't last long, because the brakes were already cooked after a couple of laps.”

Then came the moment to get into the Mercedes. In that case too, the track was wet. Musconi had at his disposal the reference data from the single-seater previously used by grand prix winner Valtteri Bottas and was impressed.

“It was his first run in the wet and he immediately found himself close to Valtteri's references at Spielberg that they had on file,” he added. “I wondered how it was possible. He had never driven a Formula 1 car: how could he already brake in that way? How did he know where to put the car in the wet? That left me speechless.”

The subsequent tests, including the one at Imola, confirmed the engineer's assessment, and he prepared a report intended for Mercedes' technical management. “After three tests I had understood that this boy was a phenomenon,” said Musconi. A conviction that would make it even more difficult to understand what would happen the following season.

A plan completed ahead of schedule

Bradley Lord, deputy team principal of Mercedes, remembers the first time he saw Antonelli in the team's garage. It was the 2018 Monaco Grand Prix, when the Italian was only 11 years old and so small that he could barely see over the workbench.

Eight years later, that child has won the F1 title. But when Mercedes decided to give him the seat vacated by seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, the objectives were different. “We hoped to develop a driver who could help us win the constructors' championship in 2026,” Lord explained. “The plan envisaged a 2025 of learning, to put him in a position to contribute significantly the following year. Obviously Kimi accelerated the programme.”

Bradley Lord Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

The choice had been a brave one. Mercedes was losing Hamilton, the most successful driver in F1 history, and instead of looking for a conservative solution, it preferred to open a new chapter. “It would not have made sense to look for a half-copy of Lewis,” said Lord. “We had to do something different, start a new story. But in the end what really matters is only speed, performance and potential. Everything else can be managed.

“Last year he learned in one season what is normally learned in three years. He had a good start, a difficult middle part and a positive finish. But above all he found the way out of the difficulties on his own. In a certain sense, for me this is his fourth season, not his second.”

Five minutes that reveal a person

Rosa Herrero, senior public relations manager, knows another Antonelli. This is the one that she has to accompany from one interview to another, protect from constant requests and guide through the commitments of a day that often does not even leave time to breathe. After 10 years spent alongside Hamilton, the switch to Antonelli was a discovery for her too and a strong bond of trust has developed between them.

But there is a small secret in Herrero’s schedule. When she plans a meeting for Antonelli with Italian journalists, she sets aside 20 minutes, but only communicates 15. The other five are a safety margin. “I know that when the interview ends he will still stay to talk, to say hello to everyone,” she revealed. “I don't want to be the one who comes in and keeps saying that we have to leave. So I leave him those extra minutes.”

It is not an occasional concession, as Herrero knows his difficulty in pulling himself away from a conversation. “He has an incredible memory for names,” she said. “You introduce him to someone and the next time he already knows who they are. He says hello to everyone, he stops to talk. I think it is something that comes from his upbringing, from his family.”

Lord also recognises in this spontaneity one of the driver's most valuable traits, revealing a surprising detail. “In all the years we have worked with him, we have done one day of media training,” he revealed. “Just one! We want authentic personalities, not robots. Kimi is himself, he is honest, transparent, open. It is one of his superpowers.”

One of the group, without needing to play a role

Kimi Antonelli and Peter Bonnington Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

Peter Bonnington has worked with some of the strongest drivers in F1 history, from 2009 title holder Jenson Button to seven-time world champion Michael Schumacher. For 12 seasons he was also Hamilton's race engineer and when he left Mercedes in 2025, a new chapter also opened for Bonnington. His particular challenge was building a relationship with an 18-year-old sensation, who suddenly found himself occupying one of the most important seats in the series.

The first time he met Antonelli, in Monaco, Kimi was still a child. Toto Wolff introduced him, announcing, almost as a joke, that one day he would be his race engineer. Bonnington smiled, without imagining that prediction would become reality.

The professional relationship grew alongside the human one. “Kimi brought a dimension of spontaneous fun into the garage, almost like a playground,” said Bonnington. “That doesn't mean there was a bad atmosphere before, absolutely not. But this boy arrived and immediately broke down certain barriers. He is one of the group, we work hard and have fun together.”

It is above all that expression, “one of the group”, that describes the way Antonelli experiences life at Mercedes. He has not tried to create distance between himself and the people who work on his car, but he prefers to sit on a stack of tyres and talk with the mechanics, share a joke and even stop when his commitments suggest going elsewhere.

It is behaviour that Lord traces back to his origins. “He grew up in racing teams thanks to Marco and Veronica, he knows what it means to be part of a team,” he said. ”You see that every day.”

Antonelli has known that world since he was a child. He learned early that behind a single-seater there are people, even before roles and responsibilities. And today, despite having become world champion, he continues to behave as he always has without needing to continually prove he is the most important driver in the garage.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The salmon, the desserts and the little secrets of hospitality

There is, however, one place at Mercedes where the world champion goes back to simply being a 20-year-old. It is the hospitality kitchen, where Zugel works as the chef who prepares meals for Antonelli and his team-mate George Russell.

Zugel has known Antonelli since his Formula 2 days and since his arrival in F1, he has started to take direct care of his nutrition, following Avila's instructions. But Antonelli is not always willing to respect the programme.

“Sometimes he tries to be smarter than Sergi, to get around the rules to eat something he shouldn't,” said Zugel with amusement. “In Singapore he came into the kitchen without me seeing him. He touched my shoulder, I turned around and found him in front of me. He asked me for a double portion of salmon. I thought it had all been agreed!”

“About 10 minutes later, Sergi arrived and asked me if Kimi had ordered anything special. I told him about the double portion. Only then did I understand that it was not authorised.” There was even another occasion in which Antonelli had attended the buffet to serve himself a steak, ignoring the menu prepared for him. And when he sees a particularly inviting dessert, he tries to convince the chef to save him a portion. “He tells me to keep something aside for him for later, but not to tell Sergi,” chuckled Zugel.

Those are small acts of complicity that have built a special relationship. Zugel now knows Antonelli’s tastes, the way he prefers his pasta and which dishes make him happiest. “Through food you learn to know a person from a different point of view,” he claimed. “You try to prepare what he likes, you change something according to his tastes and little by little you build a relationship. In the end he spends so much time here that this has almost become a second home.”

The chef, too, has been struck by Antonelli's growth. “It is impressive to see the maturity he has reached, especially mentally,” he reckons. “He doesn't seem to feel the pressure and yet, despite everything that has happened, he has remained the same boy.”

When talent was not enough

Austria 2025 Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Antonelli's rookie campaign was far from easy. Following an encouraging start, the summer of 2025 represented the most difficult moment of his journey and Musconi does not hide that that period profoundly surprised him.

“If you ask me what surprised me most in these two years, I would answer that it was the difficulties of last year,” he said. “After three tests I was convinced he was a phenomenon. At a certain point I was asking myself: what is happening? How is it possible that he cannot express what we have seen?”

The answer, at least in part, came from comparing notes with some engineers used to working with young drivers. “They pointed out something we had underestimated,” he added. “Working with a rookie is different from working with an experienced driver and I realised that many of the engineers following Kimi had never worked with a debutant.”

It was a reflection that shifts part of the attention from the driver to the structure that had to support him: Antonelli needed to learn, but Mercedes also had to adapt its working method. Lord confirmed how difficult it was to face that situation: “Only some drivers can withstand the pressure of going directly into a top team. Kimi felt the responsibility towards everyone, also because of the fight in the constructors' championship. It was an enormous weight.”

Herrero remembers Spa above all. After a particularly difficult session, she was supposed to take him in front of the television crews for the customary interviews, but she understood that he was not ready. So, she took him back to the engineers, gave him time to speak with the team to regain a little serenity. “I knew he needed time,” she said. “I kept telling him that he had to believe in himself. When you are nineteen it is difficult to bear the weight of an entire world judging you and today everything is amplified by social media.”

Bonnington also remembers that period. Mercedes had introduced modifications to the rear suspension that had not helped Antonelli, but external judgement inevitably fell on the driver. After Monza, the race engineer felt the need to have a frank conversation with him, as there were things that were not working and they had to improve.

Monza, 2025 Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

It was the beginning of a rebuilding process. Lord identified the meeting after Monza and the Baku weekend as the moment when the Italian began to find his own way. The team had not stopped believing in him. And Antonelli was learning to react.

The maturity he had acquired emerged in 2026, especially when the run of success was interrupted. “I was impressed by the way he managed the disappointment,” Lord said. “In the moment he was angry, emotionally involved, but shortly afterwards he had already turned the page and was focused on the next race.”

In Singapore, after a difficult Friday, he continued to work until he rediscovered a very high level of performance. At Austin he did even better and Lord remembered the calm he showed during qualifying in Texas. “He knew he was putting the pieces of the puzzle together and when the decisive lap came, he put them all in the right place,” he said.

A maturity that also surprises Bonnington. “The way he reads a race, picks up on the small details, describes the behaviour of the car during debriefings, they are all things you would expect from a driver with 10 years of experience,” he said. “And many of them you cannot teach. They come naturally to him.”

The champion who thinks he is only at the beginning

There is a conversation that Avila has remembered with particular pride. After the Hungarian Grand Prix, when Antonelli had already shown he could compete with the best drivers in the world, Antonelli confided to him that he still felt far from his own potential.

It was not a technical assessment. It was the awareness that he still had to learn, especially in direct confrontations with experienced rivals and in race situations he had never faced. “He told me he still needed to expose himself to many different scenarios, to gain experience. For me, hearing him talk like that was wonderful,” he said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

From karting to single-seater racing, Antonelli had never contested two seasons in the same category before F1, so constantly had to learn something new. Even with 2026 to an extent, considering the regulation change which represented a new challenge.

But today he is a world champion. He has achieved the goal he had pursued since he was a child, yet those close to him describe a boy who does not seem to consider anything concluded.

Rosa will continue to leave him five extra minutes in the schedule. Zugel will probably still have to defend a few desserts from the raids of his most famous guest. Bonnington will try to preserve that direct and spontaneous relationship he has built with his driver and Sergi, perhaps, will no longer try to convince him to stay at home on free weekends.

They are small details, far from the stopwatches and the standings, but they say something important. Antonelli has become world champion without losing the curiosity, lightness and need for authentic relationships that belong to his age.

Lord, who has known him since he was a child unable to see over the garage table, now watches with pride the driver he has become. “Out of the car he is fantastic,” he said. “But when he gets into a single-seater he is a monster. A good monster, but a monster!"

Sports.title: Piastri to receive 10-place grid drop at Las Vegas GP
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri is set for a 10-place grid drop at the Las Vegas Grand Prix for exceeding his engine allowance in the 2026 Formula 1 season.

The 25-year-old was already on the limit of four internal combustion engines for the campaign, but will need a fifth Mercedes V6 engine to finish 2026.

As it is the first time he is exceeding his ICE allowance, Piastri will be docked 10 places on Las Vegas' starting grid on Saturday night local time.

McLaren said: "Oscar will take a new Internal Combustion Engine in Las Vegas after a reliability issue. As it is his fifth of the season, he will take a 10-place grid penalty, but he has a good chance to recover positions with overtaking in Saturday's race."

The Woking squad also confirmed it will take Mercedes' upgraded turbocharger, which the manufacturer developed under the FIA's so-called Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) catch-up mechanism.

McLaren added: "Both cars, as with the other HPP-powered cars, will be fitted with a new ADUO-enabled turbo specification: the expected performance benefit is relatively small."

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

The Mercedes works team will trial the new turbo on Kimi Antonelli's car, while George Russell will stay on the original specification to avoid a grid drop, as Russell had already reached the limit of his allowance.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said: "We will have the ADUO-enabled turbo specification available from this weekend. This is primarily about proving out the development in race-weekend conditions, with the expected performance benefit relatively small.

"We anticipate running it with Kimi, whilst with George our priority is protecting his grid position with the performance benefit likely too limited to justify taking a grid penalty."

Sports.title: Alonso, Loeb join Aston Martin for 2027 Dakar Rally
Sports.content:
Two-time Formula 1 champion Fernando Alonso will headline Aston Martin’s factory entry into the Dakar Rally in 2027, joining Sebastien Loeb and Lucas Moraes as part of a star-studded line-up.

Alonso will drive a Prodrive-built Aston Martin Dreadnought in the 49th edition of Dakar, which will take place in Portugal and Morocco from 9-23 January 2027 after being relocated from its original location in Saudi Arabia.

This will mark the Spaniard’s first appearance in the world’s most popular rally-raid since his impressive debut with Toyota in 2020, when he finished 13th overall and recorded a second-place finish on Stage 8.

The 45-year-old will reprise his partnership with Marc Coma, a five-time Dakar winner on motorcycles, who will serve as his navigator for the two-week marathon.

“After deciding to continue racing in Formula 1 with Aston Martin, I thought carefully about Dakar,” said Alonso. “In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula 1 and the Dakar Rally in the same year.

“In 2020, Dakar was one of the most challenging and enjoyable experiences of my career. I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it.

"Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sebastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team.

“Formula 1 remains my priority. But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve.”

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Photo by: Aston Martin

Alonso had long harboured aspirations of returning to the Dakar, even as he continued to put his primary focus on remaining in F1. Speculation about a 2027 entry intensified after he extended his contract with Aston Martin in September.

The Spaniard is also understood to have tested a prototype version of the car in Morocco in October, before the African nation was confirmed as the primary host for the 2027 Dakar. Rally drivers regularly test in Morocco to prepare for the forthcoming season, with its vast deserts serving as an ideal testing ground for the Dakar.

Alonso’s participation in the Dakar was confirmed on Tuesday, as Aston Martin announced that it will be entering the world’s most popular rally-raid as a factory team for the first time in history.

The British manufacturer will compete for outright honours with motorsport powerhouse Prodrive, extending a successful partnership that already encompasses GT racing and previous prototype ventures.

The car that Aston Martin will enter has been badged as Dreadnought, which was first conceived as a digital-only military vehicle for the popular Call of Duty game series.

Dreadnought is understood to be the latest iteration of the prototype that previously competed as the Dacia Sandrider until the Renault Group pulled out of cross-country rallying following its victory with Nasser Al-Attiyah this year.

Prodrive, which also ran the factory Dacia programme, held discussions with multiple manufacturers about taking over the Sandrider project in the summer before reaching an agreement with Aston Martin.

“Aston Martin Dreadnought was conceived to dominate any terrain, under the most extreme circumstances, and come through it all to deliver on its mission,” said Aston Martin CEO Adrian Hallmark.

“Now along with our engineering partner, Prodrive, we will challenge this vision in the most extreme competitive environment in global motorsport – the Dakar 2027.

“It is in Aston Martin’s nature to forge forward with pioneering concepts, and just as we have always done, explore their limits on the global stage.

“We do not shy away from such challenges, but embrace them, and in Fernando, Sebastien and Lucas we have three great champions with whom to mount a formidable challenge on Dakar 2027.”

Aston Martin 2027 Dreadnought Photo by: Aston Martin

Aston Martin will also count on the experience of nine-time world rally champion Loeb, who has been part of Prodrive’s set-up since 2021, first as Bahrain Raid Xtreme and subsequently Dacia.

After holding talks with several manufacturers, including Ford and Toyota, the Frenchman will contest his 11th Dakar with Aston Martin as he continues his pursuit of a maiden win.

“Winning the Dakar is very important to me,” said Loeb. “We have come close several times, and the motivation is there to keep working until we achieve it.

"To take on this challenge with Aston Martin and Dreadnought is a great opportunity. It is a brand with a special motorsport story, and I would feel very proud to help it win the Dakar for the first time.

“This race has proved many times that it demands much more than speed. You have to manage the difficult days, look after the car and stay focused until the finish.

"With Fabian alongside me, and with Fernando and Lucas, we will bring all our experience to the preparation and development of the programme as a team. There is a lot to learn with a new car, and I enjoy that work with the engineers. The objective is to arrive at the start ready to fight for victory.”

Aston’s Dakar line-up will be completed by Moraes, who won the 2025 World Rally-Raid Championship with Toyota before moving to Dacia this year.

With both Loeb and Moraes remaining with Prodrive following Renault Group’s exit, Al-Attiyah and Cristina Gutierrez remain the only Dacia drivers left without a seat for 2027. The former, now one of the most successful rally drivers of all time with six Dakar wins, has yet to announce his plans for next season.
