Sports.title: Norris: Las Vegas GP would be "scary" with current F1 wet tyres
Sports.content:
Lando Norris hopes Formula 1 tyre supplier Pirelli will field much-improved rain tyres in 2027 as he expects the current range won't work properly at a low-downforce circuit like Las Vegas.

Following partially rain-affected weekends in Malaysia and Singapore, F1's 2026 cars went through their first proper qualifying and grand prix held in wet conditions at the Brazilian Grand Prix, with both Pirelli's full wet and intermediate compounds being put to the test at Sao Paulo. Qualifying had to be halted for over an hour due to standing water in several corners, with the risk of aquaplaning prompting drivers to run full-wet tyres in Q1 before switching to intermediates.

The race both started and finished on intermediates, with a dry middle spell, dispelling early fears over how the 2026 generation of cars would run in the wet. But while Brazil put on an entertaining spectacle and Pirelli's rain tyres largely worked as expected in the right operating window, drivers still felt this year's stiffer intermediates need work on how they perform in low temperatures as they struggled to keep their cars on the track at the start of a stint and on laps to the grid.

With Interlagos being one of the easiest circuits on the calendar to get tyres into the working range, several drivers voiced concerns that Pirelli's offering won't be robust enough on circuits where that isn't the case, like the upcoming Las Vegas street circuit.

The FIA's official weather forecast is not available yet, but other predictions suggest the chance of rain is over 50% for Free Practice 1 on Thursday evening, with conditions more likely to be dry after that.

With temperatures dipping well below 10C over the Vegas weekend and the circuit lacking any high-speed corners to put lateral load into the tyres, McLaren driver Norris said a wet practice would be quite "scary" because the intermediates don't work when they're too cold.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

"When the tyres get cold, it's pretty nasty," Norris said when asked by Autosport for his verdict on F1's first proper wet-weather weekend of this rules cycle. "On laps to the grid, when they get very cold, they felt horrible. If they get into a good window, they're good. So, I think the scary times are if you go to Vegas and you can't get any tyre temperature. You need a much better tyre than what we have here because that's going to be horrible."

Brazil runner-up Max Verstappen added: "I think it's mainly that the working range is a bit too small. When they're hot, it's okay, but when they're cold, they're really like a rock. That's something that we need to try and work on, to generate a bigger working range on the extreme wet [tyres] and the intermediates. I think that would help a lot with switching on the tyre better and then being able to run even in heavier rain."

Williams driver Carlos Sainz also felt Pirelli's entire range needed improvements. "I think the level of the wet and the inter is not good enough and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre because in the mixed conditions the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear; by the time it warms up the front is gone.

"And the extreme honestly, [in qualifying] we had so much aquaplaning and a big lack of rear grip, so still missing a bit of development on these two tyres."

Pirelli faced a difficult task developing rain tyres for F1 2026's all-new regulations suite with their high-torque power units and active aerodynamics, putting significant forces through the rubber. It meanwhile chased a moving target of just how much downforce the teams would be able to generate, with fierce in-season development already ahead of the supplier's projections.

Over the off-season the FIA implemented a partial Straight Mode in the wet to ease safety concerns, with only the front wing now being activated. Then, in April, the governing body also reduced electric output in wet conditions. Those two measures are believed to have made a big difference to the 2026 cars' ability to race in the wet relatively safely, but they obviously arrived well after Pirelli had to define its 2026 tyre range.

F1's first proper running on both the extreme wet tyres and intermediates is coming so late in the season that Pirelli can't take Brazil's lessons into account for 2027, as the Italian tyre manufacturer has already finalised its homologations for next season.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

But following earlier development work at the start of the year, it was able to conduct crucial wet-weather testing in Magny-Cours last month, trialling the various solutions it worked on over the course of 2026. At the French circuit, Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti conduced two days of testing, including one day in the wet to trial various new intermediate tyres featuring different compounds and constructions.

"We tested some solutions, especially for the intermediates, and we ended up with good options that we would like to introduce for next season," Pirelli's trackside engineering chief Simone Berra said in Mexico. "For sure the idea is to improve the wet-weather product for next year.

"We worked on the compounds, we worked on the tread thickness, we also worked on different structures. So, we worked a lot on different tyre aspects and we would like to combine the best solutions. We are working on the data now and we are going to homologate new wet-weather compound specifications."

Speaking after qualifying in Sao Paulo, Pirelli's head of motorsport Dario Marrafuschi was adamant the company has "made some steps" for 2027. "Of course, we took quite seriously the scepticism from some drivers, and we addressed the development during the year. We know there is always room for improvement and we believe we made some steps ahead for next year," he said.

"It is a great value having this information [from Brazil]. Unfortunately, it is coming only towards the end of the season. We have already closed the wet development for next year. I don't want to disclose what will happen on the wet next year, but we made the wet development based on the information we had at the beginning of the season and some of the testing we did in Suzuka, so that was good for us to address the priorities for this year.

"We had a positive test in Magny-Cours, and quite [soon] we will be disclosing the outcome of this wet test."

Sports.title: Haas sticks with Camara for Las Vegas GP, Hirakawa in for FP1
Sports.content:
Rafael Camara will race again for Haas at Formula 1's upcoming Las Vegas Grand Prix, as Ryo Hirakawa takes Ollie Bearman's seat for the opening practice session.

Both Hirakawa and Camara have now raced for the team following the dismissal of Esteban Ocon, who was stood down during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Hirakawa, contesting the World Endurance Championship finale in Monza - later winning his third WEC title - was unavailable for the previous F1 round in Brazil and this presented Haas an opportunity to bring Camara in for an early debut.

Camara will stay in the car for Las Vegas, as he gathers valuable experience for his full F1 debut next season with the team. Bearman meanwhile has only given up his seat for one FP1 session so far this year, so will do so for the final time to present Hirakawa with more track time in the VF-26.

Hirakawa scored a point in his Mexico City F1 debut, albeit after Oscar Piastri and the two Alpine drivers were handed post-race penalties, and impressed team principal Ayao Komatsu with "very good mental conviction - [he was] so clean. He delivered what we expected."

Ryo Hirakawa, Haas F1 Team Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Camara endured a tougher debut run, as conditions at Interlagos were incredibly variable. The Brazilian built up through the weekend and showed good pace by the end of FP3, but the rain arrived ahead of qualifying and made his life more difficult.

After rescuing his car from a spin in Q1, Camara got as far as Q2 - but put his car into the wall at Turn 12 having been unable to get the correct rear-axle braking in low-grip conditions.

He thus qualified 13th and started 11th with other drivers taking grid penalties, but a tough stint on the intermediates put Camara towards the back of the field.

Read Also: Formula 1 Why Camara should take heart from a tough F1 debut in Brazil

It is uncertain whether Camara will stay in the car for the rest of the season, given his position at the top of the F2 drivers' standings; he may wish to complete the season, but this will largely be at the behest of Haas and Ferrari.

Hirakawa could feasibly return to the car in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, should Camara return to F2 for those rounds.

Sports.title: What is left to fight for in F1 2026?
Sports.content:
A five-way battle for P2 in the drivers’ championship

Kimi Antonelli romped to his maiden world title to become Formula 1’s youngest world champion, but behind him it’s all to play for – and closer than ever.

As the highest-scoring driver across the latest eight rounds, Max Verstappen has climbed to second in the championship, but that doesn’t mean he’ll comfortably be this year’s runner-up. George Russell, Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris lie within 33 points of the Red Bull driver, with a maximum of 75 points still available.

Whoever takes second and third will then get the privilege to attend the FIA’s end-of-season gala as podium finishers – a prospect which typically is enjoyable to some drivers and daunting for others.

Team boss Toto Wolff said Mercedes’ priority may now be securing a 1-2 in the drivers’ championship, perhaps softening the blow of a disheartening campaign for Russell, but not everyone cares as much.

“I'm not going to say it doesn't mean anything, but it's not something I focus on,” Hamilton said of the prospect of finishing second. “I think winning the championship is the only thing any of us really care about. I mean, maybe some people do care about the other positions, but for me, my sole focus is on making sure that we secure second in the constructors' championship.”

It certainly doesn’t matter to Verstappen. “For me personally, I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth,” the Dutchman said of his championship chances back in Singapore. “It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun till the end, you know, try to go for a day’s success.” Eight consecutive podiums, including three wins from the last five rounds, seem to prove his point.

Another three chances for Oscar Piastri and Isack Hadjar to win

Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Oscar Piastri and Isack Hadjar have two things in common: they are the only top-team drivers who have been comprehensively outperformed by their team-mates and the only ones who have, so far, failed to win a grand prix in 2026.

Both of them have taken a couple of podium finishes each without ever having a real chance of victory. The fact that they never qualified on the front row doesn’t help.

That is not too surprising from sophomore Hadjar, who is paired with the formidable Verstappen, but for Piastri, it is a little more puzzling; the 2025 title contender has struggled to adapt his driving style to F1’s new machinery, especially when it comes to finding the limit.

“It's definitely something I've been working on a lot. There's been signs of progress with that, but it's just taking longer than I'd hoped,” he admitted back in Mexico.

Hadjar is in a very different situation. “This year, for some reason, I feel like I haven't driven much,” he said in Brazil, having missed three races after injuring his wrist in August. “You know, Saudi, Bahrain cancelled, and then I had a two-month break during the summer break, and now I feel like I have a lot left in the tank. I'm a bit sad that we're already on the end, because I feel like I can still go a long way this year.”

To be fair, Hadjar had his share of misfortune in the previous rounds. “That's what makes it more frustrating for me right now,” he added. “The last couple of races, I couldn't even be in the top five, except for Malaysia – there's always been something happening on Sunday.

“But it's going to click. It's just a matter of time, and on my side, I think pace has been decent, so I just want to keep pushing, and anything can happen with the conditions. So, just stay very, very sharp.” He was rewarded with a podium finish in Brazil; will he do even better next?

Red Bull vs McLaren for P3 in the constructors’ championship

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The main battle in the constructors’ championship will be Red Bull against McLaren for third position. Second-placed Ferrari admittedly isn’t mathematically out of reach, but it enjoys a 95-point advantage over Red Bull, with 129 available to score. Such a plot twist would require three debacles from the Scuderia and consistent podium finishes from Hadjar.

With Red Bull on 415 points and McLaren on 398, however, it’s all to play for. Red Bull surged to the front of the pack in the last couple of months – it collected 152 points from Azerbaijan to Mexico, with McLaren down on 59 – but the MCL40’s latest upgrade helped Norris to victory in the Brazilian GP.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies described McLaren as “a bit faster” in the Interlagos race, though the wet conditions weren’t quite representative of what they will likely be in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi – but further updates are expected in Nevada.

“It's thanks to these [latest] upgrades that we are now in condition to fight for the victory, combined with the conditions surely,” McLaren team boss Andrea Stella said. “And these upgrades, first of all, they will be complemented by some more parts that come in Vegas. And they form the foundation for what will be next year's car.

“So, it's encouraging for the trajectory of McLaren that we seem to be able to transform our development into performance on track.”

Read Also: Formula 1 McLaren to upgrade MCL40 F1 car at its bogey track Las Vegas

Haas vs Audi for seventh position

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

With Racing Bulls and Alpine solidly fifth and sixth in the standings, our attention now turns to Haas and Audi – a tale of two seasons.

F1’s new era began in impressive fashion for the American team, with Oliver Bearman finishing seventh in Australia and fifth in China. The 17 points collected across these two weekends represent more than half of Haas’ current tally of 31, as the team lost ground throughout the campaign amid consistency issues with the VF-26.

This is intriguingly reminiscent of the team’s first season, exactly 10 years ago, with Romain Grosjean then scoring 18 points in the first two events before the team’s eventual tally plateaued at 29.

Meanwhile, Audi’s maiden F1 campaign after fully taking over the Sauber squad started with low-key form, with its first power-unit somewhat struggling relative to most rival engines. But the R26 has become a consistent points scorer at the hands of Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg – hence how it has made up a 19-point deficit to Haas, now lying just three points adrift.

So the momentum firmly is with Audi, which has actually outqualified Haas in 18 out of 20 grands prix so far – especially as the second Haas car is now driven by Rafael Camara, who made his debut last time out in Brazil. Despite the rookie’s raw pace, his lack of experience might prove costly in such a tight fight.

“I really want to manage expectations here,” Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu said in Brazil. “And then that means I'm not putting any pressure on Rafa, right?

“Of course, as Haas F1 Team, we are in a tight championship battle with Audi. But, again, that's not his problem, if you like – that's on us. Our job is to really just create an environment that doesn't have any of those extra pressures.”

Read Also: Formula 1 Why Camara should take heart from a tough F1 debut in Brazil

Aston Martin to spring a surprise?

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Aston Martin’s 2026 has been nothing short of a disaster, particularly amid the Honda power unit’s lack of power, reliability and driveability – which has been painfully obvious on many occasions.

‘Painfully obvious’ might also accurately describe a dejected Lance Stroll’s lack of enjoyment, as he retires from most races and his answers to the media – which never were that loquacious in the first place – have become near-monosyllabic.

Fernando Alonso hasn’t been much happier, but to his credit, he has made an impact whenever it was remotely possible. Aston now has seven points to its name, courtesy of the two-time champion’s starring drive to eighth in Malaysia.

It’s unlikely Alonso can shine in Las Vegas – the Honda powertrain’s deficiency may be too stark with that near-2km full-throttle portion along the Strip – but a winding track like Lusail might be a decent opportunity to clinch a result for Aston.

As it happens, the team is just five points behind ninth-placed Williams – which has scored just one in the latest 14 grands prix – in the constructors’ championship. All Aston needs would be for Alonso to take one seventh-place finish, assuming its rival doesn’t score more than one point by the end of the season.

“We turn up at every event with the motivation, drive, and passion that we had earlier in the season to score every point possible,” Williams team principal James Vowles told Sky Sports F1 in Brazil. “What I'm more indicating is it's just a much harder task now, but it doesn't mean that the team isn’t motivated.

“Actually, I'd be surprised if you didn't look around and find people actually surprisingly in a good spirit. They can see what's coming in the future, but our goal still to the end of the season is to make sure that our last point scored wasn't a few races ago.” It will be a tall order.

Sports.title: Mercedes’ technical director explains how Antonelli leapt ahead of Russell in 2026 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli scored less than half as many points as his team mate in his first season of Formula 1 last year.

But he turned that around in his second season which put him in position to clinch the world championship as Mercedes produced the car to beat.

James Allison, Mercedes’ technical director who led development of their first world championship-winning car for five years, believes a shift in the handling balance arising from this year’s new technical regulations explains why George Russell lost the edge he had over his team mate.

“I would say that George – I’m more or less quoting George here – when he has been prospering, it is at a track where you can make a lot of difference from the apex and out of the corner,” he explained in a video released by the team.

“George is good at getting on the power and getting a strong exit from a corner. That certainly was true of last year’s cars and George was very strong relative to Kimi in last year’s car.

“I think this car is a little bit more conventional as a car, where a lot of the lap time is in trusting the car and the combined brake and steer on the way in: So, delivering the car to the apex, leaning on the front, trusting that the rear is not going to punish you and then arriving at the apex just that little bit quicker so you don’t have to be so aggressive on the exit.”

Antonelli’s stronger performance on the way into corners gives him an advantage when looking after his tyres, says Allison.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“That, in the race, tells because you are using less of the rear tyre. You get less tyre degradation and that – if you want to see the standout performances of Kimi this year, it’s 20 laps in when everyone else has peeled into the pits and his lap times just go level.”

Lewis Hamilton, whom Antonelli replaced at the team in 2025, has also benefited from the same change, Allison believes.

“I think that’s one of the reasons why Lewis is having something of a sort of Indian summer in his career, because that was always Lewis’s great strength is hurling the car to the apex, trusting that he’s going to manage the thing as it gets to the apex.”

Allison said he is impressed by Russell’s focus on addressing where he has fallen short compared to Antonelli this year.

“He does not hide from his own deficiencies,” said Allison. “He’s one of the most honest drivers I’ve ever had the good fortune to work with.

“He can see the areas where Kimi has been quicker than him this year and he knows that those are things that he needs to bring to the table to compete on equal or better terms with this precocious young talent. I do very much admire the fact that he looked straight down the barrel of that and I’m pretty sure that we will see, we have seen in the last couple of races some very, very strong performances from him.

“I’m pretty sure in the last three we’re going to see him, without all the burden of these championships still on any of our shoulders, looking to build the platform that is going to let him have a run at it next year, alongside an amazingly talented team mate.”

Sports.title: An early season finale? Five talking points for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 heads to Las Vegas this weekend for what is supposed to be the first of three consecutive race weekends – but doubt still hangs over the following two events in the Middle East.

Here are the talking points for this weekend’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

McLaren’s upgrade

Fresh from the team’s third victory of the season in Brazil, McLaren is bringing another upgrade for its MCL40 this weekend. However this latest package is aimed more at laying the foundations for 2027, when it hopes to reclaim the championships it lost to Mercedes last year.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit has not been a kind venue to the team in recent years. They are yet to score a top-five finish at the track: although both cars took the chequered flag inside the top five last year they were later disqualified for excessive plank wear.

Will Lando Norris be back among the victory contenders this weekend – and will team mate Oscar Piastri get a better grip on a car he’s struggled with all year?

Alpine’s last chance for a result?

Alpine’s bright start to 2026 raised hopes at the team that, having sunk to last place in 2025, they would immediately rebound by finishing in the top half of the championship this season. That looks increasingly unlikely as the team has taken only a single point over the last six rounds, allowing Racing Bulls to open up a 45-point lead in pursuit of their best-ever championship finish.

The best hope for Alpine is a repeat of the windfall result they enjoyed in the closing stages of 2024, when its drivers pulled off an unlikely double podium finish in Brazil. But if that’s going to happen anywhere for them, Las Vegas might just be the place.

The track’s long straights favour aerodynamic efficiency and straight-line speed. Pierre Gasly showed Alpine have that in abundance when he claimed a surprise pole position at Monza earlier this year. He’s shown some form at this track too, putting his Alpine third on the grid for this race in 2024.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Here to stay

Formula 1’s ambitious plan of racing on the Las Vegas Strip did not make an especially auspicious start when practice for the inaugural 2023 race was badly disrupted after a drain cover caused significant damage to Carlos Sainz Jnr’s Ferrari. At the time F1 only had an agreement to race at the circuit for three years and it remained to be seen whether the city would embrace the race for the long-term.

Now they have: this will be the first Las Vegas Grand Prix since the promoters announced a new, 10-year contract. F1’s belief it could establish a foothold in Las Vegas has been vindicated.

The new Las Vegas Grand Prix is undoubtedly more impressive than its dismal eighties predecessor and has clearly served as a useful promotional vehicle for the sport. But it’s also an event where the show unquestionably comes first and the contest feels like an afterthought. Will that change now the event’s future is assured?

Speeding down the Strip

If the Las Vegas race represents everything Liberty Media wants Formula 1 to be, it’s rather unfortunate that its latest generation of cars appear so ill-suited for the track.

F1’s energy-starved power units will have to wait a long way between recharging opportunities on the Las Vegas Strip, not to mention the other long acceleration zones dotted around the circuit.

All year drivers have been frustrated at how constrained they are by their power units, notably in Mexico, another track featuring a long acceleration zone but otherwise blessed with many other recharging opportunities. Expect the problem to be especially acute this weekend.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

The last F1 race of 2026?

Since the previous round in Brazil, F1 has abandoned its contingency plan to race at Imola if the final two races in the Middle East cannot go ahead. Andrea Kimi Antonelli can therefore forget about signing off his dream, championship-winning second season on home ground.

Instead the series will cross its fingers and hope for the best when it departs Las Vegas for Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Moto GP raced at Losail two weekends ago, though one manufacturer stayed away, deeming it too risky.

While F1 team bosses have publicly expressed faith in the FIA’s judgement over the races, they are also taking seriously the possibility they may not happen. So far all bar three* teams have confirmed they will satisfy their commitment under the rules to run four inexperienced drivers in practice by this weekend.

There is a financial incentive for F1 not cancelling two of its most lucrative races. But are all the teams and drivers satisfied this is a risk worth taking? And if not, will any be bold enough to speak out?

*Update: Ferrari have now joined Haas in confirming they will run a practice driver this weekend, leaving just two teams yet to officially announce their plans.

Sports.title: Hamilton tells F1 to spend £50 million in promoting under-represented talent | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has called on Formula 1 to publish data revealing how far the championship is representative of people from different backgrounds.

The seven-times world champion founded Mission 44, an organisation to promote black and other under-represented groups, in 2021.

Hamilton said polling conducted by the organisation shows support among fans for broadening representation. Almost two-thirds of 3,000 people polled across the UK, US and Brazil said F1’s leadership should do more to widen participation, while 55% agreed the series “talks about inclusion more than it delivers”.

In order to promote new talent in the championship, Hamilton’s review made three recommendations. These include a commitment to invest £50 million over five years promoting new talent.

The organisation’s review, called Igniting Inclusion, also recommends the series, the FIA and all 11 teams report data on representation to an independent organisation for tracking. The data would include “who joins, who is promoted and who leaves, by gender, ethnicity and socio-economic background.” This partner would “publish one, sport-wide picture each year” and give annual awards recognising progress made by teams.

Igniting Inclusion also urges teams to create a published number of early-career places each year which would “build thousands of paid routes into motorsport by 2030.”

“Formula 1 is inspiring millions of young people around the world,” said Hamilton. “But inspiration means nothing without opportunity. We can’t tell young people to dream big and then not open the doors when they try to make those dreams a reality.

“F1, the FIA and every team must push harder and move faster. We need real investment, more opportunities and greater accountability. We’ve shown that change is possible. Now we need to go further. The talent is out there, and the future of our sport depends on unlocking it.”

Sports.title: Racing Bulls boss Permane “should talk up” need for cost cap changes – Vowles | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Williams team principal James Vowles says the leading midfield team of 2026 should want to see changes to Formula 1’s cost cap.

Vowles claims the cap, introduced in 2021, has had the unintended effect of making it harder for midfield teams to catch up to the top four front-runners – Red Bull, Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren. He argues the spending limit is taken up by salary and car development costs, leaving too little for teams to invest in their facilities.

“Before the cost cap came in, there were more points scored by the teams that weren’t the top four teams,” he told The Fast and the Curious. “Quite a bit more points, actually.”

“So back then about 10% of the podiums were [scored by] the teams that were in P5 to P10 [in the championship]. Now it’s 5%.

“There’s been one winner in 130 grands prix that wasn’t a top four team, one winner.” This was when Pierre Gasly won the 2020 Italian Grand Prix for AlphaTauri, the team now known as Racing Bulls. Vowles said that was a result of “my mistake” when he was a strategist at Mercedes.

“So what I’m really bringing to everyone’s attention is the following. What we’ve done with the cost cap is we’ve made it better for the top four teams.

“The gap between all of us is bigger than it’s ever been before. The amount of points that we are scoring is less than ever before.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Vowles said other teams which are trying to catch up to the front-runners face the same problem.

“We are investing and – here’s the kicker to it, so is Aston Martin – we’re investing huge amounts more than we did before the cost cap. That was the difference.

“Williams wasn’t putting the money in, they didn’t have the money. Force India [Aston Martin’s former identity] weren’t putting the money, they didn’t have the money. So the world today is actually a completely different financial element.

“But I’m being hurt by trying to catch up to others, which is holding me back. And by the way, not just me. It’s holding back other teams as well at the same time.”

Vowles feels other midfield teams which are limited by the cost cap should be pushing for changes too. “I think Alan Permane should talk up about this as well, by the way,” he said.

Permane’s Racing Bulls team is on course to finish fifth in the championship this year behind the top four teams. However Racing Bulls shares an owner with Red Bull and largely exists to prepare new drivers for the chance to join the bigger team.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Last month Permane said he isn’t interested in significant changes to the cost cap, arguing that major investments can be spread over multiple seasons.

“I don’t think we would support a wholesale change to the cost cap rules to start being able to spend huge amounts more money because I think it’s served us very well for the six years we’re into it now. I think it’s served Formula 1 very, very well.

“I think maybe there are tweaks to do, for sure. If you want to spend a whole lot of money on [capital expenditure], you can. The mechanism’s in there.

“So if James wants to go and spend $100 million on something, he can do that. You just pay it off over the X number of years. So, the mechanism is already there.”

However Vowles insisted it is not possible to make investment on the scale teams need under the cost cap without significant compromising their competitiveness.

“We have 30 years of under-investment in Williams,” he said. “And at the moment, the way we are competing up and down the grid is whatever money you spent six years ago has defined the tools you have around you. Simple as that.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Vowles said a midfield team which wants to “fight for world championships and fight for wins” needs to be able to be able to spend more than they can at the moment without compromising their car development.

“I can do all the expenditure I want, but we wouldn’t get a car out the door if I built the facilities for a period of time because I’m having to pay this wooden amount of money that goes into a black hole as a result of it,” he said. “That’s not sporting equity at all.

“Sporting equity would be we all play with the same tools, the same characteristics. It’s unfortunate, it’s not their fault, we didn’t have investment for 30 years.

“But also, we shouldn’t define a sport by what we spent in our chequebook six years ago before the cost cap came in, which is fundamentally what we’re talking about now. So it’s not quite true to say that. You can’t spend the money without it having a large performance hit, which others won’t have to go through.”

Formula 1

Sports.title: Derek Chisora Still Waiting for the Right Wilder Money
Sports.content:
Derek Chisora says he still hasn’t been offered enough to fight Deontay Wilder again on the December 11 Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua undercard in Cardiff. He’s willing to step in for Jai Opetaia, but says he’ll stay home if the offer falls short. Asked how much it would take, Chisora kept the figure to himself.

“They already asked me, and I already told them, ‘Yes, give me the right money.’ So now we’re just talking about money,” said Chisora on talkSPORT. Pressed for a figure, he said, “A good number. A very good number.”

Given that Chisora reportedly earned between $4 million and $6 million for his first bout with Wilder, it is hard to see how he commands even a tiny fraction of that amount today. At 42 years old with 14 losses on his record, Chisora no longer has the O2 Arena farewell narrative he used to sell out London back in April.

If Dana White were running these negotiations, he wouldn’t just balk at a steep asking price; he would laugh Chisora right out of the room and refuse to even entertain the idea of using him.

If Chisora’s price stays inflated, the promoters have every reason to walk away and look at a younger heavyweight instead. Bringing in someone like Bakhodir Jalolov would give viewers a fresh matchup and let fans see how Wilder handles a younger southpaw with deep amateur credentials at a fraction of the cost.

Putting Chisora in the co-main slot doesn’t just fail to add value; it actively drags down the quality of the broadcast.

To younger American fans, Chisora is basically invisible. He hasn’t been a relevant force on U.S. television in years, and casual viewers tuning in for Fury and Joshua aren’t going to care about an aging British domestic attraction who already lost to Wilder seven months ago.

Hardcore boxing fans aren’t clamoring for it either, because everyone already knows exactly what Chisora brings to the table at this point in his career.

The bigger problem is how weak it makes the top of the card look. When you pair a faded Chisora with a 41-year-old Wilder who has lost four of his last six fights, you end up with a co-main event featuring zero top-five contenders. Following that up with Fury and Joshua means the final two bouts of the night are built entirely on nostalgia rather than elite, current division talent.

If the promoters want the card to have actual credibility with hardcore fans and younger American viewers, they need a legitimate threat or a rising contender across from Wilder, not a recycled eight-round exhibition.

Jim White wrapped up the radio segment by noting that Chisora is holding out for his magic number, prompting Simon Jordan to joke about the veteran being a “greedy little swine.”

Sports.title: Teremoana Teremoana Calls For World Title Shot After Stopping Ahio
Sports.content:
Teremoana Teremoana dropped Hemi Ahio with right hands in both rounds and stopped him at 1:36 of the second to win the vacant IBF Inter-Continental heavyweight title on Wednesday, November 18, at Pullman Melbourne Albert Park in Melbourne, Australia.

Teremoana (13-0, 13 KOs) kept his perfect knockout record intact against the most experienced opponent of his professional career. Ahio (25-2, 19 KOs) got up from both knockdowns, but referee Ignatius Missailidis checked him in the corner after the second and waved off the scheduled 10-round fight.

After the fight, Teremoana said he would take a shot at a world heavyweight title in his next bout if the opportunity came up. His goal is to fight for one within the next 12 months.

Teremoana Drops Ahio in Both Rounds

Ahio came forward from the opening bell, looking to get inside Teremoana’s jab and trade at close range. Teremoana made him pay for the approach within the first minute, catching the New Zealander with a hard right hand as he tried to close the distance. Ahio got to his feet and took more punches in combination before making it out of the first round.

The second opened at a slower pace, with some clinching and work to the body. Teremoana found room for his right hand again and hurt Ahio before putting him down with another right. Ahio beat the count, but Missailidis ended the fight after looking him over in the corner.

“I knew if I stayed close, he’d try and hit me; that’s why I stayed long. I think I handled myself well,” said Teremoana after the fight.

At 6’6″ and about 269 pounds, Teremoana had six inches in height and roughly 37 pounds on Ahio at the weigh-in. His jab made the shorter man start his attacks from farther out, and the right hand caught Ahio on the way in. Ahio kept pressing after the first knockdown, but he never found a way to get inside consistently enough to keep Teremoana from throwing at full extension.

The 28-year-old Brisbane heavyweight represented Australia at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where he lost to eventual gold medalist Bakhodir Jalolov in the super heavyweight quarterfinals. He had stopped his first 12 professional opponents inside two rounds. Ahio, 36, came in with 26 professional bouts and 19 knockouts of his own. Even with that experience, he became the 13th opponent to fall before the third round.

Matchroom Boxing CEO Frank Smith praised Teremoana for dealing with an opponent who kept coming forward. Teremoana mentioned the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury undercard as a possible place for his next fight and said he would leave the decision to his team.

In the co-feature, Joel Camilleri dropped previously unbeaten Mitchell Leek in the opening round and won a unanimous decision to claim the vacant IBF Australasian middleweight title. The judges scored it 96-93, 95-94 and 96-93.

Omar El-Abdallah knocked out Nicholas Benn in the seventh round, and Ky Hodgson won the vacant Australian super welterweight title with a third-round TKO of Victor Adis-Iosifidis. James Noonan and Matt Faron fought to a unanimous draw, with all three judges scoring it 38-38.

Sports.title: Jorge Linares Facing Deportation After El Paso Airport Arrest
Sports.content:
Former three-division world champion Jorge Linares is sitting in federal custody in El Paso, Texas, after immigration officers arrested him at the airport on Sunday. The 41-year-old Venezuelan retired in 2023, and now he is stuck in a legal battle outside the ring that looks far messier than anything he ever dealt with between the ropes.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement told reporters that Border Patrol and ICE agents picked up Linares at El Paso International Airport. According to the agency, Linares entered the United States on October 26, 2023, on temporary admission and stayed past his allowed time. ICE confirmed he will remain locked up at the El Paso Service Processing Center while his removal case moves forward.

His attorneys at Wilner & O’Reilly are fighting the government story. In a statement on Tuesday, his legal team insisted Linares is authorized to be in the country and has cooperated fully with officials. Still, his lawyers refused to say what exact status or paperwork he holds, leaving fans wondering how a former star ended up in detention after attending a ProBox TV card in town.

Linares broke the news himself on Sunday with a short Spanish post on X saying ICE had him in El Paso. WBA president Gilberto Mendoza confirmed the arrest on Monday and said he is staying in regular touch with the fighter’s family.

Fans remember Linares best for winning world titles at featherweight, super featherweight, and lightweight before retiring after his 2023 loss to Jack Catterall in Liverpool. He famously dropped Vasiliy Lomachenko at Madison Square Garden in 2018 before getting stopped by a body shot, and he hurt Devin Haney late in their 2021 title bout. Now, instead of enjoying retirement, Linares is waiting on immigration judges to decide if he can stay in the United States.

Sports.title: Jermell Charlo Wanted Errol Spence in Texas
Sports.content:
Jermell Charlo is talking mighty tough now that the fight is off the table. After watching Errol Spence Jr. return from a long layoff against Tim Tszyu in Australia, Charlo claims he is glad they never fought in Texas because he would have felt bad about what he would have done to his former gym mate.

It is easy to talk big from the couch, especially when you were trying to pick a shell of a fighter. Charlo wanted Spence for a comeback bout in Texas, mentioning a matchup between two former unified champions who both needed a payday after sitting on the shelf.

“If I’m going to come back and Errol’s been gone for a long time, let us come back and fight in Texas,” said Charlo to Fight Hub TV, arguing it was a better fight than Spence traveling to Australia for Tszyu.

What makes that sales idea so pathetic is the timeline. Charlo never called out the prime version of Spence before his horrific 2019 Ferrari crash in Dallas. Spence has looked like a shadow of his former self ever since that wreck, surviving retinal detachment surgery and a one-sided beating from Terence Crawford before stepping in with Tszyu.

“I really, really would feel really, really bad for what I would have done to him. So I’m glad that didn’t happen. And maybe one day in life we can shake hands again,” Charlo said.

Charlo called the bout terrible and trashed both fighters for having zero movement, though he still claimed Spence could have edged it with more aggression. That was a clear shot at Tszyu, suggesting the Australian was there for the taking against a diminished opponent.

Jermell is ignoring his own long stretch of inactivity since getting dominated by Canelo Alvarez in 2023. Nobody knows what Charlo has left in the tank either, and he waited around so long that Tszyu ruined his cash-out plan against Spence before he could pull it off.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Could Dump WBO Belt If Muratalla Bid Falls Short
Sports.content:
Whether Shakur Stevenson defends his WBO junior welterweight title against Raymond Muratalla or dumps the belt comes down to one thing on November 30: the size of the winning purse bid.

Dan Rafael reported Tuesday that their negotiating period expired without a deal, pushing the mandatory defense toward a purse bid where Stevenson gets 75 percent and Muratalla receives 25 percent. On paper, a 75 percent split sounds like easy money for the champion, yet the percentage means nothing until promoters put real cash on the table.

Since walking away from Zuffa Boxing over money, Stevenson has operated as a promotional free agent used to massive Saudi-funded paydays. Without Riyadh Season guaranteeing an inflated pot for this mandatory, traditional promoters have to bid strictly on what a Stevenson versus Muratalla main event can actually generate at the gate and on streaming.

Muratalla (25-0, 17 KOs) is a former IBF lightweight champion, and brings enough power at 140 pounds to make Stevenson work for twelve rounds. The problem is that Muratalla does not carry the name recognition or casual fanbase that Teofimo Lopez brought when Stevenson beat him in January. Promoters are not going to bid 15 million dollars for a risky fight against an opponent most casual fans barely know.

If the winning bid lands around 4 or 5 million, Stevenson’s 75 percent cut shrinks to roughly 3 to 3.75 million. Taking a steep pay cut off his recent Saudi numbers to fight a heavy-handed mandatory challenger makes zero business sense for a fighter chasing major names.

If the November 30 bid comes in way below his usual standard, Stevenson will likely vacate the WBO strap before he ever lets them strip him. Giving up the belt costs him leverage in unification talks at 140 pounds, yet the winning dollar figure on bid day will tell us immediately whether he keeps the title or walks away.

Without Saudi money artificially inflating the pot, platforms like Netflix and DAZN look strictly at return on investment, and Shakur’s commercial track record makes an eight-figure guarantee a tough sell.

The only way DAZN or a promoter like Eddie Hearn stretches their budget on November 30 is if they treat the Muratalla fight as a loss-leader to lock Shakur into a multi-fight deal.

They might swallow a loss on Muratalla just to secure the rights to put Shakur in unifications against Dalton Smith or Gary Antuanne Russell down the road. Otherwise, nobody is writing a Saudi-sized check for a one-off purse bid.

If the November 30 purse bid for Muratalla comes in embarrassingly low, say under $4 million or $5 million, Shakur is going straight to social media to laugh at the number before dumping his WBO junior welterweight title.

You already know how this script plays out. Stevenson has been sitting on the shelf since beating Teofimo Lopez in January, and he did not walk away from Zuffa Boxing just to take a massive pay cut against an unbeaten puncher most casual fans cannot pick out of a lineup.

With no Saudi money guaranteed to inflate the pot, promoters have to bid strictly on what Stevenson versus Muratalla can make at the box office.

The second those envelopes open, expect Stevenson to flood X with posts mocking the winning bid and claiming promoters want pound-for-pound talent on the cheap. He will tell fans he is a businessman first and insist nobody should expect him to fight a dangerous former IBF lightweight champion for chump change.

In the end, pride and purse expectations win every time. If the November 30 bid comes in weak, Shakur will drop that belt faster than a hot skillet and go looking for a bigger payday elsewhere.

In hindsight, turning down $7 million from Zuffa for a homecoming fight in Newark against Jose “Rayo” Valenzuela, only to potentially end up staring at a $3 million to $4.5 million share against a much tougher opponent in Muratalla, would look like a massive self-inflicted wound.

Sports.title: Chris Mannix Questions Diego Pacheco’s Prep for Fulghum
Sports.content:
Diego Pacheco has a preparation problem to answer for before taking an immediate rematch with Darius Fulghum. Chris Mannix said Pacheco told him before Saturday’s upset that he and trainer Buddy McGirt don’t watch tape. Fulghum’s camp studied Pacheco, and Sergio Mora saw the work show up in the opening seconds.

“Somebody in that team has got to be watching film and preparing specifically for your opponent,” said Mannix on his podcast. Mora agreed that the trainer should do the studying. He said he rarely watched much tape himself as a fighter, but his trainer would flag specific things an opponent did that Mora could take advantage of.

Mora saw Fulghum go after Pacheco’s lead arm almost as soon as the fight started. Within the first minute, Fulghum was getting low and making the taller man punch down, which gave him a chance to come over the top. He ended up outjabbing Pacheco despite giving up reach. When the distance closed, Mora thought Fulghum got the better of Pacheco there, too.

“Pacheco was a mean body puncher. Fulghum was meaner. He didn’t let him get mean,” said Mora.

Mannix credited Julian Chua with doing film work with Fulghum in Los Angeles alongside longtime trainer Darnell Pierce. The camp even looked at David Benavidez’s win over Oleksandr Gvozdyk, according to Mannix, studying how Benavidez slipped in anticipation of punches as he came forward. Fulghum told the broadcasters during fight week that he expected to get inside against Pacheco. Saturday showed why he was so sure.

Pacheco’s feet were a concern for both broadcasters. Mora said he had raised the issue before, pointing to the need for quicker movement in and out, feints with the feet, and better angles. That helps explain how Pacheco could have the longer jab on paper and still lose the battle at range. When Fulghum could draw the jab from where he wanted and close the distance on his terms, Pacheco had to do more with his feet to get back to a distance he could control.

Eddie Hearn wants Pacheco to go straight back in with Fulghum, and both broadcasters agreed. Mora called it “rematch or bust” and said he wanted to see Pacheco win decisively. Mannix floated April 2027 and said a second loss would leave the 25-year-old facing a long rebuild.

Pacheco now has twelve rounds of his own fight to work from. If the rematch happens, the first thing to watch is how he responds when Fulghum gets low and starts taking away the jab again. Fulghum made that work from the opening round. He has every reason to make Pacheco prove he can handle it the second time.

Sports.title: Josh Kelly’s Footwork Could Test Jaron Ennis’ Patience
Sports.content:
Trainer Stephen Edwards thinks Jaron “Boots” Ennis will stop Josh Kelly late in their junior middleweight unification, though he sees a familiar problem standing in the way. Kelly has the footwork to make Ennis chase him. What Edwards wants to see is whether Boots walks him down behind a steady jab or gets impatient trying to take his head off.

“His feet are a bigger deal than his hand speed. His hand speed won’t be a problem for Boots,” Edwards said to Sean Zittel’s channel. He brought up Amir Khan to explain the difference between throwing fast punches and throwing shots an opponent can see coming. Even if Kelly and Ennis look evenly matched for speed in the opening rounds, Edwards believes Ennis will read Kelly’s tells early.

Ennis’ corner has already dealt with this style

Derek “Bozy” Ennis trained Philadelphia southpaw Ray Robinson, who fought Kelly to a draw back in 2019. Edwards thought Robinson deserved the decision that night and believes having gone through that camp will give the Ennis corner plenty of confidence. Bozy brought up the draw himself at the launch press conference, so the history is already on both teams’ minds.

Kelly has obviously had years to improve since then. Edwards gave him full credit for beating Bakhram Murtazaliev, an opponent few wanted to go near. A 2019 draw only tells you so much about Kelly at 154 pounds today, especially after he proved he can beat a heavy-handed champion marching forward. The Robinson tape gives Bozy a starting point. The Murtazaliev win shows what Kelly can do when real power comes after him.

Ennis has his own history to study, too, and it goes deeper than one bad night. Across two full fights with Karen Chukhadzhian, Boots never looked comfortable dealing with that constant movement. In their rematch in front of his own fans in Philadelphia, Chukhadzhian tagged Ennis with clean right hands and made him look awkward for long stretches. It wasn’t until Chukhadzhian finally gassed out down the stretch that Ennis took control of the fight.

The problem for Kelly is that copying that blueprint takes more than quick feet. Kelly isn’t quite as slick as Chukhadzhian, and he doesn’t carry the same power or willingness to stand in the pocket and trade. Against Kelly, the temptation for Ennis will still be to load up on another power shot whenever the first one misses, giving Kelly room to step away and make him reset. Using a sharp jab to herd Kelly toward the ropes will make finding clean openings much easier, especially if Kelly lacks the pop to make Ennis respect what is coming back.

“Boots doesn’t choose the conservative route,” Edwards said. Ennis likes putting combinations together and hurting guys once he gets close. Kelly can use that aggression against him by making Ennis reach and getting away before the follow-up lands. How many rounds Kelly can pull that off without giving away points on the cards is another question.

Edwards expects the cost of all that movement to catch up with Kelly in the second half. In his view, Kelly will have to keep moving even when he wants a round to catch his breath, because standing in range gives Ennis the chance to land his heaviest shots. That is where Edwards sees the late stoppage coming. Kelly’s best chance to change that is turning his early escapes into real scoring opportunities. If all that footwork only keeps him safe, Ennis will take his time closing the distance and break him down.

Sports.title: Israil Madrimov Exposed Terence Crawford, And Walking Away Won’t Fix It
Sports.content:
Terence Crawford should come out of retirement to fight Israil Madrimov again if he wants his Mount Rushmore claim taken seriously. Beating Canelo Alvarez gave Crawford a historic achievement, but it did nothing to settle the argument over whether he deserved to beat Madrimov.

That is the stain on his legacy. Crawford left their August 2024 fight with a unanimous decision and the WBA junior middleweight title after looking completely out of ideas against the only prime A-level opponent on his resume. The scores were 116-112 and 115-113 twice, a narrow escape that looked like a gift decision to plenty of observers who saw him clearly lose.

“A win over Canelo will put me on Mount Rushmore, I really believe that,” said Crawford before their fight.

All that Mount Rushmore talk sounds like deep insecurity, as if Crawford is trying to talk himself into credentials he never earned. Truly secure all-time greats do not campaign for their own spot on the mountain. Listening to Crawford demand historical elevation after struggling so badly against Madrimov is like watching a PFC insist on being promoted to General right after failing an inspection.

Once Crawford asks for that kind of company, counting belts and pointing to an unbeaten record cannot be the whole discussion. His overall resume was already thin, padded out with unheralded contenders and aging names well past their best days. When he finally stepped in against a sharp, prime operator in Madrimov, his superiority vanished.

Madrimov gave him an awkward problem he could not solve. His feints, changes of position, and sharp right hands prevented Crawford from settling into the comfortable control he had enjoyed against lesser opposition. Crawford had to think before committing, hesitating for long stretches without throwing a punch.

The case for Madrimov winning rests on the cleaner, more effective work in the close rounds. Crawford’s supporters can point to his jab and late activity, which is precisely why running it back matters. This was not a beaten challenger begging for another payday. It was a prime opponent who exposed the limits of Crawford’s aura.

“I thought Israil Madrimov did enough to edge it here tonight,” said Eddie Hearn after the fight. Hearn promoted Madrimov, so his interest was obvious, yet his objection reflected what millions of viewers saw unfold in real time.

For fans who scored it for Madrimov, Crawford’s victory carries a permanent asterisk. Walking away without fixing it leaves a glaring hole in his career, especially since that shaky performance should have disqualified him from landing the Canelo sweepstakes in the first place.

The Canelo opportunity was already being discussed before Crawford faced Madrimov, creating an obvious financial incentive for the bigger attraction to survive. It explains why critics viewed the scorecards with suspicion, and why beating Canelo feels like an escape hatch rather than proof of all-time greatness.

Crawford could answer the boxing question tomorrow if he actually believed his own hype. Come back and face Madrimov again. Prove the first performance was an off night, take away Madrimov’s best weapons over twelve rounds, and earn the rank he keeps trying to claim.

There would also be a clear tactical reason to watch. Madrimov would need to turn his success with isolated clean punches into sustained offense, while Crawford would have to find ways to attack without spending rounds frozen by feints.

Crawford earned the money to retire, but he has not earned immunity from criticism. Until he clears up the mess he left behind against the best prime fighter he ever faced, his Mount Rushmore talk will keep sounding like a man trying to convince himself more than anyone else.

If Crawford wants another fight to save his legacy from that gift decision, Madrimov is the only call that counts.

Ghana News.title: University hostels and rent control: Examining the Law and its limitations
Ghana News.content:
Back in 1963, when Ghana passed its Rent Act, university accommodation was nothing like the commercial hostels we have today. It was mostly halls of residence, institutional, part of the educational experience. Sixty years on, that has changed. Hostels built for purpose, decent fees, private capital and company management systems have turned student hostels into big business. But the legislation that regulates residential tenancies has not changed.

And so, the question of whether university hostels are covered by the Rent Act has come up recently. If you pay for a hostel, are you a tenant? Does the Rent Control Department have the same regulatory powers as it does over other tenancies? And, most importantly, can we use 60-year-old legislation to regulate something its drafters could not have imagined?

THE STATUTORY FRAMEWORK

In Ghana there is the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220) and the Rent Control Law, 1986 (P.N.D.C.L 138). Under Act 220, Section 1 makes the Act applicable to all premises in Ghana. Section 36 makes reference to the landlord and tenant of any premises let at a rent. The Act recognises that notwithstanding the fact that the occupant of a property may not have exclusive possession of the property, a lease or tenancy may be created.

The Act however makes a significant distinction in Section 36 between premises and accommodation which is genuinely let at a rent which includes payments in respect of board or attendance. Board is meal arrangement as part of accommodation, and attendance is personal services such as cleaning the tenants’ room and other chores provided to the tenant. Therefore, in an instance where the landlord or landlady runs a boarding facility charging one price for a room, food and cleaning services, that facility is not covered by the Act. In a normal tenancy, the tenant is paying for only the premises, and the tenant arranges for anything else.

While not determinative of the university hostel concept, the distinction is important as the provision of electricity, water, security and maintenance is not considered to be board or attendance. That will depend on the package offered by the university or whoever is the provider of the service.

This distinction is further buttressed by the Rent Control Act, 1986 (PNDCL 138) which provides under section 1 for the regulation of rent in respect of certain specified classes of residential accommodation; and for related purposes; section 4 and 5 provide for the registration of tenancy agreements and the issuance of rent cards.

Of particular note is section 2(a) which provides that the law shall not apply to premises demised or held from the Government or any other agency of the State. While this may have some bearing on accommodation provided by the universities themselves, it becomes less clear where the accommodation is provided by a separate company or private provider.

It is important to note that this exception applies only in relation to section 1 of PNDCL 138 and does not exclude such premises from the operation of Act 220.

The application of the rent laws of Ghana to university hostels is therefore not just about whether or not students pay hostel fees. It depends on the nature of the transaction, the person providing the accommodation and the specific provision of the law.

LEASE OR LICENCE: THE LEGAL DISTINCTION

The distinction between a lease and a licence remains central to the controversy.

A tenancy ordinarily confers possessory rights and an interest in land, while a licence generally grants personal permission to occupy premises without creating such an interest.

In Street v Mountford [1985] AC 809, the House of Lords held that an agreement described as a licence was, in substance, a tenancy because of the rights granted to the occupant.

The principle was memorably expressed by Bingham LJ in Antoniades v Villiers [1990] 1 AC 417, at 444:

“A cat does not become a dog because the parties have agreed to call it a dog.”

The legal character of an arrangement is determined by its substance rather than the terminology adopted by the parties.

An accommodation provider cannot avoid statutory tenancy obligations merely by describing a genuine tenancy as a licence. Equally, the payment of an accommodation fee does not automatically transform a personal licence into a tenancy.

In Westminster City Council v Clarke [1992] 2 AC 288, the House of Lords considered accommodation provided in a hostel where the institution retained substantial powers concerning supervision, access and room allocation. Having regard to the purpose and operational arrangements of the hostel, the Court held that the occupant was a licensee rather than a tenant.

University accommodation may exhibit similar characteristics. Occupation ordinarily depends upon student status, is limited to an academic period and remains subject to institutional regulations concerning discipline, visitors, room allocation and maintenance.

Nevertheless, institutional control does not invariably negate a tenancy, particularly having regard to the broader definition of a lease under Act 220.

Indeed, published UGEL residence agreements expressly employ the language of tenancy and describe accommodation charges as rent or residential facility user fees. Such contractual provisions are relevant evidence of a letting, notwithstanding the institution's continuing powers of residential management.

The English authorities are persuasive but must be applied consistently with Ghana's statutory definitions. The proper enquiry remains whether the rights granted constitute a letting within the meaning of Act 220.

STATUTORY TENANCY AND THE UNIVERSITY ACADEMIC CALENDAR

In this article we discuss the distinction between a lease and a licence. The difference between a lease and a licence is crucial to this debate.

Typically, a lease provides the lessee with a right of possession and an interest in the land, whereas a licence confers only a personal right to occupy the premises and not an interest in land.

The House of Lords in the case of Street v Mountford [1985] AC 809 found an arrangement described as a licence to be, in fact, a lease because the rights conferred upon the occupier were sufficient to establish the existence of a lease.

In the words of Bingham LJ in the case of Antoniades v Villiers [1990] 1 AC 417 at 444: “a cat does not become a dog because the parties have agreed to call it a dog.” It is the substance of the agreement that determines its legal status and not the language used by the parties. Thus, a landlord cannot escape the statutory regime of leases simply by referring to what is actually a lease as a licence, and a fee paid for the accommodation does not automatically make a licence a lease.

In the case of Westminster City Council v Clarke [1992] 2 AC 288, the House of Lords found that a hostel in which the institution retained considerable control over supervision, access and allocation of rooms to be a hostel to which a licence could be granted rather than a lease.

Similarities can be drawn with student accommodation in which the right to occupy the premises is dependent on the student detaining that status and is limited to an academic period subject to the institution’s rules and regulations as to discipline, guests, allocation of rooms and maintenance. However, such control does not necessarily preclude the finding of a lease, particularly in light of the extended definition of lease under Act 220.

Indeed, it is not uncommon for residence agreements published by the UGEL to refer explicitly to a tenancy and to refer to rents or residential facility user fees. Although this does not override the institution’s residual rights as a manager of residential property, such references in the contract are a good indication that a letting has taken place. The English cases are instructive but must be interpreted in line with the statutory provisions in Ghana. The key question is whether or not the right conferred on a student is a letting within the definition of a letting in Act 220.

INSPECTION POWERS AND ACCOMMODATION STANDARDS

The Rent Control Department's authority to inspect premises must also be considered within the statutory framework.

Section 5(2)(c) of Act 220 empowers a Rent Officer to enter and view premises or order their inspection where those premises are under consideration in the lawful performance of statutory functions.

Section 11(a) of PNDCL 138 separately authorises a Rent and Housing Committee to inspect residential premises to which the Act applies, at reasonable times and concerning a matter before it.

These provisions confer statutory inspection powers, but they do not authorise unrestricted entry into every building used for paid accommodation.

The premises must fall within the relevant statutory framework, and the inspection must be connected to a function lawfully exercisable by the officer or committee concerned.

Whether students occupy as tenants or licensees, accommodation providers may remain subject to contractual obligations concerning maintenance and repairs, as well as applicable public health, fire safety and building-control requirements.

Structural defects, inadequate sanitation, dampness and unsafe living conditions should not escape regulatory scrutiny merely because the accommodation provider successfully establishes that the arrangement is a licence.

Student welfare and statutory jurisdiction are distinct legal considerations. Both require appropriate protection under the law.

THE UNITED KINGDOM'S APPROACH TO STUDENT ACCOMMODATION

The United Kingdom provides useful guidance on how legislation can recognise student accommodation as a distinct category without placing it beyond regulation.

In England, paragraph 8 of Schedule 1 to the Housing Act 1988 excludes qualifying student accommodation from the assured-tenancy regime.

The exclusion is based on specified statutory conditions rather than a general assumption that students cannot be tenants.

The distinction is important. An accommodation agreement may constitute a tenancy in law without necessarily attracting the statutory security of tenure applicable to ordinary assured tenancies.

The Renters' Rights Act 2025, with relevant reforms introduced in 2026, further recognises the peculiar character of student accommodation.

Qualifying university halls and purpose-built student accommodation may be excluded from the assured-tenancy regime where prescribed conditions are satisfied, including applicable requirements concerning approved accommodation management codes.

Ordinary private residential premises occupied by students are treated differently. The legislation also provides specific grounds upon which qualifying landlords may recover possession for subsequent student occupation.

The Housing Act 2004 establishes a framework for approved accommodation management codes addressing matters including safety, maintenance and complaints.

The significance of these statutory arrangements is that student accommodation is recognised according to its institutional purpose and operational characteristics.

The law does not need to deny the existence of a tenancy merely to accommodate the academic calendar. Instead, it expressly determines which categories of student accommodation should attract statutory protections.

Equally, exemption from ordinary tenancy protection does not excuse accommodation providers from compliance with applicable safety and management standards.

THE NEED FOR LEGISLATIVE REFORM

The circumstances under which the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220), was enacted bear little resemblance to the present university accommodation system. At the time, student accommodation was largely provided through traditional halls of residence, publicly funded and administered as part of university life. The modern hostel industry, characterised by private investment, substantial accommodation fees and corporate management structures, emerged several decades later.

Although the language of Act 220 may extend to certain hostel arrangements, it would be difficult to suggest that the peculiarities of today's commercial student accommodation were specifically contemplated by its framers. The legislation makes no express provision for the relationship between academic-year occupation, statutory tenancy protection, institutional discipline and recovery of possession.

These omissions do not place university hostels beyond the law. They reveal the limitations of applying a general residential tenancy regime to accommodation provided principally for educational purposes.

There is therefore a compelling case for a targeted review of Act 220 and the Rent Control Act, 1986 (PNDCL 138), to recognise student accommodation as a distinct regulatory category. Such reform should distinguish university-managed residences, purpose-built private hostels and ordinary residential premises occupied by students, while clarifying the legal consequences of academic-year accommodation agreements and the circumstances in which possession may be recovered.

The revised framework should also establish enforceable standards for accommodation, transparent fee structures, maintenance obligations, inspection powers and accessible complaints procedures. Any special statutory treatment should be conditional upon compliance with prescribed standards to prevent ordinary landlords from avoiding tenancy obligations merely by describing their properties as student hostels.

The United Kingdom provides a useful example of how student accommodation can be treated differently from conventional residential tenancies without sacrificing essential legal protections.

The objective of reform is to establish a legal framework that reflects the distinctive character of student accommodation while protecting the legitimate interests of both students and accommodation providers.

CONCLUSION

The present controversy raises two distinct legal questions: whether university hostel arrangements constitute tenancies within the meaning of Act 220, and whether the Rent Control Department possesses the statutory authority to regulate the particular arrangements in dispute. Both questions must be determined by reference to the relevant legislation, the terms of the accommodation agreements and the substantive rights and obligations of the parties.

The absence of an express exemption for university hostels does not necessarily bring every accommodation arrangement within the Rent Act. Equally, the institutional character of student accommodation cannot, by itself, displace statutory protections where a tenancy exists. The Department's regulatory powers must also be exercised within the limits prescribed by law.

Beyond the resolution of these questions lies a legitimate case for legislative reform. Although existing legislation may apply to particular hostel arrangements, it does not adequately address the distinctive legal consequences of academic-year occupation, institutional management and the commercial provision of student accommodation.

The appropriate legislative response is neither a blanket exemption for university hostels nor an indiscriminate extension of conventional tenancy regulation. It is a clearly defined statutory framework that reconciles the legitimate operational requirements of accommodation providers with enforceable rights and protections for students.

The present dispute may be resolved through judicial interpretation of the existing legislation. Its broader implications, however, call for legislative intervention. Parliament should take the opportunity to clarify the legal status of student accommodation and the corresponding rights, obligations and regulatory powers, thereby providing the certainty which the present statutory framework lacks.

Ghana News.title: Mahama, Ato Forson have turned Ghana’s economy around in 2 years – Ricketts-Hagan
Ghana News.content:
Deputy Majority Leader and Cape Coast MP, George Kweku Ricketts-Hagan, says President John Dramani Mahama and Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson have turned Ghana's economy around within two years of taking office.

He attributed the improvement to what he described as fiscal discipline, prudent spending and a shift towards expenditure-based consolidation.

Contributing to the debate on the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament on Wednesday, November 18, Mr Ricketts-Hagan said the government had made significant progress in stabilising the economy despite inheriting difficult economic conditions.

“His Excellency John Dramani Mahama and Dr Ato Forson have turned Ghana's economy around in two years. We still have about seven years to spare from what they told us,” he said.

He argued that key macroeconomic and fiscal indicators, including inflation and interest rates, had improved under the current administration.

Mr Ricketts-Hagan also challenged figures on Ghana's public debt cited by the former Finance Minister, insisting that the country's debt-to-GDP ratio had declined to 47.5 per cent.

He said Ghana's debt stood at $53 billion in 2024, representing nearly 70 per cent of GDP, while the current debt stock was about $59.3 billion.

According to him, applying the prevailing exchange rate to the current debt figure gives a debt-to-GDP ratio of 47.5 per cent.

He further disputed criticisms of the Bank of Ghana's losses linked to financing gold purchases, arguing that the profitability of the Gold Board's operations should be considered alongside the central bank's financial position.

Mr Ricketts-Hagan said the government had also abandoned what he described as "excessive borrowing and revenue-based consolidation pursued by the previous administration".

He explained that the current approach focuses on aligning government expenditure with available revenue rather than relying on borrowing to finance spending.

“Instead of doing an expenditure-based consolidation, they were doing a revenue-based. They were more interested in borrowing money to fund expenditure,” he said.

He added that the government was now matching expenditure to revenue and directing available resources towards priority areas of the economy.

“The discipline that we have instilled in this country, the expenditure that we are making sure that we have the revenue to fund, is what has brought us here,” he said.

Ghana News.title: GHS warns of meningitis, dehydration risks as El Niño threatens Ghana during harmattan
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Health Service (GHS) has warned Ghanaians about potential health risks associated with the anticipated effects of the El Niño weather phenomenon, cautioning that rising temperatures, prolonged dry spells and increased dust levels could heighten vulnerability to meningitis and other climate-related illnesses.

The warning comes as the country enters the harmattan season, with the Ghana Meteorological Agency forecasting El Niño conditions that could bring unusually high temperatures and challenging weather patterns.

In a public health alert issued on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Ministry of Health, through the GHS, said the anticipated weather conditions could have significant implications for public health, including increased cases of heat exhaustion, dehydration and respiratory infections.

The Service also identified meningitis as one of the major health concerns, noting that the combination of hot, dry and dusty conditions could increase vulnerability to infections and meningitis outbreaks.

It further warned of prolonged dry spells, rising dust levels and sudden rainfall, with possible flooding in parts of southern Ghana, urging the public to take appropriate precautions to protect their health.

The GHS has called on parents, teachers, traditional authorities, religious leaders, community organisations and local government authorities to intensify public education and promote preventive practices.

It particularly identified the Northern, Upper East, Upper West, Savannah, North East and Bono East regions, alongside other vulnerable areas, as locations where heightened awareness and preparedness would be necessary.

The Service, however, clarified that the anticipated El Niño conditions do not automatically mean Ghana will experience a meningitis outbreak.

It stressed that early preparedness remains essential in view of the expected hot, dry and dusty conditions.

The Ministry of Health and the GHS assured the public that they would continue to monitor the situation and provide updates as necessary.

Ghana News.title: ’24-hour economy has failed; admit it’ – Amin Adam tells Ato Forson
Ghana News.content:
Former Finance Minister, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam

Former Finance Minister Dr Mohammed Amin Adam has challenged Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson to acknowledge what he describes as the failure of the government’s 24-hour economy initiative.

According to the Ranking Member on Parliament’s Finance Committee, the government’s decision to move programmes previously associated with the 24-hour economy under its newly introduced New Economy policy raises questions about the continued relevance of the original initiative.

Speaking during the debate on the 2027 Budget in Parliament, Dr Amin Adam said he had expected the Finance Minister to admit that the 24-hour economy had not delivered on its promises.

“I was hoping that the Finance Minister would admit that the 24hr economy has failed after he moved all policies under the project to the new economy policy, he failed to do that,” he said.

He described the New Economy as a repackaging of programmes previously presented under the 24-hour economy, arguing that the restructuring had left the 24-hour economy secretariat with little justification for its continued existence.

He also questioned the allocation of GH¢165 million to the secretariat, saying the expenditure was an inappropriate use of public resources when the programmes it was expected to coordinate had been moved elsewhere.

“Taking all the programmes from the 24hr economy and putting them under the New Economy, the 24hr secretariat has nothing more to do. The Minister has allocated GH¢165m to the secretariat and I don’t think this is the way we should use our resources,” he added.
