Ghana News.title: Government steps up efforts to tackle open defecation and improve sanitation
Ghana News.content:
The Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs says it is pursuing measures to strengthen sanitation management and address persistent challenges, particularly open defecation.

The Ministry’s Technical Advisor for Sanitation and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Michael Forson, said government was working with partners to improve waste management systems and encourage private sector investment in converting waste into renewable energy.

He was speaking at the opening of this year’s World Toilet Day commemoration, where he represented the Deputy Minister.

Mr Forson said the Ministry would support such investments through policy alignment, regulation and collaboration with private investors and development partners.

“The ministry will work with partners to make sure more private sector are engaged in turning our waste into renewable energy and others. First, we will align policy so that approaches like this one are recognized and supported in our national plans.

“Second, we will give practical backing through clear regulation and help with land where it is needed. Third, we will work with private investors and development partners so that more communities benefit from such investment,” he said.

He stressed that ending open defecation would require collective action beyond government institutions and local authorities.

“No ministry can end open defecation alone, nor can any assembly end it alone. It will be ended in homes, in schools, in markets, and in places of worship if we all work together,” he added.

Ashaiman MP calls for community involvement

The Member of Parliament for Ashaiman, Ernest Henry Norgbey, also called for stronger collaboration among government, municipal assemblies and residents to improve sanitation.

He said local authorities could provide infrastructure and develop policies, but their efforts would have limited impact without public cooperation.

“Government and the Assembly may provide the necessary infrastructure and policies, but without the cooperation of the people, our efforts will not achieve the desired results,” he said.

Mr Norgbey urged residents to take responsibility for keeping their communities clean and supporting efforts to eliminate open defecation.

“I urge all residents to support the assembly's effort to eliminate open defecation by ensuring that every household has access to and use of decent toilet facilities,” he said.

Safisana advocates waste-to-energy solutions

Beyond access to toilets, the safe collection, treatment and disposal of human waste remain central to addressing Ghana’s sanitation challenges.

The Managing Director of Safisana Ghana Ltd, a company that converts faecal sludge into renewable energy, said waste recycling could help reduce environmental pollution while creating useful resources.

He warned that rapid urban growth was placing pressure on existing sanitation infrastructure, particularly sewer networks in Accra and surrounding communities.

“We live in a city and not just a Ashaiman, but also Accra that grows faster than its sewer networks. And this puts public health at risk. It pollutes the environment and it takes away the people's dignity who are not able to just go to a clean toilet,” he said.

Ghana will mark World Toilet Day on November 19 under the theme, “Safe toilets. Equal futures.” The observance highlights the links between access to safe sanitation and gender equality.

Ghana News.title: Amin Adam demands answers over Big Push projects, questions use of funds
Ghana News.content:
Ranking Member on the Finance Committee of Parliament and a former Finance Minister, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam

Former Finance Minister Dr Mohammed Amin Adam has questioned the implementation of the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme, demanding an explanation for the progress of several projects despite significant budgetary allocations.

He said the programme’s performance record raised concerns about the government’s ability to translate its infrastructure spending commitments into completed projects.

Speaking during the parliamentary debate on the 2027 Budget, the Ranking Member on Parliament’s Finance Committee said the mid-year budget review showed that a significant number of Big Push projects had recorded little or no verifiable progress as of June 2026.

According to him, only 13 projects had reached at least 50 per cent completion, while 15 were between 25 and 50 per cent. He added that the status of 59 per cent of the projects had not been accounted for.

“Even with the Big Push that they have made so much noise about, when you look at the scorecard, it doesn’t tell a good story. As of June in the mid-year budget, this was the scorecard: only 13 projects of the Big Push had reached at least 50 per cent, and 15 were between 25 per cent and 50 per cent, and a whopping 59 per cent they could not even give account of their status,” he said.

Dr Amin Adam questioned how the government had utilised the funds allocated to the programme, asking: “So where has the money gone?”

He argued that the government needed to provide greater accountability for the resources committed to the infrastructure initiative.

Ghana News.title: Secondary market turnover surges by 152% to GH¢6.86bn
Ghana News.content:
The secondary market turnover surged by 152.49% week-on-week to GH¢6.86 billion.

Trading activity shifted towards the 2031-2034 maturity segment, which dominated turnover with a 49.70% share at a weighted-average yield of 14.97%.

The 2027-2030 segment followed closely, accounting for 47.97% of turnover at a weighted-average yield of 12.92%.

The post-2035 maturities attracted a modest 2.33% share at a weighted-average yield of 14.92%.

“We expect secondary market activity to remain tactical this week as investors position ahead of the February 2027 DDEP [Domestic Debt Exchange Programme]” bond buyback,” said Databank Research. The exercise will be conducted through a Dutch auction scheduled for 23rd – 25th November 2026, with settlement on 26 November 2026.

“However, we believe the market-based pricing, capped at par value, could limit participation as bondholders weigh immediate liquidity against potential capital losses and foregone coupon income. Meanwhile, we anticipate the Bank of Ghana will maintain its policy rate at 14.00% on 18 Nov’26, reinforcing near-term interest rate stability”.

Ghana News.title: Nitiwul accuses government of buying two VIP aircraft for President in one year
Ghana News.content:
Former Defence Minister Dominic Nitiwul has accused the government of acquiring two VIP aircraft for the President within a year, questioning the purchase of an Airbus H175 helicopter alongside the Falcon 6X executive jet.

Contributing to the debate on the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament on Thursday, November 19, 2026, Mr Nitiwul argued that the Airbus H175 was designed for civilian rather than military purposes.

Referring to paragraphs in the Budget Statement, he said the helicopter should be considered alongside the Falcon 6X when assessing the government's aircraft acquisitions.

“On page 158, paragraph 475, this aircraft that you went and bought, Airbus H175, it's meant for civilian purposes. It's not a military aircraft. Same thing as 168. It's a civilian-branded aircraft. So you bought two VIP aircraft for the President. Two. In one year,” he stated.

Mr Nitiwul also accused members of the governing NDC of applying different standards to the current administration and the previous NPP government over presidential aircraft procurement.

He said the NDC had criticised the previous government over its attempt to acquire a new presidential jet, despite what he described as the absence of a formal request for a replacement aircraft at the time.

“These are the same people who, when I had not even requested a new aircraft, insulted the President, insulted myself, blasted me, made me look like I didn't know what I was doing, made me look like I was a fool,” he stated.

The government has confirmed the acquisition of a Falcon 6X executive jet and four helicopters for the Ghana Air Force as part of a broader retooling programme.

Parliament approved the aircraft procurement on December 4, 2025.

The debate on the 2027 Budget Statement is expected to continue in Parliament.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
World.content:
Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries draw condemnation from across the region.

Share Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island on social media

Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.

Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.

The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

Gulf and Arab condemnation

The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.



The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.

Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.

Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.

Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.

Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.

He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

World.title: World Bank official says Lebanon reconstruction making slow progress
World.content:
A senior World Bank official says Lebanon has been slow to use international aid to rebuild areas destroyed during the 2024 war and the renewed fighting since March 2026.

World Bank managing director of operations Anna Bjerde said she had to be “honest” about the pace of reconstruction during a visit to southern Lebanon on Tuesday.

The international financial institution approved $250m in June 2025 to help Lebanon clear rubble and repair “damaged critical public infrastructure” after the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war. But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026.

The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b.

“Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”.

Israel has continued to occupy and attack parts of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River since March, claiming to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure, while demolishing civilian homes.

On Wednesday, Israel fired artillery shells towards the towns of Baraachit and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). The towns of Rashaf and Sarbine, extending to Wadi al-Hujair, were also targeted. And Israeli earth movers demolished residential homes in the town of Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah and Haddatha.



The United Nations estimates at least 304,500 Lebanese remain internally displaced in the country, down from 1.2 million. Up to 4,500 have been killed in Israeli attacks.

Last month, Hezbollah announced it will pay up to $14,000 to families whose homes were destroyed or made uninhabitable by Israel, as the group accused the government of failing to carry out its duties to help the displaced.

Israel has refused to withdraw from southern Lebanon, citing security concerns connected to the delayed disarmament of Hezbollah and other groups, which the United States and the Lebanese government have insisted on, as part of the trilateral ceasefire framework launched in April.

“Israel will not withdraw from the current lines of these security zones, nor will it redeploy its forces,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that if tensions escalate on the various fronts, “we are fully prepared to seize additional territory”.

Bjerde said that “institutions in Lebanon are very thinly stretched” and the security situation required “very careful planning around where you can start and where you don’t start” to remove rubble and repair infrastructure.

The World Bank projected Lebanon’s economy to shrink by 6.4 percent this year, in its Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor report, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy.

“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said.

According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than one million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of hunger.

Despite this, Lebanon’s western-backed government insists it is doing all it can, given the circumstances, such as the distribution of approximately $100m in housing loans granted to 1,500 families, according to NNA.

Bjerde said the World Bank needs to be “insistent” and “very close to monitoring on a daily basis” to make sure the work gets done “because you cannot let the people down”, adding that the World Bank wants to see the reconstruction work go more quickly.

World.title: Largest US egg producer to cull 1.8 million birds after bird flu outbreak
World.content:
Cal-Maine reports avian influenza at Florida site, with 2.7 percent of its total flock affected.

Share Largest US egg producer to cull 1.8 million birds after bird flu outbreak on social media

Cal-Maine Foods, the largest egg producer in the United States, has said it would cull 1.8 million birds after avian influenza was detected at one of its facilities in Florida.

On Wednesday, the company said the 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 young hens being culled account for 2.7 percent of its flock. Production at the facility will be temporarily halted.

Cal-Maine said in a statement that it would coordinate with other production and distribution facilities to minimise disruption across the company.

The risk bird flu poses to human health is low. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there have been 74 human cases since February 2024, with no evidence of human-to-human transmission.

However, the virus continues to pose a significant challenge to the US poultry and egg industries. Some 21.5 million birds have been affected this year, following a historic surge in outbreaks in late 2024 and early 2025 that sharply reduced the number of egg-laying hens.

Approximately 50.7 million laying hens were lost between mid-October 2024 and early March 2025, when egg prices in the US reached a record high of $6.23 per dozen.

The current average retail price of eggs is $2.32 per dozen, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Despite the announcement that production at the Florida facility would be temporarily halted, Cal-Maine’s stock rose 5.3 percent in early trading.

World.title: Pax Silica is the new face of US imperialism in the Philippines
World.content:
Share Pax Silica is the new face of US imperialism in the Philippines on social media

The Philippine government is promising jobs and billions in investment through the United States-led Pax Silica initiative. But protesters see a very different future: threatened ancestral lands, environmental destruction and deeper dependence on Washington.

On November 15, ahead of Donald Trump’s visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit, Philippine police arrested more than 200 demonstrators opposing the initiative. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on protests against a project that critics see as another form of US neo-imperialism.

The Pax Silica initiative is a US-led coalition aimed at securing supply chains and countering China’s strength in critical minerals, semiconductors and other technologies essential to AI infrastructure. The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with a proposed industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac province, forming part of it. The Philippine government has promoted the proposed industrial hub as essential to economic development, projecting that it could generate more than 130,000 jobs and attract up to $70bn in investment once fully developed, a process expected to take decades. The proposed Pax Silica industrial hub, which covers approximately 1,618 hectares, raises concerns not only about national sovereignty but also about the displacement of local communities, environmental repercussions, Indigenous land rights and human security.

Critics see the project as taking land from local communities and farmers to serve foreign interests. The Aeta Hungey community in Sapang Kawayan, for example, faces relocation from land it has occupied for generations. Around 200 residents could lose access to their homes, farmland, water sources and burial grounds, while the community’s efforts to secure formal recognition of its ancestral land, dating back to 1994, remain unresolved.



Another major concern is water consumption. According to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), the proposed industrial hub could require 65–90 million litres of water daily. Although the BCDA plans to meet this demand through surface-water harvesting, concerns remain about the pressure on water resources, particularly during droughts. The Philippines is already vulnerable to drought, water shortages, agricultural disruption and climate change. On November 4, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) confirmed that a very strong El Nino was present and expected to persist into the first half of 2027.

The Philippine government must respond to the pressing needs of Filipinos instead of becoming a pawn of the United States in its geopolitical rivalry with China. Southeast Asia is a focal point of competition between the two major powers, with the Philippines serving as a key US ally. Pax Silica would position the Philippines as a central node in an emerging AI Cold War with China.

Projected as an avenue for economic progress, Pax Silica could also serve as a tool for the military expansion of the US in the region, particularly in the Philippines. Semiconductors are used in modern military production and are essential components of weapon systems in modern warfare. During his November 17 ASEAN speech, Trump highlighted US agreements across the region involving critical minerals, energy and technology, while describing the Philippines as a longstanding key ally. He also pointed to increased defence cooperation between the two countries. This cooperation already rests in part on the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), which allows US forces access to agreed Philippine military facilities.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr also emphasised the depth of the relationship between the two countries, rooted in shared history and values. Describing the extent of US influence in Philippine life, he said, “There is no part of our lives in the Philippines that is not involved with the United States in some way, in some shape or form or another.”

An unexamined alliance compromises national interests, particularly those affecting the lives of the Filipino people. Economic development should not come at the expense of human security, sovereignty and environmental sustainability.

Against this backdrop, a broad, multisectoral opposition movement against Pax Silica has emerged and is gaining momentum. It brings together diverse sectors, including Indigenous peoples, farmers, workers, scientists, environmentalists, faith leaders, students, and progressive activists.



The protests have also spread to university campuses. On November 13, university students staged coordinated campus walkouts across the Philippines. Among the major participating universities were the University of the Philippines, De La Salle University, Ateneo de Manila University, University of Santo Tomas, and Far Eastern University, among others. United in their opposition to Pax Silica, protesters repeatedly chanted slogans denouncing US imperialism. Drawing on the Philippines’ history as a former US colony, they associate the initiative with another neocolonial project by an imperial power.

In the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Mindanao, where anti-Pax Silica demonstrations took place in Marawi City and Tawi-Tawi, the opposition is particularly significant. For protesters in this predominantly Muslim region, opposition to the initiative intersects with longstanding grievances rooted in the historical dispossession of local communities whose ancestral lands were taken by settlers, reinforced by imperialist wars and oppression. They see Pax Silica as another project that could displace local communities and facilitate land-grabbing by an imperial power.

Equally important is the movement’s expansion beyond the Philippines into transnational solidarity. According to organisers, solidarity demonstrations have taken place in 23 cities across 14 countries, bringing international support to the opposition against Pax Silica and US imperialism.

As the movement gains momentum, the Marcos administration must address the legitimate grievances of the people directly affected by the proposed project. Moreover, this is not merely a concern of the Indigenous Aeta communities; it carries broader regional implications. Marcos’s reference to shared history does not necessarily mean that the two countries stand on equal footing. There is no symmetrical relationship between a coloniser and a colonised. Those subjected to imperial domination are not equal to those imposing control.

The ASEAN Way, characterised by the principle of consensus, must prevail over the competing interests of major powers. Fostering multilateralism will pave the way for cooperation, collective security and economic progress that will eventually empower ASEAN and the Global South. It is through this approach that the three major priorities of the Philippine ASEAN chairship can be realised: Peace and Security Anchors, Prosperity Corridors, and People Empowerment.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin Shake Hands as Leaders Gather in China
World.content:
As the Second World War neared an end, the soon-to-be victors — Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union, Winston Churchill of Britain and President Franklin D. Roosevelt — sat down in the Crimean resort of Yalta to discuss the fate of postwar Europe. Their decisions in February 1945 helped shape the global order for the rest of the 20th century, making Yalta synonymous with an era of great-power bargaining by outsize personalities.

On Thursday, the leaders of the world’s three largest military powers will meet again. This time it will be President Xi Jinping of China, whose nation has supplanted Britain in military might, hosting President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China — at an uncertain geopolitical moment dogged by wars, climate change and the rise of artificial intelligence — has prompted some analysts to label it “Yalta 2.0.”

That parallel has limits, historians say. For one, Yalta was a meeting of allies whose broad objectives overlapped, said Catherine Grace Katz, a historian of 20th century geopolitics and author of a book on that summit. “Or at least ostensibly still allies at the time,” she said.

By February 1945, the three Allied powers were united in their fight against Hitler’s Germany, whose defeat by then seemed inevitable. British and American troops had already stormed through France and Belgium, while the Soviet war machine was steamrolling across Eastern Europe, squeezing Germany from both flanks.

At Yalta, the allies agreed on what the Northern Hemisphere would look like after the dust of war settled.

Stalin agreed to join the fight against Japan in return for territory in the Northern Pacific. Roosevelt — by then frail, two months from his death and focused on ensuring Japan’s surrender — offered the Soviets broad leeway over Poland’s future. That set the stage for decades of Soviet domination over Eastern Europe.

David Reynolds, a professor of history at the University of Cambridge who specializes in 20th-century diplomacy, argued against overstating what was decided at Yalta.

“‘Yalta’ is a notorious word” that to many conjures the carving up of Europe and selling out to Stalin — but that is based on a misunderstanding, he said.

“The fate of postwar Europe was decided on the battlefield, not at the conference table,” he added.

By the time of the February conference, the Red Army was on the verge of taking Berlin, and both Roosevelt and Churchill had privately conceded the inevitability of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, Professor Reynolds said.

Ms. Katz said, “Short of physically pushing them out of Poland, there was not a lot that the West could do.”

She also pointed out that it was a year earlier, at a meeting in Moscow, when Churchill and Stalin scribbled out their secret “percentages” agreement on a piece of paper. That led to Europe being split between Western and Communist blocs, a division that eventually became the Iron Curtain and persisted until the end of the Cold War.

Yalta was “not the moment that the world was carved up into these spheres of influence,” she said. “That kind of gets conflated with some of the other meetings that these wartime leaders had.”

That said, she argued, Roosevelt missed opportunities to press for greater concessions from Stalin at Yalta. The president took Stalin at his word when he insisted Poland's leaders couldn’t attend the conference, she said, and dismissed Churchill for being overly concerned with Poland’s future.

“Roosevelt was woefully unprepared in dealing with Stalin and understanding Russian history and Stalin’s true objectives when it came to Poland,” Ms. Katz said. (Successive U.S. administrations would similarly underestimate Moscow’s commitment to maintaining sway over Eastern Europe, culminating in Mr. Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.)

Professor Reynolds said that several other critical negotiations were also hammered out at Yalta, which is often forgotten.

It was the scene of hard-fought bargaining by Churchill to secure protections to stop Germany from being eviscerated under a future surrender, as Stalin had wanted, he said. Churchill was adamant that Europe needed to avert a disastrous repeat of the Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War, the terms of which were so punitive on Germany that many believe it planted the seeds of World War II.

“It is not the purpose of the Allies to destroy the people of Germany, or leave them without the necessary means of subsistence,” Churchill told British lawmakers in February 1945, after he had returned to London from Yalta. “Our policy is not revenge; it is to take such measures as may be necessary to secure the future peace and safety of the world.”

Roosevelt also used the Yalta conference to advance his blueprint for a new multilateral institution that would try to resolve conflicts through deliberation rather than war: the United Nations. It was formally established nine months later.

In other words, the suggestion that Yalta was synonymous with Europe’s “carve-up” by great powers flattens the history of the war’s final years, Professor Reynolds argued. “These historical events have a memory life, and all the other aspects that don’t fit within the memory narrative get forgotten,” he said.

By the time of the February conference, the Red Army was on the verge of taking Berlin, and both Roosevelt and Churchill had privately conceded the inevitability of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, Professor Reynolds said.

Ms. Katz said, “Short of physically pushing them out of Poland, there was not a lot that the West could do.”

She also pointed out that it was a year earlier, at a meeting in Moscow, when Churchill and Stalin scribbled out their secret “percentages” agreement on a piece of paper. That led to Europe being split between Western and Communist blocs, a division that eventually became the Iron Curtain and persisted until the end of the Cold War.

Yalta was “not the moment that the world was carved up into these spheres of influence,” she said. “That kind of gets conflated with some of the other meetings that these wartime leaders had.”

That said, she argued, Roosevelt missed opportunities to press for greater concessions from Stalin at Yalta. The president took Stalin at his word when he insisted Poland's leaders couldn’t attend the conference, she said, and dismissed Churchill for being overly concerned with Poland’s future.

“Roosevelt was woefully unprepared in dealing with Stalin and understanding Russian history and Stalin’s true objectives when it came to Poland,” Ms. Katz said. (Successive U.S. administrations would similarly underestimate Moscow’s commitment to maintaining sway over Eastern Europe, culminating in Mr. Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.)

Professor Reynolds said that several other critical negotiations were also hammered out at Yalta, which is often forgotten.

It was the scene of hard-fought bargaining by Churchill to secure protections to stop Germany from being eviscerated under a future surrender, as Stalin had wanted, he said. Churchill was adamant that Europe needed to avert a disastrous repeat of the Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War, the terms of which were so punitive on Germany that many believe it planted the seeds of World War II.

“It is not the purpose of the Allies to destroy the people of Germany, or leave them without the necessary means of subsistence,” Churchill told British lawmakers in February 1945, after he had returned to London from Yalta. “Our policy is not revenge; it is to take such measures as may be necessary to secure the future peace and safety of the world.”

Roosevelt also used the Yalta conference to advance his blueprint for a new multilateral institution that would try to resolve conflicts through deliberation rather than war: the United Nations. It was formally established nine months later.

In other words, the suggestion that Yalta was synonymous with Europe’s “carve-up” by great powers flattens the history of the war’s final years, Professor Reynolds argued. “These historical events have a memory life, and all the other aspects that don’t fit within the memory narrative get forgotten,” he said.

World.title: Trump’s ‘trade deal’ with Thailand is not a done deal.
World.content:
Pinned

President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.

Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”

Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.

In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.

The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. The only event of substance on his schedule for the day — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

Mr. Trump also met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.

Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.

Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

Palace history: Mr. Marcos hosted Mr. Trump at Malacañang Palace, where the Philippine leader spent much of his childhood. He left the palace in military fatigues 40 years ago when his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, was ousted. Read more ›

Lily Kuo contributed reporting.
