World.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
World.content:
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.

The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

Read Jonathan Beale's dispatch from the front line.

World.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
World.content:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

World.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
World.content:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

World.title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
World.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have reflected on the enduring ties between the UK and India with its Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and discussed opportunities to strengthen them.

William and Catherine arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for the final leg of their three-day visit, the first official overseas trip together in four years.

The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

World.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
World.content:
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.

Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".

The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".

The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.

Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.

"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.

Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.

Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
World.content:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

World.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
World.content:
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in SuÃ¨vres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother â tested in an unrelated case â matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor AnaÃ¯s Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.

El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

World.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
World.content:
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.

"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.

But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.

Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.

Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.

"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.

He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.

"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.

Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.

Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.

He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.

"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (Â£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.

The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.

But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".

"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.

He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.

The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.

The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.

Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.

Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.

"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

World.title: Reps summon NAFDAC, police, SSS over deaths linked to suspected herbal drugs
World.content:
The House of Representatives has resolved to summon officials of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), the Nigeria Police Force and the State Security Service (SSS) to explain measures being taken to curb the circulation of fake and potentially dangerous drugs and drinks in Nigeria.

The decision followed a motion of urgent public importance moved by David Agada (APC, Benue State) during Wednesday’s plenary.

Mr Agada raised concerns over the alleged sale and consumption of an unregistered herbal medicinal product in his constituency, which reportedly left four people dead and 11 others ill.

Moving the motion, the lawmaker urged the House to intervene to prevent additional casualties.

He told lawmakers that on 31 October, three men identified as Muhammad Adamu, Musa Kala, reportedly from Sokoto State, and Muhammad Sule, from Bauchi State, allegedly introduced and sold a herbal product to residents of the constituency.

According to him, the sellers claimed the product could treat typhoid fever, waist pain and other ailments.

Mr Agada said several residents bought and consumed the product but developed severe symptoms within hours, forcing some of them to seek emergency medical attention at different hospitals.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He listed the four deceased persons as Awugo Oyije, who died on 2 November; James Onma, who died on 4 November after being referred for further treatment; Ode Ogah, who died on 5 November; and Agi Edugbeke, who died on 11 November.

The lawmaker further identified 11 other affected residents who were receiving medical attention. They include Otumala Ochele, Binta Sule, Onu Oboh, Adoga Onu, Upa James, Igbo Pius, Ochele Genesis, Otumala Amos, Uwa Baku, Ate Okpune and Roman Ehile.

Two of the affected persons, he said, had been referred to hospitals in Makurdi, the Benue State capital.

Mr Agada warned that “more residents could be at risk because some people who consumed the product might not have been identified or could be receiving treatment outside recognised health facilities.”

He also questioned the product’s composition, source, manufacturing conditions, registration status, dosage and potential adverse effects, noting that none of these had been independently established.

The lawmaker described the development as a serious public health concern requiring urgent intervention by relevant authorities to investigate the deaths, identify those responsible and prevent further exposure to the suspected product.

Debate

Contributing to the debate, the House Leader, Julius Ihonvbere (APC, Edo), said the problem of counterfeit drugs and drinks had become too widespread for NAFDAC to tackle with its existing workforce and operational capacity.

He said the agency had about 2,000 personnel, arguing that it needed at least 10,000 workers to effectively discharge its regulatory responsibilities across the country.

“NAFDAC does not have a presence everywhere; it is not in my village in Edo State,” he said.

Mr Ihonvbere called for a broader national response, warning that the circulation of counterfeit drugs and drinks could lead to more deaths if the authorities failed to act decisively.

He also urged the House to recommend severe punishments, including life imprisonment or the death penalty, for people found guilty of manufacturing and distributing dangerous products.

Ali Shettima (APC, Yobe) also called for a nationwide investigation, saying the House should not limit its intervention to the reported incident in Benue State.

He urged NAFDAC to strengthen its oversight of herbal medicine producers and called for appropriate legislation to punish those found guilty of manufacturing or selling counterfeit products.

However, Fatima Talba (APC, Yobe State) cautioned against an approach that focused solely on stopping people from patronising unregulated herbal medicine vendors without addressing the reasons behind the demand.

She argued that some Nigerians turned to such products because they lacked access to affordable and reliable alternatives, adding that concerns about fake medicines also extended to conventional healthcare facilities.

“Some of the people who patronise them do not have any other place to go to. It is not as if these people are forced to buy these products because even in the hospitals, there are fake drugs.

“We cannot tell these people not to patronise these fake herbal drug sellers because we have not given them alternatives,” Mrs Talba said.

Peter Uzokwe (NDC, Anambra) proposed holding market leaders accountable for selling and distributing counterfeit drugs.

He suggested that the executives of markets where fake medicines were produced or sold should be removed, arguing that the measure would compel market leadership to monitor traders and prevent the circulation of unsafe products.

“Let us make it a duty that in any market where fake drugs are manufactured or sold, we will depose the executives. If we do this, you will see that those executives will act as a task force,” he said.

Ismaila Haruna, who represents Toro Federal Constituency of Bauchi State, called for an investigation into deaths allegedly associated with sexual performance-enhancing drugs.

He questioned the effectiveness of existing regulatory measures, arguing that the problem was largely one of enforcement.

“There are existing laws in place guiding the regulation of herbal medicine. What is left is enforcement. Is NAFDAC doing its job?” he asked.

Mr Haruna also called for an investigation into reports of men dying in hotels, suggesting that the possible connection with sexual enhancement products should be examined.

At the end of deliberations, the House resolved to invite NAFDAC, the Nigeria Police Force and the SSS to brief its relevant committees on their efforts to investigate and address the circulation of fake herbal medicines and drinks across the country.

READ ALSO: Reps move to investigate attacks on 10 power transmission towers

Legal framework

Nigeria already has laws governing the production, distribution and sale of medicines and other regulated products.

The NAFDAC Act empowers the agency to regulate the manufacture, distribution, sale and use of drugs, herbal medicinal products and other health-related products.

Similarly, the Food and Drugs Act and the Counterfeit and Fake Drugs and Unwholesome Processed Foods (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act prohibit the production and circulation of adulterated, counterfeit, unsafe and unwholesome products.

Despite these legal provisions, there have been increased concerns about enforcement gaps and the continued availability of potentially harmful products.

World.title: Gov Lawal inaugurates campaign council, says the mission to rescue Zamfara is in progress
World.content:
Governor Dauda Lawal has reaffirmed his administration’s firm commitment to its mission to rescue Zamfara, saying the work is not yet complete and remains in progress.

On Tuesday, the governor inaugurated the Zamfara State APC Presidential and Gubernatorial Campaign Council at the Dome Arena of the Government House in Gusau.

The Zamfara State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) announced the members of its Campaign Council on Sunday, which will coordinate and lead the party’s campaign activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.

At the inauguration, appointment letters were presented to the campaign’s Director General, Mai Buhu Gummi, and other council members.

In his remarks, Governor Lawal described the inauguration as a milestone in his administration’s efforts to strengthen the Party, build on good governance, and secure a brighter future for Zamfara State.

“When we assumed office in 2023, we made a solemn commitment to rescue Zamfara, rebuild its institutions and restore dignity to governance. Nearly four years into this journey, we have demonstrated through deliberate policies, bold reforms and strategic investments that Zamfara can rise again.

“Our administration has recorded significant progress in education, healthcare, infrastructure,

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

public service reforms and economic development.

“We have also remained resolute in confronting the security challenges that have affected our communities.”

The governor emphasised that the re-election bid of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, and all the candidates contesting elective positions on the platform of our great Party must receive appropriate attention within our political planning and engagements.

“As we prepare for the 2027 general elections, I want to make one thing abundantly clear: Our campaign must be driven by achievements, sustained by credibility, strengthened by unity and ultimately judged by the people.

“We must not assume that electoral victory is automatic simply because we are in government.

“Political power is a sacred trust, and the confidence of the electorate must be earned continuously. Our achievements must speak for us, but we must also speak honestly to our people about the challenges that remain and the opportunities that lie ahead.

“We must take our message to every ward, polling unit, village and community across the 14 Local Government Areas of Zamfara State.

“We must listen to our people, understand their concerns, explain our policies and demonstrate why continuity of purposeful leadership is essential to sustaining the progress already recorded.”

World.title: Niger Miners’ Deaths: Senate demands sanctions against NSCDC officers
World.content:
The Senate has called on the federal government to prosecute or appropriately sanction officers found responsible for the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State.

The Senate also urged the government to compensate the victims’ families and implement the recommendations of the independent investigative committee that probed the incident.

The resolutions followed a motion sponsored by Mohammed Musa, senator representing Niger East, during Wednesday’s plenary.

Mr Musa raised concerns over the deaths, which occurred on 17 September, after the victims were arrested during operations against suspected illegal mining activities.

Presenting the motion, Mr Musa described the incident as a serious human rights concern that required transparency, accountability and reforms within the security agency, Punch reported.

He said the federal government had constituted a 10-member investigative committee that completed its assignment and submitted a report identifying lapses and recommending sanctions, institutional reforms, and compensation.

On 27 October, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the committee, chaired by Jonathan Kure, attributed the deaths to asphyxiation, or deprivation of adequate oxygen, following autopsies and forensic investigations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The committee had inspected the detention facility in Minna and obtained statements from NSCDC officers, survivors, relatives of the deceased and other witnesses.

Its findings also pointed to institutional failures and negligence in the handling of detainees.

The report followed public outrage over the deaths and an earlier claim by the suspended Niger State NSCDC Commandant, Suberu Aniviye, that a suspected disease outbreak had caused them.

At Wednesday’s plenary, the Senate observed a minute of silence in honour of the deceased.

It also commended President Bola Tinubu, the federal government, and Niger State Governor Mohammed Bago for facilitating the investigation.

The chamber resolved to constitute a delegation led by the Senate President to visit the bereaved families in Niger State.

It also directed its committees on Interior, Human Rights, Police Affairs and Judiciary to monitor the implementation of the investigative committee’s recommendations and report back to the Senate.

The Senate subsequently included the Committee on Solid Minerals in the oversight arrangement following an amendment moved by the Acting Chief Whip, Diket Plang, and seconded by Abdul Ningi.

During the debate, former Edo State Governor Adams Oshiomhole called for tougher measures against illegal mining, arguing it should attract the same seriousness as illegal oil bunkering.

He described illegal mining as an economic crime that deprives the government of revenue and allows individuals and criminal networks to exploit the country’s mineral resources.

However, Mr Oshiomhole cautioned against interpreting the Senate’s position as an endorsement of the deaths.

He said the victims’ involvement in illegal mining had not been conclusively established.

The Senate President also warned lawmakers against assuming that the deceased were guilty of illegal mining, stressing that they died while in the custody of a government security agency.

“The Senate must be careful not to make assumptions about their guilt or innocence,” he said.

Mr Ningi had earlier questioned the relevance of Mr Oshiomhole’s additional prayer on illegal mining, arguing that the motion should focus on the deaths, justice for the victims and accountability for those responsible.

The Senate eventually adopted the prayers, including the demand for sanctions against culpable officers, compensation for the families and reforms within the NSCDC.

The deaths occurred after the victims were arrested during operations around the Mohammed Inuwa Wushishi Estate in Minna on 15 and 16 September.

Their deaths on 17 September triggered public outrage and protests in Niger State.

The federal government had suspended Mr Aniviye and 20 other officers following the incident and ordered an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the arrests and deaths.

World.title: Tinubu receives state police bill after approval by all 36 State Assemblies
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has received the constitutional amendment bill seeking to establish state police in Nigeria after all 36 State Houses of Assembly approved the proposed legislation.

The Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, disclosed this in a statement on Wednesday, saying the bill was formally transmitted to Mr Tinubu by his Special Advisers on Senate and House of Representatives Matters, Basheer Lado and Wasiu Olanrewaju-Smart.

Mr Gbajabiamila said the president would review the bill in consultation with the Attorney General of the Federation (AGF) before assenting to it at a formal signing ceremony.

The approval by all 36 state assemblies exceeds the constitutional requirement of at least 24 states, representing two-thirds of the country’s 36 states, under Section 9(2) of the 1999 Constitution.

The development completes the state assemblies’ consideration of the proposed amendment, which seeks to provide constitutional backing for states to establish their own police services alongside the existing federal police structure.

The Senate passed the amendment on 24 June, while the House of Representatives approved it on 23 July. The bill was subsequently transmitted to the 36 state legislatures for consideration in accordance with the constitutional amendment procedure.

On Monday, 16 November, the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, announced that all 36 assemblies had approved the proposal, describing the endorsement as 100 per cent support from the state legislatures.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Senate also resolved on Wednesday to direct Mr Ogunlana to transmit the bill to Mr Tinubu for assent. It urged the president to forward the proposed national policing bill to the National Assembly for legislative consideration and passage.

National policing bill

Meanwhile, Mr Gbajabiamila said the Presidential Working Group on State Police, which he chairs, had conducted extensive stakeholder engagements and nationwide consultations towards developing a draft national policing bill.

He said the draft legislation had been submitted to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting validation.

According to him, the working group would review the validated version and present it, alongside its report, to the president for consideration.

The proposed bill is a separate legislative exercise intended to provide the legal and operational framework for implementing the proposed state policing arrangement.

The Senate’s call for its submission to the National Assembly underscores the need for further legislation to establish the rules governing the proposed system.

Background

Nigeria currently operates a centralised policing structure under the Nigeria Police Force, headed by the Inspector General of Police. State governors, although designated as their states’ chief security officers, do not exercise direct operational control over police commissioners and personnel.

The proposal to establish state police has gained renewed attention amid persistent security challenges, including insurgency, banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence across different parts of the country.

Proponents of decentralised policing argue that state-controlled forces could improve local intelligence gathering, strengthen security presence in communities and enable faster responses to threats.

However, the proposal has also generated concerns about possible political interference, abuse of police powers by governors, inadequate funding and the potential use of state police against political opponents.

The constitutional amendment is intended to provide the legal foundation for establishing state police services. However, their establishment and operation will also require the relevant implementing legislation and state-level legal arrangements.

Mr Gbajabiamila said Mr Tinubu appreciated the leadership of the National Assembly, state governors, state lawmakers and other Nigerians who contributed to the process, describing their involvement as a shared commitment to addressing the country’s security challenges.

World.title: Three killed in Jigawa farmers-herders clash
World.content:
A violent clash between suspected herders and local farmers in Garki Local Government Area of Jigawa State has claimed three lives and left two other persons injured.

The incident occurred around 3:30 a.m. on Wednesday, at Wauta Fulani settlement in Rafin Marke Ward, Kanya District, according to a statement issued by Badruddeen Mahmud, spokesperson for the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

Mr Badruddeen revealed that the crisis was triggered when about seven suspected herders, moving with an estimated 200 cattle from the Babura Local Government Area axis, encroached upon a guinea corn farm belonging to a resident, Amadu Saleh.

Trouble began when the farmers attempted to drive the cattle away to save their crops.

The herders allegedly attacked the farmers with dangerous weapons, including cutlasses, bows, and arrows.

During the initial assault, 35-year-old Amiru Saleh was killed, while two other farmers—Amadu Saleh (50) and Haruna Saleh (37)—sustained injuries.

In a swift reaction to the attack, Mr Badruddeen said other farmers within the community mobilised and confronted the attacking herders.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The ensuing reprisal led to the death of two unidentified members of the herding group, while the remaining herders fled with their cattle toward the Gabasawa Local Government Area of neighbouring Kano State.

“All three deceased individuals were evacuated to the Garki General Hospital, where medical personnel confirmed their deaths.

“While Amiru Saleh’s remains were released to his family around 11:30 a.m. on Wednesday for burial according to religious rites, the bodies of the two unidentified herders remain at the hospital morgue pending official identification and further procedures.

Meanwhile, Mr Badruddeen said the NSCDC has deployed operatives alongside sister security agencies to monitor the area, maintain law and order, and prevent a breakdown of peace in the affected communities.

Reacting to the incident, the State Commandant of the NSCDC, Muhammad Ingawa, warned residents against taking the law into their own hands or staging further reprisal attacks.

“The State Commandant strongly cautions residents against taking the law into their own hands or engaging in reprisal attacks. He urges members of the public to remain calm, exercise restraint, and promptly report any suspicious movements or security threats to the appropriate authorities,” Mr Badruddeen stated.

The NSCDC reiterated its commitment to safeguarding lives and property while fostering peaceful coexistence among farmers, herders, and other residents across Jigawa State.

World.title: 2027: Friends donate four campaign vehicles to Gov Otti
World.content:
Friends of Governor Alex Otti of Abia State have donated a brand-new coaster bus and three Sienna vehicles to support his campaign activities ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

Njoku Ukoha, the chief press secretary to the governor, disclosed this in a statement on Tuesday.

Receiving the vehicles on Tuesday, 17 November at the Michael Okpara Auditorium, Umuahia, on behalf of his campaign council, Governor Otti reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to providing a peaceful and level playing field where all political parties can freely canvass for votes ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The governor also used the occasion to highlight his administration’s commitment to political tolerance, peaceful coexistence and the protection of democratic freedoms, stressing that every political party, whether in government or in opposition, would be given the opportunity to campaign freely in the State.

“You can see that this place is very peaceful, and we have created an environment where every party, be they opposition or those in power, can freely move around and campaign. And it will continue that way.

“We believe in democracy, and it is incumbent on the people to decide who they want to vote for,” Mr Otti stated.

The governor cited the recent use of the stadium by another political party for its campaign rally, as well as the forthcoming use of the International Conference Centre by another party, as evidence of his administration’s commitment to providing a level playing field for political participation.

He noted that the development had attracted commendations from members of the public, some of whom observed that such an atmosphere of political freedom had not been experienced in the State before.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

While urging political parties and their supporters to conduct issue-based campaigns, the governor cautioned against personal attacks, misinformation and the spread of falsehood, insisting that political engagements should focus on policies, ideas and practical solutions to the challenges facing the people.

“There is a saying that people who have ideas discuss ideas. Those who don’t have ideas discuss people. So, here, we want people to discuss ideas and not discuss people,” Mr Otti stated.

The governor further maintained that political actors should refrain from making unsubstantiated claims, noting that the people were well-positioned to assess the government’s performance and make informed decisions.

Governor Otti expressed appreciation for the gesture, describing the donation by his friends as a pleasant surprise. He assured them that the vehicles would be put to their intended use of facilitating campaign activities, including the transportation of campaign personnel and supporters across the State. He also prayed that God would replenish their resources abundantly.

Remarks by donors

Presenting the vehicles earlier on behalf of the donors, Ide John Udeagbala and Ernest Udeajah said the gesture was borne out of their appreciation of Governor Otti’s leadership and the transformation taking place in Abia.

They noted that the donation was intended to support the governor’s re-election campaign activities, expressing confidence that Abians would overwhelmingly re-elect him for a second term to continue the good works.

They also said the gesture was an expression of appreciation for the governor’s commitment to the welfare of the common man, not only in Abia State but across Nigeria.

World.title: BOOK REVIEW: A Paris lunch, secret letters and Biafra’s 1969 air offensive
World.content:
In April 1969, a Swedish aviator told an American journalist about a secret military operation over lunch in Paris. Weeks before Biafran aircraft struck Nigerian military installations, senior editors at The New York Times knew what was coming. In his new book, The Day Biafra Died, Milton Allimadi uncovers the correspondence behind an extraordinary episode involving journalism, military secrecy and the Nigerian Civil War.

Published by Black Star Books in September 2026, The Day Biafra Died examines the final phase of the Nigerian Civil War through archival documents from The New York Times, the US State Department, and the White House. Beyond The Secret Air Offensive: Milton Allimadi explores President Richard Nixon’s sympathy for Biafra and the diplomatic decisions that might have altered the war’s outcome.

In April 1969, two men met for lunch in a Paris restaurant. One was Count Carl Gustaf von Rosen, a 60-year-old Swedish aristocrat and veteran aviator. The other was Lloyd McKim Garrison, an American journalist previously expelled from Nigeria for his reporting on the country’s political crisis.

Von Rosen had a secret. He was assembling a small air force to attack Nigerian military installations and challenge the federal government’s overwhelming air superiority over Biafra.

Garrison, a correspondent for The New York Times, was among the first outsiders to learn about the operation.

On April 25, 1969, he wrote to Seymour Topping, the newspaper’s foreign news editor, outlining von Rosen’s plans. The correspondence shows that senior Times editors knew about the proposed Biafran air offensive weeks before the attacks.

More than five decades later, journalist Milton Allimadi reconstructs the encounter in his book, The Day Biafra Died, drawing on Garrison’s unpublished letters and the newspaper’s archival records.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The documents reveal an unusual relationship between a war correspondent, a foreign volunteer fighting for Biafra and an American newspaper entrusted with sensitive military information.

The Journalist and the Aviator

Garrison had arrived in Lagos in 1962 as the Times’ West Africa correspondent. He subsequently covered the political upheavals of 1966, including the massacres of Igbo civilians that preceded Biafra’s declaration of independence in May 1967.

His reporting brought him into conflict with Nigeria’s Federal Military Government, which expelled him in 1967.

He continued reporting from Biafra and developed considerable sympathy for the secessionist republic.

There, he became acquainted with von Rosen, who had participated in dangerous relief flights carrying food and medical supplies into the blockaded territory.

Garrison had accompanied the Swedish pilot on one such mission, establishing a personal relationship that would later give him access to highly confidential information.

By April 1969, Biafra had lost substantial territory. Federal forces controlled major transport routes, while Nigerian military aircraft conducted bombing operations against the secessionist enclave.

Von Rosen believed a small, unconventional air force could disrupt that advantage.

Five Aircraft Against Nigeria’s Air Force

His plan involved five Malmö MFI-9B light aircraft, originally designed as trainers but modified to carry rockets.

Their small size and ability to operate from improvised airstrips made them suitable for surprise attacks.

Rather than engage Nigeria’s Soviet-supplied MiG fighters in aerial combat, von Rosen intended to destroy them on the ground.

He told Garrison that the aircraft and volunteer pilots would reach Biafra around May 21, with operations beginning shortly afterwards.

In his April 25 letter to Topping, Garrison explained:

“The first operation will be a dawn sweep of Nigerian airfields.”

The proposed targets included federal airbases and, potentially, shipping in Lagos harbour.

Von Rosen insisted that the Swedish government was neither involved in nor aware of his plans. His pilots, he said, were volunteers motivated by conviction.

Garrison recognised the significance of the information, describing the proposed attacks as “A significant, if not bizarre, story.”

He began arranging how the Times might secure exclusive coverage.

The New York Times Knew in Advance

On April 30, Garrison wrote another letter to Topping confirming that he had received approval to proceed with his reporting arrangements.

He proposed coordinating coverage from both sides of the conflict.

Raymond Walter Apple Jr., the Times’ correspondent in Lagos, could position himself near Benin City, one of the prospective targets. At the same time, Garrison travelled into Biafra to report on von Rosen’s squadron.

Secrecy was essential.

Garrison suggested informing Apple that an important development was expected without disclosing the operation itself.

He also proposed coded messages to communicate changes in the attack schedule.

One message, “Please tell parents travel plans firm as scheduled,” would indicate that the operation remained on course.

The plan was given the coded reference “Benin Talker.”

These arrangements demonstrate that the newspaper was preparing to cover an offensive about which its editors possessed advance information.

The correspondence does not establish that the Times helped plan the raids or supplied military intelligence. It does, however, raise questions about the responsibilities of journalists who learn of impending military operations.

The Editorial Dilemma

Another issue concerned photographs of the proposed attacks.

Garrison informed Topping that a senior Biafran representative had offered exclusive photographic and film rights in exchange for payment.

Garrison was interested, but Topping hesitated.

He feared that paying in advance could amount to financing a military operation.

After consulting managing editor A. M. Rosenthal, Topping instructed Garrison not to enter into an advance purchasing agreement. Photographs could be considered for purchase after the attacks.

Allimadi highlights the contrast between the editors’ concern about financing the operation and how they handled the confidential military information.

The distinction is important. Journalists often receive sensitive information whose premature disclosure could endanger lives. The surviving letters do not establish that the newspaper had an obligation to reveal von Rosen’s plans.

They nevertheless expose the ethical complications arising from Garrison’s personal relationship with the aviator and his sympathy for Biafra.

When the Biafra Babies Struck

In late May 1969, von Rosen’s plan became reality.

His squadron, nicknamed the Biafra Babies in memory of children who had died from starvation, launched surprise attacks on Nigerian military installations.

The aircraft struck targets including Port Harcourt and Benin City, reportedly damaging or destroying military aircraft on the ground.

The raids were a psychological victory for Biafra.

Despite the blockade and its deteriorating military position, the republic had demonstrated that it could strike important federal targets.

But the operation could not reverse Nigeria’s overwhelming military advantage.

Five converted trainers were insufficient to overcome Biafra’s shortages of weapons, fuel, workforce and conventional aircraft.

Their achievement was primarily symbolic, boosting morale and attracting international attention.

The Story That Finally Appeared

On May 25, The New York Times published an Associated Press report describing attacks by Swedish aircraft operating for Biafra.

The report attributed its information to Sweden’s Expressen newspaper.

Yet the Times’ internal correspondence showed that its editors had known about the planned offensive since April.

On May 26, Garrison published his own report from Biafra under the headline:

“Swedish Count Describes Bombing Raids for Biafran Air Force.”

He described von Rosen’s aircraft, volunteer pilots and the attacks.

Allimadi questions why the newspaper did not disclose its advance knowledge or secure the exclusive coverage Garrison had anticipated.

The documents do not conclusively explain the editorial decisions.

Security concerns, source protection and operational uncertainty may have influenced the newspaper. What is established is that its editors possessed confidential information about the raids before they occurred.

The Questions Behind the Lunch

The von Rosen–Garrison encounter became an important starting point for Allimadi’s investigation into Biafra.

His research into the newspaper’s archives later expanded into American diplomatic records, revealing President Richard Nixon’s private sympathy for Biafra and White House discussions about changing US policy toward the conflict.

But the Paris lunch remains one of the book’s most compelling episodes.

It illustrates how the Nigerian Civil War drew foreign volunteers, journalists and political actors into relationships that sometimes blurred professional boundaries.

Garrison was a correspondent whose access to confidential military information arose partly from his friendship with von Rosen.

The letters do not prove that he participated in planning the attacks. They establish that he knew about them and worked with his editors to prepare coverage.

They also raise a broader question: when journalists become personally sympathetic to a cause they cover, how do they preserve the independence their profession requires?

Biafra eventually collapsed in January 1970. Von Rosen’s improvised air force could not save the republic, and international humanitarian sympathy never produced the decisive intervention its leaders sought.

Yet the episode remains remarkable.

In April 1969, a Swedish aviator disclosed a secret military plan to an American journalist over lunch in Paris. Weeks later, Nigerian military installations came under attack.

The New York Times had known what was coming.

More than half a century later, the correspondence examined in The Day Biafra Died has brought that extraordinary encounter, and the questions surrounding it, back into the historical record.

World.title: Coronation Group backs Nigeria’s historic hosting of FIP World Polo Championship qualifiers
World.content:
Coronation Group supported the hosting of the Federation of International Polo (FIP) Zone E World Polo Championship Qualifiers in Abuja, marking a historic moment for Nigerian polo as the country welcomed the international competition for the first time in its 120-year polo history.

Hosted by the Nigerian Polo Association (NPA) at the Guards Polo Club in Abuja from 9 to 16 November, the four-nation tournament featured teams from Nigeria, India, Iran and Pakistan. Pakistan completed an unbeaten campaign, recording three victories against Iran (10–6), India (7–4) and Nigeria (9–5) to qualify for the championship, scheduled for 4 to 14 February 2027 in Punta del Este, Uruguay.

The FIP’s decision to award Nigeria the hosting rights recognised the Nigerian Polo Association’s efforts to develop the sport and strengthen the country’s standing in international polo. The tournament brought together players, officials, business leaders, diplomats and polo enthusiasts from the participating countries. The presence of the Emir of Katsina, Alhaji Dr Abdulmumini Kabir Usman, CFR, further reflected the sport’s longstanding cultural significance in Nigeria.

Commenting on the Group’s sponsorship, Ngozi Akinyele, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, Coronation Group, said: “Sport has a unique ability to bring people, institutions and nations together. Beyond the competition itself, it creates platforms for developing talent, building relationships and opening doors to new opportunities.

For us at Coronation, supporting the FIP World Polo Championship Qualifiers goes beyond our longstanding association with the sport. It reflects our belief that building enduring prosperity requires investment in the wider ecosystems that enable people, businesses and communities to thrive. Nigeria hosting a competition of this international standing is an important moment for the country and for African polo. We are proud to have played a part in making it possible and to support the continued growth of the sport across the continent.”

Nigeria’s polo tradition dates back more than a century, with the Lagos Polo Club established in 1904 and the Nigerian Polo Association founded in 1925. Today, Nigeria is recognised as having the largest polo community on the African continent. Coronation Group’s involvement in the sport is equally longstanding, having sponsored the Lagos Polo Tournament for over a decade.

The Group’s support for the FIP Zone E Qualifiers builds on this commitment, reflecting its belief in the value of platforms that bring people together, nurture talent and strengthen connections across business, culture and society. Through its investments in initiatives that contribute to Africa’s sporting, cultural and economic development, Coronation continues to support the ecosystems that create opportunities and enable lasting prosperity.
