World.title: Rassie Erasmus breaks silence on suspension
World.content:
Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus is set to serve out a six-match ban following a review of wide-ranging comments made at a media conference this week concerning officiating during the Nations Championship match against France last Friday.

An independent panel imposed the sanction under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, although SA Rugby has expressed a desire to take the matter to a full hearing.

However, there has still been no official response on that, and Erasmus certainly won’t be part of match day proceedings when the Springboks face Ireland this Saturday.



Taking to social media, the Springbok coach posted a simple message, while also highlighting he would welcome a ‘watch along’ of sorts with fans.

“Can sit and moan or make the best of it. I’ll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch in on my own. So let’s give it a go and hope I get the “tech” sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you’re welcome to join me. Sign up here (adults 18+): http://watchwithrassie.com. This is personal, not official.”

Can sit and moan or make the best of it. I’ll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch in on my own. So lets give it a go and hope I get the “tech” sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you’re welcome to join me. Sign up here (adults 18+): https://t.co/PXrmKbKc00.… pic.twitter.com/QUZRsWmCLV — Rassie Erasmus (@RassieRugby) November 18, 2026

Full statement from World Rugby

In explaining the full verdict handed down to Erasmus, world Rugby shared the following statement: “Having considered the comments which related to the match TMO, the standing Match Official Abuse committee, chaired by senior officer Adam Casselden SC (Australia) determined that the threshold for serious misconduct had been met.

“The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials.

“In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.



“Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension.

“The suspension applies with immediate effect, applies to international matches, and includes any match-day involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on match days; entering the stadium, coaches’ box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on match day; engaging in any ‘feedback’ process with match officials; and engaging in media duties during the suspension.

“Respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport. Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously. Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.

“Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official’s integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse.

“Erasmus is entitled to have the matter referred to a full misconduct hearing.”

World.title: Springbok star joins Rassie with big ban
World.content:
Just a day after Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus was slapped with a six-match ban for comments determined to be in breach of match official protection protocols, star eighthman Jasper Wiese has now also been suspended.

Wiese received a red card for a dangerous cleanout on France centre Kalvin Gourgues during the Springboks’ 21-19 defeat at the Stade de France, and the 31-year-old has now been handed a four-week ban.

The offence was deemed to warrant a mid-range sanction.



“To reach this decision, the FPRC considered all available evidence that included TMO footage, match official reports, and players statements,” read a Nations Championship statement.

“The FPRC had to take into account the disciplinary record of Weise, with previous instances of similar offences, but Wiese demonstrated remorse and admitted guilt of the offence.”

Springbok star could receive a minor reduction in suspension

A disciplinary committee determined that Wiese had breached Law 9.20(b), which prohibits contact with an opponent above the shoulders at a ruck or maul.

The World Cup winner could see his suspension reduced to three weeks if he successfully completes World Rugby’s Coaching Intervention Programme.

Wiese will miss this Saturday’s Test against Ireland, and the final Test of the year during the ‘finals weekend’ of the Nations Championship.

Contrasting citings

Meanwhile, as reported by TheSouthAfrican, Ireland flyhalf Sam Prendergast has received a favourable outcome from a disciplinary hearing, and he will be able to face the Springboks this Saturday.



Prendergast had been cited for a dangerous ‘knee drop’ tackle, but he was cleared on Wednesday.



“The committee unanimously determined that the player had, to the required standard, proved that the citing should be dismissed,” read a Nations Championship statement.

World.title: ‘Please stop being judgemental to applicants’: SASSA mother’s message to staff
World.content:
A tender moment of a mother holding her baby, wrapped in a blanket, with a SASSA sign. Image: Pexels/File

Bianca King has relied on the SASSA Child Support Grant for more than five years, but she says it still does not carry her family through the month.

King, who lives in the Eastern Cape, shared her experience with The South African through its SASSA grant survey. She lives in a shared family home where five people depend on the household income.

Child Support Grant runs out before month-end

King said the grant helps, but it is not enough to cover her household’s basic needs. She uses the money on a mix of essentials, and by the end of each month it has already run out.



The pressure has reached the dinner table. King said someone in her household had gone without food in the past month.

If she could change one thing about SASSA, King said she would increase the grant amount.

Jobseeker looking for retail work

King is unemployed and actively looking for work. She has experience in retail and customer service and is willing to travel between 5km and 20km for a job.

She completed some high school, and she named unemployment as her biggest financial concern.

King has also tried to access additional government support beyond her grant, but she was either declined or gave up during the process.

Long queues and ‘rude’ treatment

King said her grant payments have been straightforward, with the money deposited into her Postbank account each month. She rated SASSA’s communication with recipients as adequate.



However, applying and dealing with SASSA has been another story. King listed gathering the required documents, long queues at SASSA offices and finding clear information online as her biggest challenges.

She had a direct message for SASSA staff who deal with applicants.

“Please stop being judgemental to applicants and rude we just trying to get by,” King said.

Her experience reflects that of many caregivers who depend on the Child Support Grant while searching for work, stretching a small payment across an entire household.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Mistral AI not French president's 'personal project': CEO
World.content:
PARIS - The boss of French AI startup Mistral rejected on Tuesday that the firm was a "personal project" of President Emmanuel Macron, insisting support for artificial intelligence transcended political boundaries.

The French government holds an indirect stake in Mistral, which is considered Europe's top AI model developer, though its technology lags behind Chinese and American competitors.

Mistral's chief executive Arthur Mensch told the Semafor tech conference in California he was confident the firm, which is valued at $24 billion, would enjoy support in Europe regardless of the outcome of the French presidential election in April next year.

On stage, the moderator described Mistral as "sort of a personal project of Macron's" and asked how the company would fare under Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate currently ahead in polls for the top job.

"We are not a personal project of Macron," Mensch replied.

"We happen to have created a company that grew pretty quickly in France where the president was Macron," he said.

Macron has "been very helpful to the company in the same way the US president has been promoting US technology pretty aggressively across the world," Mensch added.

He stressed the importance of AI sovereignty -- the idea of countries developing domestic models serving their own security, privacy and business interests.

Europe's technological dependence on the United States prompted jitters in the Old Continent after Washington cut off access in June for all foreign nations to AI giant Anthropic's most powerful models for two weeks.

"Wherever we look, the realization that AI is super important goes way beyond the political orientation, so we're very confident that in Europe, we'll still have a lot of support," Mensch told the conference.

He said he had met some of the candidates running for the French presidency, but that "many of them are not technical".

"They need to get a little more technical because there's going to be five years of very technical discussions," he added, referring to the duration of the French president's term in office.

He also made a jab at US giants OpenAI and Anthropic for allegedly using businesses' data to create products that compete directly against them.

"They may deny that they're doing that," he said. "There is some track record of them doing that a little bit."

When asked whether the company would mount an initial public offering, Mensch said Europe -- where Mistral is headquartered -- was the "natural place" to do it.

"We won't be doing this this year, but we're definitely getting ready for it."

World.title: Bezos says 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as Bond
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - Amazon boss Jeff Bezos said Tuesday he was "heavily involved" in choosing British actor Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Pattinson would step into the coveted role of the world's most famous fictional spy following months of speculation.

"There was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances," Bezos said at the Semafor tech conference in California.

"Initially, I would say we were slightly biased a little against him just because he's already so famous," he added.

"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious, 'he is James Bond'".

Amazon bought the storied Hollywood studio MGM in 2022, but it was not until last year that the company struck a deal with Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson to obtain full creative control over the franchise.

It had been fiercely guarded by the Broccoli family since 1962's "Dr. No", when screen legend Sean Connery first starred as Bond, as they insisted on preserving the integrity of the character and brand.

Pattinson got his early break in "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" (2005) as Cedric Diggory, a champion for Hogwarts, but rocketed to global fame as Edward Cullen in romantic vampire saga "Twilight".

World.title: Haiti formalises security agreement with El Salvador following troop deployment
World.content:
PORT-AU-PRINCE - Haiti announced that it had formalised a "cooperation agreement" with El Salvador, the same day thousands of Haitians showed support in the streets of Port-au-Prince for soldiers sent by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs in the capital.

"The Council of Ministers has approved the Cooperation agreement between the Republic of Haiti and the Republic of El Salvador," according to a Facebook post from the Haitian executive, who called it "a new stage in strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation."

Signs carried by the demonstrators on Tuesday read "Thank you, Bukele," and "Long live Bukele," according to photographs taken by an AFP journalist.

"Bukele, the country belongs to you! Do whatever you want with it," some chanted in the streets of a capital long subsumed by gang violence that has seized control of large sections.

Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops into Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from his country went missing during an operation of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).

The new Salvadoran deployment, despite being separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought reinforcements.

"We are asking President Bukele to ignore the detractors and to continue supporting Haiti," a demonstrator who declined to be identified for security reasons told AFP.

Numerous armed forces are now operating in Haiti, with uncertain levels of coordination, including the Haitian police and army, the multinational GSF, foreign mercenaries and most recently, the Salvadoran soldiers.

Bukele, whose forceful gang crackdown at home has won public support but sparked accusations of rights violations, appears prepared for more than just finding the four lost soldiers.

On November 10, he boasted of having destroyed the "headquarters" of one of Haiti's main gangs, accompanied by video footage of the helicopter attack.

Since then, Bukele's forces have taken over a football stadium in the capital with the support of Haiti's national police.

On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called on all security forces to protect the population and resort to lethal force only as a last resort.

In the first 10 months of 2026, the UN recorded 4,595 deaths and 2,050 injuries to armed violence in Haiti.

World.title: Tiger Woods to return to competitive golf next month: officials
World.content:
BAHAMAS - Tiger Woods will return to competitive golf for the first time in more than two years next month when he tees off at the Hero World Challenge event in the Bahamas, organisers said on Tuesday.

Woods, 50, was named in the line-up for the limited field PGA Tour event taking place in Albany from 3-6 December.

It will mark the first time Woods has played an official PGA Tour event since July 2024.

The 15-time major champion has battled injuries and legal problems since his last appearance.

In March he was involved in a rollover car crash in Florida which led to him having his driver's license suspended for five years.

Authorities determined the 15-time major champion had not been drinking alcohol but found he appeared to be impaired.

Woods, who has undergone multiple back operations and surgeries on severe leg injuries suffered in a separate 2021 California car crash, had two pills containing the opioid painkiller hydrocodone in his pocket.

He refused a urine analysis and was charged, jailed and released on bond.

Woods initially pleaded not guilty to charges of DUI (driving under the influence) with property damage and refusing to submit to a lawful test.

Days later, he said he was "stepping away" to seek treatment and focus on his health.

Since the crash, Woods has travelled outside the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient facility, reportedly in Switzerland.

He made his first public appearance since his arrest at the PGA Tour's Travelers Championship in June, and later struck a plea agreement which led to his driver's license being suspended.

Woods has not won a tournament since a victory at the ZoZo Championship in Japan in 2019.

World.title: PKTT arrests suspect in MKP candidate murder
World.content:
PORT SHEPSTONE - A 44-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the murder of uMkhonto weSizwe PR Councillor candidate Lastborn Thobelani Shazi.

Shazi was killed at his home while participating in a virtual political party meeting.

He was the PR candidate for ward 18 of the Umzumbe Local Municipality and the party's Ugu regional organiser.

The Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) searched for 15 days and found the suspect in his homestead at a village near Port Shepstone.

According to the police, investigations have linked him to the murder, allegedly as one of the coordinators.

Further investigations also link the suspect to the conspiracy and murder of the alleged hitman implicated in Shazi's killing.

It is alleged that the hitman was shot and killed following a disagreement between the parties over the payment for carrying out the assassination.

The suspect is expected to appear in two separate courts on Thursday.

He is expected to appear at the Port Shepstone Magistrate's Court and Mzumbe Magistrate's Court, respectively.

He faces charges of conspiracy to commit murder, two counts of murder and possession of an unlicensed firearm and ammunition.

World.title: Douglas vote-counting disruptors permitted to vote
World.content:
DOUGLAS - Supporters of the Siyancuma Independent Forum (SIF) have been permitted to vote in the ward 3 re-vote in Douglas, in the Northern Cape.

The group, consisting of 11 people, rushed the voting station in ward 3, in the Bongani section of Douglas, on 4 November after voting had ended.

They alleged irregularities with the voting process and proceeded to damage about 100 voting ballots.

The IEC elected to cancel the results in the ward and call for a revote.

Special votes took place on Tuesday, 17 November, with the normal votes taking place on Wednesday.

The people were arrested and have since been released on bail. They are permitted to vote, on the condition that they do not interfere with the witnesses who might be at the voting station.

World.title: Hawks, police dismantle dagga plant in Magaliesburg
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Hawks and SAPS are dismantling a dagga plant in Magaliesburg.



One person has been arrested.



The plant is estimated to be worth R12 million.

This is the second dagga bust this week,

On Tuesday, police uncovered a suspected cannabis lab in Douglasdale, Johannesburg.

Two suspects have been arrested following an intelligence-led operation.

The lab is estimated to be worth R2-million.

World.title: SA Rugby slam online trolling of match officials
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africa Rugby on Wednesday condemned online trolling of match officials after coach Rassie Erasmus was banned for six matches for suggesting that the refereeing during the defeat to France amounted to match-fixing.

After the rare 21-19 loss for the world champions against the French, Erasmus questioned the decision by the television match official not to intervene on a series of French tackles.

Erasmus was banned after he blasted the match officials on Monday during a press conference ahead of the Nations Championship match against Ireland this weekend.

SA Rugby said in a statement it was "aware of the extensive public commentary, analysis and debate surrounding recent matters involving Springbok Head Coach Rassie Erasmus and World Rugby".

It added: "We are mindful that a significant volume of commentary, opinion and AI-generated content is currently circulating in the public domain, much of which does not necessarily reflect the facts, context or processes involved."

"What is deeply concerning, however, is the reaction of some individuals on social media and other platforms, particularly reports of threats and abusive conduct directed at World Rugby officials and administrators."

The statement added that SA Rugby "unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats, or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded".

Erasmus will be banned from "any match-day involvement" with his players and coaches and will not be allowed to even enter the stadium. He risks missing the final of the Nations Championship on November 29.

The Springboks' coach has criticised referees in the past, and his complaints about Wayne Barnes in 2022 led to the English match official receiving death threats.

World.title: Ruto lists measures to lower cost of living, put more money in Kenyans' pockets
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his State Of The Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18th, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

President William Ruto has outlined a raft of government interventions aimed at reducing the cost of living, increasing household incomes and creating more employment opportunities for Kenyans.

Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
World.content:
New York —

Nvidia’s board unanimously accepted former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as chief executive, board chair Harvey Jones said at the start of the company’s earnings call Tuesday night.

The announcement comes after Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO, should the board allow it. Huang abruptly resigned last week amid national security concerns and reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Jones said Nvidia’s board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent leader.

The company sought to reassure investors and offer clarity about its future in the third-quarter earnings report Tuesday evening, with Kress, saying Nvidia’s “roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”

“Our ambition will not change, our passion to innovate will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change,” Kress told investors, whose confidence in the company’s future has been badly shaken by the scandal, on the earnings call.

It’s the first financial picture investors are getting since the chipmaker was shaken last week by Huang’s resignation after three decades at the helm of the company he founded.

Nvidia more than doubled its quarterly revenue and profit from a year prior, and both figures beat Wall Street’s expectations.

Nvidia’s earnings — the numbers and executives’ comments — have long been viewed as a bellwether for the larger AI industry, with Nvidia’s technology and funding at the heart of much of the boom. That’s especially true now with questions swirling about the industry’s future without Huang, its biggest cheerleader and dealmaker, at the helm.

Nvidia shares were coming off their worst week in 19 months heading into the report. The stock is down 16.7% since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair and Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, erasing $751 billion in market value. Since Nvidia shares hit their record high on October 6, they have dropped 35%, erasing roughly $2 trillion in market value.

Ahead of the report, Siebert Financial Chief Investment Officer Mark Malek wrote that it would be the “most important in the company’s history.”

Nvidia shares have dropped for four consecutive days since Huang resigned. Shares fell just 0.44% Tuesday. But shares moved higher in after-hours trading after the earnings release and analyst call, gaining roughly 5% as of 6:10 p.m. ET.

“The massive results, strong guidance and reassurance that the strategy Huang put in place remains firmly on track show that an orderly CEO transition does not necessarily have to dilute the company’s value,” Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com, said in emailed commentary following the release. He added that Nvidia’s growth train “can continue with or without Huang, provided the company makes the right call on leadership.”

Nvidia’s board said last week that Kress, the company’s CFO of 13 years, would serve as interim CEO as it considered internal and external candidates to permanently fill the role. Nvidia’s board also said Tuesday it had established a new national security and export control oversight committee to ensure the company is abiding by global trade regulations, and that it will strengthen its internal national security and compliance initiatives.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim leader. From Nvidia

Some Nvidia employees, investors and other tech leaders had called on the board to reinstate Huang as CEO, pending the outcome of its investigation into his multiple reported extramarital affairs, including with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect as a potential Chinese intelligence asset; and at least one direct subordinate at Nvidia.

Huang said Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board decided that his “return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America,” in his first public comment since resigning.

Jones said during Tuesday’s call that he would not take additional questions regarding Huang’s resignation or the company’s investigation, but that the board would “communicate further when appropriate.” Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.

Meanwhile, Huang is set to testify on Capitol Hill on December 1. He is expected to face questions about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s sales of chips to Singapore-based Megaspeed, which some US officials believed should have been labeled a national security risk.

Some US sources say that whether or not Alice Huang was recruited by China’s intelligence service, she posed a counterintelligence risk because Chinese national security law requires its citizens to assist in intelligence-gathering efforts if asked. Concerns have been mounting that chips Megaspeed purchased were diverted to Chinese entities, potentially skirting US export restrictions.

Another strong quarter

Huang’s exit aside, concerns about whether the AI trade is a bubble about to burst, with valuations and infrastructure spending outpacing returns, had already begun to reach a fever pitch in recent months. Gary Gensler, the former top cop on Wall Street, told CNN this week that he believes the AI bubble will likely burst and cause a recession prior to the 2028 presidential election.

Nvidia’s Tuesday report indicates that, at least for now, the company’s growth continues to outpace Wall Street’s expectations.

The company posted $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% year-on-year. Profits reached more than $65 billion, up 105% year-on-year. Kress also said demand for the company’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing technology is “off to an explosive start,” with the tech already in use by customers such as Google, Microsoft and Oracle.

Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains strong, with a handful of the biggest AI and cloud companies expected to shell out more than $1 trillion in capital expenditures next year alone. But in the wake of Huang’s exit, investors have been more concerned with the company’s future business.

A close-up view of Nvidia’s Vera CPU Compute Tray is pictured during the Nvidia Product Showcase at Computex 2026 in Taipei on June 3, 2026. I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images

The report also comes after a blue wave in the US midterm elections ushered in a slate of newly elected leaders, many of whom campaigned on slowing or restricting data center development, which could dent Nvidia’s business.

Analysts with research firm IDC wrote in a report last week that the firm sees “near-term AI infrastructure demand and supply as largely locked in, so the harder questions,” like long-term bets on emerging technologies and the financing system that Jensen Huang sat in the center of, “sit further out.”

Nvidia said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to come in around $130 billion, plus or minus 3% — exceeding what Wall Street analysts had predicted, according to consensus estimates from FactSet.

Kress raised the company’s growth estimates for next year even higher from its already-ambitious targets, saying Nvidia’s revenue is expected to grow by 75% in fiscal 2028, up from 70% in the last earnings call.

Significant questions also remain about the future of Nvidia’s business in China, and potentially in Asia more broadly, as US officials react to the national security concerns surrounding the company.

Shipments of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China made up less than 1% of sales in its core data center business in the previous quarter. However, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15% of revenues when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”

The Commerce Department on Monday tightened export restrictions designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.

The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter, but it has ceased such shipments, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.

Kress ended with a rallying call to Nvidia’s investors, customers and employees: “We’ve got this.”

This story has been updated with additional details and context.

World.title: Will Putin and Trump hold separate talks in China?
World.content:
US President Donald Trump will meet on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, during unprecedented trilateral talks together with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

But that is not the only occasion Trump and Putin will cross paths in the city.

The Russian leader spoke briefly with Trump at a gala reception for Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit guests on Wednesday evening local time.

Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said Wednesday the pair could also meet tomorrow for separate talks.

“There will be a meeting, there will be. And I believe that our president and the president of the United States will speak several times over the course of APEC,” Ushakov told Russian state media outlet Vesti.

Their meeting will be an “intimate affair” without the involvement of large delegations, Vesti cited Ushakov as saying.

Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said there is unlikely to be an opportunity for “full-format talks” between the US and Russian leaders, Russian state media TASS said.

He did however say the pair will likely discuss the Ukraine conflict and possibly Iran, TASS reported.

World.title: What is APEC and why are the world’s leaders gathering in Shenzhen?
World.content:
Leaders from around the world – heads of state, business executives, policymakers and more – are gathering in Shenzhen this week for the annual summit of a group known as APEC.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) is a 21-member bloc that includes major Pacific Rim economies like the United States, Canada, Australia, Russia, China, Japan, South Korea and more. The grouping represents 61 percent of the world’s total GDP and 47 percent of global trade, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative.

They take turns hosting the summit each year, where representatives discuss trade, industry, and regional tensions and security.

This year China is hosting, with the summit held in the southern tech and manufacturing hub just across the border from Hong Kong.

There are several events on the calendar, but people will be most closely watching the Economic Leaders’ meeting today and tomorrow, where heads of state will gather and hold potentially consequential talks on the sidelines.

Past APEC summits have proved consequential – in 2018, for instance, US and Chinese leaders each delivered strongly-worded speeches as tensions rose between the two powers, with the bloc failing to agree on a joint communique for the first time in its 25-year history. Last year, Trump skipped APEC – but held a meeting with Xi just beforehand where they reached a trade deal after months of battling tariffs.

World.title: Russian military transport aircraft crashes in Siberia, killing 19, defense ministry says
World.content:
Moscow Reuters —

A military An-12 transport aircraft crashed in Russia’s Kemerovo region in southwestern Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, Russia’s defense ministry was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

“The preliminary cause of the disaster is a technical malfunction,” state news agency RIA quoted the Defence Ministry as saying.

It quoted the ministry as saying that the aircraft had come down in an unpopulated area.

Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had put out a fire. He said the main task of crews on site was to help the investigation into the accident.

Seredyuk, in a video posted online and showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when the accident occurred.

World.title: The looting of the Nile Valley’s ancient treasures
World.content:
Countless artifacts have left Egypt over the centuries, spirited away through both legal channels and illicit smuggling networks.

For more than 150 years, the country has endured the relentless plundering of its archaeological sites by organized looters who smuggled priceless relics abroad, offloading them onto black-market antiquities circuits or legitimizing them in licensed auction houses with forged provenance papers.

The most egregious waves of this systematic pillaging occurred between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries—a dark era chronicled by an American author (Brian M. Fagan) in his seminal work, “The Rape of the Nile”.

The history of Egyptian antiquities theft is rife with brazen accounts, some orchestrated by self-styled Egyptologists themselves.

Consider the case of E. A. Wallis Budge, the Englishman who served as Keeper of Egyptian Antiquities at the British Museum and had the audacity to publish memoirs detailing how he acquired and smuggled Egyptian treasures into London.

Among his most notorious exploits was the theft of the Papyrus of Ani—one of the finest and most significant ancient manuscripts ever unearthed in Luxor.

Budge devised a calculated scheme to secure it: he arrived at the antiquities storeroom bearing kebabs and wine to ply and distract the guards over a meal, while his accomplices simultaneously tunneled beneath the facility. Once inside, they extracted the papyrus and sliced it into sections to facilitate its smuggling out of the country.

One is left to wonder how the British Museum is actually managed, particularly in light of recent revelations that roughly 2,000 artifacts have vanished from its own collections.

During a live television broadcast in which I appeared alongside a British Museum curator, my counterpart had the temerity to claim that his institution safeguards Egyptian heritage better than Egypt does itself.

My response was swift and uncompromising: I reminded him that an institution incapable of securing its own galleries—having lost nearly 2,000 artifacts on its watch—has no moral standing to lecture us on the stewardship of our own heritage.

Among the most notorious figures to extract antiquities from Egypt was the Italian Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman who pivoted to archaeological excavation.

Within a remarkably brief span, he uncovered the tomb of Pharaoh Seti I, cleared the entrance to the temple of Abu Simbel, and breached the Pyramid of Khafre at Giza.

Belzoni went on to ship Seti I’s alabaster sarcophagus to England—where it remains housed today at Sir John Soane’s Museum in London—while exporting countless other statues and relics to sell to the British Museum, treating Egypt’s heritage as though it were his own personal patrimony.

Colonial consuls similarly vied with one another in plundering and trafficking Egypt’s treasures.

Foremost among them was the British Consul-General Henry Salt, who arrived in Egypt in 1815 and locked horns with his French counterpart, Bernardino Drovetti, in a fierce race to amass and monopolize Egyptian antiquities.

Encouraged by Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society, to collect artifacts on behalf of the British Museum—and finding his annual consular salary insufficient to cover his diplomatic expenses—Salt turned to the antiquities trade as a lucrative enterprise.

Drovetti, who assumed the post of French Consul in the wake of the Napoleonic expedition, pursued an equally aggressive campaign to fill European museum galleries.

The rivalry between the two diplomats grew so intense that violent clashes frequently broke out between their respective excavation crews.

Ultimately, the two men struck a cynical pact to carve up the country’s archaeological landscape: the East Bank of the Nile was claimed as Drovetti’s domain, while the West Bank fell under Salt’s purview.

Having partitioned Egypt’s heritage as though it were private property, they continued to systematically harvest and sell off artifacts to major institutions across London, Paris, and Turin.

To sustain this enterprise, both consuls deployed networks of local agents to excavate and haul monumental statuary, while currying favor with Egyptian officials to secure excavation permits. Consequently, vast troves of Salt’s acquisitions ended up in the British Museum, while Drovetti’s collections enriched rival European institutions.

This colonial scramble triggered a massive exodus of Egypt’s cultural wealth—priceless artifacts that remain on display in Western museums to this very day.

The clash between the two consuls was far more than a personal feud; it escalated into a relentless race to plunder antiquities, with each vying to reach excavation sites first—leaving Egypt as the sole victim and ultimate loser.

Consequently, iconic masterpieces were spirited out of the country, including the Bust of Nefertiti in Berlin, the Rosetta Stone in the British Museum, and the Dendera Zodiac in the Louvre.

The removal of the Zodiac is particularly notorious: in 1821, an expedition descended upon the Temple of Dendera, sawed the celestial bas-relief straight out of the sanctuary ceiling, and shipped it off to France.

For years, curators at the British Museum failed to give the Rosetta Stone the prominence it warranted, relegating it to a dimly lit corner. On one occasion, when I visited London to deliver a lecture at the museum, the director hosted a formal dinner in my honor amidst the Egyptian galleries. Following his welcoming remarks, I took the floor to respond.

I told the gathered guests that during dinner, King Ramesses II had appeared to me and whispered, “Zahi, I have lived here for over a century, and I can bear it no longer—take me back to Egypt with you.”

King Thutmose III soon approached me with the very same plea. Ultimately, the two pharaohs conferred and returned with a unified message: “Take the Rosetta Stone home with you first; it belongs to Egypt and stands as a national icon. Our turn to return will follow.”

The message was not lost on the audience, and the next morning, British newspapers splashed across their front pages that Egypt was formally demanding the repatriation of the Rosetta Stone.

Prompted by the public spotlight, museum curators swiftly relocated the artifact to a prime, central gallery, illuminating it from every angle.

The saga of the stone dates back to 1799, when Pierre-François Bouchard, an officer in Napoleon’s expedition, unearthed it near the town of Rashid (Rosetta).

The slab soon became a prized trophy in the Anglo-French struggle for dominance. Following Britain’s victory over French forces in Alexandria in 1801, London demanded the handover of all antiquities seized by the French, foremost among them the Rosetta Stone.
