World.title: Democrats formally nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, paving way for him to be the first Black speaker
World.content:
WASHINGTON — After leading Democrats back to the majority, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January.

Jeffries was nominated in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11, according to two sources in the room. It was a show of strength for Jeffries, who had faced grumbling from progressive members and activists calling for new and bolder leadership. But no challenger emerged.

Some of Jeffries’ allies had pushed for a vote by acclamation, which would not result in a tally. But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership.

“It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach,” Jeffries told reporters Tuesday, “to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision, to help move us forward in the new Congress.”

After the vote, seven of the 11 Democrats who voted against Jeffries issued a join statement explaining their position.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” wrote Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”

Jeffries was nominated by five colleagues representing the broad diversity of the Democratic Caucus: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., Rep. Derek Tran, D-Calif., Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, D-N.J., and former Majority Whip Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., one of Jeffries’ political mentors.

“This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn, a veteran of the Civil Rights Movement and former chair of the Black Caucus, told reporters before the vote.

Jeffries, a 56-year-old Brooklyn native, former attorney and former state lawmaker, is now poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House.

He campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

It means that Jeffries can afford roughly 40 Democratic defections that day and still be elected speaker. By contrast, in 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy had a razor-thin 222-212 majority; he managed to win the speaker’s gavel on the 15th ballot.

Last week, House Republicans elected Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., to be minority leader in the next Congress.

Like the speaker race, the other major Democratic leadership races are also uncontested. Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., was elected by her colleagues as majority leader, the No. 2 position. She will make history as the first woman in either chamber elected to that role.

Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., was elected majority whip, the No. 3 leader and party’s top vote counter. No Hispanic American lawmaker has ever climbed higher in the House.

Rep. Ted Lieu, another California Democrat, was elected as caucus chairman, the No. 4 leader. He will make history as the first Asian American to hold that job.

And Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., was elected assistant speaker.

The only significant contested leadership race is for vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, where Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Progressive Caucus, is running against Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., a member of the Black Caucus.

Jeffries, a Pelosi protégé, had served as Democratic Caucus chairman before he was elevated to minority leader following House Democrats’ loss in the 2022 midterms.

He spent much of Tuesday holding meetings with the various factions of his massive new majority that he will need to unite to pass legislation on issues like affordability. He met separately with the leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the two moderate groups, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs.

“It’s a great class, and they have a lot of wonderful ideas, fresh ideas, new ideas about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters.

World.title: Meghan Markle’s father faces new child sex abuse complaints in the Philippines
World.content:
Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, has had criminal complaints filed against him over alleged online child sexual abuse offences, police in the Philippines said Wednesday.

The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police told Reuters. They added that the complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu on Monday, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.

Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.

Prosecutors the evaluating the charges filed by police before they decide whether to issue a subpoena against Markle whose legal team would have 10 days to respond with a counter-affidavit. Prosecutors would then decide whether to proceed with a court case.

Prince Harry and Meghan’s spokesperson declined to comment when NBC News asked about the latest charges.

The announcement came less than two weeks after the 82-year-old was arrested in Florida and charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Justice Department.

Thomas Markle's booking photo at the Pinellas County Jail in Clearwater, Fla, earlier this month. Pinellas County Sheriff's Office via Getty

The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in Los Angeles, that contained “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, the complaint said, which added that a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle.”

Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images found in California were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document.

Markle was taken into custody in Tampa, Florida, and was later released under house arrest.

But after he cut off his ankle monitor, a federal judge ordered last week that Markle remain in custody for violating the conditions of his release.

Markle had been living in a senior care facility in Lakeland, Florida after he was forced to return to the U.S. from the Philippines when he suffered a stroke and a leg was amputated, according to The Associated Press.

The retired television lighting and photography director denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.”

Meghan Markle asaid in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny.

Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

London’s Metropolitan Police said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”

Meghan Markle and her husband, Prince Harry, stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift and moved to, leaving Britain for California.

Harry, the second son of King Charles III and the late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.”

The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

World.title: Highlights from Pope Leo’s historic, 12-day tour of South America
World.content:
LIMA, Peru — They turned out in the millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

00:00 00:00 Pope keeps energetic pace in trip to South America after surgery 01:19

For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo.

The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.

NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip.

Montevideo, Uruguay

After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.”

World.title: Jeffries wins Democratic nomination for House speaker
World.content:
Washington — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday, paving the way for his election when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Jeffries' current and incoming Democratic colleagues voted 251 to 11 to back his nomination for the gavel during a closed-door meeting where members were also choosing the rest of the House Democratic leadership. The caucus also voted to elevate Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the next majority leader, the first woman to hold that position.

The speaker is ultimately elected by the full House chamber, a vote that will occur at the beginning of the new Congress. With Democrats on track to control more than 250 seats, Jeffries' path to gaining the 218 votes needed for the speakership is all but secured. Jeffries would be the first Black House speaker in U.S. history.

The New York Democrat faced some hesitance from new progressive members heading into Wednesday's leadership vote. Seven incoming progressives who voted against him said in a statement that they were hoping to secure policy commitments from Jeffries on a number of fronts.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," the new members said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The members who released the statement were Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.

But no other Democrat put their name forward to directly challenge Jeffries' bid. And with the wide Democratic majority, individual members have limited leverage to push for concessions.

Jeffries said he wanted a tallied vote during the internal election rather than ask for a vote by acclamation. He told reporters Tuesday that it was the same approach Democrats used in their leadership elections in 2018, when they transitioned from the minority to the majority.

"Certainly seems to me it would be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision," Jeffries said.

House Democrats also voted Wednesday to fill the roles of whip, assistant leader and caucus chair in the new Congress.

Rep. Pete Aguilar of California was elected whip, Joe Neguse of Colorado won assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu of California won the vote for chair of the Democratic caucus.

House Democrats' leadership election was far less contentious than that of their colleagues in the Senate, where longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Schumer has expressed confidence that he has the votes to be elected majority leader in elections early next month.

World.title: "No indication" outages are related to cyberattacks, officials say
World.content:
Washington — Top U.S. national security officials told Congress they have found no evidence that a string of technology outages affecting airlines, banks, Microsoft services and national security communications systems were connected or caused by malicious cyberattacks, even as lawmakers pressed for answers about an outage at the National Security Agency and reports of potential Iranian attacks on U.S. soil.

At Wednesday's House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia attempted to reassure lawmakers that federal agencies were investigating the disruptions and monitoring possible threats.

"We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Mullin said, adding that DHS had contacted private industry while reviewing the outages.

Clayton said intelligence officials had reached a similar assessment after reviewing the incidents with government agencies and cybersecurity experts in the private sector.

"These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack," Clayton said.

Raia said FBI cybersecurity specialists had been involved in examining the incidents from the beginning.

"At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents," Raia said. He added that the FBI would continue working with private-sector partners "in an abundance of caution."

Rep. Dan Goldman, a New York Democrat, challenged Clayton's characterization of the recent NSA outage, repeatedly asking whether the disruption had resulted from internal software updates or other technical work.

"It's your testimony today that the technological problems that the NSA faced on Monday were from internal software and technological upgrades," Goldman said.

Clayton responded that officials had found no evidence of outside interference.

"We have no indication that they have come from external threat actors," Clayton said.

Goldman pressed for a more definitive explanation.

"It's a pretty binary. It's either external or internal, right?" Goldman asked.

Clayton described routine maintenance procedures, including software patches, system upgrades and hardware replacement, which can require systems to be taken offline and restarted.

Goldman accused Clayton of avoiding the question.

"You're a very smart person, and you're clearly not answering my direct questions," Goldman rebutted.

Clayton separately warned that advances in computing power and increasingly capable software were placing new demands on older government technology systems.

"The speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially," Clayton said.

He warned that the accelerating pace of technological development was making legacy systems obsolete more quickly, suggesting that infrastructure considered outdated only months earlier could fall even further behind as computing capabilities advance.

Mullin has already faced significant backlash for taking a government plane to a college football game one day after a FAA ground stop while the nation's airports remained chaotic. Mullin said Wednesday that it would have shown "distrust" in the nation's airspace if he had not flown.

Lawmakers also raised concerns about reports that Iranian-linked actors could be developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials using a radiological weapon, commonly called a dirty bomb, or chemical weapons.

Rep. Michael Guest, a Mississippi Republican, raised concerns about the possibility of Iranian sleeper cells operating within the United States and asked whether federal authorities were equipped to identify and disrupt potential attacks.

"Are we concerned about the possibility of sleeper cells?" Guest asked Mullin.

"Is it a concern? Of course. Are we fighting it and stomping it down every single day? Absolutely," Mullin responded.

Mullin said DHS personnel were working closely with intelligence and Justice Department officials to identify threats and prevent attacks.

Clayton also emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.

"That's not theoretical; it's real. We saw it in New York. We've seen it in other cases," Clayton said.

Raia cautioned that intelligence reporting about possible plots does not necessarily mean attackers possess the capability to carry them out.

"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean that does not mean we do not take it seriously."

He said authorities had revamped their Iranian threat mission center to strengthen efforts against potential attacks, pointing to previously disclosed investigations involving plots against dissidents.

The officials did not publicly confirm that Iranian sleeper cells were preparing attacks within the United States or that the reported dirty bomb or chemical weapons plans were operational.

Clayton said Iranian threats inside and outside of the U.S. have "dramatically increased."

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said. "These threats have dramatically increased."

World.title: Top Dem sends letters to people close to Trump ahead of probes
World.content:
Washington — The top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee sent letters Wednesday to a dozen people close to President Trump ahead of expected investigations into alleged corruption, misconduct by the Department of Homeland Security and the White House's handling of files from the investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The letters from Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to chair the Oversight Committee when Democrats take control of the House in January, went to members of the president's family, as well as former and current administration officials, and instructed them to preserve documents relevant to Democrats' future investigations.

Garcia sent notices to Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Homeland Security senior adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President J.D. Vance, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Bureau of Prisons Director WIlliam Marshall.

"Voters gave Congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people," Garcia said in the letters. "We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform."

Garcia told Donald Trump Jr., and Eric Trump that the committee will investigate alleged conflicts of interest and their stakes in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto business. He told Trump Jr. that the Oversight panel is also interested in a Russian oligarch's funding of his post-wedding festivities at a private island in the Bahamas in May.

The letter to Kushner focuses on his personal business dealings and role representing the U.S. government as a negotiator in talks in the Middle East and Russia, which Garcia said raise concerns about "transparency, conflicts of interest and the abuse of" a government position for personal profit.

His document preservation notices to Vance, Wiles, Blanche and Marshall all center around the Trump administration's handling of the release of files from the federal investigation into Epstein, or the transfer of Ghislaine Maxwell, his longtime associate, to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas last year.

Letters to Miller, Noem and Lewandowski indicate that the committee will focus on immigration enforcement operations, and for Noem and Lewandowski, specifically, allegations of corruption and pay-to-play schemes at the department.

Garcia told Guilfoyle that the committee will be investigating alleged pay-to-play schemes surrounding her ambassadorship, and notified Townsend he will be examining private donations to fund construction of the new White House ballroom.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse. These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning," the California Democrat said in a statement.

Garcia and congressional Democrats are poised to launch investigations into numerous matters arising during Mr. Trump's second term once they officially take control of the House and Senate in January and will have subpoena power.

But the White House has indicated it intends to fight back against the probes.

White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Garcia last week warning that their investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," and said any investigative acts by Congress must support a legitimate legislative purpose.

But Garcia dismissed Scharf's threat and said Congress has "wide latitude" to conduct investigations and oversight.

In addition to Scharf's letter, a U.S. attorney in southern Texas, Aaron Reitz, has sent notices to at least five House and Senate Democrats about remarks they've made about forthcoming investigations and ordered them to preserve documents.

World.title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
World.content:
In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.

Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.

What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.

There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said. "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."

What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need either a PlayStation5 or Xbox Series X or S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.

When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.

How much does it cost?

Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.

What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.

"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."

Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.

Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.

"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.

Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.

Who plays GTA?

Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.

What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.

The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.

Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.

How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

While the game has yet to officially launch, it has already racked up impressive sales. Nearly 16 million pre-order copies of the game have been sold, generating $1.5 billion in revenue, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."

An  for GTA 6 in a store ahead of its release in Amsterdam on Nov. 18, 2026. Koen van Weel / ANP /AFP via Getty Images

Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.

"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, sold more than 200 million copies. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.

How much did GTA 6 cost to make?

Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.

Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

World.title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
World.content:
Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."

Robert Pattinson attends the "Primetime" Screening during the 70th BFI London Film Festival at BFI IMAX Waterloo on Oct. 11, 2026 in London, England. Lia Toby

Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."

The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.

"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

World.title: Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
World.content:
Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast

toggle caption i Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images

A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025.

This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November .

If you plan on being one of those travelers in the coming days, make sure you know what to do in case your flight suddenly gets delayed or canceled.

Life Kit Listen to an audio version of this story here Flight cancelled again? Try these tips. Listen · 25:08 25:08

Air travel has gotten notably worse over the past decade. In 2025, cancellations and delays surged, creating the worst on-time performance for airlines in the United States since 2014, according to a 2026 report by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, a consumer advocacy group.

So, with holiday schlepping season kicking off this week, what's a weary traveler to do? Ahead, travel experts explain how to make rebooking flights less painful. Because what's worse than a canceled holiday flight is missing the holiday altogether.

Sponsor Message

Multitask! While standing in line, rebook your flight online

Most people react to a cancellation by heading straight to the nearest customer service desk and queuing up to rebook their flight. The problem with that approach? Everyone else on your flight is doing that too.

"You have 300 people getting off the plane. There's maybe one, two people trying to help everyone. That clearly is the least efficient way," says travel reporter Chris Dong.

While standing in line, open up the airline app and rebook yourself, he says. There's often a seamless way to get it done, no customer service conversation necessary. During the holiday rush, when hundreds of other passengers may be trying to rebook at the same time, getting a head start on the airline's app can make an especially big difference.

See if an agent can help you at the airport lounge

If you have a travel credit card that gives you lounge access, head there to get one-on-one customer service. "Lounge agents are much more inclined to help you and are usually not as short-staffed," Dong says. "That can get you help quickly."

If you don't already have lounge access, see if you can purchase a day pass on-site. It may be well worth it depending on your flight cost and timeline.

Sponsor Message

Know what you're entitled to from the airline

All ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they don't accept whatever the airline is offering, such as a later flight and/or travel vouchers or vouchers for hotels or meals. However, most airlines in the U.S. aren't required to compensate you for delays or cancellations unless it's the airline's fault (think maintenance issues or staffing problems).

To find out what you're entitled to, check the Department of Transportation's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard . Many major airlines have committed to giving passengers cost-free rebooking, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, hotel transportation and more.

Once you know what your airline offers, say, a hotel, you can rest easy about what to do that night — and focus on rebooking for the next day.

Check what your travel insurance covers

Once you know what your airline will cover, check what your travel insurance will cover. Many credit cards include some travel insurance coverage, which can provide everything from trip cancellation to luggage insurance to any medical needs that might arise en route.

When rebooking, choose a flight earlier in the day

If you have flight time options when rebooking or flexibility in your travel schedule, choose the early-morning flight. They're your best bet to avoid delays or cancellations, Dong says.

If you're on the first flight out, there's little chance you'll have to wait for that aircraft coming in from another city because it's likely been sitting at the airport overnight.

This is especially worth considering during the holidays, when a single disruption can have a domino effect on subsequent flights. An early departure gives you more opportunities to get rebooked on another flight that same day if something goes wrong — because nobody wants to miss that family Thanksgiving dinner!

If you want refunds or flight credits, be nice to your customer service rep

If the airline significantly delayed, significantly changed (see DOT website for details) or cancelled the flight and you originally booked your ticket directly with your airline, getting your money back should be no problem, even if the ticket is nonrefundable. But if you booked through a third party such as a travel agent or travel website, you'll have to go through them.

Sponsor Message

Remember that customer service representatives are likely dealing with hundreds of frustrated passengers during the holiday rush. Being patient and polite won't guarantee an exception, but it certainly won't hurt your chances, suggests Eulanda Osagiede , director of operations at Black Travel Alliance and chief operations officer at Black Travel Summit.

The best approach, she says, is to be "very nice, very friendly" with the customer service representative on the phone. So don't start yelling at them. Treating reps like the human beings they are can make all the difference.

Have a backup plan before you leave home

When you're traveling for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas, a delay doesn't just mean missing a few hours of vacation. It could mean missing the big family gathering or a favorite kiddo's holiday performance.

So before you leave, take a few minutes to research alternative routes to your destination. Are there other airports nearby? Could you drive part of the way? Are there trains or buses that could get you there if your flight falls through?

It's also worth saving your airline's customer service number, downloading its app, and keeping your confirmation numbers somewhere accessible offline. If you're traveling with kids, pack enough snacks, medications, entertainment and other essentials to get through an unexpected overnight stay.

You can't plan for every possible disruption, but you can make sure you're not starting from scratch when one happens.

World.title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
World.content:
Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.

Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.

"Thank you House Democrats," Jeffries wrote in a post on social media after the vote. "Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!"

Sponsor Message

The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.

Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.

It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.

He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.

Sponsor Message

Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."

Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York; New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.

Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.

Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.

Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.

Sponsor Message

Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.

World.title: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
World.content:
House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations

toggle caption i Drew Angerer/Getty Images

The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."

The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."

Sponsor Message

"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.

The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.

In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

World.title: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
World.content:
The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe

Rahul Mukherjee/NPR

This is a story that starts with a remarkable success story. However, the ending has become a cliff hanger — with potentially grave consequences.

The success is clearcut and remarkable: Both Zambia and Zimbabwe are beating back devastating HIV/AIDS epidemics. These neighboring countries in southern Africa are on the cusp of controlling the virus.

Between 2000 and 2025, new infections dropped by 76% in Zambia and 80% in Zimbabwe. In both countries, more than 95% of infected individuals are identified and 95% of them are on treatment, according to data from the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.

This progress is thanks, in large part, to billions of dollars in U.S. aid over the past two decades.

Sponsor Message

However, President Trump's new global health strategy is scrambling the landscape. After dismantling without warning the U.S. Agency for International Development in 2025, the administration is now hammering out government-to-government aid agreements as a new framework for how aid is provided.

That process leaves these two countries on very different paths and heading toward uncharted territory.

Just last month Zambian and U.S. officials signed an agreement — albeit for far less annual U.S. health aid than the country received in the past. Zimbabwe, in contrast, lost all U.S. health aid this fall after negotiations collapsed. To get an on-the-ground assessment of what has happened and what the future may hold, NPR interviewed a health worker in each country with experience in the HIV/AIDS world.

Zambia's aid agreement

When the aid agreement was announced on ZNBC — Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation on October 8 — it was branded as "a new chapter" in which the U.S. aid dollars flow primarily through the government and aims to build up the national health system.

The negotiations behind the aid agreement were secretive and became contentious, explains Asia Russell , executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP "There was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," Russell told NPR . Her organization helped expose this situation. Ultimately, the discussion about mineral rights was decoupled from the health agreement.

Sponsor Message

"I felt a bit relieved," says the Zambian health worker. But, with the aid agreement finally signed, she says, "the work now begins."

The health worker asked NPR not to use her name because she helped make public that mineral rights were in play and fears government retribution. She worries the Zambian government is ill equipped to face down the obstacles of the HIV/AIDS epidemic.

For example, homosexuality is illegal in Zambia. "Because [people are] scared of being arrested when they go to the public health facility, they would rather just stay home and face the consequences of their illness," she says, adding that such a decision not only leaves them without treatment it also lets the virus spread further via unprotected sexual relations, drug activity and other routes.

Under the previous system, huge amounts of U.S. aid went through international and local non-governmental groups who have staff specially trained to reach those vulnerable populations. This new agreement sidelines those groups and instead aims to build up the government's health systems rather than a parallel system, according to the U.S. strategy .

The Zambian health worker is also concerned the country could trumpet success in addressing HIV/AIDS but that thorough outreach and treatment records won't be kept and the right infrastructure may not be in place. For instance, she says, the government may say: " 'We've employed 5,000 community health workers!' "

But, she asks: "What is the quality? What capacity do they have? Who will they be serving? Which district? "

This health worker says many in the medical field have not received answers about what the future health systems will look like.

"It feels like a big mess, honestly. It's scary," she says, "It feels like doing it right is not the priority, but people's lives are at risk."

Sponsor Message

The Zambian Ministry of Health did not respond to requests for comment. But in the press conference announcing the agreement, Health minister Roma Chilengi said the department plans to recruit up to 40,000 health care workers, including 15,000 front line workers such as doctors, nurses, midwives, scientists, pharmacists, as well as community health workers.

However apprehensive this health worker is, she says that what's happening in Zambia is still better than the situation in neighboring Zimbabwe.

Zimbabwe's agreement collapses

In February, negotiations over the future of health aid between U.S. and Zimbabwean officials fell apart.

There was plenty of fingerpointing. Zimbabwean officials said the proposed agreement was lopsided. For example, Zimbabwe would have been obligated to provide data and biological samples of pathogens for research but would not have been guaranteed access to any treatments that result from that information. The U.S. Embassy in Zimbabwe said in a press release that the breakdown was regrettable. Whatever the reason, the result was clear. The country went from receiving well over $100 million in U.S. health aid each year to having none.

The health worker in Zimbabwe is baffled by this: "The U.S. put [in] 20 years of support — 20 years of support! — that's a huge investment which I think you cannot just throw away?" But he says that's what he's seeing.

This health worker also asked NPR not to use his name because he fears government retribution for speaking out. Without aid, he says, in his community, people's HIV medications are dwindling. "Within a period of six months or so, you will start to see a very huge impact," he predicts.

But he's concerned the world may never know the real impact. The U.S has had the best data collection and monitoring system for tracking and understanding the HIV epidemic and the response. Going forward the data coming out of Zimbabwe will be hard to verify or trust, he says. "We may not even know…if it's true or not."

Sponsor Message

The Ministry of Health and Child Care in Zimbabwe did not respond to NPR's requests for comment but this past summer, Zimbabwe's health minister, Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, pledged to expand the health workforce and infrastructure .

In a statement to NPR about the status of aid to the two countries, the U.S. State Department did not address the specific concerns of the health workers but said it's committed to working "with partner governments to define and advance shared global health priorities."

A subdued domestic response

As for public reaction in the two countries? It's been muted, the health workers say.

Both say that in their communities people are mad but that a public outcry has been muted because they fear reprisal from their governments. Russell, of Health GAP, echoed this experience saying many people who she works with are afraid to speak publicly: "The problem is retaliation" because they lived under authoritarian regimes.

"People are trying to not lose more than they've already lost," the health worker in Zambia says. "So even the anger is there, the frustrations are there, but you do not see this very publicly."

Similarly, the health worker in Zimbabwe says, "you can be mad, you can be angry, you can be whatever. But if you talk, you know the consequences of what will happen to you."

Public outcry or not, the global health world will be carefully observing how the next stage unfolds for these two countries.

Jennifer Kates , senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at the research organization KFF, says her team is scrutinizing all the information it can get about the agreement and implementation of the aid agreement in Zambia. And Zimbabwe "is an important one to watch," she says. "It's made a lot of progress, heavily relying on the U.S." — and now the future is uncertain.

Sponsor Message

World.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
World.content:
Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Her victory gives Democrats 56 senators in the upcoming Congress. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola secured a majority of first-place votes, eliminating the need for ranked-choice calculations. Her win flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. The race's final days were tumultuous due to allegations that Peltola's team tried to recruit another candidate to the race to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Trump has arrived in the Southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he is set to meet with China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday. This will mark the third time these two leaders have met this year. They are expected to discuss trade, investment and tariffs, which are currently on hold.



🎧 The meeting is about establishing a tone, as the U.S. and China have agreed to have constructive strategic stability, NPR's Jennifer Pak tells Up First. The two leaders will later be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting. The trio may discuss a peace deal for Russia's war in Ukraine, but China says that Europe must be included. Pak says China wants to show that a world leader won't make decisions without input from smaller countries. This is especially significant, Pak says, because these meetings take place on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), where many smaller nations seek a voice in regional matters.

Sponsor Message

Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in an earnings call yesterday that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct," according to Jones. Huang acknowledged he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency. The board unanimously accepted his resignation. Earlier yesterday, Huang said he would return as CEO if the board permitted it and agreed to testify before Congress regarding national security issues surrounding the company.



🎧 NPR's John Ruwitch said that Jones clearly wanted to dispel rumors, and showed support for interim CEO Colette Kress. He said she "has been at the center of the company's extraordinary growth." Kress also participated in the call, maintaining a business-as-usual demeanor, Ruwitch says. Nvidia posted revenue exceeding $115 billion for the quarter, which isn't surprising, as the numbers were secured before Huang's recent departure. Tech analyst Gaurav Gupta from Gartner tells Ruwitch that any impact from new leadership won't be reflected in the numbers for several months. Jones said the board would try to decide on a permanent CEO as soon as possible without rushing the decision.

Sponsor Message

Major organizations have been experiencing widespread crashes of computer and online systems. Apple reported significant outages yesterday, and the U.S. National Security Agency also experienced a breakdown. As of this morning, no major disruptions seem to be occurring. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that these incidents are related to one another or involve a malign actor or cybercriminal.



🎧 Cyber experts tell NPR's Greg Myre that artificial intelligence is uncovering previously undetected software flaws at an unprecedented pace. Companies are racing to patch or upgrade to address these vulnerabilities, but working under tight deadlines often leads to mistakes. As many systems undergo upgrades, people should anticipate disruptions along the way, Myre says. However, the optimistic perspective is that computer networks are expected to become more robust and resilient within the next year or two due to the improvements.

Deep dive

toggle caption i Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images

In recent years, highly concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) have emerged online and at smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. These products, available as tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolates, contain one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom. Unlike kratom leaf products, 7-OH acts more like an opioid in the human brain. Some people use kratom to maintain long-term recovery from opioid addiction. Others say it helps them feel energized or focused. Users of 7-OH and kratom can show signs of addiction, and unclear product labeling makes it hard to determine the quantities consumed. Over the past decade, the U.S. government has tried to restrict these products, but public opposition has kept them legal. Recently, this situation has started to change.

➡️ In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration restricted the manufacture and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids from 7-OH and other related compounds. They were classified under the Controlled Substances Act alongside drugs like heroin and LSD.

➡️ Kratom advocates were concerned that new rules would impact products with "trace amounts" of the opioid MGPI. The American Kratom Association filed a federal lawsuit against the DEA on Aug. 26, seeking to keep natural kratom products with MGPI legal.

➡️ On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI, leading the DEA to revise its stance to focus on restricting products with higher concentrations of these substances.

➡️ Opponents of the restriction argue that the products helped them avoid traditional opioids. Some point to the decrease in opioid deaths in the U.S.

➡️ The National Institute on Drug Abuse says that early studies indicate kratom and its compounds deserve more exploration as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder.

Sponsor Message

Real Talk With a Doc

Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR

Family physician Mara Gordon answers reader health questions monthly for NPR's special series Real Talk with a Doc . Send in your question to thrive@npr.org.

Artificial intelligence scribes help doctors take notes in various settings, from gynecologist visits to emergency rooms. Dr. Gordon says the technology saves time and allows her to focus entirely on her patients without the distraction of multitasking. But she also understands why patients might feel uneasy about new technology, and says she shares their concerns about privacy. Here's what Dr. Gordon says you should know about AI scribes:

🩺 The scribe uses "automatic speech recognition" technology to record the conversation between the doctor and the patient. After the visit, the recording is transcribed and turned into a medical note of the exam's findings and the doctor's decisions.

🩺 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance is crucial for AI scribe services to ensure they protect patient privacy. Software companies must safeguard data by encrypting it, controlling access and implementing systems to prevent data breaches. Most companies delete recorded conversations after a specified period.

🩺 AI scribes can make mistakes, which is why doctors must review AI-generated notes before signing them and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software requires doctors to sign a user agreement, making them liable for all content in the medical record.

🩺Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates have raised concerns that this could widen health disparities.

🩺 You can always opt out of using an AI scribe during your doctor's visit. But opting out of AI in medicine more broadly could be tricky.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Jawad Rizkallah

NPR's Breakfast Around the World series is spotlighting Lebanon's man'ouché, a beloved breakfast flatbread. It's a U.N.-certified part of intangible cultural heritage, with a unique twist crafted by generations of Lebanese. The Pan American Health Organization announced yesterday that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. It is now considered endemic because a strain has persisted in the country for more than a year. The oldest survivor of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Freeman Johnson, died this weekend at his Cape Cod home at the age of 106.
