World.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph
World.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

I want to tell you about the time I saw Bigfoot. I want to tell you about sitting in the rain on a city street in a muscle car and prepping to rob a bank while lightning split the sky between high-rise condo towers in the distance and the drum fill from In The Air Tonight played on the radio. I want to tell you about gunfights and fistfights, the perfect satire of radio commercials and how the sunrise looks over Ocean Beach. But more than any of that, I want to tell you about the time an alligator bit my mom.

Sponsor Message

It happened in the backyard of an abandoned house with a rotting inground pool. My mom, Mia Caminos (mother of Lucia Caminos, one of the two leads in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI, probably the most highly anticipated video game sequel of all time), was thrilled by the pool. Standing there, amid the artfully rendered weeds and trash, she spread her arms and told me to use my imagination, to see her vision for this ruin of a house with its upmarket water feature, in a scabby neighborhood on the outskirts of Vice City. She speaks in tones of increasingly frantic desperation because she has already put money down on this house, sight unseen. All of her money, actually, in hopes of flipping it and selling it fast to keep her startup real estate business afloat.

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

The pool is still half full of water. There's a dirty, sodden mattress floating in it. And as if this is the main thing standing between her and success, Mia is fixated on getting it out of the pool.

Help me, Lucia, she says.

And, dutifully, I do. Playing as Lucia, I grab hold, mash buttons, help my mom drag away the wet, heavy, stinking mattress. And just as we get it up and over the lip of the pool that's going to be the thing that makes this wreck of a house suddenly desirable – that's when the alligator lunges out of the murky water, grabs my mom by the arm and tries to drag her back in.

Sponsor Message

This is a story about folly, fixation, unrealistic expectations of success at the ass-end of late capitalism, and the vicious, whip-crack cruelty of predators who lie in wait for anyone trying to improve a terrible situation.

But then I shoot the alligator in the head before it can eat my mom. Because this is also a story about violence, and how sometimes (maybe all the times), the loud, cathartic rip of gunfire is the only solution left for people who have already lost so much and can't bear to see one more thing taken from them.

It's a story about my mom and an alligator, sure.

It is also the story of GTA6

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

But let's back up a little. For anyone who has somehow missed the shrieking, neon-and-swamp-water marketing onslaught over the past several days, weeks, months and years, Grand Theft Auto VI is the newest release from Rockstar Games. It is a Bonnie and Clyde love story, a knife-edged satire of modern American culture and politics, an unapologetic murder simulator, a love letter to 50 years of crime movies, and a thoughtful, emotional meditation on the sacrifices, small and large, that we make for family. A massive open world game set in the fictional state of Leonida (based on the very real state of Florida), it represents a return to a location that Rockstar hasn't visited in-depth since its 2002 release of GTA: Vice City, and is the first new game in the franchise since GTA5 launched in 2013. According to estimates, it already earned over $1.5 billion in pre-sales and will likely make a total of $3 to $5 billion in its first week , which could make it the largest single entertainment product launch ever.

Fans have been waiting years for it. They have created libraries worth of lore and theories and dissected trailers frame-by-frame. To discount the overheated environment into which this singular work of art is being released would be doing a disservice both to it and the legions of salivating prognosticators who have made guessing the number of bird species included in-game , or speculating on the square mileage of its map, their entire personalities.

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

Now, though, they know it all. We all do. We know that GTA6 is expansive, covering everything from the Keys (where the game starts) to the hilly, forested north, with Vice City in all its grimy, pastel-colored splendor at the beating heart of it. It is a playground, equal parts gorgeous and maniacal, and in all that space the developers have given us a thousand different things to do. You can rob a bank or take a bike ride, go fishing, hunt trophy animals, visit strip clubs, rob random civilians, street race, fly drones, eat a sandwich, work out, manage your family savings account, jump a sports car off the top of a building, steal a plane, punch out a convenience store clerk, fight a bear or, yes, just wander out toward the horizon and study the birds. And while some of that is fun and all of it is diverting (at least for a little while), none of it is the ostensible point. The game-y part of the game — the hundred extras and time-wasters that players have come to expect from open-world projects in general, and GTA specifically — is not what makes it matter.

Sponsor Message

What matters is Mia and the alligator, Lucia and the gun. It's the multi-pronged, exquisitely balanced narrative about poverty and rigged systems that makes it hard to turn away from GTA while you're playing and impossible not to think about when you're away.

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

Lucia is an ex-con, a car thief and a small-time criminal who got caught trying to rob a payday loan joint and starts the game in jail. Her partner, Jason Duval, is a veteran, dishonorably discharged, now making a living flying loads for a local coke dealer down in the Keys and living rent-free in one of his properties. Jason skims a little on the coke deals, wears flip-flops and drinks beer in the sun, and goes fishing with his best friend Cal (played with genius-level goofy, drunken paranoia and dopey bravado by Bobby Moynihan). Jason and Lucia have a kid, Tomás, who is currently living with Lucia's family, and every plan they have is about getting right by the law, making a few bucks and grabbing a chance at finally being a family.

Only there are complications — surprisingly banal ones at first (like not being able to open a checking account because of their bad credit) — that slowly ramp up into huge ones across 60-odd hours of main story gameplay that see Jason and Lucia (both of whom are playable characters) graduate from knocking over liquor stores in a beat-up El Camino, to pulling off elaborate heists in the middle of Vice City which will have you dangling from a net suspended from a cargo helicopter hauling 200 tons of cocaine. It goes from Badlands to Die Hard with the speed of a muscle car, all bright chrome and barking straight pipes. From True Romance to Heat like that's just the natural arc of any American love story.

Sponsor Message

And what's remarkable about the whole bloody delight is that it remains, until its final operatic moments, so surprisingly grounded. This is a somewhat more mature GTA than its predecessors, trading aliens, cannibal cultists and whacked-out drug trips for wellness influencers, local politics and the music industry. Jason and Lucia's relationship is the superstructure around which the entire narrative is built, and it's a dynamic thing that must be maintained in a dozen little ways — making coffee in the morning, opening doors for each other, date nights (even if that means robbing a jewelry store together), or holding hands as you walk toward yet another betrayal by someone you thought you could trust. You can switch freely between them, or just call the other one to come drive the getaway car. Let their relationship dwindle and the narrative shifts, flattens. But when they're together, the two of them talk and talk: In bed, in the car, by the pool. They reveal pieces of themselves in quiet moments, joke, tease, flirt, make plans for a future that always seems right around the next corner. And you love them for it. You can't help but love them for it, and root for them, and want good things for them, because they're just two hard-luck kids trying to do right in a world where "right" sometimes means petting a dog or helping a farmer spray manure all over his boss's house, and sometimes means stealing $10 million from South American drug lords.

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

In so many ways GTA6 is an example of inspired synthesis. Rockstar made a killing with the sunlit beauty and craziness of GTA5 more than a decade ago, a game built on deconstructing Hollywood myths and male friendships. Then it made art with a slow-burn meditation on loyalty, death and obsolescence in Red Dead Redemption 2 . And this? It is the middle path charted between those two bright stars. It has seriousness and weight and something to say. And also, you accidentally end up starring in a porno movie. Through mechanical tweaks and narrative railroading, the game trades abject chaos for consequences that force you to actually live in its world rather than just murder your way through it, but then makes the dullest, most quotidian chores (like going grocery shopping or answering your mom's texts) feel like a long, slow breath taken between gasping moments of panic.

Sponsor Message

Yes, you have to sleep. Yes, you have to eat. Yes, you have to work out and put gas in the (stolen) car. But after a while, I found myself actually wanting to do those things because doing them felt like roleplaying; like added opportunities to fully exist within the fiction of Jason or Lucia's world. And in what will no doubt enrage a million over-testosteroned 15-year-olds who want nothing more out of GTA6 than a shinier, brighter, higher-resolution playground in which to jack a Lambo and mow down pedestrians, certain mechanical adjustments in the game (like cars that exist without the tools immediately available to steal them, or how you no longer carry every gun you've ever touched, but store them in the trunk of your ride) have made it harder to jump right in and create mayhem from hour one.

Plus, the police response has been overhauled. Commit brazen crimes and cameras will capture your appearance. Witnesses will describe your clothes or getaway car. Wanted levels now measure not just the size of the armed response, but its sophistication, so speed and stealth become vital. Do a job cleanly, destroy the evidence, get out fast without tripping alarms or blowing stuff up and you're golden. Go loud and cops will search whole regions for you, using helicopters and canine units. They'll hunt you until you change your appearance, swap cars, or simply flee.

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

To call the game a masterpiece seems like a cheap, throwaway declaration because after years of development and hundreds of millions of dollars spent, a masterpiece feels… expected, right? Like if it wasn't a masterpiece, that would feel somehow personally insulting. Like they just didn't try hard enough. But the truth is, these things can go wrong so easily. They are enormous, unwieldy, lumbering projects that can fall apart for any number of reasons — and do all the time.

Sponsor Message

But this one didn't. There is a gloss on it that feels like love. A polish so fine that if you're not looking for it, you might not even notice the way the palm fronds move in the wind when there's weather coming in, or the light on the edge of a storm; how Lucia hangs her head out of a convertible when Jason is driving, or the way the sound of your tires changes depending on whether you're cruising on macadam or blacktop. Does it drag a little in the third act? Sure. Are there NPC glitches, targeting hang-ups and moments where you have to stop to puzzle out exactly who is betraying whom and how they're all connected? Absolutely. But at almost any point, you can walk away from the narrative for a while, call your better half, hop in your car and just drive. Everywhere you go, Leonida is alive around you in a way that no game has ever been before. There are a million stories here just waiting to be discovered or created. Pick one. See where it leads you.

But remember Mia and the alligator. Because at its core, GTA6 will always be a story about predators and prey. And no matter where you go or how powerful you think you are, you can never, ever be sure which one you are.

Jason Sheehan knows stuff about food, video games, books and Star Blazers. He's the restaurant critic at Philadelphia magazine, but when no one is looking, he spends his time writing books about giant robots and ray guns. Children of the Flying City is his latest book.

World.title: Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
World.content:
Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play

Esme Nicholson/NPR

If you were listening to this, you'd hear what isn't pictured: the whoops and wails of children playing on the swings and slides behind me, all under the watchful eye of Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze. The German expressionist lived just off this square in Berlin — named after her, Kollwitzplatz — and, at the turn of the 20th century, her children probably played here, too.

In the wake of World War I, Kollwitz's lithographs, woodcuts and sculptures fixated on the suffering and futility of war. They depict undernourished, wide-eyed children in the protective arms of mothers whose anguish is etched into their faces. Her statue, The Grieving Parents, stands in Belgium where her son Peter died at the front, aged 18.

Sponsor Message

As I turn my back briefly on the playground and aim my camera at Kollwitz, a boy jumps into the shot, up onto the statue's plinth. Playing hide and seek, he conceals himself behind Kollwitz. His friend finds him quickly and the two boys chase each other around the statue, inadvertently embracing Kollwitz like she does her own boys in her lithograph renderings.

The Kollwitz statue's presence is calm. She sits, charcoal in hand, poised to draw the happy hubbub of children growing up in a city that is safe. But with wars not so far away and Germany bringing back military service for a new generation, I feel a sudden urge to wrap my arms around my own child, just as Kollwitz did.

For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

World.title: Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
World.content:
Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.

"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."

Sponsor Message

But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.

"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.

Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image

Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.

The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.

Sponsor Message

Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.

On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.

Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.

"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."

Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.

toggle caption i Aaron Favila/AP

Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos

Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.

Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."

Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.

Sponsor Message

"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."

He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.

There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.

Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.

Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.

Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.

toggle caption i Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin

What's on the agenda for Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin

The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.

His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.

Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.

The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.

Sponsor Message

Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.

When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."

Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.

Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.

"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

World.title: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says of ongoing trade talks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that Canada is willing to sign a mutually beneficial deal with the Americans, but if U.S. President Donald Trump can't agree to those terms, then Ottawa will continue on its current trajectory: Aggressively diversifying away from the United States.

Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China as he wound down his nine-day trade mission to Europe and Asia, Carney said Canada continues "to have a series of issues" when it comes to trade with the U.S.

While there has been some progress, "we're not there yet" on putting pen to paper on an agreement, Carney said.

Carney met with Trump in China Wednesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit — a conversation he described as "reasonably direct" but one that didn't produce a trade breakthrough.

With the prospect of a U.S. trade deal uncertain, Carney said Canada's talks with China have gone "exceptionally well" and are "very rational," and he has secured meaningful market access for Canadian commodities in return for allowing a relatively small number of Chinese EVs to be imported at lower tariff rates.

As part of his Asian tour, Carney also brokered two free trade deals in a single day with the Philippines and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc, which combined represent a $6-trillion market.

Canada is also on the cusp of a free trade deal with India within the next three months, Carney said.

Altogether, Canada currently has free trade access to economies with some two billion people, he said, and that number will soon reach three billion.

"We'd like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy," Carney said.

Carney arrives at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Monday, ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. (Pedro Pardo/Getty Images)

Asked if the U.S. midterm results changed anything for Canada — the Democrats won both houses of U.S. Congress in a landslide — Carney said, "No, is the short answer."

Carney said the only thing that will improve relations between the two countries is a U.S. reversal of anti-Canada trade actions that are designed to destroy key sectors of the economy.

"What will change views is policy decisions that are taken and that will stick," he said. "It will take action as opposed to intent."

But even then, Carney said the government doesn't want to slide into an old pattern of ever-deeper economic integration with the U.S.

Canada doesn't want to be "coerced" or "subjugated" by the U.S., or any other major power, anymore, he said.

The overarching goal of his trade policy — brokering associate membership with the European Union and thawing relations with China — is to secure Canada's long-term sovereignty, Carney said.

"I'm not saying the transition is easy," Carney said. "It's not — there are challenges there."

World.title: Cadet captain says he's paralyzed from waist down after attack while distributing Remembrance Day poppies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A cadet leader who underwent spinal surgery after a violent attack says he is paralyzed from the waist down and will require months of physical rehabilitation.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel provided an update on his situation last week in a statement shared online by a Hamilton member of Parliament.

Kunkel says he is in continual pain and his doctors cannot give him a prognosis at this time, but he remains "hopeful and positive."

He thanked those who have reached out to express support or donated to an online fundraiser set up for his family.

Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets taking donations for Remembrance Day poppies.

They said two boys approached young air cadets who were taking donations for poppies in front of a restaurant on Barton Street East and blew an air horn "directly into their ears."

Investigators said a man who was supervising the cadets followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them, leading to a struggle.

They allege a woman jumped in to help the youths and assaulted the air cadet leader, who fell to the ground. One of the boys allegedly hit the man multiple times.

A 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman were charged with aggravated assault in the incident.

Kunkel said the youth 'tried to run away'

In his statement, Kunkel said he wanted to clarify some details of what happened that day.

He said he confronted a youth in the restaurant about assaulting one of the cadets and told him they needed to go to the front and call police. The youth "immediately tried to run away," Kunkel said, adding he grabbed the youth's backpack and started walking toward the front of the restaurant while asking staff to call police.

The youth started punching him, he said, and a woman intervened on the youth's behalf. Kunkel said he told her the boy had assaulted a cadet and they needed to speak with police.

While his attention was on the woman, the boy grabbed the lanyard holding Kunkel's car key and ripped it off his neck, he said. When Kunkel reached to grab it back, the woman "blindsided" him, slamming him into a concrete pillar, he said.

"My legs buckled beneath me and I collapsed," he said. "While I was lying on the ground helpless, the young male proceeded to violently punch me directly in the face numerous times."

Kunkel was taken to hospital and underwent surgery that night, he said.

A GoFundMe page set up on behalf of Kunkel and his family said he is the commanding officer of 826 Gryphon Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, and has been with the cadets for 20 years.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride through the American psyche
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For years, Grand Theft Auto VI has been many things: a meme for how long fans have been waiting for a new GTA title; a billion-dollar release; a potential spike in vacation and "sick" days; a talking point for unionization and workers' rights; a ticking cultural time bomb.

This week, finally, it's also ... a video game.

I've spent nearly 70 hours so far in GTAVI — which launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles tomorrow — speeding across Leonida, the satirical version of Florida built by U.S.-based Rockstar Games (published by Take-Two Interactive). I've been following the story of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a young couple caught in a web of crime and conspiracies.

After dozens of robberies and car chases, it feels like I've only scratched the surface. But it doesn't take too long to learn that beyond an impossibly lavish presentation, this is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've been waiting for.

What's the story?

We first meet our dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, in a flashback: after a chance meeting at a carjacking, they flee the police and quickly fall in love. Flash forward and Lucia, in a moment of desperation, gets arrested after trying to rob a payday loans store.

Then we get the biggest surprise that previews have not hinted at: Jason and Lucia have a newborn boy named Tomas.

An animated gif shows the jumbo screens at Sankofa Square in Toronto displaying ads for Grand Theft Auto VI on Monday, and pedestrians walking near the EB Games store advertising the latest instalment in the video game series that launches worldwide on Thursday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Some months after her arrest, Lucia gets out (an early release program, thanks to an overcrowded carceral state). She reconnects with Jason, and the two quickly go back to a life of crime with the ultimate goal of saving enough cash to live crime-free with their son, who is currently in Lucia's aunt's custody.

Jason and Lucia are the most convincingly realistic protagonists of the series, with sympathetic aspirations and struggles with relatable trauma, coupled with a cavalier criminal charisma and simmering chemistry that sells the fact that this is, above all, a love story.

Grand Theft Auto VI wears its crime movie influences on its sleeve. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

The same can't be said for most of the game's supporting cast. It's a parade of one-dimensional racial or regional stereotypes, nearly all of them contemptible by design: twitchy drug runners, gun-toting rap moguls and lecherous lawyers.

These types of unbelievable caricatures stick out more when placed next to the believable Jason and Lucia.

How does it look?

The word that keeps coming to mind about GTAVI's world is "astonishing."

The near-photorealistic Vice City feels like a living, breathing city, and it's surrounded by ocean beaches, swamplands and suburbs, along with a full-sized international airport terminal.

Public art adorns sections of Vice City in Grand Theft Auto VI, while the city streets are packed with drivers and citizens. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Convenience stores feature barred windows and fading posters. Suburban lawns are frayed and worn where they meet the roads. The concrete that makes up the massive freeway networks is mottled and cracked.

You'll see non-player characters walking or sitting while having semi-realistic background conversations. Ocean Beach is packed with sunbathers of all body types, while the Jack of Hearts strip club is filled shoulder-to-shoulder with rowdy patrons and twerking models.

How does it play?

GTAVI's critical missions play out like a major scene in a modern summer blockbuster movie: breathtaking action and a dozen things happening (or exploding) at once. Screen wipes will zip you between Jason and Lucia's points of view as a heist goes wrong or a gang war erupts.

Unfortunately, they're also the least engaging for the player.

As Lucia struggles with a mercenary in a stairwell in a scene ripped from a John Wick movie, you'll do little more than mash the square button to get out of a chokehold. Jason might fend off a dozen armed goons, but it'll only last a few seconds before you're whisked away to another scene.

PHOTOS | Grand Theft Auto VI ads hit the streets:

It feels more like you're strapped into an amusement park ride than an active participant, as the game desperately tries to prove that it's cool. (To be fair, it is very cool.)

Peel away the bombast and you'll find GTAVI's true strength in its conventional core: stealing cars, robbing stores and banks, and losing the cops.

Every stick-up could follow the same rough outline: flash your guns at the store clerks, intimidate security out of trying to shoot you down, before smashing and grabbing cash, jewelry and more, and getting the heck out of there as quickly as possible.

But there's always a tension with every new location: How many guards are there? Will someone on-site know the safe code, where the good stuff is? Will a jittery customer try to wrestle you down? Are the police too far away to respond, or just around the corner?

Players will make most of their money by stealing it, whether from banks, corner stores or hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

This is an open-world game, though, and familiar technical frustrations frequently show up.

Shooting and fisticuffs are competent, but clunky. Your AI-controlled companion might choose to slowly saunter to your getaway vehicle instead of jumping in, giving the cops precious few seconds to swarm you. Inventory management quickly becomes a mess, as you try to keep track of which guns Jason or Lucia are holding.

Speeding from the police or gang members can get hairy, with most cars swerving or spinning out more quickly than you might expect, until you shell out for high-end street racers or all-terrain vehicles.

Do I really need to buy gas for my car?

Yes, but it's only an occasional pit stop. Much has been said of the other life simulation aspects that have been added to the game.

Nearly every possible interaction will have an effect on Jason and Lucia's stats. Working out at the gym keeps their health and stamina up. Eat junk food and you'll gain weight; don't eat at all and hunger will slow your health regeneration. Even small actions like petting a cat will buff your focus meter (used to slow down time during gunfights).

Players will need to work out at the gym and eat (mostly) healthy foods to keep Jason and Lucia in peak health. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

It's a thoughtful system, but the actions aren't terribly engaging. Most gym activities simply ask you to mash or hold buttons at a certain pace, for example.

Taking the time to make Jason and Lucia hold hands, watch TV together or just give a kiss on the cheek will build their relationship meter. It's a neat bit of world-building, though ignoring it will do little to impede your journey.

How political does it get?

The GTA series has always been known for its biting satire on American culture, but even its creators have admitted the last decade's absurdities have made that more difficult, especially when things veer into the explicitly political.

To their credit, the writers walk close to that line.

A right-wing talk radio channel features a blowhard sports host who complains about trans women in sports and promises to "make sports great again." Left-wing-coded environmentalists attempt to free captive animals while spewing nonsense about energy crystals.

Tyrone, seated right, is one of your main contacts in Grand Theft Auto VI. He'll pay top dollar for stolen drugs you'll find in rival gangs' hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Every end of the spectrum appears to be fair game, but the end result feels like blanket nihilism. Everyone is either selfish, a liar, an idiot or all three. It's hard to find truly incisive humour when the only punchline is "man, that guy sucks."

The world is full of painfully obvious knock-off brands, nearly all of them sexual innuendos or fart jokes. (The finance app on your phone is called BuckMe; a popular lemon-lime soda is called Sprunk.)

Taken individually, most of these jokes are passable. Some dialogue is laugh-out-loud hilarious. Before long, though, it becomes exhausting.

Occasionally, missions veer into gritty and even chilling drama, often revolving around the gang wars in Vice City. In momentary flashes, they're as gripping as something from The Wire; but they're jarring when placed next to gags you'd find on Family Guy.

Raul Batista leads a crew of thieves and safecracking experts in Vice City. Jason and Lucia will work with his team in a series of high-stakes heist missions in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Can kids play it?

GTAVI is rated M for Mature (ages 17 and older) by the Entertainment Software Rating Board. Its description is a full bingo card of offensive content: blood and gore, nudity, strong language, use of drugs and more.

Gunplay is graphic, with blood and bits flying with a good headshot, though it's nothing you won't see in a modern shooter or horror game. Sexual content oscillates from romantic love scenes to churlish BDSM gags. Every swear word you can think of gets generous representation.

It's not a game for kids, obviously. Parents of teenagers will know what they can handle, but might want to play together and talk about it along the way.

Grand Theft Auto VI features several locations and regions outside of the Miami-like Vice City, including smaller suburbs and towns, swamplands and forests. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Should you play it?

Chances are you're among the millions of people who've already pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto VI.

So while the latest GTA won't change how designers think about open-world video games, it comes in such a lavish presentation and package most players won't care.

For them, it will be more than enough to sit back on the couch while driving down Leonida's freeways at night, with neon-soaked skyscrapers in the distance as classic '80s rock plays on the radio.

World.title: Fatal police shootings in Nunavik shattered trust. Can these new intervention teams help?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The sun is nearly set by the time Ariane Richard starts her shift in Kuujjuaq, a village in northern Quebec.

And on an evening in early November, her back seat is full — with a police officer, a new intervention worker in training and a CBC News team, in tow.

After six years working in the North as an intervention worker, Richard says she's seen a lot.

"A lot of stuff you're not necessarily ready to see," she said.

But her newest role is a bit different.

For the past year, she's co-ordinated Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) and led the unit in Kuujjuaq — pairing intervention workers with officers in an effort to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force.

Established in the northern Quebec communities of Puvirnituq, Kuujjuaq and most recently Salluit, the Inuit-led organization says the team is meant to address pressing issues: suicide prevention, intimate partner violence, mental health crises and at-risk children.

The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups.

The team was first established in the region in 2019.

WATCH | Pairing social workers with law enforcement: Could this intervention team help villages trust police in northern Quebec? | Duration closed caption 3:36 Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) in Kuujjuaq is pairing social workers with officers in a bid to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force. The initiative comes after years of distrust between Inuit and the Nunavik Police Service.

It expanded over the last couple of years in the shadow of eroding trust between Inuit and the Nunavik Police Service (NPS) — compounded by several high-profile police-involved shootings.

In 2024, communities across the province took part in marches to denounce police brutality in the region after police fatally shot 26-year-old Joshua Papigatuk and injured his twin brother, Garnet, in an incident that made headlines across the province.

Not long after, the family of Mark R. Annanack, who died in Kangiqsualujjuaq, Que., following a fatal police shooting , co-signed a letter calling for changes within the NPS .

This month, Annanack's father and Papigatuk's surviving twin brother, Garnet, issued a statement to members of the National Assembly, ministers and Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Chief of the Nunavik Police Service, Jean-François Bernier, says public trust is "coming back slowly," but that there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

The families are demanding immediate investments for an overhaul of local judicial and policing services.

"Inuit are dying and our dignity suffers," read the release, issued on a Facebook page titled "Justice for Inuit," just days ahead of the two-year anniversary of Joshua Papigatuk's death, on Nov. 4.

On Tuesday, the province's Crown prosecutor's office announced that charges would not be laid against the officers who shot and killed Joshua.

'MIT should be in every village'

Having partnerships with units like the MIT helps build trust between police and the community, says Capt. Mélanie Panneton, in charge of the southeast division for the NPS, who has worked in Nunavik for the past 11 years.

Capt. Mélanie Panneton is in charge of the southeast division for the Nunavik Police Service. She says the MIT can help build trust. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

"It helps us focus on another side of policing," she said, sitting in Kuujjuaq's police headquarters, located in the centre of town.

"It's always a learning opportunity," she said. "It's beneficial to put more [of] the focus on de-escalation."

Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, stands by the MIT approach, noting it responds to situations that aren't necessarily a policing matter.

Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, says she sees results in how the unit builds trust with families. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

According to her, "MIT should be in every village, because it's the best way to intervene."

"It's less stressful for family to see MIT coming, just Saqijuq, than [the Department of Youth Protection]," she said.

"There's the image that we're going to take children and send them down south and then family won't ever see their children again."

Bringing 'softness' and fairy wings

Nunavik police officer Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio is opening his mind to a new way of doing things.

Here he was, in the backseat of Saqijuq's MIT vehicle earlier this month, holding pink sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand.

The day earlier, he says he wore the accessories after a special request from a young girl the team was assisting.

Nunavik Police officer, Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio, seen here with Sophie Bergeron, a trainee on the intervention team, held sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand at the request of a young girl the team assisted in November. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

"And now she's actually asking for me to put it back again," he said smiling, during a ride-along with CBC News, on his way to meeting the girl for a second consecutive day.

The streets were dark as the team hurried to help transfer the child to a group home in the northern community, located along Quebec's Ungava Bay.

"I told you I had the wand," said Bertrand Dell'Accio, greeting her alongside Richard and the team's newest trainee, Sophie Bergeron.

He handed the girl a sparkly accessory as a gift and followed her up the group home's steps.

Later, back in the car, he noted despite his being on shift — and in uniform — his role that night was meant as a support.

"To show the population as well that police officer[s] are not just here to arrest people, but they're here to get involved," he said.

The MIT — when not on call — is focused on prevention and building connections by participating in local events, like karaoke, volleyball or trick-or-treating, says Richard.

Ariane Richard drove the mobile unit's car one evening in November. The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups. (CBC)

"My goal and our goal … is really to bring a little bit of softness and joy even when it's a rough time," she said.

"There's a way to bring … happiness in any of our interventions, and that's really the goal of it."

Trust in Nunavik police was at 'its lowest,' says chief

Confidence in police has historically been lower amongst Indigenous people in Canada, as outlined in a number of Statistics Canada reports.

In the 2020 general social survey , 22 per cent of Indigenous people reported having little or no confidence in the police.

When Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier first began in the role in 2025, he says confidence in the police was at "its lowest."

"I truly understand why," said Bernier. "People need answers. They need to be closer to their police force. The police force need[s] to be more transparent."

In 2025, CBC reported that the rate of fatal shootings by police officers was roughly 73 times higher in Nunavik than the Quebec average, according to the provincial police watchdog.

Since last year, Bernier says, public trust is "coming back slowly." But he says there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention.

Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier says part of his approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

Even when the Crown prosecutor determines that police acted lawfully, Bernier calls it a "lose-lose situation," that leaves families, communities — and the police service — with deep wounds.

"Because I don't know any police officers who get up in the morning and say, 'Oh, I hope I'll be involved in this serious incident and I'm going to fight for my life today,'" he said.

"It doesn't work that way."

Part of Bernier's approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible, he says, and answering hard questions.

By the end of this year, he noted he will open a new position within his executive office for an Inuk advisor that will report to him. The person's mandate will be to challenge the decisions of the police service.

Rebuilding trust, Bernier says, will take time.

"Once I get the full confidence of the public, and I will," he said. "We're never going to lose the confidence again."

Problems to continue if justice is out of Inuit hands, says elder

But Charlie Watt, an Inuk elder and former Canadian senator, says he's heard that same message many times over his lifetime.

He was one of the negotiators for the 1974 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.

The agreement was Canada's first modern Indigenous land claims treaty, and signalled a new era for Nunavimmiut to gain more self-governance, including in policing.

Charlie Watt says he is thinking about creating a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling the justice issues. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

At one point, Watt pushed for the idea of setting up the police force under Inuit control. To this day, however, he says Inuit life continues to be handled by "the outside."

"We don't have our self government in place," he said. "That's our biggest enemy at the moment."

Sitting in his living room, overlooking the Kuujjuaq River, 82-year-old Watt is surrounded by mementos from his life in politics, and photos of family growing up on the other side of the river.

The modern community of Kuujjuaq, now the largest in Nunavik, completely changed over the course of Watt's lifetime.

Kuujjuaq, located along the Ungava Bay, is the largest northern village in the region of Nunavik. (Rachel Watts/CBC)

Reflecting on justice and policing systems in his region, his perspective is that the relationship between police and Inuit never used to be this bad.

"They have [a] tendency to shoot before they open their mouth," he said, pointing to the fact that some officers get training in western Canada, through the RCMP.

"You have to train them where they [are] going to do the work."

He says Inuit also have to take on more responsibility, when it comes to policing their communities.

He is thinking about leveraging his experience to help jumpstart a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling justice issues.

When it comes to long-term solutions to systemic problems, the elder says: "They can only come from the Inuit."

World.title: Nathan Fielder lookalike contest crowns a deadpan winner
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dozens of Nathan Fielder lookalikes delighted a packed audience of comedy fans at a Toronto Theatre on Tuesday night to answer a simple, if oddly specific question: Who looks most like Nathan Fielder?

Thirty contestants sporting grey wigs took part in the competition devoted to the Canadian comedian and filmmaker with the unnervingly earnest persona — known for the docu-comedies Nathan for You, The Rehearsal and the recent hit documentary You Can See Everything.

The lookalikes came dressed for the role, with some wearing headphones and button-down shirts, while others leaned into Fielder’s signature blank stare and dry delivery.

But resemblance was only part of the assignment. Over the course of the evening at the Paradise Theatre, they faced a business pitch challenge, a staring contest and a final conversation with an Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced tech executive at the centre of You Can See Everything, impersonated by Second City alumnus Hannah Spear.

The pitch round produced schemes worthy of Nathan For You, in which Fielder plays an awkward business consultant fielding extreme, absurd marketing ideas to help real struggling businesses. One lookalike contestant named David, a drummer, proposed growing his indie band's audience on Instagram without paying for ads. He said the band had 250 followers, "and statistically 40 of those are my mom’s friends" before presenting a QR code to follow the band.

Another pitch was for a celebrity lookalike contest in which winners would pay rather than collect prize money. "This is not a prize list. This is a price list," said one contestant.

Host Andrew Phung, known for Kim’s Convenience and Run the Burbs, welcomed the crowd with a suitably grand introduction, calling Fielder "a cultural icon, a Canadian pop culture phenomenon and a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools with very good grades" — a playful nod to the opening tagline of Nathan for You and to the fact that Fielder really did earn a business degree from the University of Victoria in 2005.

Phung and Spear judged the contest alongside Kelly White and Megan Bianco, hosts of the Nathan for Us fan podcast.

Thirty contestants and fans of awkward comedy filled the Paraside Theatre on Tuesday. (Christine Pagulayan/CBC)

The judges narrowed the group to three finalists, evaluating each contestant’s appearance, costume, physicality, business pitch and improv skills. Toronto’s Jayden Williams took the crown, after staying in character throughout the competition.

"There were some Nathan ringers out there," Daniels told CBC News. "I’m shocked and flattered that I won."

Daniels said friends had repeatedly sent him a photo of the event flyer until he finally decided to enter. He also had experience: he’d already won two Halloween contests dressed as Fielder.

When asked about staying in character throughout the competition, Daniels responded with a pause and a deflection worthy of the comedian he was impersonating: "I really, I don’t know what you’re talking about."

Daniels, centre, said he’d already won two Halloween contests dressed as Fielder. (Lucky Osunbiyi Photography)

The contest attracted both longtime fans and people who had only recently discovered the comedian. Some were hooked by Fielder’s deadpan delivery; others found his comedy compelling precisely because it feels a little unsettling.

"He scares me, and that’s why I like him," one attendee said. Fielder, the fan added, seems "like an alien on Earth that’s pretending to be human."

Another fan called him "Canadian excellence," adding that his older work had found a wider audience as his profile grew.

After the winner was crowned, the crowd settled in to watch the first episode of The Curse, Fielder’s series with Benny Safdie.

The contest arrived amid renewed attention around Fielder’s work, including You Can See Everything, the hit documentary co-directed with Lance Oppenheim that examines disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Fans at the theatre said the film had introduced them to Fielder or deepened their interest in his work.

Fielder lookalike contests have also been held in cities including New York, Los Angeles and Sydney. But for one night, Toronto’s many Nathans shared a stage, and one went home with the title, "the Nathanest Nathan," as dubbed by those on social media.

Daniels said he hoped to see more lookalike contests across more Canadian cities, including Montreal and Hamilton. "But it was nice to have one in Toronto, with one of Canada’s heroes," he said.

World.title: Apartment building collapses after explosion, fire in Glace Bay, N.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Crews from several fire departments in Cape Breton are on the scene of a building collapse and structure fire in Glace Bay, N.S., that injured 17 people.

The explosion happened around 6 a.m. on Wednesday at Pizza 67, a local pizzeria. The front of the building at 130 Commercial St. collapsed, said Cape Breton Regional Police.

The force of the explosion broke windows on nearby structures.

Shortly afterward, a fire started in the building, which has the pizza shop on the ground floor and about 20 apartments on the upper level.

Crews from more than a half-dozen fire departments responded to the incident. (Ernie Bagnell)

Cape Breton Regional Municipality spokesperson Christina Lamey said 17 people had minor injuries, and 14 of them were transported to Glace Bay Hospital.

Lamey said it is still unclear if there were any fatalities.

"The activity that's currently underway is to try to ascertain how many people were actually in the building," she said.

"We of course know of the 17 people that were assessed early in the morning but it will take some time to ascertain if everybody had made it out of the building."

A CBC reporter on the scene said most of the building has collapsed, and the structure was left with only one wall standing.

The explosion happened at 6 a.m. on Wednesday. (Ernie Bagnell)

Crews from seven or eight fire departments responded to the incident, as well as police and paramedics.

Ernie Bagnell, who lives in Glace Bay, was out early this morning grabbing a coffee when he spotted smoke downtown and drove to the scene. By that time, he said, the front of the building had collapsed.

"The firemen were there on top of it, up in the air, everywhere, trying to put it out, sirens in the distance," he said.

Lamey said as of 11 a.m., crews are still fighting the blaze, watering the site and an excavator is moving debris.

Crews working on a ladder truck fight the fire. (Ernie Bagnell)

The building is located near the intersection of Main Street and is next door to the Savoy Theatre.

Lamey said there are several street closures in the downtown area, and people are being asked to stay away from the area to allow emergency responders to do their work.

A comfort centre has opened at the Glace Bay Miners' Forum for building residents.

Lamey said it's too early to know what caused the explosion, collapse or fire.

WATCH | Explosion, fire rocks Glace Bay: Building collapses after explosion in Cape Breton | Duration 0:44 Cape Breton fire crews battled a major blaze and building collapse in Glace Bay, N.S. As the CBC's Kyle Moore reports there are multiple injuries.
