World.title: Hakeem Jeffries poised to become 1st Black U.S. House Speaker, after internal vote by Democrats
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the country's first Black American with the gavel.

Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress, including Republican members, convenes in January. CNN reported that there were 11 No votes out of 262 cast.

The speaker of the House is second in the presidential line of succession, behind the vice-president.

Jeffries ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in the recent midterm elections in a rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump and the party in power.

Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of returning Democrats and newly elected members demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.

Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority.

"I embrace those conversations," he said.

Elevated to leader in 12 years

Jeffries will be part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, which would also represent historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.

Jeffries, 56, was born in Brooklyn to a mother who was a social worker and a father who was a substance abuse counsellor. He attended Binghamton University for undergraduate studies, earning a master's in public policy from Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., and a law degree from New York University.

After two unsuccessful bids for a state assembly seat in New York, he succeeded in 2006. He was elected to U.S. Congress eight years later, joining the Congressional Caucus.

WATCH | Some Democrats believe a change in approach is needed in Senate: Chuck Schumer facing challenge for U.S. Senate leadership | Duration closed caption 3:11 It's been decades since U.S. Democrats had a contested election for Senate leadership. But Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland says he'll run to oust current leader Chuck Schumer.

There are seven races yet to be projected in the 435-seat House of Representatives. Democrats have sewn up 257 seats, and with one of the biggest incoming majorities in decades, Jeffries will have room to spare, unlike current Speaker Mike Johnson from the Republicans.

When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party's electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era. Pelosi, No. 2 Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had often moved together, rising, and then stepping back, from their long-held positions.

Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.

"There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries," Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. "I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising."

The Senate Democrats will decide on their leader early next month. Chuck Schumer of New York, who has been majority leader before, faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.

Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House "are quite different."

She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others.

"His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction," Ansari said.

"It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we're going to do in the majority and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days."

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 18, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

NSA Claims “Temporary Degradation” Behind Outage of Classified Internal Network

Nov 18, 2026

The National Security Agency — the largest spy agency in the U.S. — says a “temporary degradation” is behind an outage of its classified internal network. The network, known as NSANet, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning, and some NSA staff have been unable to access their workplace systems, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for personnel. U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.

Apple and Google Hit by Widespread Service Outages

Nov 18, 2026

Apple on Tuesday confirmed widespread service outages on many of its iPhone apps, including Apple Pay and iCloud. Meanwhile, thousands of Gmail users reported disruptions that Google later said were not related to any broad internal system interruptions. This comes amidst a series of other disruptions to air travel, banking and technology infrastructure, including a massive outage at Microsoft last week that disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries.

Nvidia’s Board of Directors Reportedly Not Considering Bringing Back Jensen Huang as CEO

Nov 18, 2026

Nvidia’s board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO. That’s despite Huang releasing a statement that he would be”honored to return as CEO.” Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO, in light of his affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. This comes as Jensen Huang is expected to testify behind closed doors on December 1 before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence ​Committee.

Xi Personally Greets Trump on Tarmac in Shenzhen, Breaking Precedent

Nov 18, 2026

Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted President Trump on the tarmac when he landed in Shenzhen earlier today for the APEC summit, breaking precedent. After Trump stepped off Air Force One, he and Xi shook hands and hugged each other. The two leaders are set to hold a historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.

Alaska’s Former Democratic Congressmember Peltola Defeats Incumbent GOP Senator Sullivan

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: X/MaryPeltola

In Alaska, former Democratic Congressmember Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola becomes the first Indigenous woman from Alaska elected to the U.S. Senate. She won with 50.1% of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.8%. Her win brings the Democratic majority in the Senate to 56 seats. Peltola posted this message on social media after the race was called.

Sen.-elect Mary Peltola: “I’m so grateful you’ve put your trust in me, Alaska, and I’m ready to get to work. The future is full of opportunities for us to make Alaska a better place across the state. I’m looking forward to working hand in hand with all Alaskans over the next six years. Thank you again.”

Settlers Kill 72-Year-Old Palestinian Grandmother in the Occupied West Bank

Nov 18, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers killed a 72-year-old Palestinian grandmother and wounded at least 10 others in an attack on the outskirts of Jericho. The woman was identified as Fadda Mohammed Fheidat. She was standing outside of her home when settlers began shooting at her and her family members, fatally striking Fheidat in the head. This is a witness.

Ahmed Aref: “We went outside the house after hearing the children shouting. Then everything escalated. The settlers started shooting. I was inside the house with the elderly woman. We went downstairs, and she was behind me. She stopped at this spot, and I walked past her. I looked back and thought she was still standing, but when I looked again, I found her lying on the ground with blood coming from her head. Look, her blood is here on the road.”

Israeli settlers have recently violently moved into Jericho, seizing several Palestinian homes.

In related news, the United Kingdom has sanctioned eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, as well as a settler group blocking humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Meanwhile, Australia has imposed sanctions on three Israeli individuals and four Israeli organizations for their role in expanding illegal Israeli settlements and settler violence in the West Bank.

Guardian: IDF Uploaded 3.5 Million Photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s Platform

Nov 18, 2026

A new report by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham in The Guardian shows that the Israeli military uploaded 3.5 million photos to Amazon’s Rekognition platform to assist in its facial recognition of Palestinians soon after the invasion of Gaza in 2023. Face recognition technology is routinely used at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, and images captured at checkpoints have been used to surveil and target Palestinians.

Israeli Lawmakers Elect Matan Kahana as Speaker of Knesset in Blow to Netanyahu

Nov 18, 2026

In Israel, lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana, an ally of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, as speaker of the Knesset. It’s a major defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose candidate lost the race for speaker. Kahana was backed by both Jewish-led opposition parties and Arab-led parties.

U.N. Warns Fighting Is Worsening Health Crisis in Taiz, Yemen

Nov 18, 2026

The U.N. warned Tuesday that fighting and road closures are worsening the health crisis in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz, where water supplies meet just 8% of residents’ needs. Hospitals report thousands of cases of acute diarrhea, along with suspected dengue and cholera. This is a government employee in Taiz.

Mansour Mohammed: “We are in a situation, in a suffocating crisis, in a suffocating crisis. This siege has caused a suffocating crisis among all citizens. They can’t live, can’t get out and can’t get in. They sit silent inside and can’t earn a living.”

WaPo: Brazil Police Probes If MAGA Donor Group Linked to Vance Illegally Interfered in Brazil’s Presidential Election

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Emily J. Higgins

The Washington Post reports Brazil’s Federal Police is investigating whether Rockbridge Network, a conservative donor group co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and Chris Buskirk, illegally interfered in the Brazilian presidential election in order to favor far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the investigation after the heated runoff between Bolsonaro and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Dino cited allegations by a political activist named Renan Santos, who himself ran for president in the election and said he allegedly received messages from a Rockbridge intermediary searching for a conservative candidate that the MAGA donor group could back in the Brazilian presidential election. The probe also follows complaints by Lula’s Workers’ Party of possible U.S. interference. Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Florida last month after losing the election. He faces multiple criminal investigations back in Brazil.

AP: Immigrant Children Held in Cold, Sunless Rooms for Up to a Month

Nov 18, 2026

The Associated Press reports that immigrant children in the custody of Customs and Border Protection are being detained in cold, sunless rooms for up to a month at a time — far exceeding the legal limit of 72 hours. A legal motion filed by several advocacy groups also revealed immigrant parents held across CBP facilities in the Texas and California southern borderlands have reported widespread due process violations, including phone calls with lawyers that were restricted to less than five minutes. The parents have described being detained with their children in freezing rooms with cement floors while the lights are kept on day and night, making it hard for the children to sleep.

146,000 People Participate in Nationwide Protests in France

Nov 18, 2026

In France, about 146,000 people participated in peaceful protests across the country over the rising cost of living. High school and university students joined some private sector workers on Tuesday in the latest nationwide protests. This is a health worker.

Health worker: “We are paid a miserable amount. That’s one of our demands. We can no longer survive. I speak with my colleagues. It’s impossible to make ends meet at the end of the month. We can no longer do so, even though we have a salary. Our salaries as health workers is nearly minimum wage.”

Egyptian Writer Abdelrahman ElGendy Blocked from Entering the U.S.

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Abdelrahman ElGendy

The Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy has been blocked from entering the U.S. and is unable to attend this year’s National Book Awards. He is a finalist for the nonfiction award for his book “Huna” about his time as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy may also be ineligible for the prize since the National Book Awards rules require authors to be a U.S. citizen, a permanent U.S. resident or “maintain their primary, long-term home in the United States.” ElGendy currently lives in Europe, though he had lived in the U.S. for three years. He fled the U.S. last year fearing he would be arrested by ICE over his opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and criticism of U.S. relations with Egypt.

Bahraini Human Rights Activist Nabeel Rajab Dies at 62

Nov 18, 2026

Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab died of a heart attack Tuesday in Turkey at the age of 62. Rajab led the Bahrain Center for Human Rights and became a leading voice of Bahrain’s 2011 pro-democracy uprising. He was jailed repeatedly, spending more than six years in prison. He was most recently arrested in 2016 for criticizing Bahrain’s role in the war on Yemen and was released in 2020. He later fled to Turkey fearing rearrest. Nabeel Rajab spoke to Democracy Now! back in 2014 about his role in pro-democracy protests in Bahrain.

Nabeel Rajab: “I urge American people to pressure the American government, through your member of parliament, through your congressman, to change the situation, to ask the American government not to support dictators.”

World.title: Bedbug Epidemic in Sancti Spiritus, Cuba
World.content:
Forces the Provincial Court to close

Amidst cardboard, bags, household waste, and abandoned furniture, there appear mattresses that residents identify as infested. / 14ymedio

The infestation has spread to police stations, prisons, public buildings, and homes, while residents improvise remedies to prevent the insects from invading their houses.

Por Mercedes García (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – “Don’t sit down, there are bedbugs.” The warning, given by a police investigator to a citizen who came to file a complaint, sums up an infestation spreading throughout the city of Sancti Spíritus, one that no longer distinguishes between neglected homes, spotless households, and government offices. The insects have found shelter in furniture, mattresses, and public spaces, while residents desperately search for ways to keep them from entering their homes.

Ramón, a self-employed businessman who recently experienced an attempted robbery at his business, has had to visit the First Police Unit several times to follow up on his complaint. Each time, he tells 14ymedio, the investigator has advised him to remain standing. According to his account, the infestation affects the lobby, the holding cells, and other areas where detainees, officers, and visitors come together.

“While I was outside the station waiting, I also heard that the mattresses in Nieves Morejón prison are just as badly infested,” Ramón adds. Two women waiting to be seen to were describing the situation involving a family member imprisoned at that facility. “The prisoners would rather sleep on the floor because the beds are crawling with bedbugs,” the man says.

The alarm has also reached the Provincial People’s Court, whose headquarters had to close because of a bedbug infestation. This would not be the first time. Employees and people familiar with the building’s operations say that services had previously been suspended because of the same problem, but a higher-level order forced them to resume without removing the affected furniture.

This time, they say, the insects were visible to people arriving to conduct business. Some visitors turned around as soon as they noticed them; others preferred to wait standing rather than risk carrying an unwanted passenger home in their clothing. Finally, a decision was made to close the premises again.

For residents on the block, the problem does not end behind the Court’s doors. They fear the insects will spread from one building to another and turn their homes into another source of infestation. “It’s not easy; you lose everything. A mattress costs more than $200, and that’s where you get your rest,” says one resident, who is also worried about clothing and other belongings that could be affected.

Household ingenuity is attempting to make up for the lack of solutions. Some people place cloths soaked in bleach near their entrances and keep their shoes inside plastic bags. One grandmother in the area has gone even further: she placed all four legs of her bed inside cans containing a little kerosene. “I can’t afford to buy a new mattress, so this is what I came up with,” she explains. These are desperate measures that do not guarantee the elimination of the insects and may introduce additional health and safety risks.

The problem is not limited to the city center. In the Garaita area, a heavily traveled road between the El Parque and Kilo 12 popular councils, piles of garbage have become part of the landscape. Soviet-inspired apartment buildings and prefabricated homes stand alongside one another, housing families with widely varying economic circumstances.

Among cardboard, plastic bags, household garbage, and abandoned furniture are mattresses that residents identify as infested. Their presence is especially concerning because rummaging through discarded items to recover usable belongings has become an everyday practice. A mattress thrown out onto the street can end up transferring the problem to another home.

Fighting bedbugs is also beyond the financial reach of many households. Specialized products are difficult to find, and many are imported from other countries at prohibitive prices for people earning government salaries. City residents also question the effectiveness of the cypermethrin fumigation treatments offered by sanitation services. They say they have to pay substantial amounts for these treatments without always obtaining results.

Bedbugs can appear even in carefully cleaned spaces. They are transported among personal belongings and hide in cracks, seams, and furniture. In Sancti Spíritus, however, the combination of persistent infestations, inadequate treatments, and economic hardship threatens to turn a household nuisance into a collective problem. While institutions close their doors and families improvise barriers, the insects continue finding places to settle.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.
