The roughly 20-minute meeting focused mainly on trade, she said. Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard accompanied Sheinbaum, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer were also present. Sheinbaum said Trump was informed that “a lot of progress” has been made in bilateral trade talks and was “in a very good mood.” They agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at the Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida. 🤝 Rodríguez describes “cordial” meeting with U.S. ambassador: She said she and Ambassador Johnson reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation to manage migration flows and discussed migrant caravans, with Rodríguez reiterating the government’s public message. They also spoke about the need for U.S.-Mexico cooperation on development projects in migrants’ countries of origin, especially in Central America. The meeting came as a large migrant caravan continues to walk through Chiapas.

Why today’s mañanera matters

For a second consecutive day, President Sheinbaum joined the mañanera via video link from Shenzhen, China, where she is attending the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. She commented on her activities on Wednesday, which included a trade-focused bilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and other U.S. officials.

Later in the press conference, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez spoke about her meeting on Tuesday with U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson. Rodríguez — who is leading the federal government and the mañaneras in Sheinbaum’s absence — said on social media on Tuesday that the purpose of her meeting with Johnson was to “continue working together on migration issues for the benefit of our nations.”

Este martes sostuvimos una reunión con el embajador de #EEUU en #México, Ronald D. Johnson @USAmbMex, para seguir trabajando de manera coordinada en materia migratoria, en beneficio de nuestras naciones. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 @Claudiashein @INAMI_mx @SRE_mx @arturomedinap https://t.co/Qqic0lfdmI — Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez (@rosaicela_) November 17, 2026

Today’s mañanera underscored that there is frequent high-level engagement between Mexico and the United States on a range of issues. Sheinbaum’s meeting with Trump came at a time when Mexico and the United States are seeking to resolve a range of trade differences that contributed to the U.S. government’s decision in July to not renew the USMCA free trade agreement for an additional 16 years to 2042.

Rodríguez’s meeting with Johnson in Mexico City occurred as members of a large migrant caravan continue to walk through the southern state of Chiapas en route to Mexico City. Many of the migrants hope to eventually reach Mexico’s northern border and enter the United States.

Trump threatened last Thursday to double tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico doesn’t stop the migrant caravan.

Sheinbaum gives an update on her China trip

Flanked by Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco, Sheinbaum reported that she held a meeting on Wednesday morning with Vietnamese President Tô Lâm.

In a social media post, she wrote that the strength of the 51-year-old bilateral relationship was discussed at her meeting with the Vietnamese leader. “We expressed our interest in deepening the ties between both nations,” Sheinbaum added.

During her mañanera appearance, she also reported that she had visited a technologically advanced hospital in Shenzhen.

“We learnt about the use of artificial intelligence for health issues,” Sheinbaum said.

“We agreed to have a closer relationship with China on these issues,” she added.

Sheinbaum also said she attended a pre-APEC Leaders’ Meeting event.

On social media, she posted photos from the opening of the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. The photos include two in which she appears with Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan. Sheinbaum also posted a group photo of APEC leaders, including Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Sheinbaum reports on ‘very good’ meeting with Trump

Sheinbaum noted that she also met on Wednesday with Trump.

“Marcelo and Roberto accompanied me to a meeting with President Trump,” she said, adding that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer were also present.

“It was a meeting of around 20 minutes and we mainly spoke about trade agreements,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that Trump was informed about the progress that has been made in bilateral trade talks.

“We can say we’ve made a lot of progress,” Sheinbaum said.

“It was a very good meeting, very pleasant. President Trump was in a very good mood,” she said.

“We agreed to meet again at the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago,” Sheinbaum added, referring to next month’s G20 Leaders’ Summit in Florida.

Rodríguez reports on migration-focused meeting with US ambassador

Rodríguez described her meeting with Ambassador Johnson on Tuesday as “cordial.”

“We reviewed progress in the bilateral cooperation to manage migration flows,” she said.

Rodríguez said that she and Johnson spoke about migrant caravans, adding that she reiterated the federal government’s public message. She and Sheinbaum have stressed that no migrant caravans have reached the northern border during Trump’s second term and explained that the government tries to persuade migrants to return to their countries of origin, in part by telling them how difficult it is to enter the United States.

Rodríguez said that she and Johnson also spoke about the need for cooperation between Mexico and the United States on development projects in countries migrants are leaving, especially Central American nations.

The Mexican government has long argued that tackling poverty and crime in migrants’ countries of origin is the best way to reduce irregular migration to the United States via Mexico.

Johnson wrote on social media on Tuesday that the “meeting with Mexican authorities reinforces the work we are advancing with the Government of Mexico to combat illegal migration and dismantle human smuggling networks.”

“We are delivering results and those results are saving lives, while helping ensure that migrant caravans do not reach the U.S.-Mexico border, as President @Claudiashein has emphasized,” he added.

World.title: MND Local BCS: Stargazing, unchecked growth and an epic Baja 1000 hits the finish line
World.content:
Dark sky tourism, or seeking out night skies whose brightness is undimmed by light pollution from cities, is a fast-growing travel category. Already estimated at US $10 billion worldwide each year, per Outside, its market value is expected to double within the next 10 years. Baja California Sur (BCS), home to the lowest population density in Mexico, is poised to be a major beneficiary, with skies perfect for stargazing in many locales.

Since December 2023, the astronomical societies Mira in La Paz and Merak in Mulegé, in collaboration with the Baja California Sur Council for Science and Technology, have been tracking the quality of night skies over BCS. Last year, they reported over 70 sites around the state with apparent visual magnitudes between 18 and 21, and seven more with magnitudes above 21.5, the threshold for a pristine “astronomical sanctuary” according to Dark Sky International.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CERCA (@cercabcs)

As these regional vantage points from which to view cosmic glories have been increasingly recognized, so too have events celebrating them. The longest-running of these is “Noche de las Estrellas” (“Night of the Stars”), a national event observed in more than 120 destinations around the country, including La Paz, since 2009. The most recent edition of the astronomical fair, featuring over 20 participating organizations, took place on Nov. 14 in the state capital.

But for those who missed it, there’s another heavenly event upcoming in the state’s original capital, Loreto.

Festival Astronómico Cielo Mágico in Loreto

Loreto’s “Festival Astronómico Cielo Mágico“ (“Magical Sky Astronomical Festival”) brings together students and amateur stargazers, as well as scientists and astronomers — including David Rojas from the San Pedro Mártir Observatory in Baja California, Miguel Ángel Norzagaray from Mira, and Eduardo Sández Aguilar from Merak — for a two-day event in the Pueblo Mágico.

In addition to the telescopes set up for nighttime viewing (including at higher altitudes in the historic mountain community of San Javier), the festival will feature educational workshops, film screenings, visual exhibitions and astrophotography sessions that will help prep would-be entrants in the amateur night-photography contest.

Saturn, Jupiter, the Andromeda Galaxy and the Great Orion Nebula are all expected to be visible in Loreto in December.

Dates: Dec. 11-12

Location: Loreto and San Javier, Loreto Municipality, BCS

Cost: Free admission

Tackling unchecked growth in El Tezal

El Tezal emerged as a district composed of independent developments — from gated communities to condo complexes — about 20 years ago, and although outside the traditional boundaries of Cabo San Lucas, extraordinary growth since 2010 has brought the neighborhood within the expanding urban sprawl of the city.

Cabo San Lucas nearly tripled in population between 2010 and 2020 (soaring from 68,463 residents to 202,694), a massive leap that is still being felt in terms of the associated growing pains. This decade also saw boom times in El Tezal, as developments far outpaced infrastructure and public services. It’s not an uncommon situation in Los Cabos, but each rapidly-growing neighborhood develops its own unique collection of problems. In El Tezal, these include traffic bottlenecks, water scarcity, electrical grid overload, sewage issues and a lack of adequate parks, sidewalks and street lighting.

In an attempt to bring order to an increasingly chaotic situation, the Los Cabos City Council drafted a Partial Urban Development Plan (Programa Parcial de Desarrollo Urbano) for El Tezal in 2024, and recently opened the plan to public review and consultation before it progresses to final approval.



The consultation window runs from Nov. 12 to Dec. 2, with the first public hearing set for Nov. 17 (noon to 2 p.m.) at the Cabo San Lucas Delegation offices in Plaza León Cota Collins.

An epic finish to the 59th SCORE Baja 1000

The Baja 1000 has been run since 1967, so it took nearly 60 years for the iconic peninsular off-road race to take place entirely within the bounds of BCS, with the start and finish lines set in tourism hotspot Los Cabos (Avenida Centenario in San José del Cabo, to be exact).

It was worth the wait. The 59th SCORE Baja 1000 turned out to be one of the most remarkable in recent memory, thanks to the rugged yet picturesque routing and a record participation by Mexican drivers, with more than 121 competing, many hailing from the Baja California peninsula.

Ensenada native Alan Ampudia crossed the finish line first on elapsed time, but ultimately finished second after a post-race timing penalty. As a result, Bryce Menzies and co-driver Andy McMillin took the overall and Trophy Class crowns. Andy’s cousin Luke McMillin, who had already garnered Trophy Truck wins this year at the San Felipe 250, Baja 500 and Baja 400, finished third.

“It’s been incredible. San José del Cabo, the roads, the people,” Menzies said at the finish line. “At one point, it felt like we were racing through a forest … It was narrow and fast, with a great mix of technical terrain and wide-open stretches. That’s exactly the kind of racing I love.”

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Mexico claims narrow win over Jamaica following line-up change
World.content:
A first-half Jesús Corona goal was enough to earn Mexico a lackluster 1-0 victory over Jamaica on Tuesday night in Monterrey, setting up a Concacaf Nations League semifinal clash with Team USA in March.

The win was the first of the Rafa Márquez era and the first since Mexico defeated Ecuador 2-0 on June 30 in a World Cup Round of 32 match. El Tri had managed just two draws and lost four times since then, including a 3-2 setback against Jamaica on Saturday in the first leg of the quarterfinals.

🇲🇽 𝐆𝐎𝐎𝐎𝐎𝐎𝐎𝐎𝐋𝐋 𝐃𝐎 𝐌𝐄𝐗𝐈𝐂𝐎 🇲🇽 TECATITO CORONA EMPATA O AGREGADO PARA EL TRI 🇲🇽 MÉXICO (3) 1×0 (3) Jamaica 🇯🇲 #LigaMXBrasil https://t.co/FJaCnwiKdf — LIGA MX BRASIL 🇲🇽🇧🇷 (@LigaMexicanaBR) November 18, 2026

Although the home-and-away series ended 3-3, El Tri slipped past the underdog Jamaicans on the away-goals rule thanks to two late goals in Kingston after Mexico — No. 13 in the FIFA World Rankings — fell behind 3-0 to the 67th-ranked hosts.

Coach Márquez made six changes to his starting line-up on Tuesday after the team’s embarrassing performance in Jamaica, inserting five new players and shifting Israel Reyes to a different position on the back line.

Though El Tri dominated possession throughout (69% on the night), the team again lacked decisiveness in attack, too often playing cautiously or trying to force passes into tight spaces.

For most of the game, Jamaica sat back behind the ball, content to absorb pressure while looking for opportunities to counterattack.

The Reggae Boyz got what they were looking for in minute 24, breaking out from a poorly executed Mexico corner kick.

Renaldo Cephas beat Rodrigo Huescas to the ball, dribbled past goalie Raúl Rangel, who was out near midfield only to be chased down by skipper Erik Lira before he could get off a shot.

Ten minutes later, Mexico had the goal it needed to advance. In minute 35, Álvaro Fidalgo’s nifty pass released Julián Quiñones down the right flank. Quiñones corralled the ball, spun back toward goal and sent an angled pass into the box where Corona trapped, turned and coolly curled a left-footed shot inside the far post for the lone goal of the match.

In the second half, the more than 51,000 fans in attendance grew increasingly restless at Mexico’s inability to capitalize on its possession advantage and a crescendo of boos rained down when the referee blew his whistle at the end of 90 minutes.

While El Tri prevented Jamaica from getting a single shot on goal, its own offensive inefficiency remains a concern, especially with high-flying Team USA waiting in the semifinals.

The Americans advanced to the Nations League Final Four on the back of an 8-0 aggregate quarterfinal series victory over Haiti, while Mexico has scored just five goals in the six matches since Márquez took over.

With reports from ESPN, The Associated Press and Concacaf.com

World.title: Opinion: Why Guadalajara’s water crisis is a warning to the rest of us
World.content:
As if on cue, the moment I sat down to type this essay, the water from my faucet finally came out brown. For weeks, my friends around Guadalajara had traded stories about the city’s water crisis. In group chats, folks shared photos of brown water filling their sinks, alongside anecdotes about the new ways they’re learning to shower with store-bought water.

Paulina Cano, a lifelong resident of Guadalajara, told me the unusual smell coming from the water at her house started months ago.

“I decided to test the water at a nearby clinic, and I found out it had a bacteria that is one of the hardest to cure,” Cano told me. “Then, my mother started to get red, itchy rashes on her skin, and she needed several different creams to get rid of it.”

‘Lo que pasa en Guadalajara, pasará en tu casa’

Following weeks of protests advocating for a solution to Guadalajara’s water crisis, I knew it was only a matter of time before the situation would reach my apartment. But the moment it did, it felt like a microcosm of what Guadalajara means for the rest of the world: Simply put, it’s only a matter of time before the water crisis reaches your apartment too.

I thought of the poster I had seen repeatedly at city protests: “Lo que pasa en Guadalajara, pasará en tu casa.” — “What happens in Guadalajara will happen in your house next.”

Through my work with various environmental organizations, I have learned the phrase “sacrifice zones,” areas of the Earth we surrender to irreversible pollution, in order to create industrial projects.

Essentially, sacrifice zones are the places we collectively agree to poison, for the sake of maintaining the capitalist comforts of our society.

50 years of increasing pollution

For decades, the towns and rivers surrounding Guadalajara have become sacrifice zones for Mexican development.

Enrique Encizo, a cofounder of the local advocacy group Un Salto de Vida, recalled fond memories of growing up in El Salto near the Santiago River.

“Anytime you went to the river, there were always kids swimming and playing, women with their tubs washing baskets of clothes,” Encizo told me. “The ravine by the river was also filled with fruit trees. We would fish in the river, then harvest fruit nearby — guayabas, mangos, avocado, papaya, bananas.”

Up until the 1970s, nearby Juanacatlán Falls was known as “the Niagara of Mexico.” But in just 50 years — in Juanacatlán, El Salto and other nearby towns — corporations like Hershey’s, Nestle and IBM severely contaminated the rivers.

They became so toxic that in 2008, an 8-year-old boy died from acute arsenic poisoning after accidentally falling into the water.

Encizo noted that although El Salto contributes almost 15% to Jalisco’s GDP, it remains one of the poorest and unhealthiest towns in the state. The residents of these towns now suffer from much higher rates of hepatitis, cancer, respiratory infections and skin damage.

For example, the town of Poncitlán has some of the highest rates of kidney disease in the world. Meanwhile, other studies have shown that contamination is impacting the DNA of these populations so intensely that the next generation will inherit symptoms genetically.

Surrounded by sacrifice zones

When the water crisis hit Guadalajara these last few months, the sacrifice zone simply expanded. Those of us living in the city could no longer ignore what was happening right around the corner, in smaller towns surrounding us, because finally — and inevitably — it landed in our own homes.

In the United States, sacrifice zones similarly widen each time the government allows development on previously protected land, such as the case of Bears Ears National Monument.

At the same time, data centers — also often built near low-income communities — again expand the sacrifice zone farther and farther, contaminating nearby water sources in similar ways to what has happened in Guadalajara.

When U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently showed Congress a jar of local water from houses near a Meta data center in Georgia, it looked just like the water coming out of my friends’ faucets here.

The most important point about a sacrifice zone is that it is intentional. Corporations and governments effectively deem certain landscapes, communities and people less important than others. In Jalisco, they chose El Salto, Juanacatlán and the Santiago River.

The question then becomes: How long will it take before they choose your landscape and your community?

In Guadalajara, we now have that answer. I worry many other cities will soon get theirs too.

Failing to prevent pollution at its source

To address Guadalajara’s water crisis, President Claudia Sheinbaum promised financial resources for improving our water infrastructure.

But as journalist Jonathan Lomeli Lopez recently wrote for El Informador, “The root of many of our water-related problems lies in this obsession with prioritizing pipes and large-scale infrastructure, while failing to prevent pollution at its source.”

So long as companies can continue polluting water sources with impunity, no amount of new and improved infrastructure will make the problem go away.

Criminalizing the struggle for clean water

Unfortunately, after attending Guadalajara’s first large protest for clean water, it’s clear the government is opting to hurt and punish those protesting water conditions, rather than hold any corporation accountable. At the protest, I saw a young girl with a giant bandage wrapped around her head, as well as a young man helping carry his bloody-nosed friend by the shoulder.

For hours, police sprayed a water hose at the crowd, forming a small creek on the right side of the street — the irony of so much wasted water in a city where so many haven’t had clean water for months.

In response, the crowd chanted “Esa agua limpia, mándala a mi casa.” — “Send that clean water to my house.”

While some of the protesters in Guadalajara still face criminal charges, companies routinely contaminate water sources without facing severe consequences. And as police violence escalated during protests around the world last month, it is clear that many governments are prepared to respond in similar ways.

‘L​o que hacen en Gaza lo harán en tu casa’

It’s also important to name: Corporations have not only actively destroyed Guadalajara’s water sources, but also continue to hoard the clean water the region has left.

In her essay, “Los Acaparadores del Agua,” María Gonzalez Valencia chronicles how corporations and real estate developers essentially get first access to clean water, while the rest of the population gets stuck with whatever is left — sometimes as little as 15% of the total water available.

We have already seen this same scenario play out across Mexico — in places like Puebla and the Cholula Valley — and we’ve also seen it play out across the world.

Israel continually consumes seven times the amount of water as people in Palestine, and more recently, Doctors Without Borders spoke out against Israel’s water company systematically depriving people in Gaza of water. What’s more, this is the same water company now meddling in projects in Chihuahua, Argentina and other parts of Latin America.

At the water protest, I saw several people waving Palestinian flags. It’s clear that people recognize the connection between the water crisis in Palestine and Guadalajara, and the necessary solidarity between both places.

“L​o que hacen en Gaza lo harán en tu casa,” other protest signs read. “What they do in Gaza, they’ll do in your house next.”

Water apartheid has existed for decades, but it has become even more apparent as the Earth’s water supplies become increasingly scarce.

I worry that we underestimate the extent to which corporations and government leaders will continue doing this. And I worry about our tolerance for it — the continued respect and deference for these leaders, while those protesting their actions become criminalized.

During a recent lecture in Guadalajara, Encizo said: “The people of these towns did not kill the river. It was people whose names and surnames we know. Our streets are even named after them.”

When not seeing is not believing

The day after starting this essay, my water turned clear again. I don’t know if that means my water actually became clean, or if it just looks better, while still containing less visible contaminants that are just as dangerous.

Either way, I am starting to understand the psychological impact of all of this: how not “seeing” a social issue can turn us complacent, keep us delusional even, as we convince ourselves these issues will never reach us.

Encizo’s river memories disappeared within just a few decades. When I speak to other Guadalajara residents my age, whose families have lived here for decades, they also speak about the stark difference between their parents’ memories of Guadalajara’s rivers and their own.

“When my mother was a kid, she’d hike down to the Santiago River from the popular city trail at Huentitan, and spend the whole day there swimming,” Xochitl Esmeralda Garcia Velazco told me. “But by the time I was born, the first time I went to that same spot, it was already too contaminated. I never got the chance to do the same.”

What happens next?

I am in awe of the loss that is possible in just one generation. And I am terrified of the loss I am slowly witnessing even in the course of just a few months.

Just six months ago, I kissed a lover under the waterfalls at Huaxtla, a town 45 minutes from Guadalajara. I swam in her pools, sunbathed on rocks overlooking her turquoise water. This month, I saw photos of the same waterfall, with its pools turned brown.

Lately, I am understanding time differently. If Juanitatlán Falls became toxic in less than 50 years, how long before Huaxtla Falls goes next?

In just a few years, will I only tell my niece and nephew of the rivers I used to swim in, the water that used to be clean, the places that used to feel like they were still ours? How long before we sacrifice them too?

Amanda E. Machado (she/they) is a queer nonbinary Latine writer whose work seeks to expand the stories we tell about the outdoors. Their essays about nature and climate justice have been published in The Atlantic, The Guardian, Vox, Outside, Sierra Magazine, and many other outlets. In addition to their writing, Amanda is also a public speaker and facilitator who has worked with organizations like Patagonia, Breakthrough Institute, the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, Hip Camp, and many more.

World.title: A new museum in Yucatán tells the story of a controversial figure in Mexican history
World.content:
A museum dedicated to one of Mexico’s most notorious colonial figures has opened in a former convent in Yucatán state.

The museum examines the legacy of Diego de Landa, a Spanish friar whose campaign against Maya religious practices included burning their books and sacred objects.

But while chastised for that, he is also credited with leaving a detailed account of Maya life and religion — one that remains an important source for scholars studying the civilization he helped suppress.

The museum features nine display panels, a painting of Landa and a 25-minute video in the former San Miguel Arcángel convent in Maní, about 100 kilometers south of Mérida.

The permanent exhibition, with a title that translates as “Friar Diego de Landa: The Bishop and His Legacy,” is housed in a modest space, a room formerly used by the parish priest.

It traces his life from his upbringing in Spain to his tenure as Yucatán’s second bishop.

Born in 1524, Landa was a Franciscan missionary who arrived in Yucatán in 1549 and learned Yucatec Mayan. He became a regional leader of his religious order before becoming bishop.

He is remembered particularly for the July 12, 1562, religious proceeding in Maní known as an auto-da-fé, when Maya manuscripts, codices, religious images and other sacred objects were burned.

Historian John F. Chuchiak IV of Missouri State University researched and curated the exhibition. At last week’s opening, he challenged accounts that Maya people were burned during that event, saying the fire consumed objects and books.

That distinction does not erase the violence of Landa’s broader campaign. Encyclopaedia Britannica reports that about 4,500 Maya were tortured over three months and nearly 200 died.

Several years later in Spain, while his conduct was under investigation, he wrote “Relación de las cosas de Yucatán,” a detailed account of Maya life and religion. He died in Mérida in 1579 at age 54.

The exhibition, organized through the parish and the Archdiocese of Yucatán, also cites documents indicating that, as bishop, Landa opposed forced labor and other abuses of Maya communities.

Parts of the exhibit include QR codes that provide access to translations into Mayan, English and German.

The museum’s hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, with Monday visits by appointment by calling (997) 155-3601 or (997) 112-9774. The admission price of 60 pesos (US $3.25) includes a tour of the former convent.

With reports from Por Esto, Diario de Yucatán and Yucatán Magazine

World.title: Mexico among leaders in tech exports, ranking fourth among APEC nations
World.content:
Mexico is a leader in the percentage of exports in the medium- and high-tech manufactured goods category, ranking fourth among the 21 Pacific Rim countries gathered at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, China, this week, according to the latest APEC report.

The report shows that 70.6% of goods Mexico exported were in the medium- and high-tech categories, trailing only Taiwan (81.9%), Hong Kong (77.9%) and South Korea (75.6%). That ranking puts Mexico ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%).

Overall, trade in medium- and high-tech manufactured goods in the APEC region quadrupled between 2000 and 2025, reaching US$14.6 billion, with Northeast Asia and the Americas combining for over 82% of regional trade in these goods last year.

Mexico also ranked fourth in the region for the share of these goods in its total merchandise imports in 2025, at 61.7%, behind Hong Kong (71.8%), Singapore (64.3%), and Taiwan (62.4%).

High-tech manufacturing is gaining momentum, according to the report, with trade in these products growing faster than overall merchandise trade over the past decade.

Mexico is well positioned to build on its recent success owing to its strong manufacturing sector, skilled workforce and close trade links with Canada and the United States, particularly in high-value-added sectors such as the automotive, semiconductors and digital services industries.

APEC comprises 21 countries which, together, account for around 62% of global GDP and half of global merchandise exports.

The region is projected to grow by 3.4% in 2026, owing to significant investment in technology and trade, which has helped bolster economic activity amid higher energy prices and geopolitical tensions, another APEC report stated. However, growth is expected to fall to 3.1% in 2027.

“Rising energy costs, geopolitical tensions, increased trade restrictions and tighter financial conditions are creating pressures that could weaken growth in the near term,” Carlos Kuriyama, the director of APEC’s Policy Support Unit, stated.

Trade growth will also likely slow due to ongoing geopolitical tensions and trade policy uncertainty. While APEC’s product and service exports will increase by 6.9% in 2026, they are expected to fall to 3.8% in 2027.

President Sheinbaum is in Shenzhen, China, attending the APEC event, marking the first time a Mexican president has attended in three years. Mexico’s participation will give it the opportunity to strengthen relationships, define priorities and build agreements ahead of its hosting of the 35th Economic Leaders’ Meeting in 2028.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Sheinbaum and Xi mark a ‘new era’ in Mexico-China relations
World.content:
Listen to this article

In a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday, President Claudia Sheinbaum declared that her visit to China marks “a new era” in Mexico’s relationship with the East Asian country.

She also told the Chinese president and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party she was “convinced” that the bilateral meeting would “strengthen collaboration” between the Mexican and Chinese governments and the Mexican and Chinese people. In subsequent remarks to reporters, Sheinbaum described her meeting with Xi as “very good” and “very, very frank.”

For his part, Xi told Sheinbaum that China and Mexico are “good friends” and that advancing relations is “important for both countries,” according to a readout published by China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The two leaders and members of their respective cabinets met in Shenzhen ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting, which starts in the southern Chinese city on Wednesday. Sheinbaum previously met with Xi at the G20 leaders’ summit in Brazil in November 2024.

Mexico seeks to strengthen ties with China in areas including science, technology and clean energy

In public remarks to Xi, Sheinbaum thanked the Chinese president for his invitation to the APEC CEO Summit, at which she spoke on Tuesday.

She noted that Mexico will host the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in 2028 and told Xi it would be a “pleasure” to welcome him to that event.

Sheinbaum said that the Mexico-China relationship is “the result of deep bonds of friendship and shared principles, such as cooperation, development and shared prosperity.”

“Mexico and China share a vision of development and prosperity, and our nations have strengthened their relationship in order to cooperate on a variety of issues,” she said.

“On this occasion, we are interested in strengthening cooperation in areas related to science and technology, agriculture, clean energy, water resources, health and, of course, culture and tourism,” Sheinbaum said.

According to a statement issued by Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (SRE), Sheinbaum and Xi “highlighted opportunities to deepen bilateral cooperation on health, river cleanup and restoration, sustainable water management, biodiversity conservation, waste management guided by circular economy principles, the fight against climate change and the development of resilient cities, as Shenzhen’s model shows.”

“They also agreed to strengthen scientific cooperation by training talent, conducting joint research in strategic areas such as mathematics, agriculture, biotechnology and clean energy, and developing bilateral initiatives, including the Young Scientists Exchange Program,” the SRE said.

The ministry also said that Sheinbaum and Xi “expressed their desire to keep strengthening” the Mexico-China relationship through the two countries’ Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which was launched by Xi and former Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto in 2013.

SRE: Sheinbaum and Xi discussed ‘opportunities to deepen trade’

Mexico and China don’t have a free trade agreement, and the former country angered the latter when it imposed new and higher tariffs on Chinese goods at the start of 2026.

Mexico’s tariffs on China — seen in part as an effort to appease U.S. President Donald Trump, who has accused Mexico of being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods — were not mentioned by the SRE or the Chinese Foreign Ministry in their statements.

The SRE did say that the Mexican and Chinese presidents “discussed opportunities to deepen trade,” adding that Sheinbaum “said Mexico is interested in moving toward a more balanced and diversified economic relationship.”

China’s exports to Mexico — which include electronic equipment and electric vehicles — are worth far more than its imports from Mexico, leaving it with a large trade surplus. Some imports from China pose a threat to Mexican manufacturing sectors, giving the Mexican government added incentive to impose higher tariffs on them.

Sheinbaum told reporters in Shenzhen that she and Xi had spoken about increasing Mexico’s exports of various products to China, “from avocados to tequila.”

Asked whether she and the Chinese president spoke about Mexico’s relationship with the United States, the president responded:

“The issue was raised, but we always talk about our trade agreement with the United States, and [say] that we will always do what is best for Mexico.”

Xi says China and Mexico should ‘deepen political mutual trust’

The statement issued by the Chinese Foreign Ministry said that “given the complex and volatile global landscape, advancing China-Mexico relations at a higher level, across wider areas, and in greater depth is important for both countries as they implement their respective national development strategies and promote unity for strength among the Global South.”

The ministry said that in his meeting with Sheinbaum, “President Xi stressed that China and Mexico should first continue to treat each other with sincerity, deepen political mutual trust, keep growing bilateral relations in the right direction, enhance exchanges and cooperation in all areas and at all levels, and work together to ensure the success of events celebrating the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations next year.”

The Chinese Foreign Ministry also said that “Mexico firmly adheres to the one-China principle and attaches great importance to its relations with China.”

“In the course of implementing Plan México, Mexico is ready to strengthen cooperation with China in areas such as trade, investment, science and technology, manufacturing, artificial intelligence, agriculture and water conservancy and promote exchanges in health, education, culture and tourism, so as to elevate bilateral relations to a new height,” the ministry added.

While Mexico is clearly seeking to strengthen — and broaden — its relationship with China, Sheinbaum is mindful of the need to safeguard Mexico’s relationship with the United States, its largest trade partner. For example, the president — who will meet with Trump in Shenzhen on Wednesday — has made it clear that Mexico is not seeking a free trade agreement with China, the world’s second largest economy.

One apparent motive for China to seek closer ties with Mexico is the country’s proximity to Beijing’s foremost strategic rival — the United States.

Sheinbaum requests a panda for CDMX’s Chapultepec Zoo

In remarks to reporters after her meeting with Xi, Sheinbaum noted that a Chinese company is supplying trains to Mexico (for the under-construction Mexico City-Pachuca railroad) and reiterated that Mexico is “very interested” in learning more about China’s “smart hospitals.”

México quiere un nuevo panda en el zoológico Chapultepec: Durante su visita a China, Sheinbaum solicitó al presidente Xi Jinping un ejemplar para el zoológico capitalino 🇨🇳🐼🇲🇽 https://t.co/FMPpElrSXv — Quadratín México (@QuadratinMexico) November 17, 2026

She subsequently revealed that she asked Xi for a panda for the Chapultepec Zoo, located in Chapultepec Park in Mexico City.

One panda, a female called Xin Xin, already lives at the zoo. She was born at the Chapultepec Zoo in 1990.

Given that Mexico and China are on friendly terms and seeking even closer ties, it would appear likely that China will grant Sheinbaum’s request for a panda. According to Reuters, since its founding in 1949, “the People’s Republic of China has used panda diplomacy to boost its international image, either by gifting or lending pandas to foreign zoos as goodwill animal ambassadors.”

World.title: Sheinbaum and Canada’s Carney meet in China, reaffirming their support for the USMCA
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Tuesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, with both expressing firm support for the renewal of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement (USMCA).

Their support contrasts with mixed signals from different U.S. Cabinet members regarding elements of the agreement, sometimes to the point where the Mexican team may not be sure who they’re negotiating with. Also, U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt over whether there will be any renewal at all.

In that light, the bilateral meeting Tuesday brought together two leaders with a common challenge, though each has responded to Trump’s economic aggression (such as tariffs on both countries) in different ways — Sheinbaum seeking common ground on other issues and Carney in full pushback mode.

But those concerns gave way at the meeting to praise for how strong the mutual relationship between Mexico and Canada has grown. Both leaders agreed to deepen that bilateral relationship.

According to official reports, the leaders endorsed their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and highlighted the first anniversary of the Mexico-Canada Action Plan 2025-2028, which has launched scores of initiatives across its four pillars: prosperity, mobility, security and sustainability.

They also stressed the importance of expanding the action plan based on the positive results obtained, particularly in boosting trade and investments between both countries.

“Our trade between Mexico and Canada, Canada and Mexico has increased, and also the investments of Mexican businesses in Canada and of Canadian businesses in Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. “There is an extraordinary relationship.”

According to Canadian official figures, Mexico invested nearly CA $1 billion in mining and food production, while Canadian investments in Mexico reached CA $3.7 billion in the country’s manufacturing, renewable energy, and mining industries.

Moreover, Carney noted that bilateral trade increased 18% this year and 60% in the last five years. “We are already seeing and contemplating many more opportunities for exchanges between us,” he said.

Sheinbaum and Carney also highlighted increased market access for Canadian agricultural and agri-food products, the success of trade missions to both countries, and the potential for further growth in advanced manufacturing, agriculture, critical minerals, energy, pharmaceuticals and transportation.

Beyond trade, the leaders highlighted cooperation to strengthen health security, develop biotechnological production, facilitate labor mobility, and improve the economic well-being of Indigenous peoples.

The USMCA was, in fact, discussed, but no details were provided to the press or public.

World.title: Mexico Arrests Alleged Los Deltas Leader
World.content:
Mexican federal forces arrested a suspected cartel cell leader known as “El Topo” in Zapopan, next to Guadalajara, on Wednesday 18 November 2026. Omar García Harfuch, Mexico’s federal security secretary, announced the arrest on X.

The suspect is described as a leader of a cell of Los Deltas, the armed wing of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), which the United States designates a terrorist organisation. Three alleged gunmen died in an exchange of fire, according to García Harfuch’s preliminary report.

What We Know

The Navy (Semar), the federal Security Ministry (SSPC) and the Criminal Investigation Agency (AIC) carried out the arrest. The AIC belongs to the federal Attorney General’s office (FGR).

Authorities named the suspect as César Daniel “N”, following the Mexican practice of withholding a surname. They say he led a Los Deltas cell in the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Jalisco state prosecutor’s office obtained arrest warrants against him over the kidnappings of broadcaster Jaime Barrera and a real-estate businessman. Federal investigators also allegedly tie him to drug and weapons trafficking for Los Deltas, and possibly to money laundering, extortion and kidnapping.

García Harfuch’s preliminary report said three alleged Los Deltas members attacked agents and died in the exchange of fire. Two other people were detained with the suspect.

García Harfuch thanked the Jalisco state government for its cooperation in the operation. The federal authorities say they will keep investigating to establish the legal situation of the three people held.

The Big Picture

Jaime Barrera was abducted on Monday 11 March 2024 in Zapopan after leaving the Guadalajara broadcaster where he worked. Luis Joaquín Méndez, then Jalisco state prosecutor, said at the time that investigators pointed to a violent deprivation of liberty by three to four men.

Barrera was freed by his captors in Magdalena, Jalisco, where he asked the National Guard for help. He said in 2024 that no ransom was demanded and called it “a kind of warning” over his journalism, not a kidnapping, which is his own reading of the cause.

The federal organised-crime prosecutors (FEMDO) began the investigation behind this arrest in April 2026. Intelligence work then located three safe houses in Zapopan where he and others stayed.

On Saturday 25 and Sunday 26 July 2026, raids in the Zapopan neighbourhoods of Arboledas, Arcos de Guadalupe and Mirador del Sol led to six arrests. Authorities reported seizing weapons, vehicles, tactical gear and phones.

The public record does not say what the arrest changes for the cartel. We do not guess.

In Plain English

Los Deltas and the CJNG. Authorities describe Los Deltas as the armed wing of the CJNG in the Guadalajara area. The United States designates the CJNG a terrorist organisation. The agencies. FEMDO is the group of federal prosecutors who handle organised crime. Semar is the Navy, the SSPC is the federal Security Ministry, and the AIC is the FGR’s Criminal Investigation Agency. The letter “N”. Mexican authorities often give a suspect’s first names and an initial for the surname. The surname is withheld here.

What Is Not Known

The legal status of the two people detained with him is not confirmed. The full list of charges and the full details of the operation are also not confirmed.

The first court appearance has no confirmed date. Beyond Barrera’s own statement, no motive for his abduction is confirmed.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Guadalajara and Jalisco draw visitors, business people and American expatriates, and the operation took place in a metropolitan neighbourhood. Readers with plans there can follow statements from the federal Security Ministry and the Jalisco government.

The suspect remains an alleged offender until a court rules. We will report confirmed developments, including any court date.

World.title: US Praises Nigeria Army After 125 Rescued
World.content:
The United States has publicly praised Nigeria’s army after the country’s Defence Headquarters (DHQ), the military’s central command, reported 125 kidnapped people rescued in a single week. The Bureau of African Affairs, the State Department office that handles US policy toward sub-Saharan Africa, issued the statement on Wednesday 18 November 2026, which Premium Times (a Nigerian newspaper) says it posted on X, the social media platform.

For US readers the praise is a marker of security cooperation with Africa’s most populous country. Nigeria’s Defence Minister Christopher Musa said on Monday 16 November 2026 that US intelligence support, including satellite imagery and training, is helping Nigerian forces.

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Who. The Bureau of African Affairs, a US State Department office, praised Nigeria’s armed forces in a statement.

What. Nigeria’s Defence Headquarters counts 125 kidnapped people rescued from 6 to 12 November 2026.

Where. 119 travellers were freed near Buratai, in Biu district, Borno State, Nigeria’s north-east.

As of 18 November 2026, 16:00 GMT

Washington has praised Nigeria’s army for rescuing 125 kidnapped people in one week. The military’s own figures remain the only count of the operations behind the praise.

The Big Picture

Nigeria’s north-east insurgency, led by Boko Haram and its offshoot ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province), is about 17 years old, and the abduction of travellers on rural roads is now a recurring feature of it. In an earlier weekly briefing we reported that Nigeria Says 60 Militants Killed in a Week, so weekly military tallies are a regular DHQ product.

The State Department post, as reported by Nigerian media including Premium Times and NigerianEye (a Nigerian news site) on 18 November 2026, praises the dismantling of terrorist camps, the recovery of weapons and the clearance of explosive devices. Premium Times also reports that Washington backs Nigerian government efforts to prevent kidnappings and hold perpetrators accountable.

The post confirms that Washington is publicly backing the Nigerian campaign, and the parts reported so far announce no new aid. We found no sourced figures that compare Nigeria’s weekly rescue count with other countries in Africa, so we make no regional ranking.

File photo: the National Mosque in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. Rio Times library.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on US-Nigeria relations Email address Follow

What We Know

The 125, 8 and 10 totals come from DHQ’s weekly briefing as reported by Turkey’s Anadolu agency, while Leadership (a Nigerian daily) and the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN, the national wire service) headline only the 119. The briefing, given by spokesperson Maj.-Gen. (Major General) Michael Onoja for operations from 6 to 12 November 2026, lists 125 kidnapped people rescued, 8 terrorists killed and 10 suspected collaborators or logistics suppliers arrested.

The largest rescue involved 119 travellers abducted on Friday 6 November on the Dutsen Kura-Bulazarma-Kamuya Road in Buratai, in Biu Local Government Area (LGA, a district authority) of Borno State, the north-eastern state at the centre of the insurgency. Troops pursued the attackers along the Mangari-Dora Road, and the attackers abandoned their captives.

DHQ says the rescued were 69 men, 35 women and 15 children. Troops also found an improvised explosive device (IED, a homemade bomb) in the area.

The 125 is a nationwide weekly total, not only Biu. In Zamfara State, a north-western Nigerian state, under Operation Fansan Yamma (the military’s campaign against bandits there), troops rescued further kidnap victims, but a driver abducted with commuters on the Kombo-Gurusu Road was found dead.

In Bauchi State, a north-eastern Nigerian state, troops cleared camps at Dajin Madam in Alkaleri LGA and recovered ammunition, motorcycles and radios. In Kainji Lake National Park, a large reserve in Niger State, troops detonated five IEDs, repelled two attacks and, DHQ says, neutralised two terrorists.

DHQ’s regional breakdown does not add up neatly to the 125 total, which Anadolu gives as a summary figure. DHQ is the only source of these figures so far.

What Is Not Known

DHQ’s account does not say who the 119 travellers were beyond the counts, or whether any ransom was paid. It names the attackers only as terrorists, and the figures have no independent verification.

The published account does not reconcile the regional breakdown with the 125 total. We cannot confirm the full text of the State Department post, which we know only from the Nigerian reports.

One weekly tally cannot show whether road abductions in Borno are rising or falling. The DHQ briefing offers no earlier-week comparison for the 125, so the trend stays open.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The abduction happened on a public road, so the people most affected are Nigerian travellers and their families, not foreign visitors. We could not retrieve the State Department’s Nigeria travel advisory on 18 November 2026, so we do not state its level here.

US readers planning travel should read the current advisory at travel.state.gov before booking. Investors and aid groups should treat the weekly tallies as military claims until outside observers confirm them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the United States praise Nigeria’s military?

The Bureau of African Affairs issued a statement on 18 November 2026 that commends operations this month that rescued 125 kidnapping victims. It cited camp dismantling, weapon recovery and explosive clearance, as reported by Nigerian media.

How many people were rescued in Borno State?

DHQ says troops rescued 119 travellers abducted on 6 November near Buratai in Biu LGA, among them 69 men, 35 women and 15 children. The 125 figure is a national weekly total.

Who is Maj.-Gen. Michael Onoja?

He is the spokesperson who presented DHQ’s weekly briefing for 6 to 12 November 2026. DHQ is Nigeria’s military central command, which publishes weekly operational summaries.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to Nigeria?

We could not retrieve the State Department advisory on 18 November 2026. Travellers should read the current Nigeria advisory at travel.state.gov, which lists regional risks, before any trip.

World.title: Kenya Bank KCB Profit Jumps 24% to US$451M
World.content:
One of Kenya’s biggest banks earned more from phone loans and currency trades than a year ago. KCB Group, a Nairobi-listed lender, said in its results statement of 18 November 2026 that nine-month profit after tax rose 23.9% to KSh 58.6 billion (Kenyan shillings; about US$451 million).

For US readers, KCB is a window on East Africa’s mobile-money banking boom and on African bank stocks as an investment theme. Its subsidiaries outside the main Kenyan bank now earn about a third of group profit.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Who. KCB Group, one of Kenya’s biggest banks, listed in Nairobi.

What. Nine-month profit after tax rose 23.9% to KSh 58.6 billion (about US$451 million).

Why. Mobile loans, fee income and foreign-exchange gains grew, while bad loans fell.

Next. No dated next step is published.

As of 18 November 2026, 15:51 GMT (UTC)

KCB’s profit growth came from lending, mobile loans and currency trading, with its subsidiaries beyond KCB Bank Kenya adding a third of the total. Bad loans fell as well.

Where This Comes From

KCB Group is one of Kenya’s biggest banks, with subsidiaries in Uganda, Burundi, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Its shares trade on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, Kenya’s main stock market.

Group chief executive Paul Russo summed up the result in the statement of 18 November 2026. He said: “The results demonstrate the resilience of our business.”

Central Nairobi seen from the roof of the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) tower, 2021. File photo.

All shilling figures here use the market rate of 18 November 2026, which is KSh 129.93 per US dollar. Dollar values are rounded.

KCB said in its results statement of 18 November 2026 that nine-month profit after tax a year earlier was KSh 47.3 billion (about US$364 million). By our arithmetic, the gain is KSh 11.3 billion (about US$87 million).

Earnings per share, the profit attributable to each share, rose 24.3% to KSh 17.80 (about US$0.14) from KSh 14.32 (about US$0.11), KCB said. Total assets grew 15.4% to about KSh 2.4 trillion (about US$18.5 billion).

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Kenya 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 3 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Happened

Total operating income, the bank’s overall revenue, rose 12.3% to KSh 167.8 billion (about US$1.29 billion), KCB said on 18 November 2026. A year earlier it was KSh 149.4 billion (about US$1.15 billion).

Interest income, what the bank earns on its lending, rose 8.2% to KSh 112.9 billion (about US$869 million), KCB said. Non-funded income, which covers fees, commissions and foreign exchange, rose 21.8% to KSh 54.9 billion (about US$423 million).

Mobile loan disbursements rose 26% to KSh 492 billion (about US$3.79 billion), KCB said in its results statement. These are short-term loans issued on a mobile phone.

Foreign-exchange income rose 65.1%, mainly from Trust Merchant Bank (TMB), KCB’s subsidiary in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the statement said. During the period KCB raised its stake in TMB from 85% to 98%.

Why It Matters

The subsidiaries outside KCB Bank Kenya now carry real weight, with profit up 24.3% to KSh 19.6 billion (about US$151 million), about a third of group earnings. Burundi, South Sudan, Uganda and KCB Investment Bank, its investment-banking arm, led that growth, KCB said.

Credit quality improved, KCB said on 18 November 2026. Gross non-performing loans, which are loans whose borrowers stopped paying, fell 17.1% to KSh 184.1 billion (about US$1.42 billion) from KSh 222.1 billion (about US$1.71 billion).

The ratio of such loans to all loans dropped to 13.3% from 17.8%. Loan loss provisions, money set aside for bad debts, fell 9.1% to KSh 16.6 billion (about US$128 million).

Costs and Capital

Operating costs rose 6.1%, slower than income, KCB said. The cost-to-income ratio, the share of income spent on running the bank, improved to 43.7% from 46.2%.

Return on equity, profit measured against shareholders’ money, was 22.1%, KCB said. Shareholders’ equity rose 17.3% to KSh 362 billion (about US$2.79 billion).

The core capital ratio, a bank’s cushion of its strongest capital, was 18% against a regulatory minimum of 10.5%. Chairman Joseph Kinyua said the buffers give “sufficient headroom to absorb potential economic shocks,.”

What to Watch

No dated next step is published for KCB, such as a full-year results date or a dividend book closure. We therefore name none.

One thing to watch is whether mobile lending keeps growing after its 26% rise. Another is whether TMB’s currency income holds now that KCB owns 98% of it.

What It Means for You

For a US investor with exposure to African banks, the report shows one lender earning from lending, fees and currency trading at the same time. It describes one bank’s nine months and is not a signal to buy or sell.

For readers who bank or do business in Kenya, the numbers show where growth is coming from. Phone-based lending and regional operations are doing much of the work.

What Is Not Known

The figures are unaudited, so final audited numbers could differ. We also do not know the price of the larger TMB stake, the full-year profit or the dividend.

For background, see our report on KCB’s first-half profit and our piece on foreign investors cutting their KCB stake. More in Kenya news.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did KCB earn in nine months?

KCB reported profit after tax of KSh 58.6 billion (about US$451 million) for the nine months to 30 September 2026. That is 23.9% above KSh 47.3 billion (about US$364 million) a year earlier.

What drove the rise in KCB’s profit?

KCB said income beyond interest, which covers fees, commissions and foreign exchange, rose 21.8%. Foreign-exchange income rose 65.1%, mainly from its Congolese subsidiary, and mobile loan disbursements rose 26%.

Did KCB’s bad loans fall?

Yes, gross non-performing loans fell 17.1% to KSh 184.1 billion (about US$1.42 billion). The ratio of bad loans to all loans dropped to 13.3% from 17.8%.

What is TMB and what changed this year?

Trust Merchant Bank (TMB) is KCB’s subsidiary in the Democratic Republic of Congo. During the nine months KCB raised its stake in it from 85% to 98%.

Sources KCB Group unaudited results statement for the nine months to 30 September 2026, published 18 November 2026, including remarks by group chief executive Paul Russo and chairman Joseph Kinyua; market exchange rate of 18 November 2026 (KSh 129.93 per US$).

World.title: Morocco Education and Healthcare Explained
World.content:
Explainer: Morocco

Morocco is putting more children in school and more people on health insurance, yet many families still pay a large share of medical bills themselves. This explainer sets out how its schools, universities, hospitals and insurance fit together.

For a US reader the country matters as a destination for retirees and investors, and the home country of relatives of Moroccan Americans. We rely on official statistics and international datasets, and we say plainly where the picture stops.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Key Facts Population. Morocco had 36,828,330 legal residents on 1 September 2024, the latest census count.

Schooling. About 60% of Moroccan 10-year-olds could not read a simple text in 2023.

Insurance. AMO, compulsory health insurance, officially covered over 32 million people in 2025, about 88% of residents.

Costs. Households paid 37.25% of current health spending directly in 2023, against 10.93% in the US.

Morocco has widened school places and health insurance quickly, but learning results and out-of-pocket costs show how much work remains, and several reforms are still being rolled out.

The Big Picture

Over two decades the state has pushed towards universal schooling and health insurance. A royal social-protection roadmap, set in law as framework law 09-21 of 2021 on social protection, sets the course and drives the insurance expansion described below.

Literacy has improved, as the census presentation of the HCP (Haut-Commissariat au Plan, Morocco’s statistics office) shows. It puts illiteracy among people aged 10 and over at 24.8% in 2024, the share of that age group who cannot read and write.

Among literate people in that age group, the HCP census presentation of 2024 shows that 99.2% read and write Arabic, 57.7% French and 20.5% English. Those shares explain why language shapes both classrooms and daily life.

On health spending, the World Bank’s 2023 indicators show Morocco at 6.06% of GDP, against 4.35% in Algeria, 7.99% in Tunisia and 4.88% in Egypt. The United States spent 16.69% of GDP on health in the same World Bank series for 2023.

Doctors are scarcer, with the World Bank listing 0.74 physicians per 1,000 people in Morocco in 2021 against 3.68 in the United States in 2022. The same World Bank series shows 1.66 in Algeria (2022), 1.32 in Tunisia (2021) and 0.67 in Egypt (2020).

Lattice window in the Al-Qarawiyyin University complex in Fez, photographed on 13 May 2024. Photo: JasmineartGallery, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

In Plain English —AMO. Assurance Maladie Obligatoire, Morocco’s compulsory health insurance. —CNSS. The Caisse Nationale de Sécurité Sociale, the private-sector social security fund. —AMO Tadamon. The AMO branch for people whose premiums the state pays. —HCP. The Haut-Commissariat au Plan, the national statistics office. —GST. A Groupement Sanitaire Territorial, a regional group running public hospitals and health centres. —Bac. The baccalauréat, the national exam that ends upper secondary school.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Morocco 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 3 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

School System and Languages

Primary school, grades 1 to 6 for ages 6 to 12, is compulsory, and preschool for ages 4 to 6 is being generalised. The IEA (International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement, a research body) says so in its 2024 encyclopedia for TIMSS 2023, the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study.

Pupils then attend three years of collège, meaning lower secondary school, and three years of lycée, meaning upper secondary school, as the IEA encyclopedia describes. Lycée ends with the baccalauréat, known as the bac, the national school-leaving exam.

Arabic and Amazigh, the Berber language, are the two official languages under article 5 of the 2011 constitution. The framework law 51-17 of 2019 sets Arabic and Amazigh as languages of instruction and allows teaching of scientific subjects in foreign languages.

In TIMSS 2023 (IEA, December 2024), Morocco scored 378 in grade 8 mathematics against the TIMSS scale centrepoint of 500. In grade 4 mathematics it scored 393 against the same centrepoint.

The World Bank said in a feature of 21 May 2026 that about 60% of 10-year-olds in Morocco could not read a simple text in 2023. That finding is the backdrop to the Schools of Pioneers programme.

The Schools of Pioneers (Écoles Pionnières) started in 2023/24 as a pilot in 626 primary schools with about 320,000 pupils, the World Bank feature of 21 May 2026 reports. It now covers 4,626 public primary schools, about 54% of the total, with more than 2 million pupils, about 75,000 teachers and 960 inspectors.

A preliminary evaluation, reported in the same World Bank feature, found that pioneer pupils outperformed 82% of peers in comparable schools after one year. A secondary pilot, Collèges Pionniers, began in 2024/25 and covers 786 schools and about 678,000 pupils.

Universities

Higher Education Minister Abdellatif Miraoui said in October 2024 that Moroccan universities had about 1.3 million students that year. We give no public-private split because we could not confirm one at a ministry source.

Al-Qarawiyyin University in Fez traces its founding to 859 by Fatima al-Fihri. Guinness World Records lists it as the world’s oldest existing, continually operating educational institution.

Al Akhawayn University in Ifrane teaches in English, in contrast to most public universities. Fees for foreign students are not confirmed at an official source.

Medical and pharmacy students boycotted classes from late 2023 into November 2024 over a plan to shorten medical training. The boycott ended by agreement with the government in November 2024.

Training places for general doctors rose from 2,650 in 2019 to 6,414 in 2025, according to the government portal maroc.ma on 8 October 2025. Nursing places rose from 2,735 in 2019 to 9,500 in 2024, the same portal says.

Readers who want detail on the shared France-Morocco campus at Fez can read our page on the project. We give no figures for it here.

Public Versus Private Health Care

The US Commerce Department commercial guide of 31 July 2025 counts 164 public hospitals and over 400 private clinics, the latter with more than 15,500 beds. It says public hospitals provide 83% of care.

The IMF (International Monetary Fund) selected issues paper of 2026 puts Morocco at 7.3 hospital beds per 10,000 people in 2020, against a desirable level of 20. That gap frames the building programme now under way.

Government figures on maroc.ma of 8 October 2025 list 22 projects from 2022 to 2025 adding 2,433 beds. Another 24 projects due in 2025 and 2026 add 2,273 beds, which together come to 4,706 beds on the two government lists.

Life expectancy at birth in Morocco was 75.49 years in 2024, according to the World Bank. The figure is a national average and says nothing about the quality of any one hospital.

Health Insurance and AMO

AMO was created by law 65-00. RAMED, the former scheme for low-income Moroccans, ran alongside it until AMO Tadamon replaced it.

AMO Tadamon covers about 11 million people whose premiums the state pays (government portal maroc.ma, 21 October 2025). The self-employed regime, AMO-TNS (for non-salaried workers), covers about 4 million.

Total AMO beneficiaries passed 32 million in 2025, about 88% of the population and up from 42% before the scheme was extended. These are the Finance Ministry’s own figures from its 2026 budget presentation note, so they show registered cover rather than actual use of care.

The CNSS, the private-sector social security fund, runs AMO for private-sector employees. CNOPS, the civil servants’ insurer, handles the public-sector scheme.

What It Costs and Who Can Use It

Why it matters: when public care is thin, private spending pushes costs onto households. The World Bank puts Morocco’s out-of-pocket share of current health spending at 37.25% in 2023, against 10.93% in the United States.

The neighbours differ: in the same World Bank series for 2023 the share is 45.00% in Algeria, 37.94% in Tunisia and 57.20% in Egypt. Morocco’s share is the lowest of the four countries, below Algeria and Egypt and just under Tunisia.

AMO Tadamon beneficiaries have their premiums paid by the state, so poorer households are insured without contributing, according to maroc.ma on 21 October 2025. Doctor and public-hospital fees for non-residents are not confirmed, as we explain below.

Foreign employees with a Moroccan work contract are generally affiliated through their employer, according to consultancies, though we could not confirm this on an official page. Our guide to expat health cover gives the detail.

Reforms and What To Watch

Framework law 06-22 on the health system, promulgated on 9 December 2022, replaced law 34-09. It created the Groupements Sanitaires Territoriaux (GSTs), regional health groups that run public hospitals and health centres, under law 08-22.

Regional groups are being rolled out across the country. The government adopted decrees in December 2025 fixing launch dates, and some groups began operating in 2026, but we could not confirm which regions are still waiting.

Where the Rollout Stands —9 December 2022. Framework law 06-22 on the health system was promulgated, and it started the reform. —11 December 2025. The government adopted decrees setting launch dates for the regional groups.

On schools, the Schools of Pioneers expansion is the main programme to follow, based on the World Bank feature of 21 May 2026. We found no official date confirmed for its next stage.

What Critics Say

The CESE (Conseil économique, social et environnemental, the state advisory council) adopted an opinion unanimously on 28 January 2026 on bill 54.23, a reform of the AMO law 65-00. It calls for AMO to be universal and mandatory.

The council also asks for an actuarial study covering at least 20 years and notes that the national reference tariff has not been updated since 2006. It also warns that moving the public-sector scheme from CNOPS to the CNSS carries risks, and that unification cannot replace a financial overhaul.

The CESE further asks to keep a separate student health regime, so that students do not lose cover when their parents’ situation is precarious. Because the CESE is itself a state advisory council, these points are a critique from within the system.

Expat Practicalities

Arabic and Amazigh are official, but French is widely read: the HCP census presentation of 2024 shows 57.7% of literate people aged 10 and over read and write it. Our language guide explains where each language is used.

Families weighing schools should ask them directly, since Casablanca American School and the French mission schools publish their own fee schedules. We have not verified those fees.

Readers with Moroccan family in the United States can find context in our explainer on the Moroccan diaspora. It covers the links between the two countries beyond schools and hospitals.

What Is Not Known

Several facts we could not confirm at an official source. We list them once here instead of hedging throughout the text.

Not Confirmed —School bill. Whether a pending bill on compulsory schooling has passed Parliament and been promulgated. —AMO bill. The current legislative status of bill 54.23. —Health fees. Doctor and public-hospital fees for non-residents. —School fees. International school fees, and university fees for foreigners. —Universities. The number of public universities. —Insurance. Official AMO contribution rates for foreigners.

What It Means for You

Families moving to Morocco will meet a school system that the IEA describes as compulsory for ages 6 to 12 and taught in Arabic and Amazigh, with foreign languages allowed for science. Private and international options exist, but we have no confirmed fee data.

Retirees weighing a move face a system where the World Bank puts out-of-pocket spending at 37.25% of current health spending in 2023. We could not confirm contribution rates for foreigners.

Investors in clinics and schools face a market with over 400 private clinics, says the US Commerce Department guide of 31 July 2025. AMO covered about 88% of residents in 2025 (maroc.ma), and two government project lists add 4,706 public beds.

Americans with relatives in Morocco should note that AMO Tadamon covers about 11 million people whose premiums the state pays, per maroc.ma on 21 October 2025. More coverage is on our Morocco hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Morocco’s school system work?

Primary school runs from grades 1 to 6 for ages 6 to 12 and is compulsory. It is followed by three years of collège and three years of lycée, which ends with the baccalauréat.

How many people have AMO health insurance?

AMO covered over 32 million people in 2025, about 88% of the population, up from 42% before the scheme was extended, according to the Finance Ministry’s 2026 budget note. About 11 million are in AMO Tadamon, where the state pays premiums.

How much do Moroccan households pay for health care?

The World Bank puts the out-of-pocket share of current health spending at 37.25% in 2023. The figure for the United States is 10.93%.

What is a GST?

A Groupement Sanitaire Territorial is a regional health group that runs public hospitals and health centres. They are being rolled out across the country, and the government adopted decrees on launch dates in December 2025.

What does the CESE want changed?

The CESE, the state advisory council, wants AMO to be universal and mandatory. It also asks for an actuarial study of at least 20 years.

How many students attend Moroccan universities?

About 1.3 million students in 2024/25, according to Higher Education Minister Abdellatif Miraoui in October 2024. We could not confirm fees for foreign students.

World.title: Nicaragua History Explained, From Origins to 2026
World.content:
NICARAGUA · HISTORY

Nicaragua is a small country that empires, dictators and revolutionaries have fought over for five centuries. Its past runs from Spanish conquest in the 1520s through US occupation and a family dictatorship to a revolution in 1979.

That history matters to American readers because Washington sent Marines there, backed a rebel war and now sets tariffs on its goods. The Central Bank of Nicaragua said remittances, money sent home by workers abroad, reached US$5.24 billion in 2024, and 82.8% came from the United States.

Key Facts The arc Spanish colony, US occupation, family dictatorship, 1979 revolution and a US-backed rebel war.

Latest turn Since February 2025 a reform has made President Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, co-presidents.

Cost of 2018 The UN human-rights office counted 300+ deaths in the 2018 protests and their repression.

Money link Workers abroad sent US$5.24 billion home in 2024, 82.8% of it from the United States.

US angle Migration, remittances, tariffs and a US State Department travel warning tie Nicaragua to Americans.

A plain-English guide to how Nicaragua went from Spanish colony to revolution and war, and why its long history still shapes migration, money and policy in the United States.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Nicaragua 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Why It Matters

Nicaragua’s past reaches Americans through three channels: migration, money and policy. For calendar year 2024 the Central Bank of Nicaragua reported US$5.24 billion in remittances, up 12.5%, with 82.8% (US$4.34 billion) coming from the United States.

Many of those senders are Nicaraguans who live abroad, and the story below explains why so many left. Our Nicaragua news page tracks the daily news, and this guide supplies the background.

In Plain English FSLN is the Sandinista National Liberation Front, the party that led the 1979 revolution and governs today.

is the Sandinista National Liberation Front, the party that led the 1979 revolution and governs today. Contras were armed rebels who fought the Sandinista government in the 1980s with US support.

were armed rebels who fought the Sandinista government in the 1980s with US support. National Guard was the army and police force that the Somoza family used to hold power.

was the army and police force that the Somoza family used to hold power. OAS is the Organization of American States, a bloc of countries in the Americas.

is the Organization of American States, a bloc of countries in the Americas. Co-presidency is a 2025 constitutional change that makes Ortega and Murillo joint heads of state.

Pre-Columbian Peoples and Spanish Rule

Long before Europeans arrived, western Nicaragua was home to the Niquirano, Chorotega and Chontal peoples, a country study by the US Library of Congress says. The Niquirano were ruled by a chief named Nicarao, whose name the country carries.

On the Caribbean side, the same study says, the Miskito, an Indigenous people, emerged when a local Indigenous people, the Bawihka, intermarried with runaway slaves from British Caribbean colonies. English traders had given the Bawihka guns, which helped them dominate neighbouring groups.

The first formal Spanish expedition, led by Gil González Dávila, a Spanish explorer, in 1522, was driven back by the army of a chief named Diriangén. Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, a Spanish captain, then founded the first permanent Spanish settlements, including León and Granada, by 1524.

León became the home of liberals who wanted free trade, and Granada the home of conservatives who defended the old protected economy. Their rivalry turned violent and lasted into the twentieth century.

Nicaragua declared independence from Spain with the rest of Spain’s Central American province on 15 September 1821, then joined the United Provinces of Central America, a short-lived federation, in 1823. The federation broke apart, and a constituent assembly declared Nicaragua independent on 30 April 1838.

In the northeast, the English governor of Jamaica placed a Miskito “king” under crown protection in 1687. British control of the Caribbean coast lasted until the end of the nineteenth century.

File photo, undated. The old cathedral and the National Palace on the Plaza de la Revolución in Managua, Nicaragua. Photo: Martin Thurnherr, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article.
