Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

US Interventions

In the 1850s an American adventurer named William Walker led a private army into Nicaragua and made himself its ruler. His forces were evacuated by US Marines on 1 May 1857, the Library of Congress study says.

Walker was executed by a Honduran firing squad in 1860 after a later attempt to return to Central America. His adventures left Nicaraguans with a lasting suspicion of US designs on their country, the same study says.

In August 1912 about 2,700 US Marines landed at Corinto and Bluefields to back President Adolfo Díaz, the Library of Congress study says. US troops left in January 1933.

In 1916 the US Senate ratified the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty, which gave the United States exclusive rights to build a canal across Nicaragua. In those years the United States also helped create a National Guard, meant to be a non-partisan army and police force.

A rebel leader, Augusto César Sandino, refused to sign the 20 May 1927 peace pact and fought US and Nicaraguan government forces. On 21 February 1934 National Guard officers, on the orders of their chief Anastasio Somoza García, arrested and executed him.

Sandino later gave his name to the Sandinista movement. The movement that bears his name took power in 1979.

The Somoza Dynasty

Anastasio Somoza García won a December 1936 election and took back command of the National Guard on 1 January 1937, the Library of Congress study says. It calls the result a military dictatorship that lasted more than four decades.

On 21 September 1956 a poet shot him in León, and he died eight days later. His son Luis Somoza Debayle took over, and another son, Anastasio Somoza Debayle, won the presidency in 1967.

In December 1972 an earthquake destroyed most of Managua and killed about 10,000 people, the study says. The National Guard joined in looting, and the family’s handling of relief aid drew international criticism.

On 10 January 1978 Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal, editor of an opposition newspaper, was assassinated. In February 1978 the United States suspended military aid to the Somoza government.

File photo, March 2017. The cathedral of Granada, a city founded by the Spanish in 1524, with its red domes and yellow facade. Photo: Guillaume Baviere, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

The Sandinista Revolution

The FSLN was founded in 1961 by the student activists Carlos Fonseca Amador, Silvio Mayorga and Tomás Borge, the Library of Congress study says. It began among university students in Managua and took its name from Sandino.

In June 1979 a five-member provisional junta, a ruling council, formed in exile in Costa Rica. Its members included Daniel Ortega and Violeta Barrios de Chamorro, the widow of the murdered editor.

On 17 July 1979 Somoza Debayle resigned and fled to Miami, and on 19 July FSLN forces entered Managua. The study estimates that about 50,000 Nicaraguans had died by the time of the victory.

On 22 August 1979 the junta issued a Fundamental Statute that abolished the old constitution, presidency, Congress and courts. A consultative Council of State met from 4 May 1980, and the FSLN held 24 of its 47 seats.

Gil González Dávila leads the first formal Spanish expedition. By 1524 León and Granada are founded.

León and Granada are founded. 15 September 1821 Independence from Spain is declared in Spain’s Central American province.

Independence from Spain is declared in Spain’s Central American province. 30 April 1838 A constituent assembly declares Nicaragua independent of the federation.

A constituent assembly declares Nicaragua independent of the federation. August 1912 About 2,700 US Marines land at Corinto and Bluefields.

About 2,700 US Marines land at Corinto and Bluefields. 21 February 1934 Sandino is executed by National Guard officers.

Sandino is executed by National Guard officers. December 1972 An earthquake destroys most of Managua.

An earthquake destroys most of Managua. 19 July 1979 FSLN forces enter Managua after Somoza flees.

FSLN forces enter Managua after Somoza flees. 27 June 1986 The International Court of Justice rules against the United States.

The International Court of Justice rules against the United States. 25 February 1990 Violeta Chamorro defeats Ortega at the polls.

Violeta Chamorro defeats Ortega at the polls. 10 January 2007 Ortega is inaugurated after winning the 2006 election.

Ortega is inaugurated after winning the 2006 election. 18 April 2018 Mass protests begin across the country.

Mass protests begin across the country. 15 February 2023 A Managua court orders 94 people stripped of nationality.

A Managua court orders 94 people stripped of nationality. January 2025 Lawmakers approve the reform creating two co-presidents.

Lawmakers approve the reform creating two co-presidents. 1 September 2026 The Assembly gives first approval to a further reform extending terms to seven years.

The Contra War

Through the 1980s the Contras fought the Sandinista government with support from the United States. The US Congress cut off military aid to them under the Boland Amendment, a US law named for its sponsor, from October 1984 to October 1986, the later report of Lawrence Walsh, the special prosecutor appointed to investigate, says.

Nicaragua took the United States to the International Court of Justice, the UN’s top court, and on 27 June 1986 the court ruled for Nicaragua on key points. It found that Washington had used force against Nicaragua and broken a 1956 friendship treaty, and it ordered reparation.

Edwin Meese, then US attorney general, announced on 25 November 1986 that some proceeds of secret US arms sales to Iran had gone to the Contras. That affair became known as Iran-Contra and was investigated by Walsh.

Nicaragua voted on 25 February 1990, and Violeta Barrios de Chamorro, backed by a 14-party coalition, defeated President Ortega with 55% of the vote to his 41%, the Library of Congress study says. The FSLN handed power to her on 25 April 1990.

Ortega Returns

Ortega, who had lost in 1990, won the presidential election of 5 November 2006 with 38% of the vote against a divided opposition, the US State Department said. He was inaugurated on 10 January 2007.

In January 2014 the National Assembly repealed the constitutional ban on immediate reelection. The change paved the way for Ortega’s election wins in 2016 and 2021.

In 2016 Ortega ran with his wife, Rosario Murillo, as vice president, and won a third consecutive term. Our guide to how power works in Nicaragua explains how the couple’s circle works.

Before the 2021 vote, the UN’s Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua (GHREN) says, opposition parties lost legal status and candidates were arrested. Ortega won a fourth consecutive term.

In November 2021 Nicaragua notified the OAS that it would leave, and the withdrawal took effect on 19 November 2023, the US State Department said that day. Nicaragua also withdrew from the UN Human Rights Council in 2025, the GHREN chair told the UN General Assembly on 30 October 2025.

The 2018 Crisis

Mass protests spread across Nicaragua from 18 April 2018, after the government announced social-security changes that cut pensions. The UN human-rights office, known as OHCHR, set this out in its report of 29 August 2018.

OHCHR said in its report of 29 August 2018 that at least 300 people were killed and 2,000 injured in the protests and their repression between 18 April and 18 August 2018. The report drew on monitoring by the UN human-rights office’s regional office for Central America.

What UN Experts Documented (30 October 2025) 2021 Main independent media closed and confiscated; opposition parties lost legal status.

Main independent media closed and confiscated; opposition parties lost legal status. 2022 Thousands of non-profit groups and remaining independent media shut down.

Thousands of non-profit groups and remaining independent media shut down. 2023 Hundreds expelled, barred from returning or stripped of nationality, property and pensions.

Lost Citizenship and the 2025 Reform

On 15 February 2023 a Managua appeals court ordered 94 people stripped of nationality. The GHREN counted at least 452 Nicaraguans stripped of nationality by court order since February 2023, in its statement of 30 October 2025.

On 9 February 2023 the government flew 222 political prisoners to the United States and stripped them of nationality. The UN experts’ statement of 30 October 2025 lists hundreds more people expelled, barred from returning or stripped of nationality.

In January 2025 the National Assembly gave final approval to a constitutional reform, and it entered into force in February 2025. It creates two co-presidents who together hold the presidency.

When lawmakers first approved it in November 2024, the reform also lengthened the presidential term from five to six years, ConstitutionNet, a constitution-research site of International IDEA, a Stockholm-based democracy institute, reported. The GHREN says Ortega and Murillo now hold the co-presidency.

The experts say the Co-Presidents have merged the State and the FSLN into a unified machine of repression. They call the large-scale loss of nationality one of the most egregious practices.

The authorities have refused to engage with the group, the GHREN says. It says it has been denied access to the country.

Nicaragua Today

INIDE, the national statistics institute, estimated 6,874,748 residents for 2024. See our Nicaragua population and ethnic groups guide for the breakdown.

The World Bank, in its Macro Poverty Outlook country forecast of October 2026, says the economy grew about 5% a year on average from 2022 to 2025, helped by remittances. It estimates remittances rose from 27% of output in 2024 to 29.4% in 2025.

Remittances 2024: US$5.24 billion, up 12.5%, with 82.8% from the United States (Central Bank of Nicaragua).

US$5.24 billion, up 12.5%, with 82.8% from the United States (Central Bank of Nicaragua). Poverty: estimated to have fallen below 13% in 2026 (World Bank, October 2026).

On 12 December 2025 the US Trade Representative, the White House trade office, set a tariff on Nicaraguan goods not made under CAFTA-DR, the free-trade pact linking the US, Central America and the Dominican Republic. The duty, based on the Section 301 trade law and on labour, human-rights and rule-of-law concerns, is 0% from 1 January 2026, 10% from 1 January 2027 and 15% from 1 January 2028.

A separate notice of 28 July 2026 imposed a 12.5% Section 301 duty on most Nicaraguan goods entered on or after 24 July 2026, with exemptions listed in its annexes. The notice belongs to a wider forced-labour action that investigated 60 economies.

On Tuesday 1 September 2026 the National Assembly gave first approval to a further constitutional reform, Assembly president Gustavo Porras said, by a unanimous vote. The text would extend terms from six to seven years and restrict who may stand in elections.

A constitutional change needs approval in a second legislature before it takes effect, and the date of the next general election could not be confirmed at an official source. Our guide to the key political players covers the people who run the country.

Why Nicaragua’s History Matters in the United States

The Contra years left a record in US law and politics, from the Boland Amendment fight to the Iran-Contra inquiry. Walsh’s final report is a key record of how secret funds reached the rebels.

The International Court of Justice ruling of 27 June 1986 is the other lasting record, because it judged US conduct in Nicaragua. Our Nicaragua geopolitics guide covers the present-day rivalries.

The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, counted 92,679 Nicaraguan asylum seekers in the United States at the end of 2025. That migration is the human side of the remittance flow described above.

Remittances from the United States reached US$4.34 billion in 2024, the central bank says. The tariff spares goods made under CAFTA-DR, which the US trade office said should limit harm to US companies producing in Nicaragua.

The State Department’s advisory of 14 May 2026 keeps Nicaragua at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, citing wrongful detention and other risks. It also warns of exit bans on US citizens.

Two dated checkpoints follow from the December 2025 trade notice. The tariff steps to 10% on 1 January 2027 and to 15% on 1 January 2028.

What Is Not Known

The full-year 2025 remittance total from the Central Bank of Nicaragua was not found. The date of the next general election and the final ratification of the September 2026 reform were not confirmed at an official source.

Counts of deaths in 2018 differ between bodies, so we use the UN human-rights office figure of at least 300 killed between 18 April and 18 August 2018. How the 12.5% duty of July 2026 interacts with the December 2025 schedule was not stated by the trade office.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the history of Nicaragua?

Nicaragua was a Spanish colony from the 1520s, became independent in 1821 and had US Marines on its soil for most of the years from 1912 to 1933. It then lived under the Somoza family, the Sandinista revolution of 1979, the Contra war and Daniel Ortega’s return in 2007.

Who was Somoza?

Anastasio Somoza García took power in 1936 and founded a family dictatorship backed by the National Guard. His sons ruled after him until Anastasio Somoza Debayle fled on 17 July 1979.

What was the Contra war?

It was a 1980s conflict in which armed rebels called the Contras fought the Sandinista government with US support. The International Court of Justice ruled on 27 June 1986 that the United States had broken international law.

Why did Nicaragua protest in 2018?

Protests began on 18 April 2018 after the government announced social-security changes that cut pensions, the UN human-rights office reported. The office counted at least 300 people killed between 18 April and 18 August 2018.

Who runs Nicaragua today?

Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, hold the presidency as co-presidents under a constitutional reform in force since February 2025. The UN experts say the reform concentrates power in the presidency.

Is Nicaragua a dictatorship?

The UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua says the 2025 reform formalised virtually unlimited authority for the co-presidents. The experts say the authorities have refused to engage with them and have denied them access to the country.

World.title: Colombia Trade Deficit Hits US$2.27B
World.content:
File photo: the commercial port of Cartagena de Indias at dawn. (Photo: Reduvida3, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · TRADE

Colombia bought far more from the world than it sold in September, and the gap almost doubled in a year. The trade deficit reached US$2.27 billion, up from US$1.14 billion in September 2025, DANE, the national statistics agency, said on Wednesday 18 November 2026.

For US readers it matters because the United States is one of Colombia’s main suppliers while Chinese sellers gain ground fast. A wider gap also means Colombia needs more US dollars from abroad to pay for what it buys.

Key Facts What happened September’s trade deficit hit US$2.27 billion, almost double the US$1.14 billion of September 2025.

Imports Purchases from abroad jumped 33.7% to US$8.19 billion, the fastest rise in 12 months.

Exports Sales abroad rose 16.4% to US$5.41 billion, the highest since 2022, led by gold and oil.

Year so far The January to September deficit totals US$16.13 billion, up from US$11.74 billion a year earlier.

Imports grew twice as fast as exports in September, led by machinery, chemicals and natural gas, while gold and oil lifted what Colombia sold abroad.

The Big Picture

The September gap is part of a year-long widening. From January to September the deficit reached US$16.13 billion, against US$11.74 billion in the same months of 2025, DANE said on 18 November.

That is US$4.40 billion more, and September alone supplied about US$1.13 billion of the extra gap. Over the nine months imports including freight and insurance, known as CIF, totalled US$61.94 billion, up 19.2%, DANE said on 18 November.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Exports measured FOB, meaning the goods’ value at the port before freight and insurance, reached US$42.30 billion, up 13.3%, DANE said on 4 November. Imports are therefore growing faster than exports, and the deficit is built on that difference.

Imports: Cars, Machinery and Gas

Colombia imported US$8.19 billion of goods in September including freight and insurance, up 33.7% and the strongest annual rise in 12 months, DANE said on 18 November. Manufactured goods made up 72.8% of the total, or US$5.96 billion, up 28.6%.

Machinery and transport equipment rose 41% and chemicals rose 27.4%, DANE said. Fuels and mining products rose 91.2% to US$1.04 billion, with natural gas purchases up 350.9%.

Food, farm goods and drinks rose 30.5% to US$1.19 billion. The US$2.27 billion deficit is measured with imports at the border price (FOB), which is lower than the CIF total, so the two series cannot simply be subtracted.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Why China and the United States Matter

China was Colombia’s top supplier in September with 29.3% of imports, DANE said on 18 November. Other main suppliers, in the agency’s order, were the United States, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Trinidad and Tobago and India.

Over the first nine months of 2026, imports from China grew 26.7%, DANE said on 18 November. Imports from the United States grew 14.8% over the same period.

For US exporters that means Colombian demand is growing, but Chinese suppliers are growing almost twice as fast overall. Every extra dollar of imports widens a gap that Colombia must cover with dollars earned from exports or borrowed abroad.

Exports: Gold and Oil Lead

Exports totalled US$5.41 billion FOB in September, up 16.4% from US$4.65 billion and the highest monthly figure since July 2022, DANE said on 4 November. Fuels and mining products brought in US$2.24 billion, or 41.3% of the total.

Non-monetary gold, which is gold sold as a commodity rather than held as reserves, rose 87.5% to US$786.9 million. Oil and refined products rose 40.2% to US$1.48 billion, even though crude volume fell 5.4% to 13.4 million barrels, so the value rose much faster than the volume.

Farm and food exports rose only 2.9% to US$1.27 billion, DANE said on 4 November. Coal exports rose only 1.5%, so oil and gold, not coal, drove the gain.

What It Means for You

Readers who follow Colombian assets should note that imports are growing about twice as fast as exports, which keeps demand for dollars high. US sellers of machinery, chemicals and fuels are among those competing for that demand.

The next test is whether gold and oil prices hold, because they carried September’s export gain. If they ease while imports stay strong, the gap would widen further.

What Is Not Known

The figures show what Colombia bought, not why demand jumped, and DANE’s export numbers are provisional. The release date for October trade data is not confirmed, and we have not compared Colombia with its neighbours for the same month.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Colombia’s trade deficit in September 2026?

The deficit was US$2.27 billion, up from US$1.14 billion in September 2025. DANE, Colombia’s statistics agency, published the figure on 18 November 2026.

Why did Colombia’s trade deficit widen?

Imports rose 33.7% to US$8.19 billion while exports rose 16.4% to US$5.41 billion. Machinery, chemicals and natural gas led the import growth.

What is the difference between FOB and CIF?

FOB values goods at the port before freight and insurance. CIF adds freight and insurance, so CIF import totals are higher than FOB totals.

Which countries sell the most to Colombia?

China supplied 29.3% of imports in September. The United States, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Trinidad and Tobago and India followed in DANE’s order.

Sources: DANE (Departamento Administrativo Nacional de Estadística), imports bulletin for September 2026, published 18 November 2026: dane.gov.co imports; DANE exports bulletin for September 2026, published 4 November 2026: dane.gov.co exports.

World.title: Colombia’s Grupo Argos Buys Back US$45M
World.content:
Grupo Argos, a Colombian holding company, has bought back about US$90 million of its own shares, and its stock has climbed a quarter. The owner of cement maker Cementos Argos said on 18 November 2026 that a second offer covered 7.6 million shares worth COP 149.2 billion (about US$45 million).

A buyback means a company uses its cash to repurchase shares from investors, which shrinks the share count. For US holders of Colombian stocks, it shows how management values its business after the share rose 25% between 5 August and 18 November 2026.

What. Grupo Argos, a Colombian holding firm, awarded a second buyback of 7.6 million shares.

Price. Ordinary (voting) shares at COP 21,000 (US$6.34), preferred (non-voting) at COP 16,480 (US$4.97).

Total. Buybacks now reach COP 300 billion (US$90.5 million), 60% of the first-phase goal.

As of 18 November 2026, 15:50 GMT (UTC)

Grupo Argos is buying back its own shares at a steady pace under a plan it began in August. The second offer lifts total repurchases to 60% of the first-phase goal.

Where This Comes From

Grupo Argos said in its statement of 18 November 2026 that it presented its ACE 1.0 programme on 5 August 2026. ACE is the company’s plan to raise shareholder returns through three pillars: operating efficiency, an asset-management business and faster buybacks.

The statement sets a goal of doubling the dividend per share within 24 to 36 months. It also aims to lift consolidated Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) from COP 3.2 trillion (about US$965 million) to COP 5.6 trillion (about US$1.69 billion).

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The same statement targets a total shareholder return (price gains plus dividends) of 75% to 100%. The ordinary share traded at COP 16,400 (US$4.95) on 5 August and at COP 20,500 (US$6.18) on 18 November 2026, a rise of 25% by our calculation.

Grupo Argos announced the second offer on 4 November 2026, with bids from 5 November for four exchange business days. The first award came in early September.

La Alpujarra government district in Medellín, the city where Grupo Argos is based. File photo.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Colombia 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Happened

In its 18 November 2026 statement, Grupo Argos reported that it awarded a second buyback offer of about COP 150 billion (about US$45.3 million). The award covers more than 7.6 million shares for COP 149.2 billion (about US$45 million).

The statement says about 5.26 million ordinary shares, which carry votes, sold at COP 21,000 (about US$6.34) for COP 110.4 billion (about US$33.3 million). It says 2.35 million preferred shares, with no vote but dividend priority, sold at COP 16,480 (about US$4.97) for COP 38.7 billion (about US$11.7 million).

The offer ran through the Bolsa de Colombia, the Colombian stock exchange, using its independent mechanism of book building. In book building, sellers submit bids and a single clearing price is set.

Grupo Argos said cumulative buybacks now reach about COP 300 billion (about US$90.5 million), or 60% of the COP 500 billion (about US$150.9 million) goal for this first phase. The programme was planned to run six to 12 months from its launch, the company said on 5 August 2026.

All US$ values in this article use the market rate of COP 3,314.55 per US$ on 18 November 2026. Rounded US$ figures are our conversions.

Why It Matters

The ordinary award price of COP 21,000 (US$6.34) sits about 2.4% above the COP 20,500 (US$6.18) market price of 18 November 2026, our calculation from Grupo Argos’s statement. Sellers in the offer therefore received a modest premium to the market.

The first ACE award, in early September, covered 1,929,159 shares for COP 39.2 billion (about US$11.8 million), Grupo Argos said. That award priced ordinary shares at COP 21,900 (about US$6.61) and preferred shares at COP 16,500 (about US$4.98).

By our calculation, the second award took about four times as many shares, while the ordinary price paid fell about 4.1%. The company says buybacks aim to make the market price converge to fundamental value, meaning what the business is worth.

Felipe Aristizábal, Grupo Argos vice-president of strategy and finance, said in the company statement that ACE aims “to allocate capital only when we find opportunities able to generate attractive returns.” He said the second offer lets the company “accelerate” the buyback programme “in a significant way”.

What to Watch

Grupo Argos’s 5 August 2026 launch plan set the programme at six to 12 months, which puts its end between February and August 2027, our calculation. We found no dated next step, such as a third offer, in the material available to us.

What It Means for You

For a US investor holding Colombian stocks through an emerging-market fund, a buyback leaves fewer shares outstanding. Each remaining share then represents a larger slice of Grupo Argos, which also owns the infrastructure unit Odinsa.

Buybacks do not guarantee a higher share price, and this article offers no view on whether to buy or sell. For context on MSCI, a US stock-index provider, see our report on Grupo Argos Preferred Share Joins MSCI Small Cap Index.

Background on the business is in our Grupo Argos company profile. More stories from the country are on our Colombia news page.

What Is Not Known

Grupo Argos’s statement of 18 November 2026 does not say who sold the shares or how many bids it received. It also does not say whether a third offer will follow.

We found no detail on how the company funds the buyback beyond its statement. The cumulative COP 300 billion (about US$90.5 million) exceeds the two awards we list, and we could not reconcile the gap.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Grupo Argos spend in its second buyback?

Grupo Argos awarded 7.6 million shares for COP 149.2 billion (about US$45 million), it said on 18 November 2026. That covers 5.26 million ordinary and 2.35 million preferred shares.

What is the ACE 1.0 programme?

ACE 1.0 is Grupo Argos’s plan, presented on 5 August 2026, to raise shareholder returns. It rests on operating efficiency, an asset-management business and faster buybacks.

How far along is the buyback goal?

Cumulative buybacks reach about COP 300 billion (about US$90.5 million), Grupo Argos said on 18 November 2026. That is 60% of the COP 500 billion (about US$150.9 million) first-phase goal.

Why does a company buy back its own shares?

A company repurchases shares to shrink the share count and, in Grupo Argos’s words, to bring the market price closer to fundamental value. Buybacks do not guarantee a higher price.

Sources Grupo Argos statements of 4 November and 18 November 2026 and its ACE 1.0 presentation of 5 August 2026; Bolsa de Colombia (Colombian stock exchange) buyback notices; market exchange rate of 18 November 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Traffic Jams Doubled in a Year – Half the Roads Now Back Up
World.content:
If your drive across the Central Valley feels slower than it did a year ago, the numbers back you up. Traffic jams on Costa Rica’s roads doubled in intensity in 2025, and half of all road segments measured now back up at least once, according to the 2026 National Competitiveness Index.

The index, published Nov. 13 by the Council for the Promotion of Competitiveness (CPC), counted 117.6 jam reports for every 100-meter (328-foot) stretch of congested road. The year before, the figure was 57.4. The jam data comes from the State of the Nation Program, which draws on Waze reports shared through the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT). Of the road segments the index evaluated, 50.1% recorded at least one jam, the highest share since the series began.

The waits are getting longer, too. Drivers now lose an average of 207.4 seconds, or about three and a half minutes, on every congested 100-meter segment. CPC economist Andrés Fernández put it in starker terms. He said the average time drivers spend per kilometer (0.62 miles) of jammed road rose from about 30 minutes to about 35 in the latest edition.

Taken together, those figures pushed the index’s road connectivity score from 60.7 to 56.6 out of 100. The 4.1-point drop is the steepest since the series began in 2021. The worst-connected areas are mostly in and around the capital. San José, Escazú, Curridabat, Belén, Montes de Oca and Santo Domingo rank among the most congested, along with Corredores in the southern zone. The area of San José scored just 40.9 out of 100 on road connectivity.

The longest delays, however, turned up on the central Pacific coast. In Garabito, the area that includes Jacó, drivers lose up to 11.9 minutes for every 100 meters of congested road, the highest figure in the country. Heredia averages 5.9 minutes, while Sarchí has the shortest delays at about two minutes.

Fernández said congestion is heaviest in the Greater Metropolitan Area and on the approaches to the ports. Travel times to Puerto Caldera and to Daniel Oduber International Airport in Liberia both reached their highest levels in the index’s history. Over the past five years, 62 of the 82 areas lost ground on road connectivity, while 20 improved. Cartago, Vázquez de Coronado and San Isidro saw the sharpest declines, while Buenos Aires, Carrillo and Guatuso improved the most.

The smoothest traffic is found in Turrubares, Puriscal, Bagaces and Acosta. Congestion weighed on an otherwise improving national picture. Costa Rica’s overall competitiveness score rose 2.4 points to 58.6 out of 100, but the CPC identified worsening traffic and a 41.5% drop in real per-student investment in school infrastructure as the main factors limiting further gains.

For anyone who drives here, the index puts numbers to what the daily commute already suggests. Jams are more frequent, they cover more of the road network and they last longer than at any point on record.

World.title: Costa Rica Ties Worst Defeat in Its History With 7-0 Loss to Argentina
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national soccer team lost 7-0 to Argentina on Tuesday night in Córdoba. The result ties the worst defeat in the team’s history. The friendly at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes, which kicked off at 5 p.m. Costa Rica time, was effectively over by halftime. Argentina led 4-0 at the break and scored three more after the restart. Costa Rica had less than a third of the possession and rarely reached the attacking third.

The score matches Costa Rica’s 7-0 loss to Spain at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and a 7-0 defeat to Mexico in 1975. It is also the heaviest loss of Bryan Ruiz’s short time as head coach. Nico Paz opened the scoring in the eighth minute. Julián Álvarez doubled the lead in the 35th, Paz added his second three minutes later and Álvarez made it 4-0 just before halftime.

Franco Mastantuono replaced Paz at the break and scored in the 48th minute. Alexis Mac Allister made it 6-0 in the 78th after Costa Rica lost the ball deep in its own half. Mastantuono completed his brace two minutes from the end of regulation time.

Argentina finished as runner-up at this year’s World Cup and is playing without Lionel Messi, who has retired from international football. Lionel Scaloni’s side came into the match after a 2-1 loss to Uruguay in Buenos Aires four days earlier. Defenders Mariano Troilo and Aaron Anselmino made their senior debuts in the second half.

At his post-match news conference, Ruiz called it a very hard defeat that showed the gap between the two teams. He said the scoreline left little to add, that there was no justification for the performance and that he and his staff took responsibility. Ruiz said Argentina exposed his team in every part of the game and deserved the win. He admitted he made a mistake by having his side play out from the back. He also said he played some players out of their usual positions, including Andrey Soto, because he wanted to test him.

The coach said his staff will review every player in detail after the international window to decide who stays in the squad. He said he did not regret scheduling Ecuador and Argentina, because his players needed to see what competing at that level demands. In his view, Costa Rica is still far from it.

Tuesday’s loss ended a difficult trip to South America that began Friday with a 2-0 defeat to Ecuador in Quito. Ruiz called that performance very acceptable by comparison. Ruiz, a former national team captain, became interim coach on Sept. 28 after Argentine coach Fernando Batista was dismissed.

The Costa Rican Football Federation later named him permanent coach for the cycle leading to the 2030 World Cup. He also played in the 2022 defeat to Spain, coming off the bench with Costa Rica already 4-0 down. Midfielder Celso Borges started both matches.

Reaction at home was harsh. Commentators and sports pages across Costa Rica called the performance humiliating and questioned whether the team was ready for opponents of Argentina’s level. Costa Rica did not qualify for the 2026 World Cup, and Ruiz’s rebuild is aimed at 2030. Costa Rica has still never beaten Argentina, and Ruiz now has a long review ahead before the team plays again.

World.title: Costa Rica’s $9.8 Billion Banco Popular Has Had No Board Since July
World.content:
Banco Popular, Costa Rica’s fourth-largest financial institution by assets, has operated without a seated board of directors since July 31, and the banking regulator is now urging lawmakers to tighten the rules for who can sit on it. In a letter dated Oct. 9, Hazel Valverde, head of the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef), asked lawmakers to strengthen the legal requirements for the bank’s directors, including suitability, professional experience, technical knowledge, honorability and independence of judgment.

The regulator warned that governance weaknesses at systemically important institutions, a group that includes Banco Popular, Banco Nacional, Banco de Costa Rica and BAC, could affect the entire financial system. The stakes are large. Banco Popular reported 4.42 trillion colones (about $9.84 billion) in assets and 1.10 trillion colones (about $2.45 billion) in equity at the end of September. Dollar figures in this article use the Central Bank reference sell rate of 449.04 colones for Nov. 18, close to the record lows the dollar has hit this year.

Under the bank’s governing law, only the board can approve the annual budget and certain internal rules. The terms of all seven directors expired July 31, and the board had already stopped meeting after two members resigned on June 29 to join the boards of other state banks.

The bank’s internal audit office warned in August that management cannot take decisions reserved for the board. In September, the bank’s corporate general management cautioned that the 2027 budget, internal regulations and the external audit contract were at risk. The Comptroller General’s Office stated on Sept. 25 that budget approval is a power the board cannot delegate.

Sugef also recommended that lawmakers stagger the board’s terms. Today all seven seats run on four-year terms that expire at the same time. Banco Nacional and Banco de Costa Rica instead name directors to eight-year terms split across two administrations, three seats in one and four in the next. The regulator said that when every term ends at once, a bank can lose significant institutional knowledge and face long periods without a working board.

The government has moved to fill the gap. The Executive Decree allows the Governing Council to appoint, on an interim basis, the four directors and four alternates normally chosen by the bank’s Workers’ Assembly. Together with the three directors the Executive already names, that would complete the seven-member board.

The decree, signed by First Vice President Francisco Gamboa Soto, Minister of the Presidency Rodrigo Chaves Robles and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla, limits the government to candidates the Workers’ Assembly has already preselected. The assembly’s integration commission said last week that it had sent its shortlist to the presidential offices. As of early Wednesday, no appointments had been announced.

The leadership gap follows a turbulent stretch for the bank. On Sept. 11, Sugef lifted Banco Popular out of “financial irregularity,” a status tied to weaknesses in board governance, and placed it at normality level 3. In that resolution, the regulator rated the board’s suitability a 3 on a scale of 1 to 4, where 1 is best.

The bank’s numbers remain solid on paper. Conglomerate profit through September reached 26.4 billion colones (about $58.9 million), up roughly 47% from a year earlier, and capital adequacy stood near 22%, well above the 10% minimum. Loans sent to judicial collection, however, nearly doubled to 67.3 billion colones (about $149.9 million) from 34.1 billion colones (about $76 million).

Sugef’s letter responded to a legislative committee reviewing a bill that would fund non-contributory pensions with half of Banco Popular’s employer contribution, one of several proposals touching Costa Rica’s strained pension system. The regulator said board requirements should be examined as part of a broader review of the bank’s sustainability.

Banco Popular’s press office said the bank will respect the authorities’ decisions and that any changes will follow legal procedure. It described the interim appointment measure as relevant because it would allow a board to act on matters that cannot be decided today.

Banco Popular is one of the institutions many here use for savings, loans and currency exchange. How quickly the government seats an interim board will determine whether the bank can approve its 2027 budget on time, while the regulator’s proposals now sit with lawmakers already weighing a crowded economic agenda.

World.title: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years. What It Means for Costa Rica Travel
World.content:
The United States is no longer considered measles-free. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced today that the virus has circulated continuously in the country for more than 12 months, ending a status the US had held since 2000. If you fly between the US and Costa Rica, this is not a travel ban. It means measles now spreads inside the US on its own, rather than arriving mainly with travelers from abroad, so your chance of running into it on a trip north is higher than it has been in a generation.

The US has recorded more than 5,000 confirmed cases so far in 2026, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is more than double the 2,289 cases in all of 2025 and the highest count since 1991. PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa said vaccination remains the main way to protect yourself. He said the US is taking steps to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response.

Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles-free status, and Guatemala could follow when its 12-month review period ends on Dec. 23. Daniel Salas, a former Costa Rican health minister who now leads PAHO’s immunization program, said Mexico’s measures have sharply cut cases but warned that as long as transmission continues, so does the risk.

Costa Rica is in a different position, it has had no endemic measles transmission since 1999, and as of September health authorities had investigated about 190 suspected cases this year and confirmed five, all imported or linked to an imported case. None was fatal.

Christian Valverde, the Health Ministry’s director general, has said national vaccination coverage against measles is above 94%. PAHO considers 95% the level needed to keep the virus from taking hold, which is why every imported case gets a fast response. If you are heading to the US, Mexico or another country with an active outbreak, you can get a measles booster before you go.

The Health Ministry opened the traveler booster to anyone 15 and older, and Health Minister Mary Munive said doses are available at Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) health centers and at private clinics. Get the shot at least two weeks before you leave. The vaccine needs that time to build protection, and it is the timing the Health Ministry recommends. More than 24,000 travelers had received a booster by September.

Not sure you are covered? Costa Rica’s routine schedule gives two doses, at 15 months and at four years. Adults who have lost their vaccination card, or who were vaccinated before records went digital, are the people doctors most often advise to get another dose. Watch for symptoms for up to three weeks after you get back. Measles usually starts with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed a few days later by a rash that spreads from the face downward. Early on it is easy to confuse with other fevers circulating in Costa Rica, such as dengue.

If you think you have measles, call your EBAIS or clinic before you go in, so staff can keep you away from other patients. It is one of the most contagious diseases known, and a person can spread it for several days before the rash appears. The Americas as a whole lost its measles-free status in November 2025, after Canada passed 12 months of continuous transmission. A country can win the status back once it shows 12 consecutive months without endemic spread.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Rent-to-Own Homes With Up to 100% Financing
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Housing and Human Settlements (MIVAH) is drafting a rent-to-own model for families who can afford a monthly payment but lack the savings for a down payment or cannot prove to a bank that they can repay a loan. Housing Minister Guillermo Carazo said the model, known in Spanish as leasing habitacional, would add a rental stage of about five years before a mortgage is formalized.

Under the proposal, a trust or real estate fund would buy the property. When the home is a new apartment, the developer would be paid and exit the deal. The future buyer would then sign a lease with a purchase option, with the sale price fixed from the start, and pay monthly rent comparable to a regular lease. Part of that rent could be set aside as savings toward the down payment, although Carazo said whether that happens, and how much, would depend on each institution’s product.

At the end of the rental period, the tenant could exercise the option and take out a mortgage, subject to the lender’s approval. Carazo said the payment record built during those years would show the lender that the household can sustain a loan payment, lowering the bank’s perceived risk.

That record could also raise the share of the price a lender is willing to finance. In the minister’s example, a borrower initially offered 80% of the appraised value could reach 95% or even 100% after four to five years of proven payments, shrinking or eliminating the down payment.

Ideally, Carazo said, the rent would be close to the future mortgage payment so lenders can confirm affordability. The rental period would not be rigid and could be extended if a family’s circumstances change, for example if one partner loses a job and the household needs to delay the purchase or drop the plan.

Public and private banks, mutual housing associations, cooperatives and the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (SUGEF) are involved in the discussions. Each authorized institution would design its own product under a common legal framework set by a new law. MIVAH expects to have a draft bill early next year, which it will discuss with the Executive Branch before sending it to the Legislative Assembly. Carazo stressed that all conditions would need to be clear to buyers from the outset.

Carazo said developers believe the model would boost home and apartment sales. He offered a preliminary estimate of a 20% to 30% increase, while acknowledging the figure is difficult to calculate. The proposal targets a wide gap. A study by the University of Costa Rica’s Graduate Program in Architecture, the Federated College of Engineers and Architects (CFIA) and the organization Gestionando Hábitat found that 81.4% of renter households, about 279,890 families, face total exclusion or significant restrictions when seeking formal home financing.

Costa Rica has no specific legal framework for rent-to-own housing, although some lease-with-purchase-option arrangements already exist. A previous bill to regulate the model did not become law. Key details remain open, including interest rates, eligibility requirements and what would happen to savings built into the rent if a family walks away before buying. Those terms will depend on the products lenders design and on the final text lawmakers approve.

World.title: Horacio Zeballos and Marcel Granollers Make Winning Start at ATP Finals
World.content:
Argentina’s Horacio Zeballos and Spanish partner Marcel Granollers opened their ATP Finals campaign with a convincing victory Monday, defeating Italy’s Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori 6-4, 6-4 to take an important first step toward the season-ending doubles championship.

The third-seeded pair needed just 79 minutes to overcome their fifth-seeded opponents at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, converting all three of their break-point opportunities to begin round-robin play with a 1-0 record. The victory was particularly satisfying for Zeballos and Granollers, who had lost to the same Italian partnership during last year’s ATP Finals and again in the Rome Masters final earlier this season.

This time, the Argentine-Spanish combination controlled the decisive moments, overcoming an uneven start before establishing themselves as the stronger team. The opening set began with three consecutive service breaks. Zeballos and Granollers struck first, but Bolelli and Vavassori immediately responded to level the score.

The experienced pair broke again in the third game and protected that advantage throughout the remainder of the set. Their serving improved as the match progressed, allowing them to keep the Italian partnership under pressure without giving away further opportunities.

The second set followed a similar pattern, although both teams held serve through the opening four games. Zeballos and Granollers made their move in the fifth game, securing the only break of the set before closing out the match 6-4. The statistics reflected their efficiency. They finished with five aces, committed no double faults and landed 74% of their first serves.

They also won 79% of the points played behind their second serve, an important advantage against opponents known for their aggressive returning and strong net play. Most significantly, Zeballos and Granollers converted all three break points they created, while saving three of the four opportunities they faced.

The result evened their career head-to-head record against Bolelli and Vavassori at four victories apiece. For Zeballos, the win represents another encouraging chapter in a remarkable doubles career. The 41-year-old Argentine and 40-year-old Granollers are competing together at the ATP Finals for the seventh consecutive season, a testament to the consistency of one of the longest-standing partnerships in professional tennis.

They have been among the world’s leading doubles teams since joining forces in 2019, reaching the top of the ATP doubles rankings and winning three Grand Slam titles together. Their most recent major triumph came at the 2026 French Open, where they successfully defended their Roland Garros doubles championship.

They also reached the finals in Dallas and Rome this season, although their campaign was interrupted by physical problems following the US Open. The pair returned to competition at the Paris Masters before arriving in Turin with renewed confidence. Despite their success elsewhere, the ATP Finals title remains unfinished business.

Zeballos and Granollers reached the championship match in 2023, losing to Rajeev Ram and Joe Salisbury. They also advanced to the semifinals in 2020 and 2021. However, their last two appearances ended during the group stage, making Monday’s opening victory especially important.

Granollers previously won the ATP Finals doubles championship in 2012 alongside fellow Spaniard Marc López, but he has yet to capture the title with Zeballos. For the Argentine, winning in Turin would carry additional historical significance. Zeballos became the first Argentine to reach the tournament’s doubles final in 2023 and is now seeking to become the first South American to win the championship.

The ATP Finals bring together the eight leading doubles teams of the season, divided into two groups of four. Each partnership plays three round-robin matches, with the top two teams from each group advancing to the semifinals. Zeballos and Granollers compete in the Mark Woodforde Group, alongside Bolelli and Vavassori, American Christian Harrison and Britain’s Neal Skupski, and Germany’s Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.

The Germans, who won the ATP Finals title in 2024, also began their campaign with a victory Monday, defeating Harrison and Skupski 6-1, 6-3. That sets up an important second-round meeting between the two unbeaten teams. Zeballos and Granollers are scheduled to face Krawietz and Puetz on Wednesday, November 18, at 6 p.m. local time in Turin.

A second consecutive victory would put the Argentine-Spanish partnership in a strong position to advance to the semifinals. For Zeballos, who has already established himself among Argentina’s most accomplished doubles players, the opportunity to add the season-ending championship to his Grand Slam success remains a powerful motivation.

Monday’s victory was only the beginning, but it was precisely the start he and Granollers needed as they pursue one of the few major titles still missing from their partnership.

World.title: Killers of Costa Rica Journalist May Have Had Help Tracking Him, OIJ Says
World.content:
Investigators believe the two gunmen who killed journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri on Route 32 may have had help following him, said Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). Muñoz said today that the attackers knew which vehicle the journalist was driving.

Investigators are examining whether a second motorcycle or another vehicle trailed Rodríguez and whether the gunmen received instructions before the attack. Agents are collecting security camera footage to reconstruct the routes the suspects used to reach the scene near San Miguel de Santo Domingo, in Heredia, and to flee.

According to the OIJ’s account, the attackers knew Rodríguez was alone in a red pickup. They pulled alongside, confirmed he was their target and opened fire, then circled the vehicle and fired again from a second angle. Muñoz said the men checked that Rodríguez was dead before fleeing toward San José. Based on how they acted, he said, they apparently set out to make sure he would not survive.

Agents have also searched Rodríguez’s home in Santo Domingo with authorization from prosecutors and the Heredia Criminal Court. Muñoz said they seized electronic devices, equipment and documents that will undergo forensic analysis as investigators try to establish a motive and identify those responsible.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said prosecutors will review the allegations Rodríguez published on social media, including the people he named, along with anyone else who may have had a reason to attack him. No arrests had been announced as of Tuesday afternoon, and the OIJ has not publicly identified any suspects.

Rodríguez, 50, had spent three days with his parents in Guápiles and set out for San José around 1 p.m. yesterday, according to his brother, Andrés Rodríguez. The Costa Rican Red Cross received the alert about the shooting at 3:21 p.m., about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) from his home.

The journalist had filed about 10 complaints over threats in the past two years, according to the OIJ. Laura Lara, one of his lawyers, said he had worn a bulletproof vest for roughly three weeks as the threats mounted and had it on when he was shot. Lara said Rodríguez turned down the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program because he believed it would restrict his work. Díaz had said yesterday that the journalist declined that protection despite the threats.

International press freedom groups added their voices on today Reporters Without Borders called the killing an alarm signal for press freedom in a country long regarded as a regional benchmark. The group urged authorities to determine whether the killing was linked to his publications and the threats against him.

José Zamora, Americas director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, said authorities should thoroughly examine any link to Rodríguez’s journalism and prosecute both the gunmen and whoever ordered the killing. The Inter American Press Association demanded an exhaustive and independent investigation.

His wake was scheduled for this evening at a funeral home in central Cartago, his brother said. A funeral Mass is set for Wednesday at 2 p.m. at the San Esteban parish, known as the Iglesia del Carmen, in Cartago’s El Carmen neighborhood. The OIJ has asked anyone with information to call its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

According to the attorney general, Rodríguez is the third journalist killed in Costa Rica, after Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. Whether investigators reach anyone beyond the two gunmen is likely to define how this case is remembered.

World.title: Dollar Expected to Keep Falling in Costa Rica After Record Low of 446 Colones
World.content:
The U.S. dollar is likely to keep losing value against the Costa Rican colón for the rest of 2026, financial analysts said. Their forecast follows the exchange rate’s fall to the lowest level in the history of Costa Rica’s foreign exchange market. On Friday, Nov. 13, the weighted average rate on Monex, the Central Bank of Costa Rica’s (BCCR) foreign exchange market, closed at 446.10 colones per dollar. That was the lowest on record in Central Bank data and the eighth straight session of decline.

The close was 0.72 colones below Thursday’s 446.82 and broke the previous record of 446.80, set on Sept. 17. The Central Bank’s reference rates for Monday, Nov. 16, stood at 442.56 colones for buying dollars and 448.34 colones for selling them. By Tuesday, Nov. 17, the reference buying rate had slipped to 441.73 colones.

Traders exchanged $49.3 million in 228 transactions on Friday, at rates between 445.80 and 446.30 colones, according to BCCR data. The Central Bank bought $41.8 million of that total, or 84.8% of the day’s volume. Of those purchases, $32.3 million were stabilization operations and $9.5 million covered the needs of the non-bank public sector.

The bank uses stabilization purchases to absorb part of the dollar supply and moderate swings in the rate. Friday’s operations did not prevent a new low. Luis Alvarado, an analyst at Acobo Puesto de Bolsa, said the downward pressure could continue over the coming weeks, practically until the end of the year. He described the colón’s appreciation as a trend that has marked much of the past three years.

Pablo González, an economist at Mercado de Valores, called the recent lows small moves within an established trend. As long as the market has an excess of foreign currency, he said, a significant change in the short term is unlikely. Neither analyst forecast a specific floor for the rate.

The analysts pointed to a steady supply of dollars from foreign-currency-earning sectors, against weak demand. Seasonal factors add to the pressure in November and December, when companies convert dollars to colones to pay taxes and the aguinaldo, the mandatory year-end bonus.

The dollar opened 2026 at 497.07 colones on Jan. 2, according to BCCR records. At Friday’s close, it had lost 10.3% this year and stood more than a third below its 2022 peak. A weaker dollar lowers the colón cost of imported goods and of debts held in dollars. It also reduces the colón value of income earned in dollars, including salaries, pensions, remittances and tourism revenue.

The Central Bank publishes the Monex result after each daily session.

World.title: GTA 6 begins global rollout as early players praise graphics and gameplay
World.content:
GTA 6 begins global rollout as early players praise graphics and gameplay

By Zoila Palma: The highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) is beginning its global rollout, with players in New Zealand among the first to access the latest instalment of Rockstar Games’ popular franchise.

As the game becomes available across different time zones on November 18 and 19, early reactions have been overwhelmingly positive, with players praising its impressive graphics, realistic environments and smooth gameplay, Yahoo reports.

Early players have highlighted the quality of the game’s visuals, particularly its detailed surroundings, realistic water effects and driving experience on both roads and beaches.

As of 8:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on Wednesday, the game had reportedly become the highest-rated video game in Metacritic history, based on 167 reviews.

Digital marketing firm Sensor Tower also estimated that pre-orders had already generated more than US$1.65 billion in sales.

The global release is being staggered according to local time zones, meaning players in different regions will gain access at different hours.

While New Zealand and Australia were among the first to unlock the game, players in the United States are scheduled to gain access at midnight on November 19 in their respective time zones.

At launch, GTA 6 features a single-player experience, with no multiplayer mode available initially.

Some players have reportedly attempted to change their console region to New Zealand to access the game earlier, although PlayStation 5 users have raised concerns about potential account restrictions.

World.title: International News: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic trilateral talks in China
World.content:
International News: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic trilateral talks in China

By Zoila Palma: United States President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping have gathered in Shenzhen, China, ahead of a historic trilateral meeting scheduled for Thursday, November 19.

Trump and Putin exchanged greetings and shook hands today, marking their first face-to-face encounter in more than a year, as world attention turns to the discussions involving the three global powers.

Trump received a lavish welcome from Xi upon arriving in Shenzhen, including a red carpet ceremony, an honour guard, a military flyover and a cheering crowd, BBC reports.

The two leaders exchanged a handshake and embrace before Trump later greeted Putin ahead of a formal reception. The Kremlin confirmed that the two presidents had only exchanged pleasantries and had not yet held substantive discussions. Putin and Xi also held approximately two hours of talks earlier Wednesday.

The trilateral meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, is expected to last no more than an hour, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.

Although an official agenda has not been released, discussions could cover the war in Ukraine, tensions involving Iran, nuclear proliferation, international trade and developments in artificial intelligence. Trump and Putin are also expected to hold separate talks, with the ongoing war in Ukraine potentially featuring prominently.

The planned discussions have raised concerns in Ukraine, with President Volodymyr Zelensky expressing apprehension about decisions concerning the war being discussed without representatives from Kyiv or European countries present.

China has maintained that it remains neutral in the conflict since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while emphasizing the importance of safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability. Beijing has also rejected accusations that it has supported Moscow’s military campaign through exports of dual-use technology.

Xi described China’s relationship with Russia as stable and expressed his intention to strengthen ties with the United States through a constructive and stable partnership based on respect, fairness and equality.

World.title: Looking for night work? Cahal Pech Village Resort is hiring

Looking for night work? Cahal Pech Village Resort is hiring

The shift runs from 10pm to 6am.

The successful applicant will manage the front desk overnight, balance and close the daily accounts, and prepare end of day reports. The role also covers guest check ins, check outs and requests, along with monitoring property security.

A valid driver’s license is required.

The resort is looking for someone honest, dependable and independent, who is also an excellent team player and able to work nights, weekends and holidays.

World.content:
Sunny Wednesday with a few showers and isolated thunderstorms

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect sunny skies with cloudy spells this Wednesday, along with a few showers and isolated thunderstorms.

The National Meteorological Service says a light north to northeasterly airflow will prevail.

A few showers and isolated thunderstorms are likely mainly offshore this morning and inland this afternoon, then mostly over the south tonight. Elsewhere, showers or thunderstorms are expected to be isolated.

Coastal areas will reach a high of 87°F (31°C) with a low of 76°F (24°C). Inland areas will hit 89°F (32°C), cooling to 72°F (22°C). The hills will see a high of 76°F (24°C) and a low of 65°F (18°C).
