World.title: AI a ‘growing concern’ at ASEAN’s parliamentary org, but no concrete measures yet
World.content:
ADDRESS. House Speaker Bojie Dy delivers a speech at the opening ceremony of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly General Assembly in Manila on November 18, 2026.

'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

MANILA, Philippines – The persistent threat of artificial intelligence (AI) is a cloud hanging over the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but uncertainty remains over any concrete measure to approach the subject.

“It’s a concern for everybody, it’s a growing concern, and I think it cannot be addressed by one country. It has to be a concerted effort among the regions and other countries to be able to make sure that this is not abused,” House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, head of the Philippine delegation for the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly, said on the sidelines of the AIPA on Wednesday, November 18.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,” House Speaker Bojie Dy, current AIPA president, also said in his opening speech.

Hernandez, however, sidestepped questions about whether a resolution on AI was being drafted during the AIPA general assembly, but said any effort will be “patterned on what transpired in the ASEAN.”

In 2025, the ASEAN adopted a declaration in Kuala Lumpur establishing an ASEAN AI Safety Network, a regional mechanism aimed at promoting collaboration among member states and addressing cross-border AI risks.

AIPA, as a regional parliamentary bloc, is not as powerful as the European Parliament. Any resolution passed during the general assembly is non-binding, which means it cannot force member parliaments to pass legislation back home.

AIPA, however, can still exercise influence by encouraging member parliaments to adopt regional commitments in their own countries.

Concerns about AI come as the Philippines’ hosting of ASEAN was met with massive protests against the US-led initiative Pax Silica, which will lead to the construction of a 1600-hectare AI industrial hub in New Clark City. The project is feared to displace hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers, according to Human Rights Watch.

Only Singapore and the Philippines are ASEAN signatories to the Pax Silica initiative so far. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us
World.content:
What happens when the people you inherited a business with are also the people you can no longer work with? You can quit a job, sell your shares, or find a new business partner. But what if that partner is your brother, sister, cousin, or parent, and the company is something your grandparents spent their lives building?

I have covered Philippine business families for most of my journalism career, interviewing relatives locked in battles over ownership, leadership, inheritance, and family land. Some disputes were already playing out in court, while others were waged quietly behind closed boardroom doors even as the companies kept running. As the feud between cousins Federico “Piki” Lopez and Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III unfolded this year, I found myself returning to those stories, my interview notes, and reading Harvard Business Review research on why family businesses fight and how some survive. In June, I joined family-business adviser Enrique Soriano in an online forum with business owners across Asia to discuss why even wildly successful dynasties break apart.

The Lopez cousins are hardly the first wealthy family to face this problem. India’s Ambani brothers split up the Reliance empire their father built, while the Ortigases fought over control of their real estate business. In Singapore, a father accused his son of trying to take over the board of one of the country’s biggest property developers. Some families eventually called a truce. Others decided they could no longer be business partners, and still fought for years, burning through cash on lawyers and leaving the next generation to clean up the mess.

All of this brought me back to one big question: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

The Lopezes reach a crossroads

For decades, the Lopez name has been tied to some of the Philippines’ most famous companies: ABS-CBN, Meralco, Benpres (now Lopez Holdings), First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. The businesses changed over time, yet the family stayed connected to an empire their elders built, lost, won back, and rebuilt.

Under Oscar Lopez‘s leadership, the family published Phoenix, a book about how they bounced back from hard times. Piki wanted a different symbol for the next chapter: not the phoenix, which rises again after being destroyed, but the butterfly, which transforms into something completely new. He has also talked a lot about compounding, the idea that smart decisions made consistently over decades pay off far more than quick wins. In his September speeches to stockholders, he stressed that “direction matters more than speed,” pointing to the group’s decision ten years earlier to stop building coal-fired power plants even when coal was still making good money.

That mindset explains Piki’s game plan for First Gen’s energy investments. He believes the company must prepare for a power market that relies more and more on renewable energy. His cousins have questioned whether the bets he’s making are worth the massive price tag, risks, and years of waiting. They have also challenged his authority to make those calls on his own. Gabby and his allied cousins wanted something very different: immediate cash flow and shared family stewardship over a distressed media mission—ABS-CBN—that could not afford to wait until 2031 for long-gestation hydro projects to pay off.

The fight turned public and personal. In April, majority owners of Lopez Inc.—representing three of the four branches of the family—accused Piki of acting “like a king without accountability,” questioning First Gen’s deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure, including selling control of its natural-gas business and investing in water-pumping hydropower projects. The majority group later called the hydropower bet “a horrible deal.” First Gen pushed back on those claims, defending the business logic, pricing, and board approvals behind its deals.

The cousins reached a ceasefire in May, but it didn’t hold, and by August, Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc., the private holding company sitting at the very top of the family empire, to businessman Ramon Ang for about P11.56 billion. Meanwhile, ABS-CBN lined up fresh funding. Piki then locked down control of the boards of Lopez Holdings and First Philippine Holdings (FPH), the two companies that hold the group’s stakes in First Gen and geothermal giant Energy Development Corporation (EDC). In November, FPH approved the proposed P15.92-billion sale of its 90.74% controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Gabby’s branch’s investment firm, Crème Investment Corporation, a deal that is still waiting to close. (READ: What it took to save ABS-CBN)

Taken together, these deals suggest the cousins are moving toward a future where they no longer have to agree on how to run the same businesses.

But is splitting up actually better than staying together?

When business disagreements become family wars

One family owner wants bigger cash payouts today, while the relative running the company wants to plow back those profits into growing the business. Another thinks they should sell the company while buyers are offering a good price, while someone else wants to save it for the grandkids. One wants to ride out an industry slump, convinced a struggling business will bounce back, while another wants to stop pouring money into what looks like a sinking ship, especially when that cash could fund a different business that takes years of heavy spending before turning a profit.

Yet each walks away believing the others are greedy, reckless, or unreasonable. The real trouble starts when the people around the boardroom table aren’t just ordinary investors, but siblings who grew up competing for their parents’ and uncles’ attention, cousins who feel their branch of the family sacrificed more, or heirs who remember the founder’s wishes differently.

Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer, who advise business families and write for Harvard Business Review, explain how everyday business arguments turn deeply personal. In Why Fights Erupt in Family Businesses, they show how fights over money, power, and status get tangled up with family history. An argument over company spending can bring back old resentment over unequal treatment. A fight over who gets to be CEO can reopen old arguments about favoritism. Selling a company might look like a smart opportunity to one relative and a betrayal of the family legacy to another.

Soriano raised another complication during our webinar: many family businesses stay united for decades simply because one strong founder or family elder can settle all the arguments. Relatives might not like every decision, yet they accept the leader’s authority. Once that leader passes away, the next generation realizes it has inherited not only the businesses, but also old disagreements that were never truly resolved.

The Lopezes had larger-than-life leaders in Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr. and his brother Oscar, who died in 1999 and 2023, leaving their successors to figure out how to own and run surviving empires without those strong elders around to settle arguments.

Other Philippine families have ended up in far messier wars.

Take Banco Filipino, once the country’s biggest savings bank, famous for its slogan, “Subok na Matibay, Subok na Matatag (Tested Strong, Proven Stable).” Founded by Tomas Aguirre in 1964, the bank was shut down by the Central Bank in January 1985 before reopening in 1994 after the Supreme Court ruled the Central Bank had abused its power. But its headaches were far from over. It kept clashing with regulators over financial aid, its money troubles, and the fallout from its first shutdown.

BANCO FILIPINO. This spread in Newsbreak’s March 3, 2003 issue shows the late Don Tomas Aguirre (left) and his children, Ana Marie Aguirre-Koruga (upper right), and Albert “Bobby” Aguirre (bottom right) on a polo field. Rappler

At the same time, the Aguirre family was tearing itself apart from the inside. I covered the legal fight involving Ana Maria Aguirre-Koruga, a minority stockholder who sued the bank’s directors in 2003, including her own brother, Albert Aguirre, who was then vice chairman. She accused them of risky banking practices, conflicts of interest, and shady loans meant to enrich insiders. The directors denied the claims. In 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in Koruga v. Arcenas that her complaints belonged with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), not a regular trial court. That ruling only decided who had authority to hear the case, not whether her accusations were true. The bank shut down for good on March 17, 2011, under BSP orders. The state deposit insurer, Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, took over a bank with 62 branches, 173,480 accounts, and P17.8 billion in customer deposits. The family and regulators kept arguing over who was to blame. While the sibling feud wasn’t the sole reason Banco Filipino collapsed—its financial and regulatory problems ran much deeper—the family war played out inside a bank holding the life savings of thousands of ordinary Filipinos.

The Ilusorio family feud got even more personal. Potenciano “Nanoy” Ilusorio built a multi-billion-peso empire anchored by prime real estate, the pioneering satellite firm Philcomsat, and the exclusive Baguio Country Club. But by 1999, his six children had split into rival camps over their parents, the family fortune, and who should be in charge. When Nanoy grew old and frail, some of his children took him under their care, prompting their mother, Erlinda Kalaw-Ilusorio, to sue them for allegedly keeping her husband away from her, a battle the Supreme Court dismissed in 2001 as the “sad tale of a prominent family shattered by conflicts on expectancy in fabled fortune.” (READ: What drives people to declare war against their own flesh and blood?)

Even Nanoy’s death in June that year didn’t stop nearly 300 civil and criminal lawsuits filed between the rival camps, and according to an account Soriano published in 2016, some children only found out of Erlinda’s death four days later, leading to separate funerals. At one service, the urn reportedly held Nanoy’s ashes because another branch of the family kept Erlinda’s. Another service reportedly barred three of the sisters at the door with security guards.

A fight that started over money and power had reached the point where children could not even mourn their parents together.

In other prominent Philippine clans, the fracture began not at a parent’s deathbed, but when siblings began questioning how a brother or sister was managing inherited assets—turning boardroom suspicions into criminal complaints and proxy wars.

For the Jacintos, who built their wealth in steel, banking, and real estate, also fought over their inheritance. After their patriarch, Fernando Jacinto died, his children clashed over how family properties were being managed and sold. Musician and businessman Ramon “RJ” Jacinto stepped in after relatives questioned real estate deals handled by their sister Marilene, who was running parts of the family business. One fight centered on a large property in Misamis Oriental sold in 2007 for P226 million, which RJ’s camp argued was far below its appraised value. Another involved a Novaliches property reportedly worth about P300 million. Acting as president of family-owned Oregon Land Inc., RJ accused Marilene of faking a deed to transfer the land. Prosecutors charged her in 2012 with falsifying public documents, an accusation that led to criminal proceedings, though not a conviction. The feud showed how inheritance fights can quickly spiral into claims of betrayal and criminal charges between brothers and sisters. (READ: Shaping the future: Family legacies)

In the Yanson family, the trigger was a boardroom ouster over who would run the business. They parents founded Vallacar Transit Inc. and the Ceres bus empire, considered among the largest bus conglomerates in Southeast Asia with about 5,000 buses ferrying 700,000 to 850,000 passengers in routes across Visayas and Mindanao regions. In July 2019, four siblings—Roy, Emily, Ricardo Jr., and Ma. Lourdes Celina Yanson-Lopez—tried to oust their youngest brother, Leo Rey Yanson, from running the bus group. Their mother, Olivia Yanson, sided with Leo Rey and Ginette, splitting the family into Yanson 4 and Yanson 2 camps. They fought over who had the right to elect board directors and run the company, triggering lawsuits and battles over company records. In 2025, the Supreme Court said Olivia was mentally sound when she executed her will that designated the Yanson 2 camp as the righful heirs of their family business empire. The family still hasn’t reached the kind of broad peace deal needed to put the feud behind them. (READ: Yanson family feud gets uglier as court brands 4 siblings ‘fugitives from justice’)

This family drama resonated elsewhere in Asia where South Korea’s Lotte Group—the retail, hospitality, and confectionery giant behind Asia’s largest department stores, luxury hotels, and iconic snacks—became the stage for a succession war between brothers Shin Dong-joo and Shin Dong-bin, sons of founder Shin Kyuk-ho. The business giant had major operations in both Japan and South Korea. Dong-joo, the older brother, was prominent in Japan, while Dong-bin ran much of the Korean side. After Dong-joo lost top posts in Japan in late 2014 and early 2015, the brothers erupted into a public war over who had their father’s blessing and who should lead the empire. Their elderly father was pulled straight into the crossfire. At one point, Shin Kyuk-ho backed his eldest son, prompting Dong-bin’s camp to question whether their father was still mentally fit to make decisions. The brothers battled through shareholder votes, lawsuits, and press statements, turning their father’s mental health and legal guardianship into a court case. Dong-bin eventually won over shareholders and kept control, though Dong-joo kept fighting him. Instead of splitting the empire in two, one brother walked away with control of the main group.

Play Video

The Shin feud proved a hard truth: being the founder’s son, even being the oldest, doesn’t guarantee inheriting the throne.

Why some families choose to stay together

In Singapore, the Kwek family— the powers behind iconic skyscrapers, luxury condos, and over 160 hotels worldwide—showed how quickly a disagreement between a father and son could move from the family boardroom into the headlines. In February 2025, City Developments executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng accused his son, chief executive Sherman Kwek, of attempting a boardroom “coup” by bypassing governance rules to appoint independent directors, prompting the elder Kwek to go to court to fire his son. Trading in City Developments shares was suspended as the confrontation became public. For a listed property developer, the dispute raised questions that went beyond the relationship between father and son: Who had the authority to appoint directors? Were corporate procedures being followed? And could the company continue operating effectively while its chairman and chief executive were fighting?

Yet the confrontation ended relatively quickly. On March 12, 2025, City Developments announced that the court proceedings had been settled and would be discontinued. Kwek Leng Beng remained executive chairman and Sherman remained chief executive, while the two newly appointed independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute, Jennifer Duong Young and Wong Su-Yen, stepped down. Singapore’s Straits Times later reported that trusted family friends and senior figures had helped mediate the truce. The company continued under the same family leadership, although the settlement did not necessarily mean that every personal disagreement had been resolved.

Here in the Philippines, the Ortigas family—the landed dynasty behind Ortigas Center and Greenhills—also managed to save its core property business after years of infighting. At stake was OCLP Holdings, which controls prime Ortigas land, Greenhills Shopping Center, and Tiendesitas. To gain an edge, rival branches teamed up with competing giants: the Rafael Ortigas group with Ayala Land, and the Francisco Ortigas group with SM Prime Holdings. The battle spilled into court over board elections and whether nominees tied to a rival developer could hold seats.

Those divisions let Ayala and SM deepen their footholds in a fractured enterprise. In November 2014, the developers and Ortigas factions dropped their lawsuits and agreed to work together. The family kept its landholdings intact rather than carving them up, though peace came at a steep price: bringing in powerful giants handed outsiders major influence over an empire that had belonged to the Ortigas family for generations.

There are strong business reasons to keep a family group intact. Companies under common ownership can share cash, talent, bank relationships, and leadership, allowing a stronger sister company to help a struggling one survive a rough patch or undertake massive investments too large for one branch alone. There is also the pull of family history, where a business built by a grandfather means far more to his grandkids than an ordinary stock investment, making a sale feel like erasing part of the family identity even when the financial math makes sense.

Yet keeping a company together merely because the founder wanted it kept together can create another problem: What happens when the next generation no longer agrees on what the business should do?

Adviser Josh Baron has argued in Why Family Businesses Need to Find the Right Level of Conflict that avoiding disagreement is actually unhealthy. Families must debate tough questions rather than letting owners quietly stew over decisions they feel powerless to change. When relatives can still negotiate and compromise, staying together preserves huge value. But when every investment, dividend payout, job appointment, or asset sale becomes another war for control, the cost becomes far too high.

When separating becomes the answer

India’s Ambani family decided that the brothers were simply better off running different companies. (READ: Timeline: Key dates in India’s Ambani brothers’ dispute)

After founder Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002 without leaving a will, his sons Mukesh and Anil fought publicly over who would control Reliance Industries—India’s largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning petrochemicals, refining, telecom, and retail—until their mother, Kokilaben, stepped in to broker a June 2005 peace deal. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries and its core oil and chemical operations, while Anil took charge of telecom, power, and financial services. But it didn’t stop every argument as the brothers later fought over natural-gas supply deals in a battle that reached India’s Supreme Court. Still, they no longer had to agree on every single investment or management call.

India’s Bajaj family—one of the country’s oldest business dynasties, famous for putting India on wheels as a motorcycle, scooter, and financial services powerhouse—also split up its companies among different branches after years of fighting. Under a 2008 settlement, Shishir Bajaj’s branch took control of businesses like Bajaj Hindusthan and Bajaj Consumer Care, while other family branches kept the group’s core auto, finance, and industrial companies.

Play Video

Splitting up let each branch follow its own game plan. Their paths quickly diverged: the core Bajaj businesses boomed, while Bajaj Hindusthan struggled with heavy debt and a tough sugar market. Dividing the empire ended the fight over who was in charge, but it didn’t guarantee that both sides would win.

In Hong Kong, Walter Kwok was pushed out as leader of Sun Hung Kai Properties—the real estate titan behind the city’s tallest skyscrapers, luxury malls, and housing estates—in 2008 after clashing with his brothers Thomas and Raymond over how to run the empire. The battle pulled in their mother, Kwong Siu-hing, and tangled up the family trusts. Walter lost his executive job, though he didn’t lose his financial slice of the family fortune. He went on to start his own property company, Empire Group Holdings, while new trust rules spelled out each brother’s share of the family wealth.

Taking a different path is the Murdoch family—the real-life inspiration behind HBO’s hit drama Succession, and the media dynasty behind Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and major outlets across the US, UK, and Australia that have shaped elections and public debate for decades. After a court battle over the family trust controlling voting power in Fox Corporation and News Corp, a September 2025 settlement locked in Lachlan Murdoch’s future control. His three older siblings from 95-year-old Rupert Murdoch‘s first two marriages—Prudence MacLeod, Elisabeth Murdoch, and James Murdoch—walked away with huge payouts and exited the trust. Grace and Chloe, Murdoch’s two youngest daughters from his third wife, Wendi Deng, stayed on as financial beneficiaries under the new setup, but without the voting power given to Lachlan.

Each of these families handled their split differently. The Ambanis and Bajajs divided up operating companies. Walter Kwok stepped out of management while keeping a financial stake. The Murdochs rewrote who holds voting control over their media empire. None of them offers a one-size-fits-all recipe for solving family feuds.

ADVICE. Enrique Soriano, family business consultant of the Wong & Bernstein Group, speaks during a forum. Courtesy of the Wong & Bernstein Group

Enrique Soriano, who has advised business families across the Philippines and Asia, does not view such separations as failures, noting during our June webinar that relatives who can no longer work together are often better served by an orderly division of business interests so they can stop being business partners without stopping being family.

Of course, that is much easier said than done. A family deciding to split still has to agree on who gets what, how much each company is worth, who takes on the debts, and what happens to shared properties. One relative might want out, only to find the others can’t afford to buy their shares. Another might want to keep control, but has to bring in an outside investor to help pay for the buyout.

And a peace deal that satisfies the relatives doesn’t automatically work out for the everyday public investors who also have money riding on those companies.

Is divorce the better answer?

The Lopez cousins appear to be heading toward a more permanent split of their business interests, though whether that turns out well for their companies, outside stockholders, and the family itself will take years to see.

Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

Part 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles

Part 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

Other business dynasties offer no easy answers: The Kweks and Ortigases found ways to keep their shared businesses intact after fierce battles, though both had to make major compromises. The Ambanis and Bajajs carved up their empires. The Kwoks and Murdochs separated day-to-day control from financial ownership. The Shin brothers’ succession war left one brother running Lotte, while the Aguirres, Ilusorios, Jacintos, and Yansons showed how family fights can spiral into years of lawsuits and lasting broken relationships and personal wounds.

There is a world of difference between keeping a company together because the owners actually agree on its future, and keeping it together just because nobody wants to be blamed for breaking up the family empire. There is also a difference between splitting up to chase new ambitions and splitting it up just to stop a fight.

For the Lopezes, going their separate ways may give each branch the freedom to focus on what it values most. Piki can concentrate on long-term energy bets, while Gabby and his allies can focus on lifestyle-related consumer and media businesses. Yet, that freedom brings new pressures, and success will depend on the choices each side makes next.

A family can survive a corporate divorce. Its companies might even grow stronger because of it. Or the split could leave both sides worse off than before. But the real question isn’t just whether relatives should stay together or go their separate ways. It is whether the businesses, and all the people who depend on them, will actually be better off afterward. – Rappler.com

Part 2 on Thursday, November 19 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

Part 3 on Friday, November 20 | Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: In the Public Square: Is impeachment democratic?
World.content:
LIVE

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by lawyer and constitutionalist Michael Henry Yusingco

The on-again, off-again impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is on again this week — and according to the lead defense counsel, they have maybe eight to 10 witnesses left to present. It is possible to see the light at the end of the impeachment tunnel.

But after over four months, and over 40 trial dates, are we any closer to the ideal of “political justice”? What have we learned about impeachment as a democratic process?

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by lawyer and constitutionalist Michael Henry Yusingco. He has written often, and critically, on impeachment in the Philippines. He is a senior fellow at the Ateneo Policy Center and also at the Institute for Autonomy Governance.

Watch the episode on Wednesday, November 17, at 8 pm.-Rappler.com

World.title: NASA Voyager 1 probe believed to have reached ‘light-day’ milestone
World.content:
Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space.

The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday, November 18, at 5:16 am ET (1016 GMT).

Officials at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday, November 19, to discuss the milestone.

“Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter ‌interstellar space ⁠in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018.

A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years.

“But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen,” the JPL representative said.

Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system’s two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space.

“Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager,” Dodd said.

The Deep Space Network is NASA’s international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions.

“After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur,” Dodd said.

“We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond,” Dodd said. “Where does the sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Investing in AI Literacy Means Investing in Judgment
World.content:
Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or how it can serve other people. These questions are part of AI literacy, alongside an understanding of the technology itself. Helping people make such judgments requires education that connects AI with their circumstances and responsibilities.

For Break the Fake Movement in the Philippines, this work builds on its focus on media and information literacy and countering disinformation. In a March 2026 research interview with the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society (CAPS), co-author Paolo Miguel Ordonio, Break the Fake Movement’s executive director, explained that its AI education emphasizes foundational understanding and critical thinking, and its curriculum includes ethics, copyright, data privacy and safety. He described enthusiasm for AI that does not always translate into understanding, alongside communities where some learners still need help with basic digital activities.

A group of students accessing the AI Class ASEAN platform.

Different audiences also bring different needs. At the time of that interview, Break the Fake Movement was exploring how to adapt its AI literacy training for civil society workers through a collaboration with the Association of Foundations. Modules developed primarily for young people, parents and educators provided a starting point; understanding what civil society workers needed from AI education was part of the adaptation.

For civil society workers, AI literacy needs to address decisions they face at work: which problems AI can help solve, which tasks it can support, and where human judgment should remain central. CAPS’s report, Cars Without Roads: Investing in AI for Good Across Asia, illustrates the kinds of decisions people may face. Organizations approaching Infoxchange with plans to adopt AI sometimes discover that they first need better data management, stronger cybersecurity or a clearer definition of the problem they want to solve. In a separate CAPS interview, Hyomi Ahn, a researcher at Korea’s Beautiful Foundation, described its work to develop internal AI guidelines. She also highlighted debate among advocacy organizations about whether AI should draft public statements, raising questions about which work should remain human.

AI literacy programs can be designed for staff and leaders alike, with learning adapted to their different responsibilities. Staff may need to judge how AI fits their tasks; leaders may need to learn how to set expectations, develop guidance and provide time and resources for staff learning. The report’s findings on organizational readiness suggest that this education should also help people recognize when specialist advice is needed and what support colleagues need to apply their learning.

Yet funding for literacy education can be difficult to secure. Drawing on Break the Fake Movement’s experience, Ordonio described limited funding opportunities for literacy education, saying that funding favored infrastructure, tools and systems. His experience reflects the report’s wider concern that human capability and supporting conditions receive less investment than visible applications. In the study’s pre-interview survey of 36 organizations, 72.2% of respondents identified training and capacity-building as underinvested, the highest share for any category and more than double that of any other area.

Executive Ordonio delivering a lecture on AI usage for parents.

For funders, this means supporting AI literacy programs that adapt learning to participants’ responsibilities and provide opportunities to consider where AI fits their work, whose needs it serves and what responsibilities its use entails. Funding this learning recognizes informed judgment as a capability worth developing and an essential part of turning technological possibilities into social value.

World.title: [DECODED] Scam season and the leaks that may make it worse
World.content:
There are only 37 days before Christmas! Have you started your holiday preparations already, and are you feeling the Christmas rush yet? I’ve noticed that Metro Manila traffic has been heavier over the past week, although that may have been due to preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which just wrapped up.

Between the traffic and the shopping, the holidays are when we’re busiest and least careful, especially with our transactions. A recent survey by the global industry trade organization GSM Association (GSMA) said that Filipinos do know the risk: 76% said they “absolutely worry” about scams and 78% said they changed their behavior due to scam awareness.

And yet, scams still proliferate — and they have been evolving along with technology. Smishing (SMS phishing) has been in the public consciousness for a while now, but have you heard of quishing? It essentially does the same thing, except that it’s done via QR codes.

Rappler researcher Lourence Angelo Marcellana listed 12 types of scams to watch out for, as we approach the holiday season. He also explained how to protect yourself against scams, especially since much of our transactions now happen online, thanks to the growth of e-commerce and digital payments.

READ: 12 Christmas scams to watch out for

In the GSMA report, it said that the Philippines also has the highest rate — among Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam — of reporting scams to digital platforms (49%), compared to only 16% reporting to the police. The regional average of reporting scams to the authorities is at 36%.

This reminded me of a Decoded study we did last year on online scams. We found that government agencies were among the most active sharers of warnings online, but because each agency’s approach lacked coordination with the others, the overall effect on consumers online was dissatisfaction from all the fragmented messaging.

Users online also complained about the government hotlines set up for reporting scams, saying that they found them difficult to use and lacking a clear process to submit evidence and receive updates on their cases.

That was last year. This year, the problem has now moved from how well the public is warned to knowing what kind of personal details may already be exposed, and who might be using them.

Last Friday, November 13, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) confirmed that personal data from around 20 state agencies were exposed in recent data breaches. Rappler researcher Alex Culla looked into these agencies and listed the personal information potentially exposed, from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission, to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

READ: LIST: Personal information possibly exposed in gov’t data leaks

Among the personal details that may have been compromised are names, addresses, email addresses, mobile numbers, birth dates, genders, and even taxpayer identification numbers (TIN). Of course, these vary depending on the agency, and not everyone who deals with these agencies is necessarily affected. But it’s still worth staying alert, because while scams do happen all year, the CICC said it might become more prevalent as the holidays approach.

So if these recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start. At Rappler, Christmas isn’t the only thing we’re counting down to.

This year’s Social Good Summit is taking place this Saturday, November 21, and it will include a masterclass on data privacy and personal safety in the age of AI. There will also be discussions on technology, journalism, and human rights, as well as masterclasses on vibe coding, editorial cartooning, and crisis management.

JOIN: Social Good Summit 2026: We, The Humans

– Rappler.com

World.title: PH police file criminal complaints vs Thomas Markle, father of Meghan
World.content:
This comes less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage girls

MANILA, Philippines – Philippine police said on Wednesday, November 18, that criminal complaints had been filed against Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, over alleged online child sexual abuse offenses.

The filing of the complaints will enable prosecutors to examine evidence and decide whether charges should be filed in court.

It came less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage girls.

Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as “sick lies.”

Philippine police said complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu province on Monday, November 16, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.

Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.

Police said the complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

Forensic examination of the remaining devices surrendered in the Philippines by Markle’s son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., was ongoing and could yield further evidence to support the case or lead to additional charges, if warranted, police said.

Meghan, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage ​to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018.

She has said she was “deeply distressed” over the matter. – Rappler.com

World.title: Barbers: VP’s ex-staffers matter may be smokescreen on impeach issue
World.content:
House prosecution spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers

MANILA, Philippines — The revelation from Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp regarding her former household staff who purportedly told to sign affidavits containing “false allegations” against her could be a “smokescreen” to divert the real issue in the impeachment trial, House prosecution spokesperson, former Surigao del Norte Rep. Robert Ace Barbers said on Wednesday.

Barbers made this remark after Duterte’s legal counsel Paolo Panelo said that a staff member sought their help through a text message after being purportedly held by certain individuals who threatened their lives and forced them to sign a document against the Vice President.

READ: Sara Duterte camp: Ex-staffers pressured to make false claims vs VP

Article continues after this 

Barbers said this matter—among other issues addressed by the defense in the trial, like those pertaining to Duterte’s spouse Manases Carpio’s P256,882 purchase of Nike shoes in Malaysia and P200,000 bill in a restaurant in Japan—could serve as a smokescreen to prevent addressing the allegations on Duterte’s unexplained wealth worth P817 million.

READ: 4 more VP Sara Duterte defense witnesses subpoenaed

Article II, which centers on alleged unexplained wealth, remains the single active impeachment charge following the prosecution’s withdrawal of three other articles last month.

“What I am referring to as a diversion is the discussion of issues that are unrelated to the unexplained wealth allegation. For example, the Nike shoes, the food at the restaurant worth P200,000, and other issues they have raised that do not address or answer the prosecution’s allegations,” Barbers said in Filipino.

“Maybe these kinds of issues are also included, to be like a smokescreen. There appears to be a smokescreen to make real issues disappear,” Barbers said, referring to Panelo’s pronouncements.

Article continues after this 

Barbers further said that Panelo’s allegations raised even more questions as he advised the Duterte camp to complain to proper agencies like the Philippine National Police or National Bureau of Investigation.

“Who were the people who held them? Who were these individuals? Because if you are being held against your will, your movements are restricted, and you are not allowed to speak unless given permission, how could you possibly send text messages?” Barbers said.

Article continues after this 

“I think there are still more questions being raised than there are allegations being confirmed. These claims should be properly verified and validated,” he continued. /cb

World.title: Urgent probe into cyberattacks vs gov’t agencies needed, says ex-solon
World.content:
Former Rep. Robert Ace Barbers —Screenshot from an INQUIRER.net video

MANILA, Philippines — Former lawmaker Robert Ace Barbers on Wednesday called on the government to conduct a comprehensive investigation into the reported cyberattacks targeting government agencies and private institutions, warning that it has become a national security concern.

Barbers made the pronouncement amid reports that 20 Philippine institutions have been allegedly compromised recently by hackers.

According to Barbers, this should serve as a “wake-up call” for authorities to strengthen cybersecurity defenses, especially before it escalates into widespread financial losses, identity theft, and disruption of essential public services.

Article continues after this 

READ: China-linked hacking group targeted PH execs ahead of summit – report

“Hindi na ito simpleng problema ng computer systems o IT departments. National security issue na ito. Kapag napasok ng hackers ang ating government databases, financial institutions, at critical infrastructure, buong bansa at milyon-milyong Pilipino ang maaaring maapektuhan,” Barbers said.

(This is no longer a simple problem of computer systems or IT departments. This is a national security issue. If hackers penetrate our government databases, financial institutions, and critical infrastructure, the entire country and millions of Filipinos could be affected.)

READ: Cyberattack hits 178 websites, targets older Apple devices

The former lawmaker, who now serves as an adviser and spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, then stressed that such cases include the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Securities and Exchange Commission—which raises serious questions regarding the security of sensitive government information.

Article continues after this 

The lawmaker also warned that the Philippines cannot afford to wait for a major financial disaster before taking decisive action.

With this, he called on the Department of Information and Communications Technology, Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center, National Privacy Commission, and other concerned agencies to coordinate their investigations, determine the actual extent of the reported breaches, identify the perpetrators, and establish whether any personal information, financial assets, or confidential government records were stolen.

Article continues after this 

“Dapat malaman ng publiko ang katotohanan. Aling sistema ang napasok? Anong impormasyon ang nakompromiso? May perang nawala ba? At higit sa lahat, sino ang mananagot kung mapatunayang nagpabaya sa pagprotekta sa ating mga digital assets?” he said.

(The public needs to know the truth. Which systems were breached? What information was compromised? Was any money lost? And most importantly, who will be held accountable if it is proven that we were negligent in protecting our digital assets?)

Furthermore, Barbers also called for stronger cybersecurity investments, mandatory security audits, continuous monitoring of government networks, rapid incident-response mechanisms, and closer cooperation between government and private-sector operators of critical infrastructure. /cb

World.title: 236 Lakbayani members to be released after over 70 hours in detention
World.content:
Inquirer files

CALAPAN CITY, ORIENTAL MINDORO, Philippines — Prosecutors have ordered the release of 236 members of the Lakbayani protest caravan who were detained for more than 70 hours following their arrest during a protest in Muntinlupa City, the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) College of Development Communication (CDC) said on Wednesday (Nov. 18).

The prosecutor at the Muntinlupa Hall of Justice had decided to release the detainees for further investigation, the college announced.

The release does not mean the charges against them have been dropped, as they are expected to further legal proceedings in the coming weeks.

Article continues after this 

READ: Over 200 arrested for illegal demonstrations in Muntinlupa – SPD

The 236 were among those arrested during a police operation at Sucat People’s Park in Muntinlupa on Nov. 15, amid protests held in connection with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit and the visit of US President Donald Trump to the Philippines.

READ: CHR probes alleged rights violations during arrest of Asean protesters

They were part of the Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan delegation, composed of farmers, urban poor residents, transport workers, environmental advocates and students from UPLB. Campus journalists were also among those arrested.

The National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers earlier questioned the prolonged detention, citing Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, which sets time limits for authorities to bring arrested persons before judicial authorities. Police, however, maintained that they had followed established legal procedures and constitutional safeguards. /cb

World.title: Sara Duterte: Corruption a ‘progressive disease’ embedded in gov’t
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte attends the 52nd Philippine Business Conference and Expo of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry in October. Photo by Inday Sara Duterte/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte has described corruption as a “progressive disease” integrated into the government that hinders every Filipino to achieve a good future for them and their families.

Duterte on Wednesday shared that this was part of her message as she attended the 52nd Philippine Business Conference and Expo of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry last month.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte: Corruption a threat to sovereignty, freedom

She said that it was her dream to see every Filipino live a dignified and secure life.

“Ngunit, malaking hamon sa pangarap na ito ang korapsyon na humahadlang sa atin sa pag-abot ng mas maraming oportunidad at sa kaunlaran,” Duterte said in a Facebook post.

(But, a huge challenge to our dream is the corruption that prevents us from reaching more opportunities and progress.)

“It is a progressive disorder that has embedded itself deep within the DNA of the government—and tragically, it is the Filipino people who are left to suffer the consequences,” she added.

Article continues after this 

She then called on the Filipino people to abide by their responsibilities to help one another achieve our dreams.

She noted that such responsibilities are “to obey the law, reject corruption, protect our communities, participate in our democracy, and demand accountability from those who govern.”

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, the impeachment trial of the vice president will resume on Thursday after a three-day pause this week due to the conduct of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits.

READ: 4 more VP Sara Duterte defense witnesses subpoenaed

The defense team will continue to present their witnesses to counter the evidence submitted by the House prosecution panel on the allegations of her unexplained wealth.

World.title: Manila Water’s Luntiang La Mesa plants over 13,000 native trees
World.content:
Luntiang La Mesa clocked 25,593 volunteer hours across 84 organizational engagements from June to October 2026. —Photo from Manila Water Foundation

MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Foundation’s Luntiang La Mesa program continues to transform environmental stewardship into meaningful action, planting 13,068 native and endemic trees through sustained partnerships with public and private organizations, schools, and institutions

Luntiang La Mesa clocked 25,593 volunteer hours across 84 organizational engagements from June to October 2026, transforming environmental stewardship into a structured, multi-sectoral effort focused on restoring native habitats, promoting “biodiverCity” or biodiversity in the city, and strengthening watershed protection.

Rather than relying on one-time ceremonial tree-planting activities, La Mesa Ecopark anchored its reforestation campaign on continuing partnerships that encouraged organizations to take an active role in environmental conservation.

Article continues after this 

READ: Manila Water Ecopark now uses 100% renewable energy

Through successive planting events and volunteer activities, participants contributed to the establishment of native and endemic tree species that are essential to restoring local ecosystems and supporting wildlife within the watershed.

After planting, the La Mesa Ecopark team leads the seedling nurturing to ensure survival. La Mesa Ecopark has been certified by the DENR NCR with a 95.11% tree survival rate.

The milestone underscores the growing role of collaborative action in addressing environmental challenges facing highly urbanized areas such as Metro Manila. By bringing together diverse sectors under a common sustainability agenda, La Mesa Ecopark has created opportunities for individuals and organizations to directly contribute to ecosystem restoration while fostering greater environmental awareness.

Situated within the La Mesa Watershed, a vital resource that feeds into the system that supplies water to millions of residents in Metro Manila, the newly established trees represent a critical investment in the region’s long-term ecological and water security. Native trees help stabilize soil, reduce erosion, minimize reservoir siltation, and enhance natural flood mitigation, all of which are critical to maintaining the health and functionality of watershed ecosystems.

Article continues after this 

The initiative also supports long-term water security and climate resilience. As El Niño continues to pose challenges to water availability, healthy forest cover within the watershed helps retain moisture, reduce land degradation, and protect critical water sources that supply millions of Metro Manila residents.

READ: La Mesa Ecopark opens Phase 2 with wider green spaces, ‘BiodiverCity’

Article continues after this 

Beyond their environmental benefits, the tree-planting activities also serve as a platform for environmental education. Participants gain a deeper understanding of watershed conservation, climate resilience, and biodiversity protection, helping cultivate a stronger sense of responsibility for safeguarding natural resources.

“Environmental conservation is most effective when it becomes a shared responsibility. The collective effort of our partners and volunteers demonstrates how sustained collaboration can create meaningful environmental outcomes while helping communities better understand the importance of protecting our watersheds and natural ecosystems,” said Registered Forester Murphy Amparo, Operations Department Head of La Mesa Ecopark.

As La Mesa Ecopark continues to expand its conservation initiatives, the success of its reforestation program highlights the value of long-term partnerships in restoring biodiversity, strengthening climate resilience, and securing vital water resources for future generations.

World.title: Bayan: Rallies to continue despite Trump’s departure from PH
World.content:
Groups hold a protest along C.M. Recto Avenue on Wednesday, Nov. 18, with one of their main goals being to stop the proposed Pax Silica initiative that would allegedly displace farmers and indigenous communities. INQUIRER / Gillian Villanueva

MANILA, Philippines – Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) on Wednesday said it will continue to conduct protests even after US President Donald Trump has left the country, this time to hold President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. held accountable for wasting public funds.

“The protests will continue even if Trump is gone, because we will make sure that Marcos will be held accountable for squandering P22 billion for his [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] summit and welcome [honors] for Trump,” said Bayan secretary general Mong Palatino.

Palatino made the statement during an ambush interview on the sidelines of a protest held on Wednesday morning along C.M. Recto Avenue.

Article continues after this 

It was the latest demonstration in a series of rallies held by Bayan alongside other groups who oppose the arrival of US President Donald Trump in the country for the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits held in Pasay City.

READ: Rally vs Pax Silica greets US president’s arrival

The US President has since departed from the Philippines on Wednesday afternoon to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting to be held in Shenzhen, China.

The rally at C.M. Recto Avenue was held in time for Trump’s visit to Malacañang for a bilateral meeting with Marcos earlier on Wednesday, with protesters attempting to get closer to the area by marching towards Mendiola.

However, they were blocked by police personnel who put up barbed wires and shipping containers as barricades, forcing the protesters to conduct their rally at C.M. Recto Avenue.

Article continues after this 

During the protest, attendees reiterated their opposition to the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which intends to build a secure supply chain for semiconductors, artificial intelligence and critical minerals, in part to counter China’s dominance.

Protesters also questioned the billions of public funds that were used to conduct the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits, noting that many ordinary Filipinos continue to face economic difficulties.

Article continues after this 

READ: Youth group rallies at PNP headquarters, demands release of protesters

They also expressed concerns over the impacts of road closures and other restrictions implemented as part of the preparations for the Asean summit on the livelihoods of Filipino workers.

Moreover, they condemned alleged police brutality and harassment against protesters, citing the arrests that occurred during rallies held at Manila and Muntinlupa last Sunday.

To end the rally, protesters burned an American flag to show their opposition to US-led initiatives, such as the Pax Silica framework, as well as the construction of military bases in the country.

World.title: Prosec demands explanation of Cale88 China-linked remittances
World.content:
Former Rep. Robert Ace Barbers —Screenshot from an INQUIRER.net video

MANILA, Philippines —House prosecutors challenged Vice President Sara Z. Duterte’s defense panel on Wednesday to show the business transactions behind Cale88 Foods Corp.’s China-linked receipts, saying registration papers could not explain the money flows being questioned in her impeachment trial.

Former Rep. Robert Ace Barbers, a spokesman and adviser for the prosecution panel, demanded evidence connecting the incoming funds to actual trade.

“They should show by presenting evidence that Cale88 really had legitimate business and trade transactions,” Barbers said at an online press conference.

Article continues after this 

READ: No BIR record proving Mans Carpio sold Cale88 shares

Records from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which were presented during the trial, recorded P319.33 million in remittances from mainland China and Hong Kong to Cale88 Foods Corp.

The schedule listed 143 covered transaction reports and three suspicious transaction reports. The three suspicious reports totaled P9.78 million.

“It is on the record that there were suspicious transactions,” Barbers said.

A possible conduit role would have to be tested against the underlying bank and trade records.

Article continues after this 

Connecting a receipt to a sale requires a documented link between the payment and the underlying business obligation.

Manila Rep. Joel Chua, a member of the prosecution panel, said the prosecution was not challenging the company’s registration.

Article continues after this 

Several proposed defense witnesses are expected to discuss business or product registration and communications about food exhibitions.

The defense is due to resume presenting evidence on Nov. 19 and 20 under Article II, the remaining charge involving alleged unexplained wealth.

Barbers distinguished the demand for transaction records from a general objection to trade with Chinese companies.

READ: 4 more VP Sara Duterte defense witnesses subpoenaed

“We have companies in our country that are doing business with China,” he said.

Chua then clarified the allegation about disclosure, saying his understanding was that Cale88 had been declared as a business interest of Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Chief to Review Relations With ASEAN After Manila Snub
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing said on Wednesday his regime will review its relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in response to statements issued by the bloc at its recent summit in the Philippines.

In a three-hour speech to the military-dominated parliament in Naypyitaw, the regime chief decried the “unreasonable” position on Myanmar taken by the bloc, whose leaders met in Manila this week.

“During the ASEAN Summit held in recent days, we saw unreasonable statements… I would like to say that we have also decided to review how we will proceed with our future relations with ASEAN,” he said.

At the 49th regional summit in the Philippine capital, ASEAN leaders agreed to extend a ban on Myanmar regime leaders attending the bloc’s summit meetings, citing “insufficient progress” in implementing its Five-Point Consensus (5PC) peace plan.

In a statement, the leaders reaffirmed that the consensus remains the bloc’s main reference for addressing Myanmar’s political crisis, while agreeing to continue engagement with the country. Myanmar was represented at the summit only by a non-political representative, Han Win Aung, director-general of the regime’s ASEAN Affairs Department.

ASEAN adopted the 5PC in April 2021, calling for an immediate end to violence and dialogue among all parties. However, the regime failed to implement the agreement and subsequently rejected it.

On Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing again claimed that he had never agreed to the consensus and accused ASEAN of selectively abandoning its longstanding principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of member states.

He argued that ASEAN’s position did not represent the views of all its members, but was instead driven by the prejudices of three countries, which he did not identify.

He further accused the bloc of applying pressure exclusively on Myanmar despite political crises, election disputes and public protests in other member states.

“No other ASEAN member state has faced such political pressure or been subjected to attempts to discredit it. We see these actions being directed specifically at Myanmar,” he argued.

Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has visited several ASEAN member states in an apparent effort to restore Myanmar’s standing within the regional bloc. The diplomatic push failed to win him admittance to the latest summit, however.

The regime chief claimed the visits showed that some ASEAN member states wanted to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

“We have visited neighboring countries, including Laos, Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia and Malaysia. During these visits, the leaders of these countries openly expressed their desire for Myanmar to have normal relations within ASEAN. Some told us they wanted to see us at ASEAN meetings. Some spoke to us privately in a friendly manner, while others raised the matter during meetings. This shows that the position being pursued within ASEAN does not represent the wishes of all member states,” he said.

According to AFP, Min Aung Hlaing also told Parliament that talks were ongoing with the U.S., which shunned his country after the 2021 putsch but is now eyeing its rare earth resources.

“Now, we have discussions with our adversary, great power the United States, which has been constantly having issues with us,” the former general said.

“There is a certain level of engagement anyway. However, it has not yet been fully finalized. Relations and discussions are ongoing.”

Citing media reports, AFP said US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance joined talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw in September, in the highest-level publicly reported contact between the two countries since the coup.

The discussions reportedly focused on securing the release of a US businessman detained in Myanmar.

According to Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights organization, ASEAN said it would consider gradually restoring Myanmar’s political representation only when there is real, concrete progress on the 5PC. “If holding this criminal military junta, which has broken its promises for five years, bombed villages, schools and hospitals, blocked aid, and kept more than 15,000 political prisoners in detention, to this minimum standard is unreasonable, then nothing is reasonable,” she said.

Describing the junta as “brazen,” she accused it of complaining about the consequences of its own crimes. “The one who tried to seize the people’s power by force, who is bombing the people, who is turning international aid meant for the people into a weapon, saying ASEAN is unreasonable is laughable. ASEAN does not need reviewing. It is the junta that needs reviewing. Stop the attacks. Release all political prisoners. Let aid reach the people without discrimination,” she said.

She added that the junta is not Myanmar’s government and therefore has no role in reviewing the relationship with ASEAN on behalf of the state or the Myanmar people.

Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, urged ASEAN to continue to put strategic pressure on the junta and not to “play its game.”

Myanmar joined ASEAN in 1997.

World.title: ASEAN Leaders Accused of Enabling Myanmar Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Rights group Justice for Myanmar (JFM) has accused ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila of maintaining a status quo that enables Myanmar’s military regime to wage a terror campaign against civilians with impunity.

The bloc is aiding the regime’s war crimes through military engagement and a business-as-usual approach, JFM said on Tuesday as the 49th ASEAN Summit wrapped up.

While putschist president Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership remain barred from ASEAN summits over their failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), JFM noted that regime personnel still participate in regional meetings, defense training and military exercises. Participants include regime army, navy and police officers who are directly responsible for perpetrating war crimes under the guise of “counter-terrorism,” it added.

In September, JFM reported that regime officials have been invited to an upcoming ASEAN Regional Forum workshop on countering drone warfare, warning that the move risked technology and knowledge transfer to a military that routinely bombs civilians, schools, and hospitals.

“The Myanmar junta is a criminal cartel that should be held accountable for its international crimes, not allowed to join meetings, training, and workshops,” JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung told The Irrawaddy.

Regional cooperation only emboldens the regime to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity, she added.

Although barred from the Manila summit, regime Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin attended the 27th ASEAN Chiefs of Army Multilateral Meeting (ACAMM) in Malaysia on Tuesday.

JFM stated ASEAN’s 5PC peace plan has served as a diplomatic smokescreen while member countries and businesses continue to supply the regime with funds, weapons, and aviation fuel. It accused Thailand’s state-owned PTT energy conglomerate and Vietnam’s Viettel of bankrolling the military regime through natural gas imports and a telecoms partnership respectively.

Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand also permit domestic companies to broker sales of arms, equipment and aviation fuel to the regime, bypassing international sanctions, JFM noted, urging ASEAN to stop enabling the war crimes of a “criminal regime.”

Prominent human rights activist Thinzar Shunlei Yi said the 5PC had failed to curb civilian atrocities in Myanmar.

“They [ASEAN] must recognize that penalties imposed on the junta in 2021 were weak in their impact, which is why the violations continue,” she commented, calling for broader and more severe sanctions against the regime.

The Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute founded by military defectors, reports the regime conducted 161 airstrikes in October alone, killing 145 civilians and injuring 316 others.

World.title: Regime’s Air War in Arakan: Territorial Losses and the Growing Civilian Toll
World.content:
Myanmar’s military has lost control of much of Arakan (Rakhine) State, but it retains the power to inflict devastating destruction from the air.

Across the western state, the dangers of war extend far beyond the front lines. Airstrikes have devastated markets, damaged medical facilities, struck displacement camps and disrupted vital transport routes, leaving civilians to bear the consequences of a conflict that shows little sign of ending.

These attacks raise a troubling question: As Myanmar’s military loses territory to the Arakan Army (AA), is airpower becoming a means not only of pursuing military objectives, but also of undermining civilian life in areas beyond its control?

The question matters because the consequences extend far beyond immediate casualties. They threaten livelihoods, essential services and the ability of communities to recover from years of conflict.

Losing territory, retaining the power to strike

Since fighting resumed in November 2023, the AA, an ethnic armed organization seeking greater autonomy for Arakan, has captured most of the state from Myanmar’s military.

These losses have weakened the military’s ground positions, administrative authority and political influence. Yet losing territory does not mean losing the ability to wage war.

The military continues to use aircraft, naval firepower and long-range artillery to attack areas it can no longer effectively control on the ground.

As efforts to regain territory become increasingly difficult, airpower allows the military to exert pressure without maintaining a physical presence.

This creates a fundamental distinction between territorial control and destructive capability.

The military may no longer govern much of Arakan, but it retains the ability to make civilian life extraordinarily difficult.

For communities living under the threat of bombardment, changes in territorial control have not necessarily brought greater security.

Markets and hospitals: the wider cost of airstrikes

One of the deadliest reported attacks occurred on September 28, when military airstrikes hit the area around India Market and Kissapanadi Bridge in Kyauktaw.

According to Development Media Group (DMG), at least 50 civilians were killed and 58 injured. The United Nations cited similar reported figures, while independent investigators confirmed evidence of an airstrike and extensive damage but could not verify the full casualty toll.

The attack illustrates how aerial bombardment can devastate communities beyond the immediate loss of life.

Markets are essential to local economies. They support traders, transport workers, small businesses and families dependent on daily commerce.

When a marketplace is destroyed, livelihoods disappear, supply chains are disrupted and access to food and other necessities becomes more difficult.

In Arakan, where years of fighting and restrictions on movement have already undermined trade and driven up living costs, such destruction deepens an existing humanitarian crisis.

Healthcare facilities have also suffered.

On November 1, an airstrike damaged a temporary maternity ward in Mrauk-U. Five people, including a newborn baby, were reportedly killed. The incident was documented by Reuters and condemned by Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders).

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected.

When hospitals and clinics become unsafe, pregnant women may delay essential care, patients may avoid treatment, and already overstretched healthcare services may struggle to continue operating.

In a region facing serious shortages of medicines, medical personnel and equipment, the loss of even one functioning clinic can endanger many more lives.

The destruction of markets and medical facilities therefore cannot be measured solely by casualty figures. Its longer-term effects on livelihoods, public health and community survival must also be considered.

Nowhere safe for the displaced

The dangers are especially severe for people who have already fled their homes.

On November 13, a military airstrike hit the Byarla camp for internally displaced persons in Ponnagyun Township, killing 12 people, including children, and injuring 18 others, according to local rescue workers and witnesses.

The same camp had reportedly been bombed in October, killing six displaced people.

These incidents expose the extreme vulnerability of communities displaced by war.

Families who flee their homes often arrive at displacement camps with few possessions, limited access to food and healthcare, and little prospect of returning home.

When those places of refuge are also attacked, displacement becomes an ongoing struggle for survival rather than a temporary escape from danger.

Beyond the immediate casualties, repeated attacks can destroy shelters, interrupt humanitarian assistance and inflict lasting psychological trauma.

They also place additional pressure on local authorities and humanitarian organizations already operating with limited resources.

Damaged bridges, isolated communities

Roads and bridges have also been affected by military attacks.

In early November, airstrikes damaged transport infrastructure in Kyauktaw Township. Further attacks affecting bridges elsewhere in Arakan were reported later in the month by local sources and the AA.

Bridges may serve military purposes, but they are also essential to civilian life.

They connect farmers to markets, patients to hospitals, and communities to food, medicines and humanitarian assistance.

Their destruction can isolate entire communities, increase transport costs and further restrict access to essential services.

Under international humanitarian law, a bridge may constitute a legitimate military objective under certain circumstances. However, attacks must still comply with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians.

The central questions are whether a particular structure was a military objective, what military advantage was anticipated, and whether foreseeable civilian harm was excessive in relation to that advantage.

Not every attack on infrastructure is automatically unlawful. But a claimed military purpose does not justify unlimited civilian suffering.

A strategy of destabilization?

Taken together, attacks affecting markets, hospitals, displacement camps and transport networks have consequences extending far beyond the immediate battlefield.

Destroyed markets weaken local commerce. Damaged medical facilities undermine healthcare. Disrupted transport routes restrict the movement of people and supplies. Attacks on displacement camps increase humanitarian needs.

Collectively, these effects can make AA-controlled territories more difficult to administer.

The AA must devote scarce resources to emergency relief, infrastructure repairs, medical assistance and the restoration of essential services, even as it continues military operations.

This raises the possibility that Myanmar’s military views airpower as a means of weakening the AA’s ability to govern territories it has captured.

Unable to regain control on the ground, the military may seek to impose economic, humanitarian and administrative costs from the air.

Myanmar’s military authorities have maintained that their operations target armed opponents and have rejected allegations that they deliberately attack civilians. However, the scale and repeated nature of civilian harm demand closer scrutiny.

The consequences of an attack do not, by themselves, establish its intended purpose.

Determining whether civilian infrastructure is being deliberately targeted as part of a broader strategy requires credible evidence concerning military orders, target selection and operational decisions.

Even without establishing a single overarching strategy, the repeated devastation of civilian communities raises serious questions about the military’s conduct of hostilities.

Civilian protection and accountability

International humanitarian law requires all parties to armed conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives.

It prohibits intentionally directing attacks against civilians, indiscriminate attacks, and attacks expected to cause excessive civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

Attacks affecting hospitals, schools, displacement camps and populated areas therefore warrant credible, independent investigation.

Whether particular incidents constitute war crimes must be established through evidence and applicable legal standards.

Nevertheless, repeated civilian deaths cannot simply be dismissed as an inevitable consequence of war.

Accurate documentation by independent journalists, humanitarian organizations and investigators is essential to establishing what happened and preserving evidence for future accountability.

These legal obligations apply to every party to the conflict, including Myanmar’s military and the AA.

The AA’s responsibilities beyond military victory

As the AA consolidates control over much of Arakan, its responsibilities extend beyond military success.

Capturing territory does not automatically guarantee the safety and welfare of the population.

The AA must increasingly address civilian protection, early-warning systems, emergency shelters, healthcare access and assistance for displaced communities.

It must also take feasible precautions to reduce risks to civilians in areas under its control.

These responsibilities are particularly demanding in a region facing continued aerial attacks, economic disruption and limited humanitarian access.

Ultimately, the credibility of any governing authority depends not only on the territory it controls but also on its ability to protect civilians and provide essential services.

Military victories alone cannot establish effective governance.

The real test beyond the battlefield

Arakan’s war has exposed a widening gap between territorial control and civilian security.

The AA controls much of the state, yet it cannot fully prevent airstrikes against communities under its authority.

Meanwhile, Myanmar’s military retains the capacity to destroy infrastructure and disrupt civilian life, even where its administrative control has collapsed.
