But destruction cannot restore political legitimacy. Nor can the fear created by aerial bombardment be mistaken for genuine public support.

The future of Arakan will not be determined solely by the number of townships controlled by either side.

It will also depend on whether children can safely attend school, patients can reach hospitals, traders can rebuild their livelihoods, and displaced families can eventually return home.

Myanmar’s military may have lost much of Arakan, but it retains the power to destroy. Yet the ability to destroy is not the ability to govern, and civilian fear is no substitute for political legitimacy.

The ultimate measure of the conflict will lie not only in military victories or territorial gains, but in whether the lives, security and fundamental rights of civilians can be protected.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Regime Blames Thailand for Border Scam Hubs While Shielding Militia Allies
World.content:
The Myanmar military regime has again attempted to shift the blame to Thailand for online scam operations along the border, with Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin calling on Bangkok to do more to cut off essential supplies to scam syndicates operating in Karen State.

During talks with Pana Claewplodtook, commander-in-chief of the Royal Thai Army, on the sidelines of the 27th ASEAN Chiefs of Army Multilateral Meeting in Malaysia on Monday, Kyaw Swar Lin said Thailand should cooperate in blocking the flow of food supplies, fuel, electricity and telecommunications services used by scam syndicates operating along the border, according to regime media.

The regime said the meeting also covered military-to-military cooperation, border security and efforts to combat narcotics trafficking and illegal cross-border trade.

The junta has repeatedly sought to blame Thailand for the flourishing online scam industry centered on Myawaddy and Shwe Kokko on the Thai-Myanmar frontier. Since early 2025, regime officials have argued that scam compounds rely on electricity, internet connections and other logistical support originating from the Thai side of the border.

Kyaw Swar Lin also told the Thai army chief that scam syndicates were operating under the protection of certain insurgent groups, as he sought to distance the Myanmar military from notorious scam hubs. He did not mention, however, that the organizations he blamed are aligned with the Myanmar military.

Among the most notorious figures linked to the industry is Border Guard Force commander Colonel Saw Chit Thu, whose forces control Shwe Kokko and who has been sanctioned by the U.S. over his alleged involvement in online scams.

International pressure on scam networks along the Thai-Myanmar border has intensified since last year. The United States and China have both pushed for tougher action against syndicates operating in Karen State. The FBI is collaborating with the Royal Thai Police to crack down on the scam industry on the border, including Chinese transnational criminal organizations, which, according to U.S. officials, defraud Americans of US$10 billion annually from scam centers based in Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said the regime was trying to distance itself from online scam operations as both Washington and Beijing view the issue as a top priority.

“Given that these major powers are treating the issue with such concern, it is hardly surprising that the military regime is scrambling to deny any involvement and distance itself from the problem.”

The U.S. Embassy in Yangon on Monday again shared a reward offer of up to US$10 million for information leading to the recovery of assets linked to the Tai Chang scam network operating in areas controlled by the junta-aligned Democratic Karen Benevolent Army. The same day, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, arrived in Bangkok to discuss joint efforts against transnational scam networks.

Earlier this month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told the Myanmar regime to prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, months after Beijing hailed the “success” of a trilateral mechanism involving Bangkok and Naypyitaw launched in March 2025 to fight scam compounds in the border town.

While the regime portrays the fight against online scams as a national priority, the industry has spread far beyond the borderlands. Recent crackdowns have uncovered scam operations in Yangon and Mandalay, reinforcing findings that syndicates have established permanent footholds in Myanmar’s major cities while continuing to operate from militia-controlled enclaves along the Chinese and Thai borders.

In October, Kyaw Swar Lin warned senior army officers to steer clear of fraud, online gambling and narcotics.

“It is common knowledge that various levels of the regime have been involved and benefited from online scam operations and the drug trade, and are implicated in those activities,” said Htin Kyaw Aye.

Former regime spokesman Major General Zaw Min Tun previously acknowledged that senior officials from regional and state governments had been implicated in online scam operations and that major disciplinary action had been required against some of those involved.

World.title: Regime Minister Turns to Migrant Workers in Malaysia to Plug Foreign Currency Gap
World.content:
Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint, admitted while talking to Myanmar workers in Malaysia last week that the junta is increasingly relying on migrant workers to bring in foreign currency as sanctions and declining export earnings squeeze its finances.

“The world sanctions us,” Maung Myint said during his visit to the country. He also claimed that one of the reasons for the decline in Myanmar’s international revenue was that the regime had deliberately “reduced” exports of natural resources.

Following the 2021 coup, Western countries and blocs including the U.S., the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada imposed targeted economic sanctions on senior Myanmar regime officials, including coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, as well as state enterprises and military-controlled banks.

The sanctions remain in place, leaving some foreign development assistance programs suspended and interrupting international banking transfers, fueling the country’s foreign currency shortage and exacerbating an economic crisis caused by the regime’s mismanagement.

While Maung Myint claimed the regime had deliberately reduced natural-resource exports for environmental reasons, a World Bank report suggests that natural gas exports to Thailand and China—one of Myanmar’s major sources of foreign income—dropped by US$200 million in 2025-26 due to “reduced output” from existing offshore operations.

As international sanctions began to bite, the regime imposed remittance rules and enforced tax laws targeting overseas workers in 2023, aiming to extract funds from them. Foreign remittance value reached US$5.6 billion in 2025, and Maung Myint is hoping to match that figure this year.

“We’re trying to cover the shrinking income with remittances from workers,” he said in a video posted on his TikTok channel on Sunday.

He added that the rules and restrictions targeting migrant workers would be only temporary, claiming that potential increases in revenue from rare earths and a major deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea would eliminate the need for them.

However, he cautioned that rare earth sites “are not under the government’s control,” and are a “prospect” for foreign revenue once the regime gains control of them.

The majority of Myanmar’s approximately 600 rare-earth mining sites are concentrated on the China-Myanmar border in Kachin State under the control of the Kachin Independence Army. The rest also lie beyond the Myanmar regime’s control in eastern Shan State, in territory run by armed groups over which China exerts a great influence, including the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Its lack of control over these deposits deprives the regime of billions of dollars in potential revenue, as global powers like the U.S. and India court it for access to the critical minerals.

He said the deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea’s Block M-15 could earn $400-500 billion. According to the World Bank report, the project could produce up to 94.6 trillion cubic feet of usable gas “if confirmed”, but its output “is not expected soon.”

Maung Myint last week turned his focus to Malaysia, which hosts the second-largest population of Myanmar migrant workers, after his efforts to extract more foreign currency met with resistance from migrant workers in Thailand.

Since being appointed labor minister in October, he has been pushing hard for workers to comply with the new remittance and tax rules, particularly the Certification of Identity (CI) process.

The push sparked widespread boycotts in Thailand, where only 15,000 of nearly 750,000 undocumented Myanmar workers applied for the CI. Workers refused to apply for fear of funding the military’s war on civilians and exposing themselves to military conscription.

In Malaysia, he used flattery, calling workers national “heroes” and comparing them to soldiers who “sacrifice their time with families to serve the country.”

World.title: All Quiet in Northern Shan—and for Good Reason
World.content:
For several months, speculation has swirled over whether northern Shan State could see a return of resistance offensives on the scale of Operation 1027. But what is the likelihood of a resurgence of fighting?

The speculation appears to stem from signs of friction between Beijing and Myanmar’s military regime over how the ethnic armed organizations are to be managed, as well as the regime’s recent efforts to restore ties with the U.S. and Japan.

Yet the differences between China and the military regime are not fundamental—they do not amount to a strategic or ideological split.

China has not abandoned its long-held view that the military is a central pillar in maintaining stability in Myanmar. What has changed is Beijing’s growing recognition that the crisis cannot be managed through the military alone.

The fact that Beijing now acknowledges other forces has become a source of discomfort for the regime. But that is not a policy shift, only a tactical adjustment in how China seeks to implement its existing policy.

Beijing’s position on border stability remains unchanged. China does not want to see a return of armed conflicts to northern Shan, which shares a 200-km stretch of border with Yunnan.

All the rare-earth mines and other major investments operating in areas controlled by Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan involve Chinese capital. Given the technical requirements involved in rare-earth extraction, the companies operating these projects are more likely to be state-linked Chinese enterprises than private firms. The Chinese government is unlikely to allow such investments to be jeopardized.

One point of frustration for China has been the regime’s handling of border trade. Naypyitaw frequently claims that cross-border trade was disrupted by ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) that now control the major border trade routes. Yet Beijing is well aware that the military has also restricted border trade with Thailand, even though it fully controls the trade corridor there. From China’s perspective, regime policy puts up more barriers to trade than the MNDAA or TNLA.

Estimated at US$6 billion annually, that business is relatively small compared with the scale of the Chinese economy. The more pressing concern for Beijing has been online scam operations. Since the MNDAA and TNLA established control over large parts of the border, scam syndicates targeting Chinese citizens have been brought under much tighter control. The central military regime, by contrast, failed for years to address the problem.

Chinese policymakers may therefore calculate that restoring central military control across northern Shan could revive the criminal networks Beijing has made considerable effort suppressing. The financial and political costs of that scenario would surely outweigh the benefits of expanded border trade.

The EAOs themselves have little incentive to launch new offensives. The MNDAA and TNLA now control substantially more territory than before Operation 1027, and arguably more than they had dared to dream of. Having achieved those objectives, neither group has a pressing need to expend additional force.

Beijing may have a similar view and is therefore likely to restrain them from fighting the regime again. That means there is virtually no prospect of the MNDAA or TNLA initiating hostilities. The only realistic scenario under which fighting might resume would be if the military regime attacks first.

For its part, Naypyitaw expects China to pressure EAOs to return all the territories in northern Shan State to it. That is how the regime recovered the northern Shan capital of Lashio. Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun’s recent proposal of “high-level autonomy” for ethnic forces was therefore a bitter pill for the regime to swallow. And soon after Deng made the proposal, the regime dispatched reconnaissance planes to northern Shan.

Having survived the military disasters of 2023 and 2024 in large part because of Chinese intervention, the military’s top brass is now dreaming of eventually reclaiming all lost territory by force. Such thinking is hardly surprising for an institution that seized power by forced and continues to view military means as the answer to political problems.

But here dreams and reality collide. Before Operation 1027, the Northeastern Command was backed by roughly 20 infantry and light infantry battalions, in addition to artillery, logistics and support units. It was further reinforced by as many as seven or eight division-sized formations rotated through the theater.

That force no longer exists. Now only about 10 infantry and light infantry battalions remain under Northeastern Command, dispersed across Muse, Tangyan and Mongyai. The military now fields only a single major combat formation across the region, spread among Nantlan, Kyaukme, Hsipaw and Nawnghkio, while smaller units are deployed in Mongmit and Mogoke.

Indeed, since the ceasefire with the MNDAA and TNLA, the regime has moved an estimated seven division-sized formations out of northern Shan State to active fronts in Rakhine, Chin, Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay.

That mean it simply does not have the strength to maintain more than a presence in northern Shan and hold existing positions. The convoys that are regularly observed traveling between Taunggyi, Kho Lam, Mong Nawng, Mongyai and Tangyan do not represent substantial reinforcements: they mainly transport batches of new recruits to and from military training facilities.

The military’s ability to sustain operations elsewhere, then, depends heavily on the fact that northern Shan remains relatively quiet. To reopen that front, it would first have to withdraw troops from other battlefields, which would risk repeating the overstretch that contributed to the military’s earlier defeats.

In essence, the regime would be creating a new battlefield at a time when it can barely manage the existing ones.

No matter how much it resents the loss of northern Shan’s borders, there is nothing it can do about it. In addition, any attempt to violate the Beijing-brokered ceasefire could invite retaliation from China itself. Unlike Thailand, which has repeatedly shown restraint when fighting spills across its border, Beijing is unlikely to tolerate renewed instability along a frontier it regards as strategically vital.

In other words, the regime would be digging its own grave.

Moe Set Nyein Chan is a military analyst

World.title: Dozens of Civilians Killed in Myanmar Regime Strikes as ASEAN Leaders Meet
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has continued bombing civilian targets nationwide after its leaders were barred from attending the ongoing 49th ASEAN Summit for rejecting the bloc’s peace plan.

Rakhine State has borne the brunt of attacks, which have killed over a dozen civilians in the past week as the ethnic Arkan Army (AA) pushes to seize the state capital, Sittwe, and Kyaukphyu, home to China-backed mega projects.

Junta warplanes pounded residential areas in the AA-held town of Kyauktaw on Monday night, but casualty figures were unclear as of press time. The strike followed an Oct. 28 attack on the town’s busy market that killed 50 civilians including children and wounded 60, drawing international condemnation.

The AA also reported another deadly strike on a displacement camp in Ponnagyun Township on Friday evening. Twelve people were killed and 18 injured as blasts ripped through the Byar La shelter for war-displaced civilians. The attack came just weeks after two regime fighter jets bombed the same IDP camp, killing eight civilians and destroying homes and shops on October 4.

The airstrikes continued Sunday as ASEAN leaders gathered for their summit in Manila, with Myanmar’s crisis topping the agenda.

Blasts destroyed bridges in the Rakhine townships of Minbya and Ramree, according to the AA. The attacks followed a Nov. 1 airstrike on a Kyauktaw bridge that killed seven commuters and injured seven others.

Meanwhile, the regime’s Taung Maw Oo naval base used drones and artillery to destroy around 60 homes Kyaukphyu’s Sane town at the weekend, months after it was abandoned by civilians.

Former army captain Zin Yaw, who defected following the 2021 coup, said the regime is targeting bridges to cut supply lines of the AA, which is pushing to seize the regime’s last remaining toeholds in Rakhine.

“The regime has failed to meet its military objectives, so it is now attempting to destroy the enemy’s administrative and supply chains,” he said.

Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and relief worker, said regime forces are destroying bridges to slow the AA’s advance.

The AA has seized 14 out of Rakhine’s 17 townships plus Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State since launching a major offensive in November 2023.

The ethnic army has also expanded offensives across the border into Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady regions.

World.title: UN Chief Backs Engagement With Myanmar But ‘Violence Needs to Stop’
World.content:
MANILA—UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed support Monday for fresh diplomatic efforts to engage with Myanmar’s post-coup government, but said that “violence needs to stop.”

Guterres made the remarks in Manila, where leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) agreed Sunday to pursue a “calibrated engagement” with the war-torn country.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021, but the regional bloc is seeking a path towards normalizing diplomatic relations.

“We have never opposed the idea that it is always necessary to engage with whoever is involved in a conflict,” Guterres told a press conference on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

While “engagement is not appeasement,” Guterres said the “intolerable violations of human rights in Myanmar” must end.

“Violence needs to stop, humanitarian access needs to be granted, and all those arbitrarily detained must be immediately released,” Guterres said.

“And these are the conditions that could allow for what everybody should will [to happen], which is that Myanmar will find a way to move… to a true democratic situation.”

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” in an effort to implement ASEAN’s long-languishing five-point plan to end the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders adopted that language on Sunday in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach,” according to the joint statement.

Guterres’s remarks came as the UN’s International Court of Justice prepares to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalized Muslim Rohingya minority.

World.title: Four Kazakh Boxers Reach No. 1 in World Boxing Ranking
World.content:
ASTANA — Four Kazakh boxers have claimed the top spots in their respective weight categories in the latest World Boxing rankings, while several other members of the national team also secured places among the world’s top 10, the Kazakhstan National Olympic Committee reported.

Sanjar Tashkenbay (up to 50 kilograms), Torekhan Sabyrkhan (up to 70 kg), Natalia Bogdanova (up to 70 kg) and Aibek Oralbay (over 90 kg) lead their respective divisions.

Nazym Kyzaibay (up to 48 kg), Makhmud Sabyrkhan (up to 55 kg), Alua Balkibekova (up to 51 kg) and Aida Abikeyeva (up to 65 kg) rank second in their categories.

Nurbek Oralbay (up to 85 kg) and Dina Islambekova (over 80 kg) are ranked third.

Other Kazakh boxers also placed among the top 10. Sabyrzhan Akkalykov (up to 75 kg), Nurbek Oralbay (up to 80 kg) and Nadezhda Ryabets (up to 80 kg) hold fourth place in their respective categories.

Orazbek Assylkulov (up to 60 kg) and Viktoria Grafeeva (up to 60 kg) rank sixth, while Yeldana Talipova (over 80 kg) is seventh.

Yertugan Zeynullinov (up to 65 kg), Sultanbek Aibaryuly (up to 85 kg) and Sagyndyk Togambay (up to 90 kg) hold ninth place. Bakyt Seidish (up to 70 kg) rounds out the list in 10th place.

World.title: Almaty SuperSki Construction Advances as Kazakhstan Targets Its Opening in December 2028
World.content:
ASTANA — Construction of Kazakhstan’s Almaty SuperSki mountain resort is entering an active phase, with cable car foundations underway and international engineering and architecture firms joining the project as the government targets a December 2028 opening.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov reviewed the project’s progress on Nov. 18 at a meeting of the Board of Directors of Kazakh Tourism Development, where officials reported that construction is proceeding according to the approved schedule, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Work on the foundations for the cable car systems has begun in cooperation with French company POMA, which is responsible for building 11 cableways. Equipment manufacturing is also underway, with technical specifications tailored to the resort’s requirements.

The project is also creating opportunities for domestic manufacturers. Following an assessment of potential local suppliers, POMA qualified a Kazakh producer to manufacture selected structural components for the cableway systems in line with European quality and safety standards. The initiative is expected to facilitate technology transfer and develop new industrial capabilities in Kazakhstan, extending the project’s economic impact beyond tourism infrastructure.

International expertise shapes resort development

The latest decisions also advance the project’s architectural and engineering components, based on a concept developed by British architecture firm Foster + Partners. Swiss company Blumer-Lehmann will design, manufacture and supply the timber load-bearing structures for the resort’s base and upper stations, while providing technical support during installation.

Denmark’s Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) was selected following an international competition involving 24 companies to develop the concept for the mountain village. A key element of BIG’s proposal is its cooperation with Canadian company Ecosign, which specializes in ski resort master planning. The company has completed more than 1,000 projects in 46 countries and brings experience in integrating accommodation, transport and tourism infrastructure into mountain resorts. Its expertise includes developing accessible transport systems and ski-in/ski-out concepts, allowing visitors to reach ski slopes directly from accommodation facilities. BIG is also working with a British architectural firm whose portfolio includes a resort village in Finland, a mountain complex in Switzerland and a building featuring a ski slope on its roof in Denmark.

The selection of international partners follows earlier project decisions announced in June, when French company POMA was selected to build the cableways, Canadian company StructureCraft was brought in to work on timber engineering solutions, and U.S.-based Hill International was engaged to coordinate project management, construction and compliance with schedules.

Bektenov instructed officials to accelerate construction and maintain oversight of project timelines and quality. The next board meeting is scheduled in two weeks, when responsible officials will report on construction progress.

The government’s immediate priority is to keep Almaty SuperSki construction on schedule and deliver the resort by December 2028.

A broader ambition for Almaty’s mountain tourism

Almaty SuperSki is part of the broader Almaty Mountain Cluster initiative, which aims to transform the region into a year-round tourism destination and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in the regional tourism market. According to project figures presented during a May 2026 discussion hosted by the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, Almaty SuperSki is planned across 1,022 hectares, with 17 ski lifts, more than 60 kilometers of ski slopes of varying difficulty levels and a 20-hectare mountain village. The wider mountain cluster concept envisages up to 30 cable cars, nearly 151 kilometers of ski trails and capacity to accommodate up to 30,000 visitors daily. Beyond winter sports, the plans include hiking routes, cycling and mountain biking infrastructure, visitor centers and an integrated mountain safety system. The project aims to expand the region’s tourism offering beyond the existing ski resorts and make the mountains accessible to a broader range of visitors year-round.

The ambition comes amid growing demand for tourism in Kazakhstan. The country’s tourism sector contributed 5 trillion tenge (US$ 9.26 billion) to the economy in 2025, while investment in the industry reached 1.25 trillion tenge (US$ 2.31 billion), up 32.6% from the previous year. The country received 15.7 million foreign visitors in 2025, including 11.1 million classified as tourists. Domestic tourism is also expanding, with 8.7 million Kazakh citizens traveling within the country in 2025. Almaty’s mountain destinations are already an important part of this growth. The Almaty Mountain Cluster accounted for nearly half of domestic tourism flows in Kazakhstan’s growing nature-based tourism market.

The economic potential is accompanied by questions about environmental sustainability and visitor safety. During a May discussion on the mountain cluster, project developers highlighted cooperation with specialists in ecology, hydrology, zoology and sustainable land use to minimize pressure on the Ile-Alatau mountain ecosystem.

The Astana Times also reported in May that authorities were considering a registration system for visitors entering mountain routes around Almaty amid growing concerns about unprepared hikers and emergency response coordination. These considerations will remain important as the region develops its tourism infrastructure and attracts larger visitor flows.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Fixed-Capital Investment Rises 4.9% to $38.8 Billion
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s fixed-capital investment rose 4.9% year on year to 18.3 trillion tenge (US$38.8 billion) in January-October 2026, according to data the Bureau of National Statistics published on Nov. 18.

The increase was recorded in comparable prices, compared with the same period in 2025. The strongest growth was registered in the Ulytau Region, where fixed-capital investment rose by 74.4%. The Zhambyl Region followed with a 29% increase, while the Pavlodar and Turkistan regions recorded growth of 13.4% and 13%, respectively. Investment also increased by 11.4% in the Almaty Region, 10.6% in the East Kazakhstan Region, 8.2% in the Aktobe Region and 4.5% in the Mangystau Region.

Meanwhile, several regions reported declines. Fixed-capital investment fell by 31.7% in the Zhetysu Region, 8.7% in the Karagandy Region and 3.4% in the Akmola Region.

Astana accounted for 11.7% of total fixed-capital investment, while Almaty accounted for 10.3%.

The figures reflect investment trends across Kazakhstan’s regions during the first 10 months of 2026.

World.title: Kazakh PM Assures Samruk Kazyna Will Meet Obligations Despite Corruption Probe
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will honor all financial and contractual obligations to international investors and creditors, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said on Nov. 18, seeking to reassure financial partners following the detention of senior executives at Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and its national railway company.

“All companies within the group continue to operate as normal. The fund’s long-term strategy remains unchanged, and the implementation of its investment and infrastructure projects will proceed in accordance with approved plans,” Bektenov said in a statement published on Samruk Kazyna’s official website.

“All financial, contractual and debt obligations to investors, creditors, banks and international financial institutions will continue to be honored in full and on time,” he added.

The assurances come amid a high-profile corruption investigation involving Nurlan Zhakupov, chairman of Samruk Kazyna’s management board, and Yelzhas Otynshiyev, head of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy national railway company.

“Law enforcement authorities are currently conducting investigative proceedings involving certain officials. The circumstances surrounding these developments are being established as part of the ongoing investigation,” said Bektenov, noting that the investigation is under “direct oversight” of the President of Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan’s National Security Committee announced on Nov. 12 that the two executives and several other individuals had been detained on suspicion of a corruption-related offense.

“The competent authorities will ensure that the investigation is conducted thoroughly, objectively and in full accordance with the law,” said Bektenov.

Bektenov, who also chairs Samruk Kazyna’s board of directors, emphasized that the investigation should not cast doubt on the operations of the wider group. A new chairman of the Samruk Kazyna management board will soon be appointed, according to him.

Samruk Kazyna controls some of the country’s largest strategic enterprises with holdings spanning oil and gas, transportation, energy and telecommunications, among other sectors, including Air Astana airline ​and ​KazMunayGas oil and gas company. It also plays a central role in financing and implementing major national infrastructure and investment projects.

“Full continuity of leadership and uninterrupted operations of the fund will be ensured,” he said.

Reaffirming the government’s commitment to the fund’s long-term strategic direction, Bektenov said Kazakhstan would remain a reliable partner for the international investment and financial community.

“We highly value the confidence placed in us by our investors and creditors and remain firmly committed to building long-term, mutually beneficial partnerships,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Approves 2027–2029 Budget, Advances Online Platform Regulations
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Kurultai approved the country’s 2027–2029 national budget, advanced legislative amendments to regulate online platforms and mass media and also ratified international agreements with Singapore during a Nov. 18 meeting.

Deputies supported amendments increasing planned expenditures for 2027, including additional funding for presidential initiatives announced in his Oct. 28 address.

A total of 114.1 billion tenge (US$257 million) was allocated for these measures. Of this amount, 75.9 billion tenge (US$171 million) will go toward raising the minimum monthly wage from 85,000 (US$191) to 110,000 tenge (US$248). Another 20 billion tenge (US$45 million) is earmarked for salary increases for employees of primary healthcare organizations, while 600 million tenge (US$1.4 million) will support the introduction of artificial intelligence in secondary education.

An additional 101.5 billion tenge (US$228.6 million) was allocated to implement other presidential instructions. This includes 34.5 billion tenge (US$77.7 million) for the construction of a water pipeline from the Satpayev Canal to Astana, 21.9 billion tenge (US$49.3 million) to modernize and equip border checkpoints, and 16.2 billion tenge (US$36.5 million) for surveying work related to the proposed Balkhash nuclear power plant project.

The budget also provides 5.5 billion tenge (US$12.4 million) to expand staffing and improve the technical equipment of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.

Separately, deputies supported amendments allocating 47 billion tenge (US$105.9 million) for regional infrastructure projects. Another 2.5 billion tenge (US$5.6 million) will go toward the construction and development of healthcare facilities, and 6.5 billion tenge (US$14.6 million) will support special economic zones. Air transport development and Ministry of Emergency Situations facilities will each receive 2.5 billion tenge (US$5.6 million).

New rules proposed for online platforms and mass media

The Kurultai approved in the first reading draft legislation aimed at improving regulation of online platforms and mass media.

The proposed amendments seek to protect citizens’ rights, strengthen safeguards for minors online, increase the accountability of digital platforms and promote a more transparent information environment.

Under the proposals, online platforms would be required to establish representative offices in Kazakhstan and face liability for failing to comply with orders to remove illegal content.

According to the Ministry of Culture and Information, authorities identified 128,500 pieces of illegal content during the first 10 months of 2026.

The draft legislation also supports mechanisms to identify users and public communities with audiences exceeding 5,000 subscribers.

A separate set of measures focuses on protecting children online. The proposals would restrict registration on online platforms for children under 16 and introduce age-verification mechanisms. The restrictions would not apply to messaging services used to communicate with parents, relatives and teachers.

The proposed changes would also introduce licensing for the distribution of television and radio channels through audiovisual platforms and require online cinemas to appoint legal representatives in Kazakhstan.

Other amendments seek to strengthen protection of citizens’ honor, dignity and right to their own image. They would introduce administrative liability for defamation on online platforms and the use of obscene language in mass media and online.

The proposals also include labeling official responses from government agencies in the media and improving transparency around educational courses and occult services.

Kazakhstan and Singapore strengthen legal cooperation

The Kurultai ratified an agreement between Kazakhstan and Singapore on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters. The agreement is intended to strengthen cooperation between the competent authorities of the two countries in investigating and prosecuting criminal cases.

It provides for the exchange of evidence, searches and other procedural measures, access to bank account information, action against proceeds of crime, expert examinations and the collection of witness testimony.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan’s Economic Ambitions Depend on Multilateralism That Delivers
World.content:
ASTANA – At a time when international institutions face growing pressure and trust between major powers is weakening, Kazakhstan is making the case for a more practical approach to multilateral diplomacy, one that connects global commitments with regional cooperation and tangible results. The idea is reflected in an article in Vision for the Future edition 2026 by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Kairat Umarov, who reiterates that diplomacy should be measured not by the number of agreements reached, but by what international cooperation changes in people’s lives.

The argument also resonates with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s October state-of-the-nation address. Assessing the international environment, Tokayev pointed to a crisis of trust among major powers, the UN’s weakening authority and the erosion of international law. Amid all these, he stressed the importance of strengthening Kazakhstan’s sovereignty while maintaining a balanced foreign policy.

According to Umarov, for a country situated between major political and economic centers, these questions are closely connected to its development priorities.

“As the world’s largest landlocked developing country, our prosperity depends on open connections, peaceful relations, responsible management of shared resources and cooperation across borders. Geography has taught us a simple lesson: lasting progress cannot be built in isolation,” Umarov writes.

This perspective places regional cooperation at the center of Kazakhstan’s international engagement. Rather than treating diplomacy as a separate sphere of activity, it connects foreign policy with issues that directly affect economic development and public welfare, including transport connectivity, water security, climate resilience and digital transformation.

“We continue to pursue a balanced and constructive foreign policy, privilege dialogue and support a strong UN. For Kazakhstan, multilateralism is not an abstract preference; it is a strategic necessity,” Umarov writes.

From global commitments to regional solutions

One example is the UN Regional Center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty. According to Umarov, the center was established through General Assembly resolution 79/268, initiated by President Tokayev and co-sponsored by 152 UN Member States. Its purpose is to bring together UN expertise and coordinate assistance around regional development priorities.

The initiative reflects a broader question: how can international institutions become more responsive to regions’ specific needs rather than operate through fragmented projects and overlapping mandates?

“The true measure of multilateralism is not the number of declarations we adopt, but the difference cooperation makes in people’s lives,” Umarov writes.

This emphasis on practical results also aligns with the economic priorities outlined in Tokayev’s address. He called for Kazakhstan to strengthen its position in international transport networks, develop domestic logistics operators and expand its participation in global production chains. For a landlocked country, these ambitions depend on more than national infrastructure investment. Efficient transport corridors require coordinated border procedures, reliable regional partnerships and access to international markets. Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, illustrate how domestic economic objectives are closely tied to cooperation beyond its borders.

Water management offers another illustration of this interdependence. Central Asian countries share river systems and face growing pressure on water resources, making national policies closely dependent on cooperation with neighboring states.

Umarov identifies water security as one of Kazakhstan’s most urgent national and regional priorities. He points to the modernization of water infrastructure, water-saving technologies and digital monitoring, as well as Tokayev’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under UN auspices.

“Water agenda remains one of our most urgent national and regional priorities.… At the international level, President Tokayev has proposed the establishment of an International Water Organization under the auspices of the UN. Such an organization could bring greater coherence to fragmented international efforts, strengthen coordination, raise water higher on the global political agenda, accelerate progress towards water-related commitments by 2030, and help shape the global water agenda beyond that timeframe,” Umarov writes.

The proposal illustrates how Kazakhstan’s domestic priorities can become part of a wider international agenda. Water infrastructure, resource efficiency and cross-border coordination are not only environmental concerns: they affect agriculture, energy security, investment and long-term economic stability.

Digital transformation beyond national borders

A similar connection can be seen in the digital sphere. Tokayev’s address placed technological modernization, AI and stronger domestic production capabilities among the country’s development priorities. Umarov, meanwhile, notes that digital transformation should be approached through regional cooperation, including shared expertise, skills development and common principles for the responsible use of artificial intelligence.

“The objective is not digitalization for its own sake, but better public services, stronger human capital and broader participation in future growth,” he writes.

The regional dimension is reflected in the Asian and Pacific Digital Solutions Center for Sustainable Development in Almaty, an initiative of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. The center aims to help countries exchange solutions and build capabilities in the digital economy.

This approach aligns with Kazakhstan’s broader economic ambitions. In his address, Tokayev emphasized the importance of strategic partnerships with international technology leaders, deeper industrial processing and greater integration into global production chains. However, access to technology alone does not guarantee economic transformation. The challenge is to develop domestic expertise, strengthen institutions and ensure that technological advances translate into productivity gains, better services and opportunities for businesses. Regional cooperation could support these objectives by allowing countries to share expertise and address challenges that extend beyond national borders.

The role of Middle Powers in a changing global order

For Umarov, practical multilateralism requires more than establishing new institutions or expanding international dialogue. It depends on whether cooperation translates into implementation, with clear objectives, adequate resources and measurable results.

“These initiatives suggest three priorities for practical multilateralism. First, trust must come with effective architecture. New mechanisms succeed only when they respond to real demand and have the support of those they serve. Second, partnerships must lead to implementation, with clear objectives, responsible actors, adequate resources and measurable results. Third, progress must be inclusive. Women, young people, local communities, scientists, entrepreneurs and vulnerable groups must have a voice in shaping the solutions that affect them,” Umarov writes.

This distinction between political commitments and implementation is particularly relevant as the UN faces growing calls for institutional reform. The challenge is not simply to make international organizations more efficient, but to ensure that they remain capable of responding to the needs of countries with different economic capacities and development priorities.

The role of middle powers is another important part of this discussion. Kazakhstan does not seek to position itself as a global power, but its geographic location, resource base and regional ties give it an interest in maintaining open channels of cooperation.

“Kazakhstan seeks to contribute in precisely this way: not by claiming exclusive leadership, but by offering solutions and creating space for cooperation,” Umarov writes.

This approach is consistent with the emphasis on sovereignty and pragmatic international engagement in Tokayev’s October address. He linked Kazakhstan’s economic resilience to stronger transport connectivity, energy security, technological development and partnerships with major international economic players.

For Kazakhstan, maintaining a balanced foreign policy is therefore closely connected to its ability to diversify economic relationships and participate in international markets without becoming excessively dependent on any single route, partner or source of technology.

At the same time, the effectiveness of regional initiatives will depend on their implementation. Establishing new centers and cooperation mechanisms can provide a framework for joint action, but their value will ultimately be determined by the projects they deliver, the resources they mobilize and the problems they help solve.

The connection between Umarov’s diplomatic perspective and Tokayev’s domestic agenda lies in this emphasis on practical outcomes. Transport connectivity, water management, digital transformation and industrial development are national priorities, but their implementation increasingly requires regional coordination and international partnerships. For Kazakhstan, multilateralism is thus both a foreign policy principle and a practical instrument for addressing development challenges.

As the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals approaches, the broader question is whether international cooperation can keep pace with the economic, technological and environmental challenges facing countries across the region.

“The question is not whether multilateralism should endure, but whether it can deliver,” Umarov concludes.

The article was published in Vision for the Future, the annual international publication of the Global Partnerships Forum, which brings together contributions from representatives of international organizations, diplomatic, academic and business communities on issues of global cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exports to EU Rise as France, Greece and Spain Lead Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with the European Union (EU) increased by 8.2% year on year to $31.6 billion in January-August 2026, with France, Greece and Spain accounting for 96.5% of the growth in Kazakh exports to the bloc, according to an analysis by the Association of Financiers of Kazakhstan (AFK).

According to the report, Kazakhstan’s exports to the EU rose 12.2% to $25.3 billion during the eight-month period. However, the bloc’s share of the country’s total exports declined from 44.6% to 41.8%. Mineral products saw the largest export increase, rising by $2.4 billion, followed by chemical products, which increased by $439.4 million.

France recorded the largest growth in imports from Kazakhstan, with shipments increasing by $1.6 billion. Exports to Greece rose by $627 million, while those to Spain increased by $382 million. Together, the three countries accounted for 96.5% of the increase in Kazakhstan’s exports to the EU.

The AFK noted that the figures point to export growth concentrated in a small number of European markets rather than an evenly distributed expansion across the bloc. Meanwhile, imports of European goods to Kazakhstan declined by 5.4% to $6.4 billion. The largest decreases were recorded in machinery, equipment and transport vehicles, down $191.5 million, and chemical products, down $109.3 million.

According to AFK analysts, the decline was largely associated with the irregular nature of major investment-related purchases. In particular, imports of aircraft from France decreased by $322.7 million.

Germany remained Kazakhstan’s largest European supplier, with imports totaling $2 billion, followed by Italy at $898 million and France at $808 million. Together, the three countries accounted for 57.6% of Kazakhstan’s EU imports.

Amid rising exports and falling imports, Kazakhstan’s trade surplus with the EU rose 19.6% to $18.9 billion, up from $15.8 billion a year earlier. The country’s overall trade surplus reached $17.8 billion in the first eight months of 2026.

The EU remains one of Kazakhstan’s key trading partners, accounting for nearly 42% of the country’s exports and 15% of its imports. However, trade continues to be dominated by raw materials, particularly oil and uranium products.

According to the AFK, further expansion of trade with the EU will depend on Kazakh manufacturers gaining access to European markets with higher-value, more-processed products.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Maldives Agree to Double Weekly Flight Allowance at ICAO Conference
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has agreed with the Maldives to double the number of permitted regular flights between the two countries from seven to 14 per week for designated airlines, the Ministry of Transport reported following bilateral meetings at the seventh ICAO World Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) in Montreal, Canada.

The agreement was reached during a meeting between Saltanat Tompiyeva, chair of the Civil Aviation Committee of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, and Abdul Haris, head of the Civil Aviation Authority of the Maldives. The sides discussed expanding air connectivity, strengthening bilateral cooperation and developing tourism links.

They also discussed the possibility of operating flights under fifth freedom traffic rights, which would allow airlines to explore additional commercial opportunities on international routes.

Kazakhstan discusses aviation cooperation with international partners

Kazakhstan also held talks with Guyana on prospects for cooperation in civil aviation. Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev met with Deodat Indar, Guyana’s Minister of Public Utilities and Aviation.

Lastayev outlined Kazakhstan’s reforms aimed at improving flight safety and aviation security, strengthening state oversight and aligning national aviation legislation with international standards.

According to the ministry, Kazakhstan’s compliance with ICAO standards in flight safety increased from 47% in 2009 to 82% following the 2025 audit. Effective implementation of aviation security standards reached 95.7%, compared with 62% in 2009.

Lastayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s open skies policy, introduced in 2017. Kazakhstan became the first country in Central Asia to implement the regime, which provides foreign airlines with fifth freedom traffic rights and allows flights without restrictions on destinations, frequency or aircraft types.

The discussions also covered cooperation between aviation authorities and coordination on shared priorities within the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).

Meetings with Croatia, Equatorial Guinea and Central American partners

Tompiyeva also met with Ana Kapetanović, director of Croatia’s Civil Aviation Agency, to discuss bilateral cooperation and the exchange of experience in aviation regulation and flight safety oversight. The sides considered the implementation of ICAO international standards and recommended practices, as well as professional cooperation between their aviation authorities.

During a separate meeting with representatives of Equatorial Guinea, Kazakhstan signed a memorandum to expand cooperation between the countries’ aviation authorities. The meeting brought together Tompiyeva, Santiago Oyono Afugu Eyenga, director general of Equatorial Guinea’s Civil Aviation Authority, and Estanislao Esono Anguesumo, the country’s permanent representative to the ICAO Council. Discussions focused on strengthening institutional ties and exchanging experience in civil aviation regulation.

Kazakhstan also held talks with representatives of Belize and the Central American Corporation for Air Navigation Services (COCESNA). The meeting was attended by Nigel Carter, director of Belize’s Civil Aviation Authority, and Juan Carlos Trabánino Aguirre, executive director and general director of COCESNA, alongside representatives of Costa Rica and Belize.

Established in 1960, COCESNA provides air navigation services to six Central American countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua. The participants discussed potential long-term cooperation, particularly in flight safety, aviation security, training aviation inspectors and air navigation services.

Tompiyeva presented Kazakhstan’s aviation development priorities, including work with ICAO on a General Plan for Civil Aviation Development through 2050. Belizean representatives expressed interest in signing a memorandum of cooperation and studying Kazakhstan’s experience with the ICAO Global Ambassadors Program, for which Tompiyeva serves as the national ambassador.

World.title: ‘Economic development must not come at expense of sovereignty’: Views on mountain resort project in Abkhazia
World.content:
The president of Abkhazia has announced plans to begin construction of a mountain resort in the Aibga mountain range.

Aibga, however, is a 160 sq km territory whose border between Abkhazia and Russia has never been formally delimited.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, one part of Aibga fell on the Russian side and the other on the Abkhaz side. The Psou River serves as the de facto boundary between them. Russia lays claim to the other part of the mountain range, a claim that Abkhazia firmly rejects.

Abkhazian President Badra Gunba has announced plans to build a joint year-round ski resort on the slopes of Mount Aibga in cooperation with the Russian ski resort of Krasnaya Polyana.

“These territories are located opposite each other, and everyone who visits would have the opportunity to ski down the slopes of Krasnaya Polyana, then head up the slopes of Aibga and enjoy the unique opportunities it offers as well.

“So there should be no competition here. On the contrary, we should work together on joint projects,” Gunba said.

Former Abkhaz parliament member Ilya Gunia discusses the ski resort project in the context of the territorial dispute in his blog.

Ilya Gunia:

“The project is being presented as a strategic economic breakthrough that could attract investment, create jobs and give the republic’s development fresh momentum.

I agree that tourism needs to be developed and investment attracted. However, I believe that behind the economic prospects lie questions of national importance that cannot be ignored.

Aibga is first and foremost a matter of Abkhazia’s state border and territorial integrity.

A joint Russian-Abkhaz commission on the delimitation and demarcation of the border has been operating for many years. I served as a member of this commission during my time as a member of parliament. It was precisely over the Aibga section that the commission’s work reached a deadlock. The two sides failed to reach an understanding on the issue.

As a former member of the commission, I believe it is necessary to highlight three fundamental problems.

First. Any large-scale infrastructure project in territory whose status remains the subject of an interstate dispute could trigger a serious political crisis. A commercial project cannot begin in an area where the state border has yet to be legally established between the two sides.

Second. Attempts to circumvent existing disagreements under the pretext of creating a unified cross-border space raise serious questions. International cooperation must not become a pretext for weakening state control over one’s own territory.

By taking part in such projects, Abkhazia must act exclusively as an equal partner. Investors’ economic interests cannot take precedence over national interests, and the republic’s laws must remain an absolute priority.”

Third. If the interstate commission has been unable to find a solution to this issue for many years, how does the executive intend to resolve it now? On the basis of what agreements? Within what boundaries will the project be implemented? What are the terms of Russia’s participation, and who will exercise state control over the territory? The people of Abkhazia have the right to know what commitments their state is undertaking.

I am not opposed to developing tourism, attracting investment or building modern resorts. But all this must take place within the law and exclusively on territory whose status is clearly defined and legally protected.

We have no right to put the country’s territorial integrity at risk for the sake of economic prospects.

Abkhazia paid too high a price for its independence for us to treat questions of sovereignty today as a mere formality or a technical obstacle to an investment project.

I therefore urge the republic’s leadership to refrain from making any decisions on the Aibga project until the border dispute has been fully resolved.

The first priority must be to ensure transparency in the negotiations, establish the state border and guarantee the protection of Abkhazia’s national interests. Only then can we have a substantive discussion about implementing projects of this kind.

Economic development is necessary, but it must not come at the expense of sovereignty.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: NGOs in Azerbaijan face re-registration as experts warn of tighter rules
World.content:
Re-registration of NGOs in Azerbaijan

All non-governmental organisations (NGOs) operating in Azerbaijan, as well as branches and representative offices of foreign NGOs, will have to undergo state re-registration. The requirement is set out in amendments to the Law on Non-Governmental Organisations (Public Associations and Funds). The draft legislation has been included on the agenda of Milli Majlis sessions scheduled for 17 and 18 November.

Once the law comes into force, organisations will have just 30 days to bring their statutes into line with the new requirements and apply for re-registration. Authorities will suspend the activities of any organisation that fails to apply or whose application they reject. They will then file a lawsuit seeking its dissolution.

Over the past decade, Azerbaijan has repeatedly tightened the legislation governing NGO activities.

What will the re-registration process mean for these organisations, and who will decide their fate?

What does the draft law provide for?

Re-registration. Local NGOs registered before the law comes into force will have to apply to the “relevant executive authority” within 30 days. Branches of foreign NGOs whose agreements have expired or which have no agreement in place will have to sign a new agreement or extend their existing one within the same period.

New requirements for statutes. Organisations will have to include internal financial control procedures in their statutes, establish supervisory bodies and provide for measures to reduce the risk of terrorist financing. The law will also define different types of NGOs, with each organisation allowed to belong to only one category.

Tenfold increase in the minimum capital required for foundations. The current minimum statutory capital for a foundation is 10,000 manats (approximately $5,882). The draft law proposes raising it to 100,000 manats (approximately $58,820).

Suspension of activities without a court order. This is one of the most significant changes proposed by the draft law. Under the current legislation, only a court can order an NGO to suspend its activities. Under the proposed rules, the executive authority would be able to suspend an organisation for up to one year without going to court. Grounds for suspension would include:

failure to ensure transparency in the organisation’s activities;

failure to comply with requirements on combating corruption, money laundering and terrorist financing;

failure to update the state register within three months of the expiry of the head of the organisation’s term of office;

expiry of an agreement with a foreign NGO branch.

New grounds for dissolution. Under the current law, a court can generally order an NGO’s dissolution if it has received more than two written warnings within a year. The draft law expands the list of grounds for dissolution. These would include posing a “threat to the interests of the state and society protected by law”, failing to hold a general meeting for three consecutive years, remaining inactive for more than three years, and carrying out activities that do not correspond to the organisation’s stated objectives.

Who will decide what constitutes “transparency” or a “threat”?

The draft law uses broad terms such as “failure to ensure transparency” and “threat to the interests of the state”. However, it does not specify the criteria for applying these provisions. If adopted, the law would allow the executive authority responsible for registering NGOs and overseeing their activities to make decisions that previously fell to the courts.

Lawyer Narmin Ahmadli told the Musavat newspaper in a comment that 30 days would not be enough for many NGOs. She said that amending their statutes would require them to draw up internal financial control procedures, which takes time. Lawyer Bakhtiyar Hajiyev, meanwhile, pointed out that the requirement would apply to all public associations and foundations registered before the law comes into force.

Raising the minimum statutory capital to 100,000 manats would make it significantly harder to register small initiatives as foundations. By comparison, this amount is around 85 times the country’s average monthly salary.

Previous tightening of NGO legislation

This is not the first time Azerbaijan has tightened its legislation governing NGOs. In February 2014, President Ilham Aliyev signed around 50 amendments into law. They prohibited banks from processing transactions under unregistered grant agreements, required Azerbaijani citizens to head branches of foreign NGOs and increased fines. The then-chairman of the NGO Forum, Gubad Ibadoghlu, said the changes would severely restrict civil society activities. US, EU and UK diplomats also expressed concern.

In July 2025, new requirements were introduced for registering service contracts funded by foreign sources, along with additional fines. In its 2024 report, international human rights organisation Human Rights Watch urged the Azerbaijani government to review its NGO legislation in line with recommendations from the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

Against the backdrop of the “NGO funding case”

The draft law is being considered amid ongoing criminal proceedings against NGO representatives. In February 2025, the Prosecutor General’s Office reopened the so-called “NGO funding case”, which it had launched in 2014 and suspended in 2022. According to human rights organisation Amnesty International, at least 50 civil society representatives have since been questioned as witnesses or suspects.

Asef Ahmedov, head of the Ganja Regional Public Centre, was sentenced to eight years in prison. Zamin Zakiyev, head of the Ubuntu Association for Social Work initiative, received a seven-year-and-three-month sentence. Prosecutors have requested a nine-year prison term for Bashir Suleymanli, head of the Institute for Civil Rights. The next hearing in his case is scheduled for 19 November. The defendants reject the charges and say they acted within the law.

There has been no announcement of who drafted the bill or which executive authority will oversee the re-registration of NGOs. Government agencies have also yet to explain the reasons behind the proposed changes.

Re-registration of NGOs in Azerbaijan

World.title: Deutsche Bank leak: Bank linked payments to Trump companies in Baku to ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’
World.content:
Trump-linked companies in Azerbaijan

According to documents leaked from Germany’s largest bank, Deutsche Bank, between 2014 and 2020 the bank repeatedly flagged as suspicious payments received by two companies linked to Donald Trump‘s hotel project in Baku. Some of the funds came from companies associated with a money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The findings were reported in an international journalistic investigation, Inside Deutsche Bank, published on 17 November. More than 200 journalists from over 50 media outlets took part in the investigation. The section focusing on Azerbaijan was published by the Russian-language investigative outlet iStories.

The journalists obtained more than 15 million internal bank files, including email correspondence, client documents and risk assessment materials. The files were provided by two whistleblowers to journalists in India and South Africa.

Trump’s unfinished skyscraper in Baku has been the subject of numerous reports in the past. This time, however, the investigation focused on a different question:

Where did the funds that the bank considered suspicious come from, and what do these findings reveal about the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”?

Unfinished skyscraper in Baku

Trump International Hotel & Tower in Baku / Archive photo, 2015

The project in question is the 33-storey Trump International Hotel & Tower complex in Baku, construction of which began in 2012. However, the building was never put into operation. Trump’s partners in the project were relatives of Azerbaijan’s then Transport Minister Ziya Mammadov. As iStories notes, the family amassed a multimillion-dollar fortune through government contracts.

Trump’s company withdrew from the project in late 2016. According to Trump’s financial disclosure, he received around $2.5m for managing the project in 2015 and just over $300,000 in 2016. In 2017, the Trump Organization told The New Yorker that Trump had played a “passive role” in the project and had merely licensed the use of his name.

The project was managed by two US companies, DT Marks Baku and THC Baku Services. It is their bank accounts that are covered by the documents obtained by journalists through the leak.

Which transactions did the bank consider suspicious?

According to iStories, Deutsche Bank first flagged a payment to DT Marks Baku as suspicious in August 2014. The funds came from an unnamed client of Danske Bank’s Estonian branch. Deutsche Bank was unable to establish the purpose of the payment or the nature of the relationship between the sender and the recipient.

In April 2015, THC Baku Services received just over $141,000 from Faberlex, a UK-registered shell company. Faberlex was one of the key participants in the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The bank continued to identify suspicious payments in subsequent years. As reported by the Dutch investigative platform Follow the Money, Deutsche Bank’s internal analysis linked the funds to both the “Azerbaijani Laundromat” and a Russian money-laundering network associated with oligarchs close to the Kremlin.

According to an internal bank document dated May 2020, the total value of suspicious transactions involving the accounts of Trump’s companies in Baku exceeded $3m.

What was the ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’?

The “Azerbaijani Laundromat” was a money-laundering scheme exposed in an investigation published in September 2017 by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), an international investigative journalism network.

According to the investigation, around $2.9bn was transferred through UK-registered shell companies between 2012 and 2014, primarily via the Estonian branch of Danske Bank. Journalists found that some of the funds were channelled to European politicians, while others were spent on luxury goods and other expenses of members of the elite.

The Azerbaijani authorities rejected the investigation’s findings at the time. Presidential spokesman Azer Gasimov described the investigation as “absurd and biased”. The OCCRP website was blocked in Azerbaijan.

In subsequent years, European courts handed down several sentences in cases linked to the scheme. In 2021, former member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) and Italian politician Luca Volontè was sentenced to four years in prison for accepting bribes from Azerbaijani officials. According to iStories, the funds were transferred to him through Faberlex.

Former German Bundestag members Eduard Lintner and Axel Fischer also received suspended prison sentences for accepting bribes in connection with lobbying for Azerbaijan’s interests.

According to the documents, Faberlex and two other companies involved in the scheme, Hilux Services and Polux Management, were formally owned by Maharram Ahmadov, a driver from Baku.

What is the situation now?

The document leak comes amid closer ties between Trump and Baku. In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a joint declaration at the White House with Donald Trump and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.

Deutsche Bank said that the law prohibited it from disclosing information about suspicious transaction reports. In response to journalists’ questions, the bank noted that the events in question had taken place “many years ago”, stressing that “we are a different bank today”.

The Trump Organization did not respond to journalists’ questions, while the White House referred them to the company. Danske Bank said that money laundering “should never have happened” and noted that the case had been closed in 2022 following decisions by the Danish and US authorities.

The Azerbaijani authorities have yet to comment on the newly leaked documents.

World.title: ‘Traffic jams are not caused by buildings’: Yerevan mayor responds to prime minister’s wife
World.content:
Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

“Traffic jams are caused by cars, not buildings. Armenia is experiencing economic growth and an inflow of money. People now have more opportunities – and they are buying cars,” Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan said today.

He was effectively responding to Anna Hakobyan, the wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. A few days ago, she posted a video on social media showing traffic jams in the capital. She said Yerevan was gradually becoming “the most unfriendly city” to live in.

The prime minister’s wife asked what the authorities should do to prevent life in the city and getting around it from becoming “a reason for a heart attack”. She pointed to economic growth, the rapid construction of new buildings, a rising population, more cars on the roads and an influx of tourists.

“Some people have a professional duty to find an answer to this question. But this task is far more difficult than issuing construction permits to companies investing millions of dollars. ‘Approved’ is a magic stamp that requires minimal effort but has an enormous impact [on the situation],” Hakobyan stressed.

According to the mayor, the city authorities issued a record 108 permits for apartment blocks and residential complexes in 2021. Those are the buildings now being completed and handed over to residents. Avinyan noted that the authorities have not issued as many permits in any year since then. For example, they issued just 37 in 2025.

The mayor acknowledged that the current situation is causing a certain degree of “tension” – and said he shares those concerns. However, Avinyan called for an analysis of the problems and appropriate solutions.

Tigran Avinyan’s explanation apparently failed to satisfy Anna Hakobyan. She immediately posted another video, this time about the “catastrophic traffic jams”. In her post, the prime minister’s wife urged women drivers to stop being patient:

“Keep noisy objects in your cars. Every time you find yourself stuck in traffic for hours, make a loud noise. Make it loud enough for those who have a duty to use their brains and solve the problem to hear you.”

Prime minister’s wife: “You need an astronaut’s health to get from point A to point C”

In her first post, Anna Hakobyan said that getting around the capital required “an astronaut’s health” – in other words, a strong cardiovascular and nervous system.

She also expressed confidence that scientific disciplines exist that can help calculate how many cars Yerevan will have in 25 years, based on current development trends. They can also help determine what measures the authorities need to take now to prepare for that future.

Hakobyan suggested that, alongside the buildings springing up across the city “like mushrooms after rain”, the authorities should build flyovers, as well as elevated, underground and bypass roads.

“You have to actively seek out this knowledge yourself. Nobody will serve it up on a silver platter as a ready-made, multi-million-dollar project that only needs a ‘approved’ stamp,” she said, again alluding to the construction permits issued in the capital.

In her view, traffic planning must take into account how much the population could grow in the coming years and how many more cars the city might have.

“What will happen if between 300,000 and 500,000 people return to their homeland to live permanently over the next five years? And what if 250,000 of them bring their own cars? What are we going to do? Will the same number of people have to leave so that we can all fit on the streets?” Anna Hakobyan asked.

Mayor: “Possible solutions will be presented to the public”

According to Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan, traffic congestion in the capital has three main causes: the growing number of private cars, driving culture and the need to give public transport priority.

He said the city authorities would soon present various possible solutions for public discussion. Avinyan outlined some of the measures under consideration:

fully separating bus lanes from other traffic;

introducing measures to reduce traffic violations;

restricting car use on public health grounds.

On the last point, the mayor clarified that the restrictions would not apply to vehicles coming to Yerevan from other regions. He said the aim was to reduce the overall number of cars within the city.

Tigran Avinyan believes the growing number of private cars is the main cause of traffic jams. He argues that public transport should take priority.

He expects new road construction to help improve traffic flow to some extent. However, he warned that new roads alone would not solve the problem. They would soon become congested again unless the authorities introduced measures such as restrictions on car use, dedicated lanes and tougher fines.

The mayor also addressed environmental concerns. Avinyan identified nitrogen dioxide as a specific pollutant whose levels in Yerevan are rising rapidly year after year as the number of cars increases. He said it causes lung and respiratory diseases.

“The most dangerous thing is that children are the first to suffer from these problems,” Avinyan stressed.

First lady’s appeal

In response to the Yerevan mayor’s remarks, Anna Hakobyan published a new video, saying that people had thanked her for raising the issue.

“They tell me: ‘At last, someone has had the courage to speak about this.’ Every day, hundreds of thousands of people suffer in Yerevan’s traffic jams. So does complaining about the situation now require ‘courage’?”

Hakobyan urged women drivers to stop putting up with the situation and called on men to show greater determination. She suggested that women should make a loud noise whenever they get stuck in traffic.

In her view, government institutions never hear complaints that people “do not dare to voice”.

“Otherwise, we might end up blaming the previous authorities for Yerevan’s traffic jams [the current government, led by her husband, often blames its predecessors for various problems]. If Armenia’s economy had developed in a balanced way over the past 30 years, and the number of cars had increased gradually rather than exponentially, the situation in the Armenian capital would be completely different today,” she said.

Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

World.title: ‘Сake will be divided without us’: Analyst on Georgia’s foreign policy
World.content:
According to analyst Paata Zakareishvili, the appointment of Giorgi Zurabashvili, first deputy foreign minister, as the Georgian prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia gives the Kremlin a new channel for direct political communication with Georgia’s foreign ministry. This could pave the way for existing negotiation formats to be weakened.

Russia has already established contact with the new special representative, Giorgi Zurabashvili. His Russian counterpart will be Mikhail Galuzin, Russia’s deputy foreign minister. According to the Russian side, the main topics for discussion will include increasing trade and tourism, expanding transport links and promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.

Paata Zakareishvili believes that placing the special representative’s post within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is a dangerous decision. In his view, the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia should be an independent figure, rather than a serving senior official in the foreign ministry.

“Georgia and Russia have not maintained diplomatic relations since the August 2008 war. At the same time, Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and the political confrontation between the two countries require a special format for relations.

“It was precisely for these reasons that the Karasin-Abashidze format was established. Under this arrangement, Georgia’s former special representative, Zurab Abashidze, met with Russia’s deputy foreign minister, Grigory Karasin,” the analyst says.

According to Zakareishvili, the format was important because it kept talks with Russia on practical issues separate from discussions about the conflicts. It also allowed Georgia’s foreign ministry to make its position clear during international negotiations.

“Russia constantly says that diplomatic relations with Georgia should be restored. The Georgian authorities remain silent on this issue. Against this background, they have suddenly taken a step in Russia’s favour. Russia needs to ‘get its foot in the door’ of Georgia’s foreign ministry and hold talks with the first deputy minister,” Zakareishvili says.

He is particularly concerned about the possible weakening of the Geneva International Discussions. Established after the 2008 war, the talks involve representatives of Georgia, Russia and the United States, as well as the European Union and the OSCE. Zakareishvili believes the Georgian authorities’ latest moves could eventually be aimed at reducing the importance of this international format in favour of direct bilateral contacts.

According to the analyst, the replacement of Lasha Darsalia as Georgia’s representative at the Geneva talks also carries symbolic significance. Zakareishvili says Darsalia clearly articulated Georgia’s position during the negotiations and regularly used the term “occupation” when referring to Russia’s actions.

“The time will come when they start singing a new tune: ‘Georgia’s foreign ministry is already dealing with Russia, so why do we need Geneva?’ Their primary aim is to weaken the Geneva format, which is visibly losing ground,” Zakareishvili predicts.
