He also believes that the location of the first meeting between Giorgi Zurabashvili and Mikhail Galuzin will be particularly important. He considers holding the meeting in Moscow a disastrous political move, as it would give Russia an opportunity to symbolically demonstrate that it controls the process.

In Zakareishvili’s view, Prague would be the most logical venue, as it hosted meetings between Karasin and Abashidze for years.

“Russia needs symbolic victories. If the meeting takes place in Moscow, the message will be that Russia is in control of the process. That must not be allowed under any circumstances,” the analyst says.

Zakareishvili also links the Georgian authorities’ new approach to relations with Russia to a shift in the country’s foreign policy. In his assessment, the government is gradually moving away from the European Union and NATO, while seeking to build closer ties with Russia without making any formal commitments to direct integration or cooperation with Moscow.

In this context, the analyst also points to the possibility of Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution being repealed. It obliges state authorities to take all necessary measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

According to Zakareishvili, the initiative to ban opposition parties and the Georgian authorities’ efforts to secure a constitutional majority are part of a broader political process that could undermine the institutional foundations of Georgia’s commitment to Western integration.

Paata Zakareishvili

“It is not Bidzina Ivanishvili who is Russia’s project, but Russia that is Ivanishvili’s project. For now, however, this suits Russia. Russia has other priorities at the moment, and it is not Russia that is working on Georgia – it is Ivanishvili who is working for Russia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the message the Georgian authorities are sending to the Kremlin is this: Georgia no longer intends to move towards the European Union and NATO, but it also has no plans to join the political and economic blocs established by Russia. Zakareishvili believes the authorities are using this approach to preserve room for political manoeuvre while avoiding public discontent that an overt shift towards Russia could trigger.

The analyst believes that if the authorities continue with their current policy, by the time Bidzina Ivanishvili’s political influence comes to an end, support for Georgia joining the EU and NATO could be significantly weakened, leaving the political space open to groups advocating neutrality.

Turning away from Brussels and the threat to Georgia’s role as a transit hub

Another key focus of Zakareishvili’s criticism is Georgia’s absence from a ministerial meeting in Brussels dedicated to security and connectivity.

The meeting brought together representatives of the European Union, Central Asian countries, Armenia and Azerbaijan. Zakareishvili sees Georgia’s absence not simply as a diplomatic mistake, but as a significant loss for the country’s long-term economic and geopolitical interests.

He says the connectivity ministerial was not about EU enlargement. Its main focus was the development of transport, energy and economic links across the region – an area in which Georgia could play an important role because of its geographical position.

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, and the country’s position has deteriorated further compared with the previous year. The Commission says the Georgian authorities took no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine recommendations set out as conditions for advancing the country’s EU accession process.

Zakareishvili stresses that international transport and trade routes are constantly changing. A country that does not take part in the relevant negotiations may eventually lose the opportunity to benefit even from its own geographical advantages.

“If Georgia does not take part, someone else will take its place and share the spoils! If you do not show up to a party, the party will go on without you – and someone else will eat the slice of cake that was meant for you,” he says.

In the analyst’s view, Georgia should pay particular attention to the development of a new transport corridor through Armenia, including the so-called “Trump Route”, which could significantly reshape the transport geography of the South Caucasus.

Zakareishvili fears that if Georgia does not actively participate in regional connectivity projects, a significant share of international freight could bypass the country. Georgia would then lose the economic and political advantages built up over decades through its Black Sea ports, railway, pipelines and East-West transit corridor.

The analyst draws a historical parallel with the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline. He says that, as a result of political decisions made at the time, these projects were routed through Georgia rather than Armenia. But the situation could now change: new transport routes in the region could allow Armenia to become a transit country at Georgia’s expense.

Zakareishvili believes Turkey will play a particularly important role in this process. The development of new routes and the redistribution of transport flows could increase the importance of Turkish ports and Mediterranean routes, affecting the competitiveness of Georgia’s Black Sea ports.

“As long as Georgia has pipelines and ports, and still has a chance to take part somewhere, to get a foot in the door and claim a share – if not a piece of the cake, then at least a seat at the table – it should do so. Otherwise, these processes will move forward without Georgia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his view, the authorities’ refusal to attend international meetings, justified on the grounds of protecting the country’s dignity and sovereignty, could in reality damage Georgia’s economic interests.

“EU candidate status is becoming little more than a formality”

Zakareishvili identifies the Georgian authorities’ decision to suspend political dialogue with the European Union as one of the main reasons for the country’s growing distance from Brussels.

In November 2024, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028. The announcement came after the EU had effectively suspended Georgia’s accession process and stepped up its criticism of the government’s policies.

Zakareishvili believes that instead of meeting the conditions set by the European Union, the Georgian authorities chose political confrontation. He says candidate status alone does not mean progress towards membership: the country must fulfil specific commitments.

The analyst points to Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro as examples of countries that continue to implement reforms as part of their efforts to move closer to the EU.

“The European Union did not write an application saying, ‘I want Georgia to join.’ It was Georgia that said it wanted to join the European Union. It is all very well to want to join the EU, but you need to look at its standards, its economy and its relations. The EU’s conditions include judicial reform, de-oligarchisation and many other things that the ruling Georgian Dream party does not like,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the EU’s declining political attention to Georgia is not limited to deteriorating diplomatic relations. The country could also gradually be left out of regional developments in which its geographical position and transit potential once gave it a significant advantage.

The analyst warns that Georgia’s international role is not determined by geography alone. A country may lie on a transit corridor on the map, but to gain real economic and political benefits, it must take part in the processes shaping the region’s future transport, energy and security architecture. Otherwise, Georgia risks finding itself surrounded by new political and economic partnerships while remaining on the sidelines.

Paata Zakareishvili on Georgia-Russia relations

World.title: Part of Crimean Bridge collapses into sea: what damage to one of Kremlin’s key propaganda symbols means
World.content:
On 17 November 2026, the Crimean Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, was severely damaged in another Ukrainian attack. Video footage and photographs circulating online appear to show a large metal arch and a section of the road deck collapsing into the sea. Both road and rail traffic across the bridge have been suspended.

The attack is particularly significant because the Crimean Bridge is a vital land corridor linking the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014, with Russian territory. Moscow has also used the bridge to supply its military forces.

For years, the Crimean Bridge was regarded as one of Vladimir Putin’s largest infrastructure projects and a symbol of Russian control over Crimea. Its damage creates several problems at once: it complicates Russian military logistics, increases the cost of supplying Crimea and shows how difficult it is for Moscow to secure one of its most heavily protected strategic assets.

It is important to note that the collapse on 17 November was preceded by an attack on 16 November, which also reportedly damaged the bridge’s structure. This means the bridge has been hit in a series of successive strikes rather than in a single isolated incident.

According to Anton Herashchenko, an adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, the attack involved a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Russian authorities confirmed the attack and the suspension of traffic across the bridge, but have yet to issue an official statement about its collapse.

The Russian outlet Agentstvo reports that federal television channels did not mention the attack on the Crimean Bridge in their morning news bulletins. Instead, they covered strikes on several bridges in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

The collapsed Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

What does the collapse of the bridge arch mean from an engineering perspective?

To understand the scale of the damage to the Kerch Bridge, it is important to know how it is constructed.

The bridge is approximately 19 kilometres long and consists of two independent parallel structures: one carries road traffic and the other railway traffic.

Both structures rest on concrete supports. However, the navigable section of the Kerch Strait features large metal arch structures that support the corresponding spans and provide sufficient clearance for ships to pass underneath.

According to reports published on 17 November, a roughly 227-metre-long arch of the road bridge collapsed into the sea, along with the section of road deck connected to it. The adjacent railway arch was also damaged but has not collapsed.

Why does this matter?

The arch is not a decorative feature of the bridge but a key load-bearing element. Its damage means that the load in the affected section can no longer be safely distributed.

This creates several technical problems:

Damage to the load-bearing structure: After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles.

After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles. Risk of damage to adjacent elements: The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans.

The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans. Safety of the railway infrastructure: The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure.

The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure. Possible disruption to shipping: Debris from the collapsed structure could also obstruct the shipping channel used by vessels.

It is important to stress that the collapse of the arch does not mean the entire 19-kilometre bridge has been destroyed. However, one of its most important sections has been damaged. Restoring traffic will require a detailed structural assessment, the removal of debris and the necessary engineering and repair work.

Rebuilding such a large load-bearing element is a far more complex, time-consuming and costly process.

What does the collapse of the Kerch Bridge mean symbolically?

For Russia, the bridge is one of the most visible political symbols of the annexation of Crimea.

When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of Moscow’s main challenges was establishing a land link between the peninsula and Russian territory, as the Kerch Strait separates Crimea from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. By building the bridge, the Kremlin overcame this geographical barrier.

Vladimir Putin personally championed the project. In May 2018, he drove a lorry across the bridge and officially opened its road section. The event was broadcast on Russian state television and became an important part of the Kremlin’s propaganda narrative.

For Moscow, the bridge carried several key messages:

Consolidation of the annexation of Crimea: The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory.

The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory. Putin’s political project: Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities.

Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities. Demonstration of Russian control: The bridge signalled that Moscow intended to maintain a long-term presence in Crimea and had no plans to return the peninsula to Ukraine.

Russia decided to build the bridge in 2014, following its annexation of Crimea. Construction began in 2016. The road section opened on 15 May 2018, while rail traffic began in December 2019.

The bridge is considered one of the longest in Europe. Its construction cost around 228 billion roubles (approximately $3.5–3.8 billion at the exchange rate at the time).

The project involved extensive engineering work. The structure includes supports on both land and underwater, while specially designed high arches allow ships to pass through the navigable section of the strait.

After the first explosion in 2022, the damage to the bridge was seen in Ukraine as an important moral and symbolic victory. At the time, Al Jazeera reported that the attack had heightened the perception of Russia’s vulnerability.

Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

How many times has Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge before?

Before the attack on 17 November 2026, Ukraine had carried out three major successful operations against the Kerch Bridge. Ukrainian officials subsequently confirmed or acknowledged responsibility for them.

The strike on 16 November 2026, which directly preceded the attack on 17 November, should also be treated as a separate incident.

8 October 2022: First major explosion

A lorry travelling across the bridge exploded, damaging several road spans and causing some of them to collapse. The blast also set fuel tankers on a passing railway train on fire. Four people were killed.

Ukraine subsequently acknowledged its involvement in the attack. Repairs to the damaged sections took several months.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge on 8 October 2022

17 July 2023: Sea drone attack

Ukraine attacked the bridge using Sea Baby naval drones. The road section sustained damage, and one of its spans collapsed. Two civilians were killed in the attack, and their child was injured.

Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out the operation.

Sea drone attack on the Kerch Bridge in 2023

3 June 2025: Underwater explosion

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detonated explosive devices near the bridge’s underwater supports. According to the Ukrainian side, the blast had an estimated force of 1,100 kilograms of TNT.

The SBU said the operation had been in preparation for several months and that the bridge’s supports had sustained significant damage. The agency claimed that the structure had been left in a critical condition.

Underwater explosion on the Kerch Bridge in 2025

16 November 2026: Another strike

The Ukrainian drone attack damaged the bridge’s structure. Russian authorities initially described the damage as minor, but traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended and later partially restored.

16 November 2026: Another strike on the Kerch Bridge

What did Russia use the Kerch Bridge for?

For Russia, the bridge was not just a transport link for Crimea’s population. It was also one of the key logistical routes used in its war against Ukraine.

Military role

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the bridge acquired particular strategic importance. It allowed Russia to transport military supplies from its territory to Crimea and then onwards to the occupied regions of southern Ukraine.

These supplies included:

military equipment and armoured vehicles;

ammunition and weapons;

fuel and other military supplies;

military personnel and logistical resources.

The bridge allowed Russian forces to move military supplies relatively quickly from Russian territory to Crimea and then distribute them towards the front line in southern Ukraine.

In March 2024, Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), said Russia had significantly reduced its use of the bridge to transport military equipment following Ukrainian strikes.

According to Maliuk, 42–46 trains carrying weapons and ammunition crossed the bridge every day before the attacks. After the strikes, that number fell to four or five.

Civilian and economic role

The bridge is also an important transport route for Crimea’s residents and tourists.

It was used to deliver:

food;

fuel;

consumer goods;

construction materials;

various industrial products.

The bridge also carried passenger trains and cars travelling between Russia and Crimea.

A prolonged disruption would therefore affect not only military supplies but also everyday economic life in Crimea, the cost of delivering goods and the tourism industry.

The collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge

What alternatives does Russia have?

Disabling the Kerch Bridge does not mean that Russia will lose the ability to supply Crimea altogether.

Moscow can use the land corridor through the occupied parts of southern Ukraine. It links Russia’s Rostov region with the occupied territories of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and Crimea.

However, this route has several drawbacks. It is significantly longer, runs close to active combat zones and is itself vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes.

Russia could also use the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, but it would not be able to fully replace the bridge’s capacity.

Disabling the Kerch Bridge therefore represents a serious logistical blow to Russia, even if Moscow continues to supply Crimea via alternative routes.

Why is this attack significant?

From a military perspective, Russia is losing – at least temporarily – one of its most important transport corridors, which it used to supply its forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine.

From an economic perspective, a prolonged closure of the bridge will increase the cost of supplying Crimea and put additional pressure on alternative transport routes.

From a political perspective, it is another blow to Putin’s project, which has become a symbol of Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

It is also particularly significant that the bridge was considered one of Russia’s most heavily protected strategic assets. It was guarded by air defence systems, maritime barriers and other security measures. Yet Ukraine has managed to strike it repeatedly.

However, the ultimate strategic impact will depend on how long the bridge remains out of service, how severe the damage is to its supports and the adjacent railway structure, and how quickly Russia can increase the capacity of alternative routes.

One thing is clear: the Kerch Bridge is one of the most important symbols Putin has created since the annexation of Crimea. Its repeated damage sends Moscow a clear message: in its war against Ukraine, no infrastructure asset is safe or beyond reach.

World.title: EU foreign policy chief: ‘Syria must withdraw recognition of occupied territories in Georgia and Ukraine’
World.content:
EU foreign ministers have called for closer relations with Syria. However, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that any association agreement with Syria should include a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine, alongside commitments to protect human rights.

Kallas made the remarks at a press conference following a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

According to Kallas, EU member states agreed that maintaining relations with Syria was important. Without EU engagement, other actors would fill the existing political and diplomatic vacuum in the country.

Kallas said the EU was considering signing an association agreement, negotiations on which began in 2008. The agreement would provide a common framework for cooperation between the two sides. At the same time, the EU would begin work on a new mandate to modernise the agreement.

“The question now was the status of the agreement. Negotiations on it took place in 2008, quite a long time ago. So the question arose as to whether we should make changes to it.

“The EU works in such a way that decision-making takes time. That is why the compromise would be to sign the 2008 association agreement. This would give us a framework within which we could work on all the issues that matter to both sides. At the same time, together with the Council, we will begin work on developing a new mandate for a modernised agreement,” Kallas said.

Kaja Kallas

Kallas said EU foreign ministers had called for several key issues to be addressed in the agreement. These include clear conditions on human rights protection and a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine.

She explained that the issue concerned the territories whose independence was recognised by Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

“We are now working in technical groups on the details, both technical and legal, but we are making progress,” the EU foreign policy chief said.

At the press conference, Kallas also commented on the architecture of European security. She said that Russia had been a party to several international agreements that laid the foundations for European security. However, the main problem was not the existence of these documents, but Moscow’s failure to honour its commitments.

In this context, Kallas cited the Helsinki Final Act, the Paris Agreement and the Budapest Memorandum.

“The problem is not with the agreements themselves, nor with Ukraine’s position on this issue. The problem is that Russia violates these agreements and fails to comply with their terms. So the main question is: how can we restore the European security architecture?” Kaja Kallas said.

Background

On 29 May 2018, the regime of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad recognised the independence of Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). Tbilisi responded by severing diplomatic relations with Damascus. The EU condemned the decision on the same day, saying it violated international law and the principles of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Assad’s decision followed Russia’s military intervention in the Syrian civil war. Moscow was one of the main supporters of Assad’s government, and Damascus’s move was seen as serving the Kremlin’s interests.

In June 2022, Syria also recognised the independence of Ukraine’s occupied territories of Donetsk and Luhansk. Ukraine responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Assad’s regime fell in December 2024, and a new government took power in Syria. Against this backdrop, Tbilisi called on Damascus to withdraw its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

Ukraine restored diplomatic relations with Syria in September 2025. The association agreement now under consideration by the EU could therefore mark a new stage in relations with Syria. However, the territorial integrity of Georgia and Ukraine remains one of the key conditions in this process.

World.title: Old links on Aliyev’s X account redirected users to opposition videos: cyberattack or global vulnerability?
World.content:
Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

On 15 November, links in some old posts on President Ilham Aliyev’s account on X redirected users to videos featuring opposition politicians and bloggers, as well as footage of protests. Most of the posts dated from 2010–2011. The links led to videos featuring Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, and bloggers Mehman Huseynov and Gabil Mammadov.

The posts themselves remained unchanged, but the links they contained began directing users to different pages. The altered links remained accessible for several hours, and users shared the posts across social media.

That evening, the Azerbaijani president’s press service issued a statement:

“Cyberattacks are currently targeting the social media accounts of Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Relevant agencies are taking the necessary measures to prevent these attacks and investigate the incident.”

The statement did not specify which platforms had come under attack, how the attacks were carried out or who was behind them.

Similar incidents affected the accounts of several prominent politicians, government agencies and companies around the world on the same day. This raises the question:

Were the president’s accounts actually hacked, or was the incident the result of a global vulnerability that affected numerous accounts, including those of Donald Trump and McDonald’s?

Trump, Gates and Burger King among those affected by similar incidents

According to a CNN investigation published on 15 November, links in old posts by politicians, government agencies and companies on X began redirecting users to unrelated videos, images and websites over the weekend.

The largest number of such cases involved the personal account of US President Donald Trump. Links in at least 12 of his posts began directing users to other websites. Similar changes affected posts by Bill Gates dating from 2010 and former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau from 2011.

A link in a 2011 Burger King post listing the locations of its restaurants redirected users to a page listing Nazi concentration camps. A link in one of McDonald’s posts led to a page about the 11 September attacks. Similar cases also affected posts by the FBI, the US Department of Defence and former Vice-President Mike Pence.

All the links had been shortened using Bitly, a service that turns long web addresses into shorter ones. The service was widely used on Twitter, now known as X, between 2009 and 2014. According to CNN, Bitly links do not expire, and users with paid subscriptions can change the addresses to which they redirect.

Bitly said it had identified “an issue that allowed malicious actors to reuse some old, inactive links”. The company said it had suspended the accounts used to change the links and deactivated the links themselves. However, Bitly did not say who was behind the activity.

No password required

An attack of this kind does not require access to an account password. The original post remains unchanged; only the destination address of the shortened link changes. As a result, someone clicking a link in a post published by the president 15 years ago ends up on a completely different page.

IT expert Osman Gunduz also believes that the problem stems not from hacked accounts but from a security vulnerability in Bitly’s system. He recommended that government agencies and other organisations check their old links, deactivate potentially dangerous ones and use their own domains wherever possible.

Ari Lightman, a professor of digital media at Carnegie Mellon University, told CNN that many old accounts remain inadequately monitored. He described the situation as “problematic”.

Government agencies have not yet confirmed that the incident involving the president’s account was linked to a Bitly vulnerability. The president’s press service has issued no further statements on the matter.

Who appears in the videos?

The videos feature some of the most vocal critics of the Azerbaijani authorities.

Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, has been under arrest since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of actions aimed at violently seizing power. Karimli rejects the charges, calling them fabricated and politically motivated. The investigation ended in October. If convicted, he faces a prison sentence of 12 years to life. On 12 November, he received the Magnitsky Human Rights Award in London.

Blogger Mehman Huseynov was sentenced to two years in prison in 2017 on defamation charges. He was released in March 2019. Following the incident, Huseynov sarcastically “thanked” the president on Facebook for sharing a video featuring him: “Thank you, Mr President!”

Blogger Gabil Mammadov, who lives abroad, has been convicted in absentia in Azerbaijan. The Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

What does “cyberattack” mean?

In the past two months, the Azerbaijani authorities have reported cyberattacks for the second time. On 13 October, more than 100 government websites came under attack. At the time, the State Service for Special Communication and Information Security said when the attack began, which systems it targeted and that its impact had been limited. The agency blamed an unnamed “foreign hacker group”. However, the pro-Iranian group 313 Team, which is believed to operate in Iraq, claimed responsibility. Its members said they had acted in protest against the ban on wearing hijabs in schools.

The statement about the attack on the president’s accounts, however, provided no similar details.

Previous cyberattacks on social media accounts in Azerbaijan have mainly targeted independent media outlets. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, an international press freedom organisation, almost all Azerbaijani-language posts disappeared from Meydan TV’s Facebook page in June 2020. In August this year, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets operating in exile issued a joint statement. They said a series of coordinated copyright infringement complaints had led to the suspension of several of their Facebook and Instagram accounts.

This time, the incident affected the president’s own account. It remains unclear who changed the links and why they chose opposition videos as the new destinations. Bitly has not disclosed who owned the accounts it suspended.

Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. On November 18, an Azerbaijani parliamentary delegation led by Sahiba Gafarova, Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament, paid a working visit to Turkmenistan to participate in a Council meeting and the 61st plenary session of the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly, the Press and Public Relations Department of the Azerbaijani Parliament reported.

The Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament was met at Turkmenbashi International Airport by Bayramgozel Myradova, Chair of the Committee on Science, Education, Culture, and Youth Policy of the Mejlis of Turkmenistan; Dmitriy Kobitskiy, Secretary General of the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly; Gismat Gozalov, Azerbaijan’s Ambassador to Turkmenistan; Aydin Jafarov, Plenipotentiary Representative of the Azerbaijani Parliament to the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly; and other officials.

World.title: Azerbaijan and Vietnam: Two economic transformations, one bridge between regions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Although thousands of kilometers separate Azerbaijan and Vietnam geographically, historical ties, economic transformations, and aligned strategic interests bring the two countries closer together. In the past, Azerbaijani specialists helped rebuild Vietnam’s industry and develop its oil sector, while Vietnamese students traveled to Baku to pursue their education. Today, decades later, this cooperation extends far beyond traditional humanitarian and energy-related links: Baku and Hanoi are exploring opportunities for joint investments, industrial development, renewable energy, transport logistics, and new technological projects.

The economic history of both states adds a special dimension to this process. Azerbaijan and Vietnam have followed different, yet in many ways comparable, paths of transformation. Both countries leveraged their available economic resources, implemented consistent state programs, and opened up to external markets to accelerate development, strengthen their industrial capacity, and enhance their roles in the global economy.

These processes now lay the foundation for a new phase in bilateral relations. The focus has shifted beyond the mere trade of Azerbaijani oil toward the creation of complementary economic ties. In this framework, Azerbaijan could serve as a gateway for Vietnamese businesses to access markets in the Caucasus, Central Asia, and Europe, while Vietnam could become a key partner for Azerbaijan in the dynamically developing region of Southeast Asia.

From historical friendship to strategic partnership: bridge whose construction began decades ago

The history of Azerbaijani-Vietnamese relations predates the establishment of formal diplomatic ties between the two independent states. Its foundation was laid during the Soviet era, thanks to the engagement between the National Leader of the Azerbaijani people, Heydar Aliyev, and President Ho Chi Minh.

In 1959, Ho Chi Minh visited the Azerbaijan SSR. During the visit, discussions were held on how to assist Vietnam in developing its oil industry, training specialists, and rebuilding the country. Subsequently, thousands of Azerbaijani engineers, oil workers, and other professionals took part in the development of Vietnam’s infrastructure and industry.

A significant milestone in the history of bilateral relations occurred in 1983, when Heydar Aliyev, then serving as First Deputy Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR, led a Soviet delegation to Vietnam. This visit held both diplomatic and practical economic importance.

This historical engagement also left a notable mark on the educational sphere; during the Soviet era, approximately 5,000 Vietnamese citizens received their education in Azerbaijan.

The ties between the two peoples also found a geographical expression: in the early 1980s, Baku and the Vietnamese oil-industry city of Vung Tau established a sister-city relationship. A Baku Street was created in Vung Tau, while a Vung Tau Street can be found in the Ahmadli settlement of Baku.

Following the restoration of Azerbaijan’s independence, the relationship was given a new diplomatic framework. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were established on September 23, 1992. A key development was the state visit of the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, to Vietnam in 2014, which helped to invigorate political contacts and expand bilateral cooperation. The next significant milestone was the state visit of the General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam, To Lam, to Azerbaijan on May 7–8, 2025. Following talks with President Ilham Aliyev, the two sides adopted a Joint Declaration on the Establishment of a Strategic Partnership.

Thus, a relationship whose foundations were laid more than half a century ago has attained a qualitatively new political status.

Two economic success stories: different models, shared logic of transformation

The growing rapprochement between Azerbaijan and Vietnam is compelling not only from the perspectives of diplomacy and geography. It offers an opportunity to compare two economic narratives in which state policy, the leveraging of national advantages, and integration into the international economy have played pivotal roles.

At first glance, the economic trajectories of Azerbaijan and Vietnam appear markedly different. One possesses vast hydrocarbon reserves, which it utilized to attract international capital and develop export infrastructure. The other achieved rapid industrialization through reforms, the export of manufactured goods, and integration into global production chains.

Yet, upon closer inspection, a common logic emerges.

Both countries viewed economic development as a long-term state objective. Both sought to harness international cooperation to secure technology, capital, and professional expertise. Both placed a strong emphasis on infrastructure, human capital development, and the expansion of foreign economic relations.

Energy cooperation remains one of the most well-developed areas of the Azerbaijan-Vietnam relationship. However, its nature is gradually evolving: while the partnership was initially centered on crude oil supplies and the exchange of professional expertise, the two sides are now exploring opportunities to expand cooperation into oil refining, petrochemicals, field exploration, oilfield services, liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, and renewable energy.

Azerbaijan has already established a foothold in Vietnam’s energy supply system. Since 2023, more than 1.1 million tons of Azerbaijani crude oil have been delivered to the country.

The history of cooperation in this sector spans over a decade. A notable example is a contract between SOCAR Trading and the Vietnamese company Binh Son Refining and Petrochemical (BSR) for the supply of five million barrels of Azerbaijani "Azeri Light" crude oil to the Dung Quat oil refinery.

A new phase of energy cooperation gained further momentum in May 2025, when SOCAR and PetroVietnam signed a memorandum of understanding. During the same period, a cooperation agreement was also formalized between SOCAR Trading Singapore and Binh Son Refining and Petrochemical.

In discussions held in October 2026, the parties explored the further expansion of cooperation in the exploration and development of oil and gas fields, oil refining, petrochemicals, and oilfield services. Prospects for the supply of liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Vietnam were also discussed.

For Azerbaijan, this opens up opportunities not only to maintain its existing export position but also to expand its presence in one of Asia’s most dynamic energy markets. For Vietnam, cooperation with SOCAR offers an opportunity to diversify its sources of raw material supplies and expand its partnerships with international energy companies.

Moreover, the prospects for cooperation aren't limited to traditional hydrocarbons. One of the most promising areas is the development of renewable energy sources. During To Lam’s state visit to Baku in 2025, President Ilham Aliyev invited Vietnamese companies to invest in renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan and expressed the Azerbaijani side’s readiness to consider investments in similar projects in Vietnam.

A practical follow-up to these agreements was a memorandum signed between the Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan and the Vietnamese firm ROX Group on September 25, 2026, during the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum.

The document outlines the exploration of two potential projects: a 600 MW wind power plant in Azerbaijan and a 200 MW solar power plant in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. As part of this collaboration, the parties intend to conduct feasibility studies, assess grid connection capabilities, and examine prospects for exporting the electricity generated.

ROX Group is also exploring investment opportunities in Azerbaijan’s renewable energy and real estate sectors. Thus, the interest of the Vietnamese business community is gradually extending into new sectors of the economy.

Industry and technology: opportunities beyond raw material trade

Another significant area is industrial cooperation. Of particular interest is potential collaboration with the Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup and its subsidiary, GSM (Green Smart Mobility), which focuses on the development of eco-friendly transport solutions. During discussions between the Azerbaijani delegation and representatives of Vingroup, the parties explored the possibility of assembling electric vehicles in Azerbaijan, as well as potential cooperation in the real estate sector.

A significant institutional milestone was reached in May 2025 with the signing of a memorandum on cooperation in technology, innovation, and development between the relevant ministries of the two countries.

Cooperation in the defense industry also warrants special attention. During To Lam’s visit to Baku in 2025, a document on collaboration between the two countries' defense agencies was signed.

Looking ahead, industrial cooperation could encompass equipment manufacturing, technical maintenance, engineering services, digitalization, and professional training. However, specific projects in these areas will require further development.

Transport and logistics: Azerbaijan as a link between Vietnam and European markets

While the energy sector has historically served as the foundation for economic ties, transport and logistics could become a key driver for their further expansion.

Vietnam is a major export-oriented manufacturing hub in Southeast Asia. A significant portion of its output is destined for international markets, primarily in the US, Europe, and other parts of Asia. Situated at the crossroads of the East-West and North-South transport corridors, Azerbaijan is well-positioned to offer Vietnamese exporters alternative logistical routes. In this context, the Middle Corridor, which connects China and Central Asia to Europe via the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye, is of particular significance. For Vietnam, utilizing this route could be advantageous for diversifying the paths used to transport goods to Europe.

Notably, this cooperation is already yielding practical results. According to the Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan, transit shipments involving Vietnam and passing through Azerbaijani territory increased by more than 200% in 2025. From January through September 2026, this growth reached approximately 600%.

Aviation is another equally vital component of transport connectivity. In November 2026, AZAL (Azerbaijan Airlines) held discussions with representatives from the Vietnamese airline Vietjet Air, as well as the Sovico Group and Vingroup. The talks focused on the prospects for establishing direct air links between Azerbaijan and Vietnam, the potential for Vietjet Air to operate flights to Baku and other regional airports in Azerbaijan, and opportunities for collaboration with AZAL.

The launch of direct flights could provide fresh momentum not only to tourism, but also to business ties, investment negotiations, educational cooperation, and corporate partnerships.

Trade and investment: goal of diversifying mutual exchange

Despite historically strong relations and the significant potential of both economies, the current level of trade between Azerbaijan and Vietnam does not yet fully reflect the true scope of their bilateral partnership.

A defining feature of the existing trade model is the substantial role played by Azerbaijani oil. As President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev stated while delivering a press statement alongside General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam, To Lam, there is a need to balance trade turnover between the two countries.

"Unfortunately, the dynamics of trade in the economic and trade sectors depend on Azerbaijan's oil sales to Vietnam. When oil sales are high, trade increases, and when they drop, it decreases too. Of course, we would like to see our trade become more balanced, and to achieve this, information exchange is necessary, of course. What projects are implemented in our countries, what investment opportunities there are, what rules, legislative framework, and tax administration there are – all these issues should be clear to business circles. If this is the case, I am sure that trade will not depend on the oil factor alone," the head of state remarked.

Therefore, a key priority is to expand the mutual supply of non-oil sector goods. Vietnam holds potential for Azerbaijani producers in areas such as agricultural products, textiles, processed goods, and industrial items. Azerbaijan, for its part, can offer the Vietnamese market energy resources, petrochemical products, agricultural goods, and logistics services.

A significant milestone was reached on July 16, 2025, with the inaugural meeting of the Joint Azerbaijan-Vietnam Business Council and a business forum held in Hanoi. The event brought together representatives from government bodies, investment agencies, and leading companies from both countries. During the forum, cooperation agreements were signed between the Azerbaijan Export and Investment Promotion Agency (AZPROMO) and the Vietnam National Association of Enterprises (VINEN), as well as between companies from both countries in sectors including cotton products, agriculture, and other areas.

The third meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission on Economic, Trade, and Scientific-Technical Cooperation took place in Hanoi on July 17, 2025. The parties reviewed 58 initiatives across 17 priority areas for the 2025–2027 period.

Thus, the next phase of cooperation should focus on increasing the participation of the private sector, raising awareness among companies regarding market opportunities in both countries, and establishing conditions for long-term investment.

Political dimension: shared approaches to international relations and mutual support

The economic component of the Azerbaijan-Vietnam partnership is developing against the backdrop of a traditionally friendly political dialogue. Despite their geographical distance, the two countries share many common approaches to issues concerning international law, state sovereignty, territorial integrity, and multilateral cooperation.

The establishment of a strategic partnership in May 2025 served as a significant affirmation of both sides' political will to further deepen their relationship.

The Joint Declaration places particular emphasis on strengthening engagement within the framework of the United Nations, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA). Furthermore, the parties expressed their readiness to foster cooperation between Azerbaijan and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as well as its member states.

The interaction between the two countries within international organizations is of significant importance.

During the 44-day Patriotic War, Vietnam, as a member of the Non-Aligned Movement, supported the inclusion of references to the 1993 UN Security Council resolutions regarding the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict in a draft statement by the UN Security Council President. Azerbaijan views this move as a significant demonstration of support for its position.

Thus, political engagement creates a favorable foundation for economic cooperation, as the relationship is built not only on commercial interests but also on mutual trust and aligned approaches to a range of international issues.

A key feature of the economic and political relations between Azerbaijan and Vietnam is that they are underpinned by more than half a century of human-to-human contact.

Assistance provided by Azerbaijan to Vietnam in the wake of natural disasters holds a special place in their humanitarian cooperation.

In September 2024, through its International Development Agency (AIDA), Azerbaijan allocated $200,000 in humanitarian aid to address the aftermath of Typhoon Yagi. From September through October 2025, an additional $100,000 in aid was provided to Vietnam to help address the consequences of flooding.

Another symbol of this cooperation was the opening, on March 18, 2026, of a new building for the Tran Phu School in the Luc Yen district of Lao Cai province. The educational facility, designed to accommodate 1,400 students, was constructed with support from Azerbaijan as part of the recovery efforts following Typhoon Yagi.

Ultimately, the engagement between Azerbaijan and Vietnam could serve as an example of how two countries, situated in different parts of the continent and operating under distinct economic models, can combine their respective strengths to create new opportunities.

The bridge between the Caucasus and Southeast Asia, the foundations of which were laid as far back as the last century, is now taking on new substance. It has evolved beyond a historical bridge of friendship into a prospect for a long-term economic partnership, one capable of linking the industrial capacities of Asia, the energy potential of the Caspian region, and the markets of Europe.

World.title: Azerbaijan, US discuss strategic partnership charter, TRIPP project (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov met with Aryeh Lightstone, Senior Advisor to the US Special Representative for Peace Missions, to discuss the Charter on Strategic Partnership between the two countries and the TRIPP project, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported.

During the meeting, the parties exchanged views on Azerbaijani-American bilateral relations and regional issues, including prospects for specific cooperation projects under the Charter on Strategic Partnership.

They also discussed the development of regional ties, the Middle Corridor, and transportation and logistics capabilities. In this context, they highlighted the contribution of the TRIPP project to strengthening regional transportation and economic ties, as well as ensuring unimpeded connectivity between the main part of Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan.

The meeting also addressed the normalization process between Azerbaijan and Armenia and other areas of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan and Georgia discuss military and naval cooperation (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. The official visit of the Chief of Defense Forces of Georgia, Lieutenant General Giorgi Matiashvili, and his accompanying delegation to Azerbaijan is underway, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense reported.

Pursuant to the visit itinerary, the First Deputy Minister of Defense – Chief of the General Staff of the Azerbaijan Army, Colonel General Karim Valiyev, together with the Georgian delegation, visited a Navy unit. Commander of the Azerbaijan Navy, Rear Admiral Shahin Mammadov, briefed the delegation on the operational activities of the Naval Forces and the ongoing structural reforms. Subsequently, the delegation viewed an exhibition of military-technical equipment currently in service of the Naval Forces and observed a tactical demonstration conducted by naval special forces.

The visit involved discussions on expanding bilateral naval cooperation and advancing ties in the field of mutual experience exchange.

Additionally, the guests toured the Jamshid Nakhchivanski Military Lyceum under the National Defense University.

At the lyceum, the delegation received a comprehensive briefing on the educational system and the organization of the academic process at both NDU and the Military Lyceum, followed by a Q&A session addressing matters of common interest.

While touring the institution, the guests visited the Heydar Aliyev Museum. It was specifically emphasized that military lyceums play an exceptional role in training professional personnel for the Azerbaijan Army, and that the establishment of this premier military educational institution was made possible by the far-sighted policy of National Leader Heydar Aliyev.

Following the visit, Lieutenant General Giorgi Matiashvili signed the Book of Honour and expressed his sincere gratitude for the warm hospitality extended to the delegation.

World.title: Azerbaijan Audit Chamber warns of pension fund financial risks
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. The incomplete reconciliation of the State Social Protection Fund’s (SSPF) calculations regarding government obligations, as well as discrepancies in the determination of expenditures to be financed from the state budget, poses risks to the fund’s financial stability.

This was stated in the Audit Chamber’s report on the draft budget of the State Social Protection Fund under the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection for 2027.

The report notes that inconsistencies in the amount of government obligations have created conditions for the fund to include additional categories in these obligations—categories that were absent in previous years—and, as a result, to unilaterally increase the total amount of obligations.

Furthermore, it is reported that the inclusion in the financial statements of debt amounts not recognized by the state, as well as the omission of accounts payable related to payments made from contributions to mandatory state social insurance, complicates the determination of the limits of financial coverage for expenditures in future years.

According to the Audit Chamber’s report, a letter sent in 2025 by the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection to the Ministry of Finance noted that between 2018 and 2025, a total of 10.437 billion manat ($6.14 billion) was transferred to the State Social Protection Fund to finance state budget obligations for the purpose of balancing the budget.

At the same time, the fund noted that the amount of obligations accrued during this period but not covered by the state budget totaled 9.848 billion manat ($5.79 billion).

The report also drew attention to factors influencing the growth of government obligations.

In addition, it was noted that following the amendments made to the Law “On Labor Pensions” effective January 1, 2023, supplements to labor pensions for civil service tenure are also indexed annually on January 1 in accordance with the growth rate of the nominal average monthly wage for the previous year.

“This, in turn, led to an increase in expenditures on government obligations as part of pension expenditures in 2023–2025,” the report states.

The Audit Chamber also noted that, unlike in previous years, the fund took into account the cases provided for in Articles 8 and 9.2 of the Law “On Labor Pensions” when determining government obligations.

These refer to benefits related to a reduction in the length of the insurance period. According to the data presented, the calculation of the amount in this category is based on the principle of contributions to mandatory state social insurance that were not paid into the fund.

According to the Audit Chamber’s assessment, the total amount of the government’s liability, based on the fund’s own calculations, amounted to 3.412 billion manat ($2.01 billion) in 2025. The bulk of this amount was attributable to liabilities related to service periods before 1992.

In addition, the report notes that the funds allocated from the state budget in 2025 amounted to only 46.9% of this commitment.

As for the funding of the areas identified as obligations, it was noted that the allocated funds were primarily directed toward financing allowances. Thus, the total amount for allowances and benefits amounted to 92.3% of the funds allocated from the state budget.

The Audit Chamber believes that the complete lack of alignment between the amounts of government obligations could create conditions for financing payments not based on the insurance principle, including through contributions to mandatory state social insurance.

“This circumstance is ultimately assessed as a risk factor for the fund’s financial stability,” the report emphasizes.

World.title: Fossil teeth discovery supports multiple human species lived in rainforests
World.content:
Troves of fossilised teeth collected by ancient Chinese porcupines in two caves show that Homo sapiens were not the only human species to adapt to rainforests.

Trace chemical elements in the teeth of Homo erectus and a bevy of forest animals have helped scientists fill in gaps about when the ancient hominin lived in the region and how it survived.

Two studies in the journal Nature — from Australian, Chinese and European researchers — identified Homo erectus teeth dated between 324,000 and 184,000 years old in southern China and reconstructed the ancient ecosystems this species called home.

The discovery means Homo erectus lived in mainland Asia longer than thought, and challenges assumptions that they did not have the skills to live in rainforests.

Homo erectus teeth from Baxian Cave. (Supplied: Yingqi Zhang/IVPP-CAS)

Homo erectus were an ancient ancestor of modern humans that lived from 2 million to 108,000 years ago. They migrated from the cradle of Africa out to Europe and Asia about 1.8 million years ago.

Until now, the youngest Homo erectus fossil in China was about 400,000 years old.

Kira Westaway, a geo-chronologist from Macquarie University, said it had previously been thought that Homo erectus went extinct as their preferred landscapes, grassland savannas and open woodlands, changed into rainforests.

"But this assumption has been challenged by our new Homo erectus evidence from two neighbouring caves in southern China," Professor Westaway said.

"They give evidence of Homo erectus surviving in rainforests."

The studies indicate the species may have not just survived in rainforests but also travelled great distances instead of staying in a single location.

How the teeth were found

Nine hominin teeth were found across two caves, Baxian and Naxian, about 20 kilometres north of the city of Chongzuo in China's south.

The entrance to Baxian Cave in southern China. (Supplied: Yingqi Zhang/IVPP-CAS)

Eight of the teeth were linked to Homo erectus, while the ninth tooth was from another unidentified species of ancient human.

Scientists also discovered fossils from a range of animals including elephants, bears, canines, pigs, rhinos and monkeys.

Study co-author palaeontologist Yingqi Zhang, from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the two fossil deposits contained some bone fragments but were mainly teeth.

He said the teeth, which were in sediment estimated to be 324,000 to 184,000 years old, were likely gathered by ancient porcupines.

"Porcupines have this kind of habit [where] they collect bones and gnaw them to sharpen their incisors," Professor Zhang said.

"These teeth we found in a cave are the things they [porcupines] left behind because teeth are the hardest tissue in our body."

What was in the teeth?

Several tests, including the analysis of the metal strontium, which is found in the enamel of teeth, were used to figure out what Homo erectus and the other animals ate.

Study author and geo-chronologist Renaud Joannes-Boyau, from Southern Cross University, said it appeared Homo erectus was living in a dense rainforest at the top of the food chain.

To find out how Homo erectus survived, the researchers cut into the tooth enamel to see bands of growth and figure out what the hominin ate at different stages of life and where.

And it appeared that, at an early point in life, these ancient hominins ate food about 250km away in what is now Vietnam.

"They're very flexible, they're adaptable, and they're mobile, which I think is something that we believe was only [possible] for Homo sapiens," Professor Joannes-Boyau said.

Griffith University palaeontologist Julien Louys, who was not involved in the study, said the research represented the first evidence that Homo erectus lived in rainforest environments.

"While the sample size for this conclusion is small, if substantiated it would suggest a degree of ecological flexibility unmatched in the hominin lineage until the later arrival of Denisovans and modern humans."

La Trobe University archaeologist Jesse Martin, who was not involved in the study, said it was not shocking that the species was able to survive in rainforest environments, as it lasted in Indonesia until about 100,000 years ago.

"Indeed, this study reinforces the fact that Homo erectus continued to survive in rainforest environments long after the species had gone extinct elsewhere."

What happened to Homo erectus?

There is still plenty of mystery surrounding why Homo erectus became extinct.

Professor Joannes-Boyau said the next big question to answer was how the species may have interacted with other hominins.

The researchers speculated the mystery ninth tooth could have belonged to a Denisovan (Homo longi), a type of human that appears in the fossil record from about 200,000 years ago in China, or a new species altogether.

The oldest Homo sapiens teeth in the country have been dated between 120,000 and 80,000 years old.

Yingqi Zhang excavating in Baxian Cave. (Supplied: Kira Westaway)

Professor Louys said the studies suggested the three species almost overlapped in time.

"Certainly they are found much closer in time than previously demonstrated," he said.

"Overall, it really highlights how little we know about hominin evolution in this part of the world.

" The studies raise a whole bunch more questions about the uniqueness of our own species. "

Dr Martin said Homo erectus likely encountered Denisovans, Neanderthals, and us towards the end of their global domination as a species.

As a result, he said, increased competition for resources may ultimately have driven the species extinct.

"Understanding the rise and fall of Homo erectus highlights that humanity isn't, and never has been, immune to the impacts of climate change."

World.title: Xi gives Trump personal welcome ahead of historic trilateral talks with Putin
World.content:
Xi Jinping's personal welcome to US President Donald Trump at Shenzhen airport on Wednesday for a summit made him China's first paramount leader in decades to greet a foreign counterpart on arrival.

After Air Force One touched down, Mr Trump descended to the red carpet, where the Chinese president himself was waiting to greet him.

The men shared a brief hug, before walking together to their cars beside a crowd of cheering performers waving pom-poms.

It stood out among other world leaders' arrivals in Shenzhen this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, where Mr Xi, Mr Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin will hold historic three-way talks on Thursday.

Xi Jinping is hosting historic talks with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. (AP: Iori Sagisawa)

A US official has also told Reuters Mr Trump will have a one-on-one meeting with Mr Putin while in China, although no date or time has yet been given for that.

Mr Putin, who arrived in the early hours of Wednesday, was met by Mr Xi's right-hand man Cai Qi.

But Mr Trump's personal welcome is believed to be the first by a paramount leader in China in decades — and marks an upgrade to his high-profile summit trip to Beijing in May, when Vice President Han Zheng was there to meet him.

Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, said Mr Trump was "visibly delighted by Xi's gesture".

China's President Xi Jinping's treatment of various global leaders is being closely watched as he hosts the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

"Given Beijing's overriding objective of extending the fragile calm in the US-China relationship for as long as possible, Xi will look for opportunities to extend courtesy and respect to Trump during his visit, like he did in greeting Trump on the tarmac upon arrival," Mr Hass told AFP.

"It set a positive tone for Trump's visit, marking a contrast from the swirl of news around the Jensen Huang scandal that preceded Trump's arrival in Shenzhen."

Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a low-key reception as tensions between Beijing and Tokyo remain frosty. (cnsphoto via Reuters)

Mr Huang last week resigned as chief executive of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia after admitting to an affair, reportedly with a woman some US officials suspect to be a Chinese spy.

Mr Xi's warm greeting of Mr Trump was also reciprocal.

When Mr Xi travelled to the United States in May, the US leader also met him on arrival, reportedly the first American president in decades to do so, if visits from the Pope are not included.

Albanese warns Putin in APEC meeting Anthony Albanese has called for an end to global conflicts ahead of talks between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Mr Xi told Mr Trump on the tarmac on Wednesday that during his state visit to the United States, the "presidential couple came to the airport in person and hosted a grand welcome ceremony", according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Mr Xi also noted that "China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill", the Xinhua report said.

Although several other leaders arriving in Shenzhen for the APEC summit got cheering crowds or bouquets of flowers, one arrival stood out for its relative lack of ceremony.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was greeted not by a top minister, but by military guards and a woman whom Japanese media named as the Chinese foreign ministry's ambassador of protocol.

Long-frosty ties between the countries have worsened since Ms Takaichi suggested last year that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan, the democratic island Beijing claims as its territory.

AFP

World.title: Surge in complaints, compensation claims after Telstra outage
World.content:
A woman unable to receive updates about her critically ill mother was among more than 13,000 Australians who lodged official complaints with the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) in the September quarter.

The 12-hour Telstra network outage on July 8 fuelled a 72 per cent surge in complaints that mentioned network outages, including domestic violence victim-survivors, people in ill-health and customers in financial hardship.

In total, telcos were forced to pay out $1.9 million in compensation to 2,267 complainants in the quarter, via a combination of direct compensation, bill adjustments, refunds and account credits.

Network outages are an increasingly common and expensive headache for phone and internet customers, according to the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN).

Its chief executive, Carol Bennett, said the ombudsman complaint figures were "only the tip of the iceberg" when it came to customer harm caused by outages.

"Since April 1 this year, Optus has had 110 outages, and Telstra has had 334," Ms Bennet said.

" Outages are not only inconvenient, they are a huge impost on consumers and a drain on our productivity. "

Outage cost half a billion

Modelling by FTI Consulting estimates the July 8 Testra outage cost the Australian economy $552 million and the 2023 Optus outage in the order of $2 billion.

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) Cynthia Gebert said telcos should act swiftly and fairly to address the harm caused by phone or internet outages.

Cynthia Gebert is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. (Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman)

She added that consumers always had the option to lodge a complaint with the TIO seeking compensation if they were unsatisfied with their provider's response.

"Losing service can be much more than an inconvenience," Ms Gerbert said.

" It can affect someone's ability to earn a living, manage their health, access support or contact emergency services. For a small business, losing a phone or internet service can mean losing customers, sales and income. "

Disputed charges top complaints

Overall, complaints about telcos rose 8.4 per cent on the previous quarter, with the top three complaints being disputed charges (4,151 complaints, down 7.3 per cent on the previous quarter), compensation for poor experience or inconvenience (2,032 complaints, up 58 per cent) and complaints about 'no service' (1,311, down 9 per cent).

The number of complaints to the ombudsman seeking compensation for a poor customer experience or for being inconvenienced by their telco provider has doubled over the past year.

Carol Bennett says the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

A spokesperson for Telstra said 99 per cent of consumer and small business customers who had complained directly to the telco about the July 8 outage had had their complaint "resolved and closed".

"We have processed credits of almost $1 million for consumers and businesses who contacted us or lodged a complaint on the July 8 outage," the spokesperson said.

"We encourage anyone that believes they still require assistance to reach out to us."

Telstra typically dominates the list of most complained about telcos, in part due to its large customer base and large regional and remote coverage.

Onus 'should not be on customers'

ACCAN's Ms Bennett said the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers to prove their damages to get redress.

" Right now, if your service goes down, it's largely up to you to chase your telco for compensation, and any goodwill gesture is entirely at their discretion. That isn't good enough for an essential service. "

Consumer groups are pushing for telco customers who suffer outages to be awarded compensation automatically, similar to what happens in the energy sector when service disruptions occur.

Telstra CEO 'deeply sorry' for outage Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady apologises to the company's customers, saying the telco let them down and that investigations into the cause of Wednesday's Telstra outage are continuing.

ACCAN is also calling for enforceable standards to ensure companies invest sufficiently in networks to provide reliable services, along with the implementation of 'domestic mobile roaming' so that customers can connect to another provider in the case their network fails in an outage.

This echoes the findings of a Senate inquiry in September that recommended the federal government mandate domestic mobile roaming for both voice calls and text messages.

It also recommended the introduction of "substantial" civil penalties for telcos that fail to meet reliability and performance standards, and to introduce "a comprehensive automatic compensation scheme for those directly or indirectly affected by service outages."

World.title: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Cher to headline Glastonbury
World.content:
Harry Styles, Sam Fender, Billie Eilish and Cher will headline Britain's Glastonbury Festival next year, the organisers have said.

The announcement was made on their official website and social media accounts on Wednesday, as the sold-out festival returns after taking a year off in 2026.

The line-up poster for the event, held at Worthy Farm in south-west England since 1970, was captioned, "Many more acts and attractions still to be announced".

British singer Harry Styles, who recently completed a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York, will play the festival for the first time.

Billie Eilish last played Glastonbury in 2022. (Reuters: David Swanson)

Cher will take the Sunday legend's slot at the age of 81. US star Eilish will headline for the second time after her first appearance in 2022.

British singer Fender will take one of the coveted top spots for the first time.

He posted on his Instagram page, "Headlining the best party on the planet".

Festival organiser Emily Eavis said: "We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists.

"We are beyond excited about how it's all shaping up.

"We will bring you even more names in the new year and can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"

Sam Fender will headline on the Friday night. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Glastonbury often sells out before any headliners have been announced.

Tickets were snapped up in 42 minutes last month.

"Tickets for Glastonbury 2027 have now sold out," the organisers posted on social media, less than an hour after the general sale began.

The festival was not held in 2026, known as a fallow year.

Every five years or so, the farm's pastures need to recover from the impact of having over 200,000 people on site for the event in June.

Crowded House, Massive Attack, Chase & Status, the XX and Lily Allen are amongst the other acts who will perform at the festival.

Glastonbury 2025, which was attended by some 210,000 people, featured Neil Young and Rod Stewart, as well as performances by Raye, The Prodigy, Alanis Morissette and Snow Patrol.

The gates will open on June 23.
