She was quite impressed and would shop there from time to time but always making sure that she immediately decanted her Aldi purchases into the more upmarket Marks & Spencer branded bags.”

“Inspired by Jim Dewar of Davistown, my near neighbourhood, I offer the following”:

The service we used to get,

At David Jones was admired,

But now they’ve closed half their stores,

And half the staff have been fired,

Do we now have to go and get ‘Myered’?”

Many thanks, Aidan Cuddington of Umina Beach.

Not to be outdone, Jim offers his take on the recently discussed courtesy bus (C8):

On duty day and night,

Unceasingly polite,

A well-coached bus

Is such a plus -

A transport of delight!

George Zivkovic of Northmead steps up for the spies of the sisterhood: “If Amazon MGM Studios were serious, it would have recast the new 007 as Jamie Bond, with a licence to thrill men. Think about it, worked well for the Time Lords in Doctor Who.”

“Heavens to Betsy, Clytie Williams! Her Majesty (C8) would never have risked eating a dodgy mollusc,” says Serge Nemaz of Illawong. “With her busy schedule she couldn’t afford to be sitting on the ‘throne’ all day could she now? Wearing pearls would’ve been the closest she ever got to oysters.”

World.title: ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa
World.content:
Updated SportBall tampering ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa Daniel Brettig, Daniel Lo Surdo and Andrew Wu Updated November 18, 2026 — 8:53pm ,first published 7:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cameron Bancroft has alleged the whole team knew he was using sandpaper in South Africa, in an explosive statement that challenges Pat Cummins’ recollection of the scandal and contradicts former coach Darren Lehmann’s claim he did not know of the plot. But Cummins hit back late on Wednesday through his manager, who said the Test captain stood by what he said at his lengthy media conference last Friday. Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images Bancroft’s extraordinary 4000-word statement was released on Wednesday night, hours after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum for members of the 2018 tour to speak honestly and privately about the events of the infamous series. Bancroft revealed at length how he became involved in the use of sandpaper on the ball, at the initial suggestion of David Warner.



He also detailed meetings showing how widely the team knew about what he was doing, including repeated feedback conversations with all the bowlers about how much he was doing. Bancroft claims that Lehmann had knowledge of the plot, in addition to bowling coach David Saker, and alleges that after captain Steve Smith said he did not want to know about the plot, former media manager Kate Hutchison had been the only member of staff to raise strong objections. Video of Cameron Bancroft in Cape Town. “The recent release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface,” Bancroft wrote. “It was freeing to hear on a personal level the truth of the chronology of events finally out there. A burden I have carried all these years. “But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference. It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.”



But Cummins’ manager Neil Maxwell issued a statement to this masthead hours after Bancroft’s statement was published. “Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he’s been through, there’s nothing in the statement that hasn’t been answered by Pat in his press conference,” Maxwell said. Loading Bancroft recalled Lehmann and Saker allegedly being involved in conversations at the tea break on day two of the second Test of the series about how to get the ball reverse swinging more drastically. After Warner’s suggestion of sandpaper, Bancroft claims he took it with him for the final session. “I walked onto the field for the final session of day two carrying sandpaper. When I collected the ball, I used it,” he wrote.



“The result wasn’t immediately noticeable to me and I felt uncertain about how effective my twist and turns were on the ball. I had never done this before. Related Article Australian cricket Boon, Greenberg try to take Sandpapergate civil war behind closed doors “During that period, I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to. I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough. “I was physically altering the ball with sandpaper. I was discussing its performance with teammates who knew I wasn’t just plucking at the quarter seam, but that I was actually using sandpaper. “Those two things were connected in my mind. And they remained connected throughout the Test. It’s not rocket science these events and the burden of carrying them around has caused me a lot of pain all these years.”



The following morning, after Bancroft had been given a team shoutout about what he was doing, he alleges that Hutchison spoke up against the team’s failure to play by the game’s laws. “Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening,” he wrote. “I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion. Loading “I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.” Cricket Australia interim chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg announced the forum for members of the 2018 touring party in South Africa to safely share memories and divulge details without fear of recrimination or sanctions.



After Bancroft’s statement was released, CA revealed its own, much shorter, statement. “We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments,” CA said. Loading “We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events. “We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible.”



The Bancroft statement also prompted Khawaja to cancel his scheduled appearance on The Grade Cricketer on Thursday. In Cape Town, Bancroft said that while it was true he was approached by Saker to do more work on the ball, he also got similar feedback from other members of the team. “It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker and it is true,” Bancroft wrote. “Once again the same conversations we had on the field in Port Elizabeth continued. Me asking for feedback from Starcy, Pat, Josh and Mitch about working on the ball like the Test earlier.



“They all told me what I was doing wasn’t enough. The conversations I remember having with the bowlers about the ball’s movement have troubled me enormously in the years since. “When I later heard public statements denying knowledge of sandpaper being used, I struggled to reconcile those denials with my memories. I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used.” When Bancroft was sprung by South African broadcast cameras at Newlands, he recalled how it had in fact been Lehmann – via reserve batter Peter Handscomb – who had demanded the sandpaper be taken off the field. Lehmann had told the 2018 investigation he had no idea about the use of sandpaper. “Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I’d been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants,” Bancroft wrote.



“He said to me, ‘I think it’s time I take that off you now’. And Pete was doing his job after Boof shouted to him on the walkie-talkie ‘get the f---ing sandpaper off Bangers now’. Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Broken trust is the biggest obstacle facing Boon’s Sandpapergate truth forum “In my opinion, if he didn’t know he wouldn’t have said that. And if it wasn’t clear enough before, then it was obvious now. Once again. WE ALL KNEW.” Bancroft believes his chances of an international career were destroyed by the scandal. He also remembers that in the team meeting mentioned by Khawaja about collective accountability, no-one had denied they were aware of what he had been doing. “Nobody in that meeting stood up and said they had been completely unaware of my use of sandpaper. Not one person,” Bancroft wrote.



“[On the] contrary everyone started to give me advice about what I should say and what I shouldn’t say to minimise the damage on the team related with the sandpaper saga. “I had convinced myself that I was carrying out a role for the benefit of the team. Now I was facing the possibility that my international career might be over. As it turns out I ended up becoming the scapegoat for the entire team.” Cricket Australia was contacted for comment. World.title: ‘We’ve got a lot of work to do’: Australia’s batters fall short as England wins one-day series 2-1; Green subbed out with concussion
World.content:
On a day when the word truth was getting a big workout in Australian cricket, the old enemy England gave Australia’s one-day side some home truths of their own.

In the deciding game of their three game series, England out batted Australia setting them 329 to win and then decimated their top-order, with the exception of another stoic knock from Matt Renshaw (55 runs from 70 balls), to win the match by 97 runs and take the series 2-1.

Cooper Connolly is bowled out. Getty Images

This match was played on a batting friendly pitch at Bellerive Oval in Hobart and in as neutral conditions as teams could want for limited overs cricket - that was what made England’s win so instructive and Australia’s shortcomings so apparent.

“There are lots of areas of improvement for our team - we’ve got a lot of work to do,” Australian captain Mitch Marsh said post game.

“While we haven’t won and were outplayed, I’m still excited about this group. They are a good group of young players and the [ODI] World Cup is 12 months away, bring it on.”

Australia’s opening bowlers lacked penetration and without the lead spinner Adam Zampa, who was a late withdrawal due to back spasms, the slow bowling was left to all-rounder Cooper Connolly (1-44) and batters Renshaw (3-51 from 10 overs) and Travis Head (1-33).

Ben Duckett celebrates his century. Steve Bell/Getty Images

The trio did their best and took a few wickets between then but not before player of the match Ben Duckett (133 runs from 115 balls) plundered Australia during the first half of the innings, laying the groundwork for their total, one that could have been even bigger if not for some brave bowling at the close by the home side, led by seamer Jack Edwards (4-31).

But when it came to Australia’s batting, star openers Mitch March and Head were gone inside the first two overs and Josh Inglis joined them in the sheds before the innings was eight overs old as Australia slumped to 3-34 as the speed and movement Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker proved too much for them.

Renshaw and Alex Carey gave Australia hope making 74 for the fourth wicket but when Renshaw hit the ball back to spinner Liam Dawson, Australia’s chances were all but gone.

Cam Green and Carey had a horror mix-up that saw Carey run out and soon after, Green was hit in the grill by a steep bounce from Atkinson and it not only cut his mouth but forced him off with a suspected concussion.

Green retired hurt and walked from the pitch, giving a thumbs up to England and to fans and, hopefully, he can recover quickly given the big load Australia hopes he can play this summer.

That saw young batter Ollie Peake subbed into the game in a rare use of the sport’s concussion substitute but Peake only lasted six balls before he was dismissed.

Cameron Green leaves the field after being hit on the grill. Getty Images

Final pair Spencer Johnson and Mahli Beardman both reached double figures in a spirited final stand but they were stalling the inevitable.

There is one home truth that England needs to take away and that was their catching as they dropped three sitters, including Renshaw twice.

It didn’t cost England on this night but history has shown us that catches win matches and drops do the opposite.

Australia won’t play another 50-over international for the next nine months due to the hectic schedule of Test matches and the Indian Premier League in April and May.

With the World Cup to come next year, the limited overs leaders need to find some solutions for the shortcomings shown in this three-match series led by their poor batting against spinners in the middle overs and their early dismissals at the top of the order.

There is time enough, the question is whether Australia are good enough to find those answers.

England’s Tom Banton was named player of the series.

World.title: Eight years of carrying the burden of the country on my shoulders. Now it’s time I told the truth
World.content:
NationalAustralian cricket Eight years of carrying the burden of the country on my shoulders. Now it’s time I told the truth Cameron Bancroft November 18, 2026 — 10:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

On Wednesday morning, Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg announced that CA will open an independent forum for all those who were on the 2018 South African tour. I appreciate Todd’s comments and the chance for players and staff to have an opportunity to speak. Transparency is a way to acknowledge our respect for cricket, a game we love and something that is bigger than all of us. And that is why I will attend the forum. But it’s also why the public needs to know my story today. For eight years, I shared the burden of this story for the whole team.



This was a burden which was heavier than my capacity and I took the bullet for everybody, and it was my choice. I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learnt from one of Australian cricket’s darkest moments. However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened. It was not just the three of us – Steve Smith, David Warner and I – who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team. When I was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.



I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me. The recent release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface. It was freeing to hear on a personal level the truth of the chronology of events finally out there. A burden I have carried all these years. But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian Cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference.



It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone. What I saw, experienced and lived with – not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa – is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time. In addition to what Usman already mentioned I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying. There are also conversations and moments that I believe remain untold. I want to share those now. It’s time. My cricket career has been destroyed, and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.



But I have reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth. Eight years is long enough. A culture that existed before South Africa To understand what happened in the Second and Third Tests in Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha) and Cape Town, I believe it is important to understand the environment I entered as a young Australian Test cricketer. In doing so, I need to take you back to my first Test match against England in the Ashes of the 2017/18 season. David Warner had carried significant responsibility for maintaining the condition of the ball within our team for a long time. He understood reverse swing, understood how to look after the ball and was highly regarded for his knowledge in that area.



Ball maintenance was a normal part of our cricketing conversations. Dave did this selflessly for the team. I remember during my first Test match being instructed, along with other members of the team, to push the quarter seam of the ball together after the team took a wicket. Manipulating that area could help create a rougher surface and encourage reverse swing. It was something the group was directed to do, and as a young player entering the Australian team, I accepted it as part of how we operated. I never questioned the distinction between legitimate ball maintenance and deliberately altering the ball’s condition. But at the time, these practices were so normalised that I barely gave them a second thought.



This was the beginning of my journey in the Australian cricket team. We were ruthless and willing to do these sorts of behaviours and cross boundaries to give ourselves an advantage, to win. Casting forward to the First Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used. There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking; this practice became so normal after my First Test. Importantly for the chronology of events, I was not responsible for the ball in that Test. However, what happened in the Second Test in Port Elizabeth was different. It was a significant escalation. And it was where I became directly involved.



Port Elizabeth: Where the sandpaper began After winning the First Test in Durban we were on top of the world as a team. We were slightly arrogant about winning that game, and emboldened by the scars we felt we had left on the South African team. We sensed blood in the series. That’s exactly what we wanted to continue into the Second Test at St George’s Park, Port Elizabeth. We would do literally whatever it took to achieve that – and here is why and what happened.



In the first innings we were bowled out for 243. It was a slightly green wicket, a bit challenging, and we were put on the back foot immediately. By tea on the second day, South Africa had reached 2/153. The match was finely balanced, but the momentum was moving towards South Africa. They were gaining control of the match and we were struggling to find a way to make the ball move, and the pressure within our team was growing. By the tea break on day two, there was a clear sense that we needed something to change. It was a short break, only 20 minutes, and like most intervals during a Test match, coaches were moving around, checking in with players and discussing the state of the game and what we could do more to take some wickets and create some pressure. All the coaches and players were involved in these discussions in the dressing room with the intention to improve our position in the game.



Some players were more opinionated, but we were all invested and working towards the same goal of winning the Test match for Australia. This happens in every change room and team I’ve played for, from club cricket all the way up to international cricket. This is also happening concurrently with players hydrating, eating, receiving physio treatment and mentally resetting before starting again. Towards the back end of that interval, a conversation developed in the changing rooms about getting the ball to reverse swing. I remember bowling coach David Saker being involved in those conversations. Coach Darren Lehmann was also present. Other players were moving in and out. The need to get the ball moving through the air was openly acknowledged, and the more vanilla methods like shining the ball normally and using saliva weren’t cutting it.



We were under pressure. It was in that environment that David Warner raised the possibility of using sandpaper to roughen one side of the ball. Dave explained he could not personally carry out the task because of the attention the television cameras were paying him throughout the series. This was something widely acknowledged by our whole touring party during the series. It’s why we joked about it and Dave started writing funny words on his finger tape. He had been under intense scrutiny, and he knew the cameras were watching him closely. I don’t believe Dave was acting purely for himself. I understood his suggestion as an attempt to help the team regain control of the match. That doesn’t excuse his involvement or mine. But I think it matters that the conversation took place within a wider team environment where we were collectively desperate to make something happen.



We did this together for the bowlers especially, but more widely the team and to win the game. I recall people in the room agreeing with the proposal. Saker and Lehmann were certainly present, although I cannot speak for every word shared. Captain Steve Smith came into the conversation and, as I remember it, made it clear that he wanted no part in it, before distancing himself. There were also people who expressed caution to me. I remember being warned to be careful, and others suggesting they would not do it if they were in my position.



Not everyone was in the changing room at the time, but the conversation was not confined to Dave and I. I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised. I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating. But I also saw an opportunity to contribute. I was a youngster playing in his seventh Test match. If you asked me to run through a brick wall at that time I would have. That’s how naive and impressionable I was. I just wanted to be accepted by my teammates beyond the runs and catches I took. This was an opportunity for that. Additionally, being relatively new, I was desperate to establish myself and eager to be someone my teammates could rely upon.



That desire to belong clouded my judgment. I agreed. What happened on the field As spoken about in Usman’s book, there was an understanding of when the ball could most easily be altered without attracting attention. This was an awareness we had as a team. When we returned to the field after the break, the umpires would leave the ball on the outfield, a short distance away from the boundary line. From a broadcast perspective, we knew that the cameras didn’t pan onto us as a team until we were about halfway out.



This was because the country logos would pop up on the telecast as an intro to the session. This is common practice. We’ve seen this before. Dave explained to me why that presented an opportunity. It was also what seemed to be the safest time to do it. Others in the group agreed and gave their opinions on this. I walked onto the field for the final session of day two carrying sandpaper. When I collected the ball, I used it. The result wasn’t immediately noticeable to me and I felt uncertain about how effective my twists and turns were on the ball. I had never done this before. During that period, I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to.



I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers – Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh – about whether it was reverse swinging enough. I also spoke with Tim Paine, who was in a key position behind the stumps to observe how the ball was moving. I wanted and needed feedback. How else am I to know if what I’m doing is effective or not if I don’t have these conversations with the bowlers bowling with it and the wicketkeeper? Additionally, they need to actually turn the ball the other way to test if it is reversing and, as you will see watching the game, it clearly was. All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful. Is it going yet? It’s not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.



There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious. The conversations about the effect the sandpaper was having on the ball were regular, very natural and organic on the field. It is as it is. I also remember expressing my disbelief to teammates about what I was doing. It was so taboo and against the grain. Everyone would laugh and speak about it sporadically on the field. We were all well aware of the riskiness of my behaviour. As time elapsed in that session, there was excitement about the movement we were getting from the ball.



And there was an uncomfortable sense that something we all knew was wrong had become part of our effort to win the Test match. We took 4/28 in that final session. That is game changing! This was not something I did just once in the playing area after returning to the field from the tea break. This was an act I did nearly every over the whole last session on that day to begin with, and then for the remainder of that Test match, up until I was caught in Third Test in Cape Town. Yes, I chose to carry out this role for the team. I remember Mitchell Marsh taking wickets and joking about how much the ball was swinging and how he never used to swing it like that. There was laughter and celebrations when wickets fell.



I was amazed that sandpaper could have such an effect on a cricket ball. I was stoked my impact was leading to the team doing well. It was the same for my teammates, and I remember their praise to me for that whole final session when we were taking those wickets. “Great work Bang. Keep it up.” Yet also “be careful”, and as Steve said, “I don’t want to know about it”. We were down the rabbit hole so far. I was physically altering the ball with sandpaper. I was discussing its performance with teammates who knew I wasn’t just plucking at the quarter seam, but that I was actually using sandpaper. Those two things were connected in my mind. And they remained connected throughout the Test. It’s not rocket science that these events and the burden of carrying them around has caused me a lot of pain all these years.



The meeting that has stayed with me On the morning of day three in Port Elizabeth, we gathered for our usual team chat before warm-up. We spoke about the day which had gone, celebrated the moments that occurred, but more importantly, emphasised the points which were key for a successful day ahead. I remember my ball tampering with the sandpaper the evening before being discussed and my role being acknowledged in front of the group. Much like the celebrations when we took 4/28 the evening before, I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker.



It reinforced the sense that what I was doing was being accepted as part of our collective effort. This event is crystal-clear in my mind. Not only for the praise I received. But I also remember a very different reaction. Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening. I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion. I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.



Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it. I cannot speak for Kate’s thoughts beyond what I remember her saying and doing. She deserves the opportunity to give her own account. But her reaction is important because it completely challenges the idea that nobody had an opportunity to question what was happening. We did. I did. And I chose to continue. South Africa ultimately won the Test, with AB de Villiers playing a magnificent innings that helped turn the match decisively in their favour.



Whatever advantage we thought we were gaining, it wasn’t enough. We had compromised our integrity and still lost. From Port Elizabeth to Cape Town There was a substantial break between the Second and third Tests. I remember spending time exploring South Africa. I went swimming with sharks, visited Camps Bay, walked alone to the top of Table Mountain, and enjoyed a day visiting wineries around Stellenbosch with teammates. They are memories that should have been among the highlights of my first Test tour of South Africa.



Or the fact that I probably played the best innings of my career in the first innings of that Cape Town Test match. I scored 76 off 103 balls against Philander, Rabada, Morkel and Maharaj. Instead, I now look back on that period knowing what I had been doing on the field. The sandpaper had become part of what I perceived to be my responsibility within the team. I was worried about it. Before the Cape Town Test, I remember speaking with Kate Hutchison at training. I asked what would happen if I was caught tampering with the ball. She did not want to engage in that conversation because of the seriousness of the consequences, but her response was “not good”, and she walked off.



Cape Town: The moment everything unravelled The changing rooms at Newlands was unusual in its layout, something Usman has described in his book. I remember sitting next to Usman and Tim Paine in the smaller change room. It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings, telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker, and it is true. Once again the same conversations we had on the field in Port Elizabeth continued. Me asking for feedback from Starcy, Pat, Josh and Mitch about working on the ball like the Test earlier.



They all told me what I was doing wasn’t enough. The same feedback was given behind the stumps when I asked Tim and the guys in the slips. This Test match it wasn’t as effective using sandpaper due to the conditions and moisture. The conditions were difficult for reverse swing. The central wicket square was green, and the ball wasn’t behaving in the way we wanted. I continued trying to alter it. The conversations I remember having with the bowlers about the ball’s movement have troubled me enormously in the years since.



When I later heard public statements denying knowledge of sandpaper being used, I struggled to reconcile those denials with my memories. I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered, and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used. Then came the moment the cameras caught me. The sandpaper was exposed. And everything changed. Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I’d been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants. He said to me: “I think it’s time I take that off you now.” And Pete was doing his job after Boof shouted to him on the walkie-talkie “get the f---ing sandpaper off Bangers now”.



In my opinion, if he didn’t know, he wouldn’t have said that. And if it wasn’t clear enough before, then it was obvious now. Once again. WE ALL KNEW. The press conference and another lie After I was caught in Cape Town, there were frantic conversations about how we should respond.



I remember there being a preference among some people to wait until the following day, to sleep on what had happened and consider a more measured public response. Steve Smith wanted to address the situation immediately. He believed owning up to the incident would help contain the damage and allow us to move forward. Steve just wanted to clear it so he could focus on batting. I went with him because I believed I needed to accept responsibility for my actions. But even then, we did not tell the complete truth. Before the press conference, I recall David Saker specifically warning against identifying sandpaper as the material used.



Other coaches, management and players agreed, some disagreed. “We cannot say we used sandpaper.” We listened to that advice and we followed it. There was concern about the implications of that admission. So we acknowledged ball tampering while giving an inaccurate account of the material involved, describing tape and material collected from the ground. It was another lie. One told while we were supposedly taking responsibility. I look back at that press conference with enormous regret. We were frightened. We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us. The investigation and the silence



The remainder of the Cape Town Test was intense. There were private conversations, uncertainty about what would happen next and an overwhelming sense that our world was falling apart. The prime minister even weighed in. After the match, I remember a lengthy meeting involving players and staff on the tour. We discussed how to respond to the scandal and the information that would need to be acknowledged publicly. By then, it was clear that the use of sandpaper could no longer be concealed. Nobody in that meeting stood up and said they had been completely unaware of my use of sandpaper. Not one person.



On the contrary, everyone started to give me advice about what I should say and what I shouldn’t say to minimise the damage on the team related to the sandpaper saga. I had convinced myself that I was carrying out a role for the benefit of the team. Now I was facing the possibility that my international career might be over. As it turns out, I ended up becoming the scapegoat for the entire team. Two words that changed everything In 2021, while playing county cricket for Durham, I gave an interview to The Guardian. During that conversation, I was asked about the awareness of the Australian bowlers.



I was caught off guard. I had spent years trying to move forward, trying to focus on my cricket and trying not to reopen the events of South Africa. When pressed, I answered the question of awareness as “self-explanatory”. I had not intended to make a major public revelation. But those few words reignited the entire controversy. Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon subsequently released a joint statement denying that they knew sandpaper had been taken onto the field to alter the ball before the television footage appeared at Newlands. Reading that statement was deeply painful. I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest.



Yet I also knew that I had never publicly given a full account of those conversations. I did this for the same reason Usman never spoke, Dave never spoke, and for what has transpired in the last week, Mitch Marsh in his interview before the ODI series against England never said anything. That reason is the want and desire to represent Australia. To do so goes against the story of events, puts CA under pressure and the lies which were already told. That is the contradiction I have wrestled with for years. I felt hurt by the public response, the reaction of those bowlers and finding meaning in my life post it. The career I thought I could rebuild



When I accepted my punishment in 2018, I believed that Dave, Steve and I taking sole responsibility for the entire team, serving my suspension and demonstrating that I had changed would eventually allow me to rebuild my international career. I also hoped that the people who had shared that dressing room would understand the responsibility I had taken on. I believed that, with time, my performances and conduct might earn me another opportunity to represent Australia. There have been periods in Sheffield Shield cricket when I was out of touch and wasn’t at the top of the list for Test selection. But there were other times I genuinely believed I had done enough to warrant selection. I have continued to train, compete, make runs and pursue the dream of wearing the Baggy Green again. Yet the opportunities I hoped for have not materialised in the way I expected.



Selection is complicated. There are cricketing reasons, competing players, different conditions and decisions that I have not been part of. For many years, I believed I would be selected because I trusted the selection process. But I would be lying if I said I had never wondered whether the unresolved tension surrounding these events in South Africa had played a part. Because in spite of having scored the most hundreds of any player in the competition in the last six years, including featuring in the top three run-scorers for over half that period, I have never had a look-in. After my “self-explanatory” public statement in 2021, I felt increasingly uncomfortable around some of the people involved. I wondered whether my presence in an Australian dressing room might bring back questions that others wanted to leave behind. I wondered whether the easiest option was simply not to select me, which I believe to be quite unfair in my opinion. The hardest part has been feeling that nobody fully understood my perspective and the complete truth that was South Africa and the Sandpapergate. This includes Australian selectors and coaching staff making these cricket decisions.



I made a terrible decision because I wanted to belong in the Australian team. I made mistake, I owned my mistake, I served the severe punishment, I came back, scored runs, in the hope I would be selected again in the Australian team. Which has not eventuated yet. And in the years that followed, I have sometimes felt that this incident has left me permanently an outsider. Conclusion For eight years, I suffered silently. I cannot change the past. But I can change what I do now.



The release of Usman’s book has reassured me that the events of South Africa have never truly been resolved. There are still unanswered questions, conflicting recollections and people who have lived with the consequences in different ways. I do not claim that my account alone settles every question. This is the truth that I am now prepared to give openly and in full. As the person at the centre of this, all I am doing this now is because I can’t handle the burden any more of carrying for everyone what happened in South Africa.



Nobody has pushed me to write this. I don’t feel obliged or benefit financially by sharing this. Michael Clarke in an interview last week said: “Now we’ve got this opportunity. I would just like to see whatever the truth is for it all to come out, allow people to finally tell the truth, and move on. Fans have not moved on”. And, as I wrote earlier, I am looking forward to being part of the CA forum and to speak as specific and detailed as possible without being general. I am inspired by Michael Clarke’s comment and I agree the fans deserve this. This is my responsibility.



And here it is. Published with the permission of Cameron Bancroft. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Kidnappings, cocaine drops and a love story: GTA VI delivers
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games Opinion Kidnappings, cocaine drops and a love story: GTA VI delivers David Swan Technology editor November 18, 2026 — 10:00pm

November 18, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Grand Theft Auto VI is Bonnie and Clyde on meth. It’s a love story for the ages and has a different tone to any GTA game before it. Rockstar Games has taken a big swing with its first new Grand Theft Auto in 13 years, and the result is one of the best games ever made. Within the first few hours, I’d escaped masked men in a hospital wheelchair, kidnapped a doctor for his painkillers and flown a plane on a cocaine drop. By then, I knew this was the most outrageous game I’d played. GTA VI is a big swing that pays off. The game is full of moments like that, vivid, outrageous and a lot of fun in equal measure. It drags you in and keeps you playing until 1am. It is worth the 13-year wait, and you can feel the effort that has gone into every corner of it. Grand Theft Auto is a crime series that drops you into a sprawling fictional American city and lets you roam on foot or in whatever you can steal, taking jobs from crooks as a story unfolds. This one follows Jason and Lucia, a criminal couple, through Vice City, Rockstar’s version of Miami, and the surrounding state of Leonida. The usual car chases, drug deals, set-ups and jewellery store heists are all here, with everything dialled up to 11.



The plot itself starts slowly, then escalates into a heady mix of Goodfellas, Heat, Tiger King, True Romance and Pulp Fiction. I won’t spoil where it goes. What holds it together is Jason and Lucia. The game tracks their relationship as you play, and keeping it healthy never feels like a chore; it adds to the realism. Their relationship and the game’s writing give the game an emotional weight no previous GTA has had. For me, it doesn’t quite hit the highs of Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar’s cowboy epic and probably my favourite video game of all time. But ask me again in another 40 hours. What holds it together is Jason and Lucia. The world they move through is kaleidoscopic and technicolour, crammed with stories, activities and people who feel real. You can’t walk into every building, but it’s close. It can take more than half an hour of real-world time to drive from one end of the map to the other.



Some of the best moments are the smallest: the parody ads on the radio, the small talk between pedestrians, and side-missions that send you down strange rabbit-holes. There is so much game here that after more than 40 hours, I still haven’t finished the main story. It looks extraordinary, to the point that clips of the game have been mistaken for real footage. It looks extraordinary – another high-water mark for the series. Clips of the game have been mistaken for real footage on social media. That realism takes some adjusting to when you’re committing acts of ultra-violence. As a former music journalist, I’ll stick my neck out: this is probably the strongest soundtrack of any video game to date. French electronic duo Justice composed the score, and the accompanying album has new tracks from Travis Scott and Lana Del Rey, with Aussies Tame Impala and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard guesting on a Justice song. The needle drops at key moments lift those scenes the way a great soundtrack lifts an action movie. Related Article Video games Bikies, bands and billions: The Australians riding the GTA juggernaut



Underneath the chaos, the game has a lot to say about Trump’s America, a place that already borders on self-parody. Vice City is outlandish, corrupt, weird and deeply funny. The strange part is that it still works as escapism, even though what you’re escaping into is effectively a mirror of the world outside your lounge room. It isn’t perfect. One problem has dogged GTA for years is back: while there’s so much to do, some missions can feel repetitive. Drive somewhere, steal something or kill someone or blow something up, then drive away and shake the cops. Another is getting around. There’s no fast travel. You can book a ride through Ryde Me, the game’s version of Uber, and pay extra to skip the trip, but mostly you drive, and that gets tedious. Some of the realism tips into chores as well: filling cars with petrol, remembering to eat, assembling furniture. Realism for its own sake doesn’t always add to the fun. It isn’t perfect. But it’s close. I also hit small bugs, such as pedestrians walking into walls and getting stuck. Nothing broke the game, and on a pre-release build of something this size, that’s about what you’d expect.



None of that dents what Rockstar has pulled off. In an era of AI slop, this is a game that feels deeply alive and human, which is fascinating given how many people it took to make and how long it took. It’s also deeply impressive on a purely technical level: there are almost no load times, despite its mammoth download size of more than 200 gigabytes. Related Article Opinion

Video games I’m taking a week off to play a video game. I can explain Roy Ward Sports writer People – gamers and non-gamers alike – will get lost in it for years. I expect it to outsell a Taylor Swift album or a new Avengers film, and to reopen the debate about whether games are art on a par with TV and film – a debate that should have been settled long ago. It will also revive the often reductive argument about violence in games and its incredibly tenuous links to real-world violence. There’s no escaping that. The game is rated R 18+ for high-impact violence, sex scenes and drug use, and it earns every bit of that. It’s not one for the kids, and if hyper-realistic violence turns your stomach, skip it. Everyone else should buy it. It costs $129.95 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, with no PC version yet. Spread over the 40-plus hours I’ve played so far, that’s about $3 an hour, and I’m nowhere near done with Vice City.



This is grand theft of the highest order. What it steals is your free time. Fact box Game: Grand Theft Auto VI

World.title: ‘More dialogue, less conflict’: Albanese backs historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaChina relations ‘More dialogue, less conflict’: Albanese backs historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin Lisa Visentin and Natassia Chrysanthos Updated November 18, 2026 — 9:35pm ,first published 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Shenzhen: Russian President Vladimir Putin has touted “big potential benefits” from historic talks with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese backed the dialogue while calling for de-escalation in Ukraine and the Middle East. Albanese took part in a group photo at a gala dinner at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Wednesday evening, in which Xi, Putin and Trump stood centre stage, despite political pressure at home for him to opt out in protest against Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Albanese stood in the back row next to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, after both leaders indicated they did not want to disrespect China’s role as host. As the carefully choreographed photo was being arranged, Trump and Putin greeted each other with an extended handshake and had a brief informal chat in a huddle with Xi before the other leaders were ushered into place. The moment provided the first images of the three men together, serving as an early preview of the history-making photos expected from their unprecedented trilateral talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit on Thursday.



Leaders pose for a group photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. Iori Sagisawa/Kyodo News Pool via AP Ahead of the trio’s talks, Albanese said on Wednesday that the conflicts had not only taken a heavy toll on human lives but also damaged the global economy. “We want to see more dialogue, less military conflict,” Albanese said as he endorsed the three-way meeting, adding that any solution and peace needed to be on Ukraine’s terms. View post on X Putin used the rare spotlight of the international stage on Wednesday to pitch Russia as resilient and confident, while taking a swipe at “formerly dominant powers” and their sanctions.



Addressing a forum of business executives, Putin asserted Russia was staring down “failed attempts to isolate our country” with dignity, saying that while sanctions could halt development they were “not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying the economies of the competition.” In reality, five years of war has heavily strained Russia’s economy, stalling growth while defence costs mount and inflation rises. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Of course you shouldn’t’: Albanese under fire over possible Putin photo Putin’s decision to attend APEC in Shenzhen, China’s tech capital – his first appearance at a major multilateral forum with Western leaders in years – is part of his renewed push for legitimacy in the face of a Western-led campaign of economic isolation since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. His presence poses potential diplomatic awkwardness for Albanese, who, along with other leaders, has publicly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and helped Kyiv’s efforts to repel Putin’s armed forces. Albanese made a quick stop at high-end supermarket Ole when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, where he tasted Australian beef, looked at lobster and inspected domestic imports of grocery products and fresh food with ambassador to China Scott Dewar.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tours a high-end grocery store ahead of the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China. AAPIMAGE In an address to the APEC CEO summit afterwards, Albanese spruiked Australia’s artificial intelligence policies and encouraged investment in the country. He said there was “nowhere you’d rather be” than Australia, with its universities, resources and room to build renewable energy. “We have deep ties with the fastest growing populations in the world … Not least is our ties with the People’s Republic of China,” he said. China ‘committed to true multilateralism’



Many US allies are anxious that Trump is facilitating Putin’s pitch for rehabilitation by agreeing to a trilateral summit, and Putin is widely expected to use the meeting to push for favourable terms for Russia ending the Ukraine war. However, analysts are sceptical the meeting will produce concrete outcomes, and have generally dismissed attempts to liken it to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when the leaders of the Soviet Union, the UK and the US sat down to carve up the postwar world into spheres of influence. Xi Jinping greets delegates after speaking at the 2026 APEC CEO Summit. AP Meanwhile, Xi used his opening address to the APEC CEO summit to portray China as a leading advocate of the international rules-based trading system, in a speech designed to draw a contrast against the tariffs and transactionalism pursued by the Trump administration. “China has stood up to unilateralism and protectionism and remained committed to true multilateralism,” Xi said, adding that “no matter how the international landscape changes, China will not waver in its pursuit of win-win co-operation with all other countries.”



Xi is due to hold bilateral talks with Trump on Thursday before their joint meeting with Putin. Related Article Analysis

Foreign relations Secret meetings and maybe a photobomb: What to expect when Trump, Xi, Putin get together The fallout of the Nvidia scandal will hang over the leaders’ talks, potentially destabilising a fragile trade truce struck between the pair at last year’s APEC summit in South Korea. Trump’s visit to China comes after Washington announced further restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, while Beijing has accused the US of fabricating a spy scandal as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade and vowed to take countermeasures. Trump landed in Shenzhen in the afternoon (China time) after meeting key regional allies in Manila during the week.



Xi greeted the US president at the airport, reciprocating Trump’s gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met. President Donald Trump speaks with China’s President Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Shenzhen. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein They had a brief hug and a short exchange before walking along the red carpet to their motorcades. The US president met Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in the Philippines on Tuesday night, marking his first appearance at a Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue) leaders summit. Trump described the Quad countries as “the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific” in his official remarks at the beginning of the meeting.



“We talk a lot. When they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you,” he said. With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Bowen’s bid at UN conference: Not too late to turn down the temperature
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate policy Bowen’s bid at UN conference: Not too late to turn down the temperature Nick O'Malley November 18, 2026 — 9:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has told the UN’s climate conference that it was not too late for the international community to “bend the global emissions curve” by embracing electrification, even as a new study finds Australia is not moving fast enough to comfortably meet its interim climate goals. According to a new report from BloombergNEF, a global energy think tank, the country faces a gap between current market trends and what is required to limit global warming. The current pace of Australia’s renewable rollout risks its 2030 renewable-electricity target and puts its 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution – the country’s official Paris Agreement climate pledge – out of reach, making net zero emissions by 2050 harder to achieve. Chris Bowen at the COP31 Climate Conference in Antalya, Turkey. Getty Images The report outlines two main pathways for Australia’s energy future. Under the Economic Transition Scenario, a business-as-usual forecast driven purely by market forces and economics without new policy interventions, emissions will fall by 32 per cent by 2035 and 56 per cent by 2050. However, this trajectory aligns with roughly 2.4 degrees of global warming by 2100, falling well short of international climate targets.



In contrast, reaching net zero by 2050 requires the Net Zero Scenario, an aggressive road map that demands the rapid elimination of nearly all fossil fuel use. Achieving this net zero pathway will rely heavily on switching to clean electricity and widespread electrification, which together will deliver 76 per cent of the required emissions reductions through 2050. For harder-to-abate sectors such as aviation, shipping, heavy industry and steel, cleaner alternatives like clean hydrogen, bioenergy and carbon capture and storage – a technology that traps industrial carbon emissions and stores them underground – will play a vital role. Bowen, in Antalya to lead United Nations climate talks as president of negotiations, is advocating for a global goal to accelerate electrification. “In the last quarter of last year, renewables generated more electricity across Australia’s national grid than fossil fuels,” Bowen said in his address to the climate summit. “This is not only cutting emissions. It is making our energy system more secure, more sovereign and less exposed to global fuel shocks. “The transformation is also reaching our roads. One in four new passenger vehicles sold in Australia this year has been electric. Five years ago, it was just one in 50.



“Australia’s experience shows what becomes possible when households, businesses and governments move together. One home with solar and a battery does not transform an energy system. But millions of individual choices can.” Related Article Paris Agreement Bowen has drawn battlelines with his climate proposals. Now comes the hard part According to the Bloomberg NEF report, the transition to net zero does not require dramatically more overall investment, but a dramatic shift in where capital flows. The net zero path requires $2.6 trillion in investment between 2026 and 2050, which is only 3 per cent more than the standard economic transition. Bowen said that Australians’ enthusiastic uptake of rooftop solar, home batteries and electric cars showed change could be made at scale. “Australia’s experience proves something more: climate action can strengthen energy security, attract investment, create jobs and build economic resilience,” he said. “Australians are already demonstrating that transformation, rooftop by rooftop, battery by battery, community by community.”



A draft deal issued by Bowen on Monday in his role as president reflected the extent of disagreements between the nearly 200 countries represented at the talks and highlighted the challenge of agreeing to a meaningful deal by the conference’s official close on Friday. Bowen said the 18-page draft was crucial to the debating process and sought to reflect the range of views. The draft contained two sets of phrasing around fossil fuels. One reiterated wording agreed in 2023 around “transitioning away” from their use, and another more ambitious clause talked about their “phase out”. Both could be omitted from a final deal. with Reuters Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.
