“Christine Perrott’s mention of pride in the distinctive David Jones bag (C8) brought back memories of when Aldi first arrived in the UK,” says Pauline McGinley of Drummoyne. “My mum-in-law was initially reluctant and needed to be persuaded to peruse the aisles. She was quite impressed and would shop there from time to time but always making sure that she immediately decanted her Aldi purchases into the more upmarket Marks & Spencer branded bags.”

“Inspired by Jim Dewar of Davistown, my near neighbourhood, I offer the following”:

The service we used to get,

At David Jones was admired,

But now they’ve closed half their stores,

And half the staff have been fired,

Do we now have to go and get ‘Myered’?”

Many thanks, Aidan Cuddington of Umina Beach.

Not to be outdone, Jim offers his take on the recently discussed courtesy bus (C8):

On duty day and night,

Unceasingly polite,

A well-coached bus

Is such a plus -

A transport of delight!

George Zivkovic of Northmead steps up for the spies of the sisterhood: “If Amazon MGM Studios were serious, it would have recast the new 007 as Jamie Bond, with a licence to thrill men. Think about it, worked well for the Time Lords in Doctor Who.”

“Heavens to Betsy, Clytie Williams! Her Majesty (C8) would never have risked eating a dodgy mollusc,” says Serge Nemaz of Illawong. “With her busy schedule she couldn’t afford to be sitting on the ‘throne’ all day could she now? Wearing pearls would’ve been the closest she ever got to oysters.”

World.title: ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa
World.content:
Updated SportBall tampering ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa Daniel Brettig, Daniel Lo Surdo and Andrew Wu Updated November 18, 2026 — 8:53pm ,first published 7:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cameron Bancroft has alleged the whole team knew he was using sandpaper in South Africa, in an explosive statement that challenges Pat Cummins’ recollection of the scandal and contradicts former coach Darren Lehmann’s claim he did not know of the plot. But Cummins hit back late on Wednesday through his manager, who said the Test captain stood by what he said at his lengthy media conference last Friday. Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images Bancroft’s extraordinary 4000-word statement was released on Wednesday night, hours after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum for members of the 2018 tour to speak honestly and privately about the events of the infamous series. Bancroft revealed at length how he became involved in the use of sandpaper on the ball, at the initial suggestion of David Warner.



He also detailed meetings showing how widely the team knew about what he was doing, including repeated feedback conversations with all the bowlers about how much he was doing. Bancroft claims that Lehmann had knowledge of the plot, in addition to bowling coach David Saker, and alleges that after captain Steve Smith said he did not want to know about the plot, former media manager Kate Hutchison had been the only member of staff to raise strong objections. Video of Cameron Bancroft in Cape Town. “The recent release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface,” Bancroft wrote. “It was freeing to hear on a personal level the truth of the chronology of events finally out there. A burden I have carried all these years. “But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference. It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.”



But Cummins’ manager Neil Maxwell issued a statement to this masthead hours after Bancroft’s statement was published. “Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he’s been through, there’s nothing in the statement that hasn’t been answered by Pat in his press conference,” Maxwell said. Loading Bancroft recalled Lehmann and Saker allegedly being involved in conversations at the tea break on day two of the second Test of the series about how to get the ball reverse swinging more drastically. After Warner’s suggestion of sandpaper, Bancroft claims he took it with him for the final session. “I walked onto the field for the final session of day two carrying sandpaper. When I collected the ball, I used it,” he wrote.



“The result wasn’t immediately noticeable to me and I felt uncertain about how effective my twist and turns were on the ball. I had never done this before. Related Article Australian cricket Boon, Greenberg try to take Sandpapergate civil war behind closed doors “During that period, I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to. I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough. “I was physically altering the ball with sandpaper. I was discussing its performance with teammates who knew I wasn’t just plucking at the quarter seam, but that I was actually using sandpaper. “Those two things were connected in my mind. And they remained connected throughout the Test. It’s not rocket science these events and the burden of carrying them around has caused me a lot of pain all these years.”



The following morning, after Bancroft had been given a team shoutout about what he was doing, he alleges that Hutchison spoke up against the team’s failure to play by the game’s laws. “Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening,” he wrote. “I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion. Loading “I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.” Cricket Australia interim chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg announced the forum for members of the 2018 touring party in South Africa to safely share memories and divulge details without fear of recrimination or sanctions.



After Bancroft’s statement was released, CA revealed its own, much shorter, statement. “We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments,” CA said. Loading “We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events. “We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible.”



The Bancroft statement also prompted Khawaja to cancel his scheduled appearance on The Grade Cricketer on Thursday. In Cape Town, Bancroft said that while it was true he was approached by Saker to do more work on the ball, he also got similar feedback from other members of the team. “It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker and it is true,” Bancroft wrote. “Once again the same conversations we had on the field in Port Elizabeth continued. Me asking for feedback from Starcy, Pat, Josh and Mitch about working on the ball like the Test earlier.



“They all told me what I was doing wasn’t enough. The conversations I remember having with the bowlers about the ball’s movement have troubled me enormously in the years since. “When I later heard public statements denying knowledge of sandpaper being used, I struggled to reconcile those denials with my memories. I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used.” When Bancroft was sprung by South African broadcast cameras at Newlands, he recalled how it had in fact been Lehmann – via reserve batter Peter Handscomb – who had demanded the sandpaper be taken off the field. Lehmann had told the 2018 investigation he had no idea about the use of sandpaper. “Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I’d been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants,” Bancroft wrote.



“He said to me, ‘I think it’s time I take that off you now’. And Pete was doing his job after Boof shouted to him on the walkie-talkie ‘get the f---ing sandpaper off Bangers now’. Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Broken trust is the biggest obstacle facing Boon’s Sandpapergate truth forum “In my opinion, if he didn’t know he wouldn’t have said that. And if it wasn’t clear enough before, then it was obvious now. Once again. WE ALL KNEW.” Bancroft believes his chances of an international career were destroyed by the scandal. He also remembers that in the team meeting mentioned by Khawaja about collective accountability, no-one had denied they were aware of what he had been doing. “Nobody in that meeting stood up and said they had been completely unaware of my use of sandpaper. Not one person,” Bancroft wrote.



“[On the] contrary everyone started to give me advice about what I should say and what I shouldn’t say to minimise the damage on the team related with the sandpaper saga. “I had convinced myself that I was carrying out a role for the benefit of the team. Now I was facing the possibility that my international career might be over. As it turns out I ended up becoming the scapegoat for the entire team.” Cricket Australia was contacted for comment. News, results and expert analysis from the week in sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Housing market sitting out economic recovery - Infometrics
World.content:
Audio player for " Is it time to get my money out of AI? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2671943%2Fhousing-market-sitting-out-economic-recovery-infometrics

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

New Zealand's economic recovery will be more difficult because the housing market isn't joining in, but it should put the country in a stronger position, Infometrics says.

It has released its latest Quarterly Economic Monitor, which shows activity improving.

It said economic activity rose 2.4 percent per annum in the September 2026 quarter, and was up 2.1 percent over the year to September 2026.

"All but one of 16 regional economies expanded in the September 2026 quarter," said principal economist Nick Brunsdon.

"Most regions grew by at least 2 percent this quarter. Taranaki was the only regional economy to contract this quarter, driven by declining production from ageing gas fields.

"Job growth remains a couple of steps behind, with employment up 1.1 percent per annum nationally in the September quarter, and growth spreading to 13 regions according to Infometrics' analysis of tax-based jobs data. Employment growth in Auckland picked up to 1 percent per annum, a key step in the national recovery given Auckland is home to a third of New Zealand's population."

He said it had largely been public sector jobs such as in healthcare, education and public administration growing.

"There is a private sector recovery in activity, but there's not really a private sector recovery in jobs just yet."

Higher fuel prices were likely to exacerbate the uncertainty many were feeling and limit growth over the next few months, he said. Brunsdon said it could take a year or two for business confidence to translate to more hiring.

"Job ads aren't really going anywhere... Again, businesses have more work to do, but they feel like they can cope with the staff they've got."

He said growth was still strongest in the South Island but it was encouraging to see that some of the indicators were broadening.

Residential building consents lifted 18 percent in the year to September 2026, supporting an early recovery in construction jobs.

Nick Brunsdon. Supplied / Infometrics

But he said that would be limited because the housing market remained lacklustre, with house values easing 0.9 percent in the year to the September 2026 quarter.

"We don't have a housing market-led recovery this time around, and that's helped us in the past, from a job point of view, because as soon as interest rates go low and people get excited about the value of their house, they start spending money on builders and things like that, and that's really got it quickly kicking things into gear.

"The conditions just aren't there, and obviously we're on an interest rate increasing cycle, not a decreasing cycle, so I don't think we're going to have a recovery that feels like some of those past recoveries that we've had."

He said it was harder for an economic recovery to happen when the housing market was weak.

"Construction is quite a great industry for recovery because you don't need quite so much premises. The ute and the dog cliché is quite good because you can scale up without a lot of fixed resources.

"But it does put us in a more resilient position if our economic recovery is not predicated on asset prices, potentially bubbles in asset prices.

"It's the same if you look at household finances. Household incomes are growing. People are being incredibly tight with their consumer spending. That's a really good thing for household finances, because it means they've got more resilience. They've got more in the bank, they can roll with the punches, but that's not great for the retail or hospitality sector if everyone's holding on to their money."

Marketview card spending data showed a 1.3 percent increase in retail spending in the year to September 2026. Infometrics estimated spending volumes fell 0.4 percent over the last year once retail inflation was accounted for.

"Households are spending more than they were a year ago but are sacrificing spending across most categories to cope with higher fuel costs."

World.title: Māori business leaders have more positive outlook
World.content:
Māori business leaders maintain a more positive view of business performance and a long-term planning perspective, but immediate commercial pressures are drawing increasing focus.

That's according to the eighth edition of BDO Pūrongo Pakihi Māori, the BDO Māori Business Sector Report, which surveyed 159 Māori business leaders.

BDO national Māori business sector leader Solomon Dalton (Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Porou) told RNZ Māori business leaders tended to be more positive about business performance than most other sectors, second only to agribusiness.

"Māori businesses remain optimistic, but financial pressures are still making it harder to turn those opportunities into sustainable results ... some of the key findings that have come out of this report, is that 62 percent of Māori business leaders are positive about business performance, which is on par with previous years."

Fifty-nine percent were positive about their pipeline of work, but only 42 percent were positive about their financial performance and cash flow.

Dalton said the real challenge was turning that pipeline of work into actual profits and revenue.

BDO national Māori business sector leader Solomon Dalton. Supplied / BDO

Another key finding was that just 17 percent were planning beyond five years, down from 25 percent last year.

"Many Māori businesses, we're always thinking long-term, but given the current climate that we're in, what we've seen is that they're having to focus on the here and now to just make it through these challenging times," he said.

The survey also highlighted that financial pressures were taking a greater toll on the wellbeing of Māori business leaders, 46 percent felt less mentally healthy due to their business' financial performance and cash flow problems, almost double the 24 percent reported in 2025.

Dalton said that pressure was not just about profitability, it was also about the whānau and community that made up and supported Māori businesses.

"To be able to maintain a happy and well-being whānau, and look after your community or give back to your community, you need to have a financially stable and strong business ... so that's kind of why we're feeling that pressure."

Dalton's advice was for business owners to focus on what they could control, so understanding their margins, understanding their business and to keep chasing opportunities.

Dalton said Māori businesses were spread across a range of sectors, including tourism and construction, but were especially connected to agribusiness, where Māori business leaders showed a correlation with agribusiness leader sentiment trends.

"A lot of our asset base is in whenua, and so that's why we have that correlation between agriculture, forestry, farming, horticulture. So we're predominantly land-based organisations, and so that's why we kind of see those two and two go together."

The findings of the report were derived from an online survey conducted in September 2026 among 159 Māori business leaders from across Aotearoa.

Dalton said the definition of a Māori business for the survey came down to ownership, if a business had over 50 percent Māori directors, trustees or the like, they qualified.

World.title: NZ catching up to Australia for worker satisfaction, but only because Australia is getting worse
World.content:
Audio player for " Is it time to get my money out of AI? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2671941%2Fnz-catching-up-to-australia-for-worker-satisfaction-but-only-because-australia-is-getting-worse

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

The grass may only be slightly greener for workers in Australia according to new research from Telus Health, which recently ran its Mental Health Index in Australia and New Zealand over the same fortnight.

Managing director Jamie MacLennan said scores had been stronger for Australia in the past few years, but they were starting to even out.

"Realistically the pressures on New Zealand workers are the same as Australian, so I think those who've moved to Australia thinking that was a strong economy [with] better opportunities are finding right now that's really not the case."

New Zealand workers scored 62.2 out of 100 for mental health, while Australian workers were only slightly ahead on 62.5.

Australians felt better paid. Only 14 percent of Australians said they were not fairly paid for the work they do, compared to 18 percent of New Zealanders.

Money stress was affecting New Zealand workplaces to a greater extent.

The research found 12 percent of New Zealand workers were considering leaving their jobs because of financial stress, compared to 10 percent in Australia. Seven percent of New Zealand workers had missed work because of financial stress compared to 5 percent in Australia.

Just over a third of New Zealand workers had no emergency savings compared to 31 percent in Australia. But 52 percent of New Zealanders said they were in a good financial position, compared to 49 percent of Australians.

New Zealand workers were less likely to believe their employer cared more about productivity than wellbeing.

MacLennan said the comparative improvement in New Zealand compared to Australia was less that New Zealand had picked up and more that Australia had deteriorated.

"The [Australian] Reserve Bank moved interest rates again recently. That's now five in a row. And I think you've hit a tipping point in Australia where the cost of living pressures are suddenly getting extreme.

"But it's moving into the stage that New Zealand's been at for quite some time now, so I think it's more deterioration on this side of the pond than New Zealand getting better, unfortunately."

He said there were clear correlations between financial wellbeing and overall mental wellbeing.

"If you're wondering where the next bill is going to come from or what to do if a family member becomes ill, you can't just switch that concern off when you come to work.

"So those pressures are very significant and they impact all workers in the economy, but particularly certain groups are under a lot more pressure. And what we see consistently is younger workers under a lot more pressure than the older workers.

"But what is concerning in this latest report is probably managers feeling a lot more under pressure and parents feeling a lot more under pressure. So I think the strain on the workforce is getting more significant because it's beginning to spread out to other groups more than it has done previously."

One woman who moved to Australia in early 2020 said she had noticed more mental health awareness there.

"I think there is more awareness in general, but also the younger generations are more aware and open about it, so there is a cultural change happening. I think it also differs by industry, bigger industry tries to tick more of the boxes. Financially I think it is much easier here. There are still people who struggle, but it's much easier to get ahead even without qualifications, as long as you're willing to work."

More than just about pay

MacLennan said organisations needed to understand that their workforces were under pressure and consider what could be done to help.

"If I talk to businesses about financial well-being, they often say, 'oh, you just mean pay people more'. Really, there's a correlation between salary and financial well-being, but actually, what we try to point out is it's a lot more than that.

"Financial well-being can be much more practical than just salary. People are really crying out for things like financial literacy, help with budgeting, so you can do workshops on budgeting, how you can build up emergency savings. Retirement is horribly misunderstood.

"People have very little understanding of what's going to happen when they retire - how does KiwiSaver pay out for them? So there's a lack of financial literacy across the workforce.

"And I think it's those kind of elements that organisations can help their staff with that can help alleviate a number of these concerns. So it's not just salary, it's much broader than that."

Earlier, BNZ chief economist Mike Jones said the gap between the Australian and New Zealand economies was narrowing.

"Australian economic growth is slowing, the labour market is losing steam and house prices are falling, so there's an element of catch-down happening," he said.

"At the same time, the NZ economy is managing to maintain momentum, with forward indicators still consistent with reasonable growth ahead.

"It's notable that NZ's economic recovery, underwhelming though it's been, has closed the growth gap to Australia. Annual growth in the second quarter was 2.6 percent, above Australia's 2.1 percent.

"It's nonetheless important to emphasise that the bar for some NZ growth catch-up has been low, given the weak economy of the past few years, and a faster rate of NZ growth over the next 12 months or so will not close the gap in the level of activity that opened up as the NZ economy struggled through 2024 and 2025."

World.title: Earth Sciences looking into cause of wave activity that triggered tsunami alert
World.content:
Earth Sciences is working to determine the cause of wave activity that triggered a tsunami alert on Wednesday.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) issued an advisory about 5.40pm, saying strong currents and unpredictable surges at the shore could be expected in coastal areas on the East Coast of the North Island.

It came after strong currents were picked up on tidal gauges at Napier and Gisborne, but with no sign of an earthquake.

No evacuations took place and the advisory was cancelled 15 minutes later.

NEMA said mobile alerts were not sent because it would have been premature to do so.

The agency's deputy chief executive John Price said it didn't want to get the public involved unnecessarily, but said civil defence partners needed a precautionary warning in case action was required.

Earth Science duty seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said sensors initially recognised wave peaks of up to 30 centimetres about 10 minutes apart.

"Think about it like a fast moving tide. The height of that isn't going to inundate you, or drown you, or destroy a building necessarily but the currents that come with that amount of water coming in and out at that sort of speed are what is dangerous," Taylor-Offord said.

He said initial theories were that the cause was either an underwater landslide, caused by the collapse of sediments built up from river outflows, or the interaction of multiple swell systems against the coast.

Taylor-Offord said Wednesday's alert was a reminder that damaging wave systems could occur without storms or earthquakes.

"They can sweep in and they can flood things and they can pull things out with them.

"It could be a beautiful day and you wouldn't see it because the actual height of the tide in this case is not that large but the effect can be really significant," he said.

World.title: Gisborne police say they're cracking down on rising gang tensions
World.content:
Extra police will be on duty around Gisborne as police crack down on rising gang tensions.

Eastern District Commander Superintendent Joel Lamb said police had been responding to incidents of firearms being discharged at houses over the last week.

He said four gang members were arrested in two traffic stops near Te Reinga on Tuesday.

Officers seized two loaded firearms along with ammunition, knuckle-dusters and drug utensils.

Police also searched two homes in Elgin and Te Hapara on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.

"The public will see an increased Police presence around the wider Gisborne area as we address gang tensions.

"Police won't tolerate behaviour from gangs that place innocent members of the public at risk," Lamb said.

World.title: 'It's a disgrace': Pike River families on 16-year wait
World.content:
Pike River families say it is a disgrace they are still waiting for a decision on whether criminal charges will be laid, as a result of the disaster that left 29 men dead 16 years ago.

In February, police said they were nearing the final stages of their criminal investigation into the disaster that killed 29 men on the South Island's West Coast mine on 19 November 2010.

Eight months on, police assistant commissioner Corrie Parnell reiterated that point.

"Operational security around the next phase of the investigation is critical, and therefore it is not appropriate to comment further at this time."

The investigation was reopened in 2018, and figures showed since then it had cost more than $35 million, with around half of that spent on consultants, specialist fees and overseas travel.

Corrie Parnell . RNZ / Angus Dreaver

In September 2022, police announced they were reopening the borehole drilling operation as part of the investigation and 10 boreholes were drilled, imaged and resealed.

Human remains were found in the mine in 2023. In November 2024, Police said they were working with the Crown solicitor and considering whether to lay charges over the disaster and it was hoped a decision would be reached in the first half of 2025.

Back in February, police said they had been working with the Wellington Crown solicitor on the "legally complex" case for more than 18 months.

Crown Law referred questions to police.

A 16-year wait for accountability

Some family members of those who died in the disaster said it was not good enough.

Sonya Rockhouse, whose son Ben was 21 when he was killed in the explosion, said it was "bloody frustrating" and "absolutely ridiculous" to still be waiting for a decision.

Police had been in touch with her last week, but they did not have any new information.

"I said to them, 'You know, people are starting to die, it's been so long', and we just don't understand the hold up really - it just beggars belief."

Lawyer Nigel Hampton KC, who represented the miners' union at the royal commission inquiry and the victims' families, was gravely ill, as were others connected to the disaster.

"Anna's [Osborne, fellow widow] living on borrowed time, her five years was up last year and thankfully she's showing no signs of anything happening," Rockhouse said.

"But you just don't know. I'm getting older, I'm 68 next birthday, I could have a heart attack and drop dead tomorrow."

She said those deciding whether to prosecute "need to get their flippin' act together and make the right decision".

"We've warned them, we've told them that if we don't get the result that we want, then they're going to hear a hell of a lot more from us.

"If we've got to go back and protest and do what we did before, then we will - I'll retire from work and we'll go for it."

Meeting with minister a 'waste of time'

On the 16th anniversary, Rockhouse said she and Osborne would be in Auckland for the 2026 New Zealand Screen Awards, where the feature film Pike River about the mining disaster had received 15 nominations.

"It's better than last year on the 15th anniversary, we were meeting with Brooke van Velden and that was a flipping waste of time."

She said they had not heard anything since meeting with the former minister for workplace relations and safety, but still wanted to see a corporate manslaughter charge introduced in New Zealand.

Anna Osborne and Bernie Monk. RNZ

Bernie Monk, whose 23-year-old son Michael died in the mine, said it had been a 16-year wait for redress. He said some of the families were told three months ago that a decision on charges was weeks away, but then nothing had happened.

"It's a disgrace. We've got one of the biggest industrial homicides in New Zealand's history and we've had to wait 16 years to get justice and accountability.

"We are never going to go away until something is done."

Monk said on the 16th anniversary, he would be at the opening of the memorial at the mine site, which he expected would become a major asset for the West Coast and those wanting to commemorate the lives of the 29 men.

'Very odd' events on the night - Brownlee

In response to questions from Kathryn Ryan on Nine to Noon about whether it was appropriate that families were still waiting for a decision on a prosecution, 16 years on, Parliament speaker Gerry Brownlee said it was not, but that he had to be careful about what he said.

"What I will say is that it surprised me, I got there a few hours after it happened on the night, up on the mountain and from that moment - the police who should have been in charge and were in charge legally, had the [Pike River] company representative as a spokesman.

"At the time, I found that very odd because there had to be questions about what actually happened here. That's all I'll say about that."

He said there remained questions over how the Pike River disaster was able to happen.

There was no ability for the methane to escape the mine before the explosion, he said, and it was his personal opinion that there should have been a second entrance into the mine.

"In the film footage you see on television of the stack, so-called breather stack, that's 180 metres above the drift and there were flames coming out of that, so the intensity of that inferno was something wicked. Why wasn't there a second entrance?"

He said he met the mine rescue crew that day with then prime minister John Key.

"I met them on the night it happened and they weren't going in there. They made it very clear, no - methane level's too high, it's dangerous."

He and Key met with them again the following Monday and asked each of them if they would go in, and they all said no.

Department of Conservation Greymouth operations manager Chris Hickford said the organisation had been working with the families on the memorial to commemorate the 29 men who died in the disaster.

He said details and photos of the memorial would be released once families had been to the site for an invite-only event for the 16th anniversary on Thursday.

The upper valley and memorial would remain closed to the public until visitor access, interpretation, and other facilities were completed - likely in mid-2027, he said.

World.title: Gloriavale meal plant fire caused by open boiler door
World.content:
A fire at Gloriavale Christian community's meal plant broke out because the door to a boiler had not been shut properly, the workplace safety regulator says.

A firefighter was taken to Greymouth's Te Nīkau Hospital in a moderate condition following the boiler shed blaze at Gloriavale's Value Proteins plant late on 14 August.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said the firefighter suffered a "medical event".

A WorkSafe spokesperson said staff did not carry out a formal investigation into the fire.

"Our initial enquiries concluded that the door to a boiler had not been shut properly. Burning material fell out and caused the fire. The boiler that caught fire is no longer operational and will be replaced," the spokesperson said.

"WorkSafe plans to visit the site later this year to check on progress."

A FENZ spokesperson said the fire was a result of "human error".

Gloriavale declined to comment.

Value Proteins is a rendering company that takes freezing works waste and turns it into bulk pet food ingredients for local sale and export.

Photos of the fire seen by RNZ showed flames engulfing the shed, a hose spraying water to cool fuel tanks nearby and firefighters later working in the charred remains of the building.

In a statement at the time, a Gloriavale spokesperson said the processing plant had been temporarily shut down because of the damage.

"Safety protocols were successfully activated and there were zero injuries," they said.

"Value Proteins extends its gratitude to Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) and our on-site team for their professional response, which quickly brought the situation under control.

World.title: Youths forcefully obtain keys, escape care and protection facility
World.content:
Youths at a Christchurch care and protection facility have escaped more than once in the past week after forcefully obtaining keys from staff.

On each occasion the youths remained close to the residence and were found.

An internal investigation is now underway into what happened at Te Poutama Ārahi Rangatahi - a care and protection facility run by Barnardos Aotearoa.

According to Barnardos Aotearoa's website, it is a "comprehensive, integrated therapeutic residential treatment programme for boys aged 12-18 with at-risk behaviour". They are referred to the facility by Oranga Tamariki.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Barnardos Aotearoa CEO Matt Reid confirmed in a statement to RNZ that over the past week "serious incidents" took place in the facility involving youths "obtaining keys through force and absconding".

"Oranga Tamariki was notified and also involved in offering ongoing support to Barnardos. Police were also involved and continue to support.

"The rangatahi involved are now safe and secure."

Te Poutama Ārahi Rangatahi is located in Christchurch. Supplied / Google Maps

Reid said following the recent incident, Barnardos Aotearoa had focused on the safety and wellbeing of the youths and staff on site.

"Following our usual processes, we have an internal investigation underway."

RNZ asked how many incidents there had been, and how far the youths got.

In response, a spokesperson said the incidents were currently under a "thorough internal investigation".

"And part of this is to understand exactly what has happened. What we can confirm at this stage is that over the past week, serious incidents took place in our facility involving rangatahi in our care obtaining keys through force and absconding, and each time, they remained close to our residence."

Asked why they could not say how many times, the spokesperson said the statement was "all we are prepared to comment on at this stage".

Canterbury Police's rural area commander inspector Peter Cooper told RNZ Police had been called to the facility "multiple times in the last week".

"The nature of the incidents varies and include reports of youths absconding and assault. One instance reported on Friday, 13 November has resulted in a charge for assault and a 14-year-old will appear in the Christchurch Youth Court today.

"Police are aware of the ongoing concerns for the behaviour of some residents and continue to support staff at the care facility when required."

An Oranga Tamariki spokesperson said they had been notified of the incidents.

"We are actively working with Barnardos to provide support."

Barnardos Aotearoa said all youths who come through Te Poutama were "under the care of the state and have been referred by Oranga Tamariki for specialist support".

"Rangatahi who come through Te Poutama have faced complex and often traumatic experiences, many have lived through things no child should ever have to.

World.title: England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton
World.content:
Australia has crumbled to a one-day international series loss to England, with star all-rounder Cameron Green forced from the field after being struck by a bouncer.

Chasing 329 to win the deciding game three in Hobart on Wednesday, the hosts were bowled out for 231 in the 47th over.

Green was substituted out of the game in the 27th over after being felled and left with blood in his mouth following a Gus Atkinson delivery.

Ben Duckett scored a vital 133 for England as the tourists set Australia a big total in the third and final ODI in Hobart. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

The loss came on another turbulent day for Australian cricket, with former opener Cameron Bancroft claiming the whole Test side and coaches knew of sandpaper ball tampering in 2018.

Earlier, Ben Duckett scored 133 off 115 balls to help set the platform for England's big total.

England got off to a flying start but were pulled back through the middle overs by the part-time spin of Matt Renshaw.

Renshaw picked up 3-51, which included a flighted delivery to bowl Joe Root (12) in the 15th over, the scalp of Jordan Cox (12) stumped and Duckett off a top edge in the 39th over.

Matt Renshaw's impressive spin bowling brought three vital wickets for Australia against England in the final ODI in Hobart. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Australia's chase started poorly with openers Travis Head (four) and Mitchell Marsh (one) gone inside the first two overs.

Shifted to No.3 at the expense of Cooper Connolly, Renshaw (55) launched a salvage mission before being caught and bowled by spinner Liam Dawson.

It got worse a few overs later when Alex Carey (37) was run out, leaving Australia 5-115 in the 27th over, before Green (three) was forced off shortly afterwards

Connolly, who had been batting at No.3, managed 29 at No.7 before being bowled by Dawson.

Young England quick Sonny Baker was the pick of the bowlers with 4-45.

Australia, who were beaten comfortably by England in game two, now face a dearth of ODI cricket before the World Cup begins in October.

AAP

World.title: Sydney's Papley banned for three games after roadside drug test
World.content:
Sydney's Tom Papley will miss the Swans' preseason game and the first three matches of the 2027 season after being banned by the AFL over a failed roadside drug test.

The AFL banned Papley for conduct unbecoming, giving the Swans small forward a notifiable adverse finding under the league's Illicit Drugs Policy.

He was also given a suspended $5,000 fine.

NSW Police stopped Papley on November 2 for a roadside licence check.

He was issued with a court attendance notice for driving with a suspended licence, due to an unpaid parking fine.

The Swans player then completed a random drug test that gave a positive initial result. Today, the AFL said the secondary sample had confirmed the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

NSW Police has fined Papley $722, and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Swans culture issue Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich expresses "bitter disappointment" after Tom Papley's drug test result hurls the AFL club back into the spotlight.

AFL COO Tom Harley said the sanction reflected the seriousness of the breach.

"AFL players are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with illicit drug use," Harley said in a statement.

"The player is being held accountable for his actions and has acknowledged he made a grave mistake."

Papley apologised for his behaviour in a statement released by the Swans.

"I am extremely sorry for my behaviour which has caused distress for my family, everyone connected to the Club and broader industry," he said.

"I accept my actions have fallen well short of the standards that is expected of me at this football club, and I will work very hard to win the trust back of everyone in the wider community.

"Road safety is something that affects everyone in our community, and I take full accountability for my mistake.

"I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my wife, my family, my manager Winston, the Club, my teammates, the AFLPA and all those who have supported me over the last fortnight."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich said Papley understood the sanction and was taking responsibility for his mistakes.

"While we are very disappointed in his actions, he is an important member of the team, and we will work closely with him and the entire AFL program to reinstate the high standards the Club expects of everyone.

"We need to be better, and change must occur."

World.title: Sandpapergate coach has 'nothing to hide' after forum announced
World.content:
Former Australian Test coach Darren Lehmann, who led the side during the Sandpapergate incident in 2018, has said he has "nothing to hide" after a new forum into the saga was announced.

Cricket Australia on Wednesday announced a voluntary forum for players and staff involved in the Test match at Cape Town, where Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, to discuss their recollection and perspective of the incident.

Warner wants Sandpapergate 'public inquiry' as CA announces safe-space forum Cricket Australia has announced a new forum for players and staff to discuss the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, but whether it will achieve anything has already been questioned.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were suspended for their roles in the ball-tampering, but the saga was thrust back into the spotlight last week following the release of Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr.

In the book, Khawaja says he knew the ball-tampering was happening, while former player Chadd Sayers has since claimed he believes everyone knew.

Australia's bowling unit has consistently denied they knew about sandpaper being used on the ball.

Lehmann, who has also denied knowing about the ball-tampering plot, has said he supports Cricket Australia's forum.

Darren Lehmann says he will be happy to be part of Cricket Australia's Sandpapergate forum. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Asked if he would be happy to participate while on the ABC Sport broadcast of Australia's third ODI against England, Lehmann said: "Yeah [I would speak to them], I've got nothing to hide."

"I think this gives everyone who didn't get a chance to speak [a chance now].



"It gives everyone a bit of clarity for the Cricket Australia board to make a decision from there [once people are heard]. I think it's a good thing."

The reaction to Khawaja's chapter about Sandpapergate has led to a turbulent fortnight for Australian cricket.

In the book, Khawaja said the whole team should have taken responsibility for the incident and the brunt of punishment should not have been put on Bancroft, Smith and Warner.

Khawaja said he knew the ball-tampering was happening, and even told Bancroft to be careful.

Since the book's release, there has been a frenzy over who knew what and whether the entire team knew of the ball-tampering.

Warner said the claims detailed in Khawaja's book are "100 per cent accurate", and has accused Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation as "botched".

Former Test player Chadd Sayers, who was in the 2018 touring squad, says 'everyone knew' about the use of sandpaper.

Loading...

Current Test captain Pat Cummins held a 70-minute press conference in the wake of the book release, repeating the bowlers' stance that they knew nothing of the ball-tampering, and said his friend had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, said the announcement of a forum by Cricket Australia let him "see some light at the end of the tunnel".

"I haven't been great [for me since the topic re-emerged]," he said.

"People close to me know that. It happened in 2018, it's a long time ago.

"[I] went through health troubles then, and a triple bypass; mentally I wasn't great either.

"The last couple of weeks have been tough, but that's for everyone involved."

World.title: Thieves steal 1948 Caulfield Cup from Caulfield Racecourse
World.content:
Thieves have smashed their way into Caulfield Racecourse and stolen the 1948 Caulfield Cup.

That theft is believed to be one in a string of break-ins at the track during Melbourne's Spring Racing carnival.

Victoria Police confirmed this afternoon that an alleged offender or offenders entered the Caulfield premises on four occasions between November 4 and 11.

Red Fury won the 1948 Caulfield Cup. (Supplied)

"Alcohol and trophies, including the Caulfield Cup, were allegedly stolen during the course of offending," the police spokeswoman said.

"A 39-year-old was arrested at a residence on Orrong Road in Elsternwick on 16 November.

"He was charged with attempted burglary and possess drug of dependence (methylamphetamine)."

The police spokeswoman said the Elsternwick man was charged and bailed to attend Moorabbin Magistrates Court on March 1 next year.

A broken display at Flemington Racecourse where three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva were stolen on November 16. (ABC News)

It comes after another brazen heist at Flemington this week, where thieves disguised as construction workers stole three Melbourne Cups won consecutively by legendary mare Makybe Diva in 2003, 2004 and 2005.

"Detectives are investigating if (the Caulfield Cup) incident is linked to the theft of the three Melbourne Cup trophies on 16 November," the police spokeswoman said.

Following the theft earlier this week, a Melbourne Racing Club spokesman said the cup was stolen along with some bottles of wine and some other "low-value" items.

"The club has been requested by Victoria Police not to speak to the media during the investigation," a MRC spokesman said.

"As this is an active police investigation, the Club can make no further comment at this stage."

It is understood the 1948 Caulfield Cup, won by then five-year-old Australian thoroughbred Red Fury, had been kept in a secure area of the racecourse off-limits to the public.

The cup, worth $55,000, was sold in March and was on loan to the MRC during this year's racing festivities.

The 2026 theft is not the first time the very same Caulfield Cup has been stolen.

A painting of Red Fury with jockey William Briscoe with the Caulfield Racecourse grandstand in the background. (Supplied: Leski Auctions)

Three men were committed for trial over the theft of the 1948 cup, less than two years after Red Fury's racetrack success.

In 1950, The Argus newspaper reported that the cup was stolen from the now-defunct Ress-Astoria Hotel in central Melbourne when it had a value of 200 pounds (about $15,500 in 2026, adjusted for inflation).

One of the men accused of the theft was later acquitted.

World.title: 'Why are they selling pies?' What surprised O'Connell about AFL footy
World.content:
When Irish AFLW import Siofra O'Connell arrived in Australia, she wasn't entirely sure what to expect.

She had watched AFL games on TV, time zone permitting, and braced herself for the transition from limited-contact Gaelic football to the heavy contact of Australian Rules.

"I was like, 'This is chaos,'" O'Connell told ABC Sport, who signed for Carlton in December 2024. "It's been a learning curve."

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

But then all the quirks and traditions came along with the more than 130-year-old sport.

"I was like, 'Why are they selling pies at a game?' O'Connell laughed. "That was very eye-opening … The chicken and chips is a big one.

"And even the fact that there's alcohol on the ground. You're only allowed it outside the stadium (in Ireland). You can't bring it to your seat.

"So when I went to my first AFL game, and people were a bit tipsy beside me, I didn't know what was going on."

Siofra O'Connell was surprised by the food choices at AFL games. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Media)

Just how much Melbourne is "an AFL city" also took O'Connell by surprise.

"You start getting used to that as well, in a way, because it's on the TV every night of the week almost, and from March to November," she said.

And playing at a big Victorian club like Carlton inevitably puts you in the headlines.

"I work one day a week in the club shop … and that opened my eyes to the supporters and the fan base, and how big the club is," she said.

"You can appreciate it a lot more when it's post-game, and you're engaging with the fans … I'm so not used to all the numbers and spectators. So, it's just amazing to hear a crowd."

Carlton beat Hawthorn in the semifinal to send them to a preliminary final match-up with Melbourne. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

There was a crowd of over 5,000 for the Blues' qualifying final against North Melbourne, and then about 4,000 for the semifinal against Hawthorn.

"You see the number on the board, and I never would have dreamt that there'd be 5,000 at a game before. (In Ireland), We might go to a game, and we have great support at home, but it's just not as big.

"And the platform isn't as vocal as it is (in Australia)."

Darcy Vescio sealed the semifinal victory for the Blues in their 100th game. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

That crowd made itself known for the Blues' win over the Hawks in inaugural player and fan-favourite Darcy Vescio's 100th game.

The two-time All Australian sealed the victory with their second goal of the night, prompting the stands to fill with signs celebrating the beloved player.

In the lead-up to the game, Carlton organised speeches honouring Vescio and had special shirts made to mark the occasion.

"Being able to celebrate Darcy today, and seeing that players are getting to 100 games, I just didn't realise how big an achievement it was coming in last season," O'Connell said.

"Because we don't celebrate these kinds of things at home. To see that it's so special, and it's for that person for the week … You're just so excited to go out and play with them, and it lifts you. It lifts your spirits."

World.title: Rockliff says 'no surprise' if Hobart stadium cost exceeds $1.13b estimate
World.content:
Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has told parliament the final cost of Hobart's planned stadium will be made public next week, while avoiding questions about whether he'll stick to the $875 million public spending cap.

The last cost estimate of the stadium put it at $1.13 billion, but that was from about a year ago.

Since then, world events have resulted in prices going up, and it seems Tasmanians can expect the same for the waterfront, 23,000-seat, roofed stadium.

The roofed stadium at Macquarie Point is a condition of Tasmania being granted entry to the AFL competition. (Supplied: MPDC)

Under questioning in parliament, Mr Rockliff said he would be "very surprised" if the cost hadn't escalated.

"I'm not aware of the cost, however everything has gone since the 28th of February where there was an invasion in Iran," he said.

"Houses have gone up, buildings have gone up … there'd be no surprise if there was some cost escalation.

" I don't know the figure … but that is no reason to kill this project. "

An artist's impression of the Macquarie Point stadium's entry gate four. (Supplied: Mac Point Site Master Plan Report)

Over the past two days, Mr Rockliff has repeatedly faced questions as to whether he will stick to the $875 million public spending cap or bring it back to parliament for approval to exceed it.

It was a commitment he made to Upper House MLC Bec Thomas last year to secure her support for the project.

But Mr Rockliff was evasive, saying only that budgets go before the parliament.

Rosalie Woodruff: "I just want a simple yes or no for Tasmanians. Will the premier come back to parliament to ask … or are you just going to break the promise you made?" Jeremy Rockliff: "We have budgets alright and the budget's gone through the parliament. There'll be a budget go through the parliament as well."

Asked again later in the sitting, Mr Rockliff said the parliament had already spoken on the project.

"The parliament has overwhelmingly voted on this project and made that call, and I know you don't like it."

Liberals' vote hits 25-year low as One Nation continues Tasmanian surge Support for the Liberal government in Tasmania has fallen to its lowest result in an EMRS poll since 2001, as Labor and One Nation appear to make inroads by focusing on healthcare and cost of living — the two biggest issues on voters' minds.

The government has also been under pressure to reveal the final cost of the stadium before parliament rises for the year.

It is facing a motion, which is likely to get up, from independent Kristie Johnston to release the cost by tomorrow evening.

The preferred builder, BESIX Watpac, has given Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) its updated cost, but the government says that is not the final price.

That final costing was due to be made public in early December, but in question time today, Mr Rockliff said the MPDC is now working to have it ready by Monday.

"This is the most scrutinised project in Tasmania's history, and we need to get on with it," he told parliament.

"There is a view it should be released before this house rises, so we are working with the MPDC to condense the next two weeks' work into one week.

"Notwithstanding that, it's likely to create significant challenges, and possibly more costs, but we will have the updated costings by Monday next week.

" We'll get those out, and I'm sure we'll give everyone in this house plenty to talk through next week. "

Independent wants details of contract

The government says the final cost is likely to be made public Tuesday, but for Ms Johnston that's not enough.

"It's important we get [the BESIX Watpac] lump sum design and construct offer price," Kristie Johnston said.

"It's also important that we get the full project number, which the premier has committed he will deliver to the parliament.

"Combined these two prices tell us a lot. It tells us about what's included in the contract, what's not included in the contract and importantly what's still yet to come when it comes to the final project number."

Labor appears likely to support the motion.

"We support scrutiny and transparency. That's why we said we'd support the motion," Labor Leader Josh Willie said.

"The government has said there are probity issues, but the figure will be revealed.

" We need to make sure people's intentions are clear. Kristie Johnston does not support the stadium. She wants to kill the stadium. "

Funding uncertainty

Even once the figure is revealed, the question of how much taxpayer money is going towards it will not go away.

Ms Thomas said she expected the government to honour her agreement.

"The government made a clear commitment, a written commitment, to the parliament and the people of Tasmania that it would cap the state's contribution at $875 million," she said.

"If any additional funding is required, the government is committed to seek it from additional sources," she said.

" If the government can't seek that funding from additional sources, the contract ought not be signed. "

Loading...

Greens Leader Rosalie Woodruff said if the taxpayer spend was more that $875 million, the premier had to bring parliament back and put the question again.

"Parliament can exercise its right to make the government bring it back for approval if we had the numbers," she said.

"We've seen signatures from across MPs who voted for and against the stadium, wanting the premier to bring it back to parliament and consider whether the stadium bill needs to be reassessed."

World.title: Warner wants Sandpapergate 'public inquiry' as CA announces safe-space forum
World.content:
Cricket Australia (CA) has announced a new forum for players and staff to discuss the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, but whether it will achieve anything has already been questioned.

CA CEO Todd Greenberg and board member David Boon announced the forum on Wednesday, following a turbulent fortnight for the game.

The notorious 2018 Cape Town Test match where Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, leading to his suspension as well as that of captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner, was thrust into the spotlight after Usman Khawaja revealed he knew about the ball tampering in his new memoir, Sabr.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. That is all for our live coverage Thank you for joining us this afternoon. Cricket Australia has announced a new forum for people to discuss their recollections and perspectives of the Sandpapergate saga. Meanwhile, Usman Khawaja and David Warner have questioned if the forum will achieve anything if all the information is not made public. This is where we end our live coverage of the media conference and the reaction. You can get all the latest sport news and analysis on the ABC Sport website. Sport Khawaja and Warner both say they want to move on from Sandpapergate David Warner says he does not want any more penalties handed to players or staff in relation to Sandpapergate. The former Test opener says he would like to see "transparency and accountability". Both he and Khawaja have also said they want all of Australian cricket to be able to move on from this scandal. Warner "I think everyone just wants to see cricket played on our TV. It's about the Australian public, the fans of the game. " Yes, people want to talk about moving on, but in this safe environment, we want every single person that was there to be able to speak." Khawaja "We all want to move on. There's no clearer thing from everyone that we want to move on. The question is, will this allow us to move on. That's the question that has to be asked." Khawaja says he has heard some former CA staff 'aren't allowed to talk' Usman Khawaja is speaking again. He has taken issue with the findings of the forum potentially not being fully available to the public. Todd Greenberg said in the press conference that Cricket Australia would need to wait until the conclusion of the forum before deciding what information was made public. Khawaja said he had a lot of respect for Greenberg, but worried about what the point of the forum was if all the information was not made public. At the end of the day, if you're going to cherry-pick what is said in this report, the board can choose whatever they want to come in or come out. Are we just going around in a circle? Khawaja then references his understanding that some people "aren't allowed to talk" about Sandpapergate. What he means there is not clear. "Plenty of guys, including staff who have left CA, from all reports I've heard, aren't allowed to talk about the situation. Are they allowed to talk about it in this forum? I don't know. But how are we supposed to get the truth if they can't talk about it?" Show more

Since then, former player Chadd Sayers says be believed everyone in the team knew about the tampering, something strongly denied by the bowling unit, including current captain Pat Cummins.

The new forum will be voluntary, and has been described as a "safe space" for players and former staff to discuss their recollections and perspectives on Sandpapergate.

Loading...

Greenberg said this forum was not an investigation, there would not be a new investigation, and there would be no penalties or sanctions to come out of the forum.

"The game is genuinely hurting at the moment. It's not good for anyone," Greenberg told media in Hobart, ahead of Australia's third ODI against England.

"We need to find a path through and we need some time to heal. As part of this process, and so that all parties who wish to can tell their version of events, we have set up now an independent forum."

Asked if the public would find out what is discussed in the forum, Greenberg did not commit to making anything public.

"Ultimately, that will be a matter when we get through the end of this with the Cricket Australia board on what we can disclose," he said.

"And we will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward."

Warner wants 'public inquiry' as Khawaja questions value of forum

Greenberg and Boon's press conference on Wednesday came just as Fox Cricket, broadcaster of Australia's ODI match with England, went to air.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner have responded to Cricket Australia's announcement of a Sandpapergate forum. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Khawaja and Warner both appeared on Fox commentary and responded immediately to the press conference.

Both men questioned whether the forum would achieve the desired result of bringing closure to the ugly chapter in Australian cricket if CA was the one who chose what information was made public.

Warner said he wanted a public inquiry into Sandpapergate.

"Where do we actually end here, because it is upon the board to review what they want to be published. Yes that's a safe space, but is everyone able to talk?

"I would have liked an open public inquiry and the people that were there at the time can come forward and speak.

Khawaja said he had a lot of respect for Greenberg and believed CA had its heart in the right place with the forum, but he too worried about what the point of the forum was if all the information was not made public.

"At the end of the day, if you're going to cherry-pick what is said in this report, the board can choose whatever they want to come in or come out. Are we just going around in a circle?" he said.
